lessons.title: How US and Florida real estate law is organized
lessons.html:
2. Why it matters

Every exam question is answered by one specific source of law, and many questions are worded straight from Florida's statutes. If you know which source governs a situation and which body acts, you can eliminate wrong answers even when you do not remember a detail. This is also the first place where the Portuguese and Florida systems differ in structure, not just in detail.

This is a bridge lesson: the textbook assumes you already know how American law is layered. Everything in Chapters 2–7 builds on it.

3. Simple explanation

Two levels of government make law in the United States.

  • Federal law applies in every state. In real estate it covers national issues: fair housing, lending disclosures (RESPA, TILA), lead-based paint, disability access (ADA), environmental cleanup (CERCLA) and income tax.
  • State law applies inside one state. Licensing real estate professionals is a state matter. There is no national real estate license; a Florida license is valid only in Florida.

Inside Florida there are four layers you will meet constantly:

  1. The Florida Constitution — the top state law. Example: homestead protection from creditors (Article X).
  2. Florida Statutes (F.S.) — laws passed by the Legislature, organized in chapters. The real estate license law is Chapter 475. Chapter 455 sets general procedures for every profession the DBPR regulates. Others you will meet: Chapter 83 (landlord–tenant), 689 (deeds and conveyances), 718 (condominiums), 201 (documentary stamp tax).
  3. Florida Administrative Code (F.A.C.) — rules adopted by state agencies using power a statute gives them. The Florida Real Estate Commission's rules are Chapter 61J2 (escrow deadlines, advertising, offices, education). A rule has the force of law but cannot go beyond its statute.
  4. Case law — decisions of the courts. Florida, like most of the US, is a common-law system: courts' decisions create binding precedent. For this exam the key case is Johnson v. Davis (1985): a seller must disclose known hidden defects that materially affect value.

Who does what. Two state bodies regulate real estate licensees, and the exam constantly asks which one acts:

  • FREC (Florida Real Estate Commission) — 7 members appointed by the Governor. It makes rules (a quasi-legislative power) and decides discipline — fines, suspension, revocation (a quasi-judicial power).
  • DBPR (Department of Business and Professional Regulation), through its Division of Real Estate — processes applications, issues licenses, keeps records and investigates complaints. It provides the FREC's administrative support.
  • Courts — only a court can impose criminal penalties (prison) or award civil damages to a consumer.

How to read a citation. "s. 475.25(1)(d)1., F.S." means Florida Statutes, chapter 475, section 25, subsection (1), paragraph (d), subparagraph 1. "Rule 61J2-14.009, F.A.C." means rule chapter 61J2, part 14, rule .009. You do not need to memorize citations for the exam, but recognizing them lets you check sources yourself.

4. Key terms

Term Meaning
Statute A law passed by the Legislature (e.g., Chapter 475 F.S.)
Administrative rule A rule adopted by an agency under a statute (e.g., 61J2 F.A.C.)
Case law Law created by court decisions
Common law A legal system that relies on court precedent as well as written law
FREC Florida Real Estate Commission: rules and discipline
DBPR Department of Business and Professional Regulation: licensing, records, investigations
Quasi-legislative An agency's power to make rules
Quasi-judicial An agency's power to decide cases and impose discipline
Licensee A person holding a real estate license (sales associate or broker)

5. Practical example

A buyer signs a contract for a resale condo in Fort Lauderdale and gives a $25,000 deposit to the seller's broker. The deal falls apart and both parties demand the deposit.

Question Source that answers it
Must the broker account for the money? Chapter 475 F.S. (statute)
How many business days to notify the FREC and choose a procedure? Rule 61J2-10.032 F.A.C. (15 / 30 business days)
Could the buyer cancel because the condo documents arrived late? Chapter 718 F.S. (condominium statute)
Did the seller have to disclose the roof leak she knew about? Johnson v. Davis (case law)
Who investigates if the buyer files a complaint? DBPR
Who can fine or suspend the broker? FREC
Who can send the broker to prison if he stole the money? A criminal court

6. Portugal comparison

Familiar principle: both countries regulate brokerage through a statute and a regulator. In Portugal that is Lei n.º 15/2013 and IMPIC; in Florida it is Chapter 475 and FREC/DBPR.

What changes:

  • Level of government. Portuguese real estate law is national. In the US, licensing is decided state by state, while some topics (fair housing, lending, environment) are federal.
  • Who is licensed. In Portugal the IMPIC license belongs to the mediation business. In Florida each individual needs a license, and a sales associate can only work under a broker.
  • Entry test. IMPIC requires commercial good standing and liability insurance. Florida requires a 63-hour course and a state exam.
  • Legal method. Portugal is a civil-law system built on codes (Código Civil). Florida is a common-law system where court decisions such as Johnson v. Davis create binding rules.

Exam implication: never reason from the Portuguese structure. If a question asks who issues licenses, the answer is the DBPR; who disciplines, the FREC; who imprisons, a court.

7. Legal and numerical requirements

Memorize exactly

  • Chapter 475 F.S. = Florida real estate license law.
  • Chapter 455 F.S. = general law for all DBPR-regulated professions.
  • Chapter 61J2 F.A.C. = FREC's rules.
  • DBPR issues licenses and investigates; FREC makes rules and disciplines; only courts imprison or award damages.

Understand

  • Federal law → Florida Constitution → Florida Statutes → administrative rules. A lower layer cannot contradict a higher one.
  • Agencies (FREC, DBPR) act administratively. Criminal and civil liability belongs to the courts.

8. Visual explanation

Federal lawFair housing · RESPA · TILA · ADA · lead paint · CERCLA · income tax
Florida ConstitutionHomestead (Art. X)
Florida StatutesCh. 475 license law · Ch. 455 DBPR procedures · Ch. 83 · 689 · 718 · 201
Administrative rules61J2 F.A.C. — FREC rules (escrow, ads, offices, education)
Courts (case law)Interpret all layers · Johnson v. Davis
Body Makes rules Issues licenses Investigates Disciplines Imprisons / awards damages
FREC ✔ — — ✔ —
DBPR — ✔ ✔ — —
Courts — — — — ✔

9. Common misconceptions

  • "The FREC is a court." It is an administrative commission. It can revoke a license but cannot imprison anyone or order a licensee to pay a consumer's damages.
  • "The DBPR punishes licensees." The DBPR investigates and prosecutes; the FREC decides discipline.
  • "A rule is weaker than a statute, so it is optional." Rules are binding law. They simply cannot exceed the statute that authorizes them.
  • "The REALTOR® association regulates agents." It is a private trade association. The state regulates licensees.
  • "My Portuguese experience or AMI license counts." It does not; Florida licenses individuals under Chapter 475.
  • "Federal law licenses agents." Licensing is state law.

10. Memory sheet

  • 475 = license law · 455 = all DBPR professions · 61J2 = FREC rules.
  • DBPR digs, FREC decides, courts jail.
  • Federal: fair housing, RESPA/TILA, ADA, lead paint, CERCLA, tax. State: licensing, escrow, disclosures, landlord–tenant.
  • Johnson v. Davis: disclose known latent material defects.
  • Florida licenses each person; Portugal licenses the business.

lessons.title: The real estate business: sectors, specialties and organizations
lessons.html:
2. Why it matters

This is one of the smallest exam areas (1% in the official content outline), and much of it is familiar from your work in Portugal. It still matters because it introduces the vocabulary the exam uses for property types and roles, and it contains one classic trap: confusing REALTOR® membership with a license.

3. Simple explanation

Property types. The course groups real property by use:

  • Residential — homes, condos, apartments.
  • Commercial — income-producing business property: offices, retail, hotels.
  • Industrial — manufacturing, warehouses, distribution.
  • Agricultural — farms, groves, ranches, timberland.
  • Special-purpose — properties with a unique use: churches, schools, hospitals, cemeteries.

Specializations. Brokerage (residential or commercial sales and leasing); appraisal (estimating value — a separate license in Florida); property management (leasing, rent collection, maintenance for owners); financing (mortgage lending); development and construction (turning land into finished property); counseling (advice for a fee).

Organizations. The National Association of REALTORS® (NAR) is the largest trade association. REALTOR® is a registered trademark that only members may use; it is not a license. In Florida the state association is Florida Realtors, and local boards and associations run the MLS in their areas. The National Association of Real Estate Brokers (NAREB) uses the term Realtist.

Real estate vs real property vs personal property. Real estate is land plus permanent improvements. Real property is real estate plus the bundle of ownership rights. Personal property is movable (furniture, cars — and, importantly, cooperative shares).

4. Key terms

Term Meaning
Special-purpose property Property with a unique, limited use (church, school, hospital)
Property management Managing property for owners: leasing, rent collection, maintenance
REALTOR® Trademark for NAR members; not a license
Realtist Member of NAREB
Real property Land, improvements, and the rights of ownership
Personal property Movable items not attached to land

5. Practical example

You meet a new Miami colleague whose card says "REALTOR®". That tells you she belongs to NAR (through her local association). It tells you nothing about whether her license is active — you would check that on the DBPR license search. Another agent who is not an NAR member can be fully licensed and may not call herself a REALTOR®.

6. Portugal comparison

Familiar: the sectors (residential, commercial, industrial) and specialties (sales, management, valuation) work the same way in practice.

Different: in Florida the trade association (NAR/Florida Realtors, which runs much of the MLS infrastructure) is separate from the state regulator (FREC/DBPR). Membership is voluntary; the license is mandatory. Appraisal is also separately licensed in Florida (Part II of Chapter 475), and a sales associate may not call a market analysis an "appraisal".

7. Legal and numerical requirements

Memorize exactly

  • Five property categories: residential, commercial, industrial, agricultural, special-purpose.
  • REALTOR® = NAR membership trademark, not a license.

Understand

  • Licenses are issued by the state; associations are private.

8. Visual explanation

Category Florida examples
Residential Single-family home in Kissimmee; Brickell condo; duplex in Tampa
Commercial Strip mall in Orlando; office building in Fort Lauderdale
Industrial Warehouse near Port Everglades
Agricultural Citrus grove in Polk County
Special-purpose Church, school, hospital

9. Common misconceptions

  • "REALTOR® is a license level." It is a trade-association mark.
  • "Every licensee must join NAR." Membership is voluntary.
  • "A CMA is an appraisal." A licensee may prepare a CMA, but must not call it an appraisal (Chapter 16).

10. Memory sheet

  • R-C-I-A-S: Residential, Commercial, Industrial, Agricultural, Special-purpose.
  • REALTOR® = membership, not license. Realtist = NAREB.
  • Real property = real estate + rights. Co-op shares = personal property.

lessons.title: Who needs a license: the three-part test
lessons.html:
2. Why it matters

Unlicensed activity is a third-degree felony, and "does this person need a license?" is one of the most common question shapes on the exam. The questions hide the decisive fact — usually how the person is paid — in the middle of a sentence.

3. Simple explanation

A Florida license is required when all three of these are present:

  1. A real estate service — the activities listed in Chapter 475. The course mnemonic is A BAR SALE: Advertise, Buy, Appraise, Rent, Sell, Auction, Lease, Exchange. The statute's definition is broader and also covers acts such as negotiating, listing, and procuring buyers, sellers, tenants or landlords.
  2. For another — for someone else, not for yourself.
  3. For compensation — anything of value: money, a gift card, a car, a discount. Compensation that is only promised or expected still counts.

Remove any one element and no license is needed. A homeowner selling her own house (not for another) needs no license; a friend who shows a house with no expectation of pay (no compensation) needs no license.

4. Key terms

Term Meaning
Real estate service An activity listed in Chapter 475 (A BAR SALE and related acts)
For another On behalf of someone other than yourself
Compensation Anything of value, paid, promised or expected
Sales associate Licensee who performs services under a broker
Broker Licensee who performs services for others in their own name

5. Practical example

Carlos, unlicensed, tells his cousin he can find a tenant for her Orlando condo. She says, "If you do, I'll take you to dinner at a steakhouse." He finds a tenant and enjoys the dinner.

  • Service? Yes — renting/leasing for another.
  • For another? Yes — his cousin's condo.
  • Compensation? Yes — a dinner is something of value, promised in exchange.

Carlos needed a license. The size or form of the payment does not matter.

6. Portugal comparison

Familiar: in both systems, intermediating property deals as a business is regulated.

Different: Florida's test is applied to each individual and turns on compensation. In Portugal the IMPIC license attaches to the mediation business, and consultants commonly work under the agency's license. In Florida, an unlicensed assistant who is paid per showing or per closing is breaking the law even though the brokerage itself is licensed.

Exam implication: whenever a scenario mentions pay per transaction, per showing, per closing, or a bonus tied to a deal, treat it as compensation for a real estate service.

7. Legal and numerical requirements

Memorize exactly

  • Three elements: service + for another + compensation.
  • A BAR SALE: Advertise, Buy, Appraise, Rent, Sell, Auction, Lease, Exchange.
  • Unlicensed practice = third-degree felony (Chapter 6 covers penalties).

Understand

  • "Compensation" includes promised or expected value, not only money received.

8. Visual explanation

Is it a real estate service (A BAR SALE…)?
No → no license needed
Is it for another person?
No (own property) → no license needed
Is there compensation — paid, promised or expected?
No → no license needed
Does an exemption in s. 475.011 apply? (next lesson)
Yes → no license needed
Otherwise → a license is required

9. Common misconceptions

  • "It's only illegal if you're paid in money." Any thing of value counts.
  • "Doing it once is fine." There is no one-time exemption.
  • "The brokerage is licensed, so its assistant can show homes for per-showing pay." Each person performing services for compensation needs a license.

10. Memory sheet

  • Service + for another + compensation = license.
  • A BAR SALE.
  • Promised or expected pay counts. Per-deal pay is the giveaway.

lessons.title: Exemptions from licensure
lessons.html:
2. Why it matters

Exemptions are where the exam tests reading precision. Each exemption has a condition — usually salary, not commission or within the scope of another profession — and the question changes one word to remove it.

3. Simple explanation

Section 475.011 lists persons who do not need a real estate license even though they may perform real estate activities. The main ones:

  • Owners selling or leasing their own property — unless they use commissioned agents to sell to the public in the ordinary course of business. Corporate officers selling the corporation's own property for a salary fall here.
  • Attorneys at law acting within their duties as attorneys. Earning a brokerage commission takes them outside the exemption.
  • Certified public accountants acting within their duties as CPAs.
  • Attorneys in fact acting under a power of attorney to execute contracts or conveyances only (signing for the owner — not marketing or negotiating for a fee).
  • Court-appointed or will-appointed fiduciaries: personal representatives, receivers, trustees, and others acting under a will or court order.
  • Salaried employees of public utilities, railroads and government agencies handling their employer's real property, with no compensation beyond salary.
  • Salaried employees of an owner (or of a broker for an owner) of an apartment community working in an onsite rental office in a leasing capacity.
  • Salaried condominium or cooperative managers renting units for terms of 1 year or less.

Two exemptions in the study manual need correction: the manual mentions "radon professionals", which does not appear in the statute, and it describes the attorney-in-fact exemption as "a single specific transaction" — the statute says "execution of contracts or conveyances only" (verification V-14).

4. Key terms

Term Meaning
Exemption A category of person who need not hold a license
Attorney in fact Someone holding a power of attorney (not necessarily a lawyer)
Attorney at law A lawyer
Personal representative The court-appointed administrator of a deceased person's estate
Onsite rental office Leasing office located at the apartment community

5. Practical example

Three people rent apartments at a 300-unit complex in Jacksonville:

  1. Maria works in the complex's leasing office for a salary paid by the owner — exempt.
  2. João is paid $250 for every lease he signs, by the owner — license required (compensation per transaction).
  3. Lena manages rentals for twelve different owners across the city for 8% of rents — license required (managing for others for compensation; not an onsite salaried employee).

6. Portugal comparison

Requires care: In Portugal you may be used to seeing staff of a developer or an agency intermediate deals under the company's license. Florida asks a narrower question for each person: is there an exemption, and does its condition (salary only, onsite, scope of profession) still hold?

7. Legal and numerical requirements

Memorize exactly

  • Salaried onsite apartment leasing employees are exempt; per-lease pay removes the exemption.
  • Condo/co-op salaried managers: rentals of 1 year or less.
  • Attorneys and CPAs: only within their professional duties.
  • Attorneys in fact: executing contracts or conveyances only.

Understand

  • Each exemption has a condition. The exam changes the condition.

8. Visual explanation

Person Exempt when… Not exempt when…
Owner Selling/leasing own property Uses commissioned agents in the ordinary course of business
Attorney at law Acting within legal duties Earns a brokerage commission
Attorney in fact Executing contracts or conveyances only Markets or negotiates for a fee
Owner's onsite leasing employee Salaried, onsite rental office Paid per lease
Condo/co-op manager Salaried; rentals ≤ 1 year Paid by commission

9. Common misconceptions

  • "Lawyers never need a real estate license." They do if they earn a brokerage commission.
  • "Attorney in fact means lawyer." It means anyone holding a power of attorney.
  • "Any employee of an owner is exempt." Only if salaried and, for apartment leasing, working onsite.

10. Memory sheet

  • Salary yes, commission no.
  • Lawyers and CPAs: only inside their own profession.
  • Power of attorney: sign the documents only.
  • Condo/co-op manager: rentals ≤ 1 year.

lessons.title: Qualifying and applying for a sales associate license
lessons.html:
2. Why it matters

These are exact-recall facts — ages, hours, scores and time limits — and the mutual recognition rule is a favourite trap because it depends on residency at the moment of application. It also affects you personally: you are a nonresident-born professional entering Florida licensing.

3. Simple explanation

Applicant requirements (sales associate):

  • At least 18 years old.
  • High school diploma or equivalent.
  • A U.S. Social Security number.
  • Not required: U.S. citizenship, Florida residency, a college degree.

The path: complete the 63-hour pre-license course (63 hours of 50 minutes, including the course exam) → apply to the DBPR with fingerprints and fees → pass the state exam (100 questions, 3.5 hours, 75 correct to pass) → license issued. The course completion becomes invalid if you do not pass the state exam within 2 years after completing the course, and the application expires 2 years after the DBPR receives it if you have not passed (s. 475.181(2), verification V-31 and V-32). The license is inactive until the licensee is registered with an employing broker.

Criminal history and honesty. Applicants must disclose criminal history. A record does not automatically disqualify; the FREC looks at the nature of the offence, time elapsed, rehabilitation and honesty (good moral character). A false answer on the application is itself grounds for denial or revocation and is a crime. A denied applicant receives written notice and may request a hearing.

Mutual recognition. Florida has agreements with certain states. A licensee from one of those states who is not a Florida resident when applying can obtain a Florida license without the 63-hour course by passing a 40-question Florida law exam with at least 30 correct. Florida residents cannot use it, and the other state's license must have been earned through that state's own course and exam. In October 2026 the DBPR Division home page lists nine states (Alabama, Arkansas, Connecticut, Georgia, Kentucky, Mississippi, Nebraska, Rhode Island, West Virginia) and shows the Illinois agreement as dissolved on December 31, 2025. The list changes over time, so it is low priority for the exam (verification V-22).

4. Key terms

Term Meaning
Pre-license course 63-hour FREC Course I
Good moral character Honesty, trustworthiness and fair dealing required of applicants
Mutual recognition Agreement letting nonresident licensees of certain states qualify by passing a Florida law exam
Registration with a broker Required before a new license can be used

5. Practical example

Two applicants:

  • Inês, a Portuguese citizen living in Miami with a green card and a Social Security number, finished high school in Portugal (with an equivalency evaluation). She qualifies to apply: citizenship is not required. She must take the 63-hour course and pass the state exam.
  • Mark holds an active Georgia license and lives in Savannah. If Georgia has an agreement with Florida when he applies, he can take the 40-question law exam. If he first moves to Jacksonville and then applies, he is a Florida resident and must take the full course and exam.

6. Portugal comparison

Different: Portuguese mediation licensing has no state exam or course-hours requirement (IMPIC lists good standing and insurance). Florida's requirements are educational and exam-based, and your Portuguese experience does not reduce the 63 hours. Mutual recognition covers only certain US states — not foreign countries.

7. Legal and numerical requirements

Memorize exactly

  • 18 · high school diploma or equivalent · SSN.
  • Not required: citizenship, Florida residency.
  • 63 hours; must PASS the exam within 2 years of finishing the course. Application expires 2 years after receipt without a pass.
  • Exam: 100 questions, 3.5 hours, 75 to pass.
  • Mutual recognition: nonresident at application; 40 questions; 30 to pass.

Understand

  • Honesty on the application matters more than the record itself.
  • A new license cannot be used until registered under a broker.

8. Visual explanation

Course63 hrs · valid 2 yrs for exam
ApplicationFingerprints · fee · valid 2 yrs
State exam100 Q · 3.5 h · 75 to pass
License issuedInactive until a broker registers you
First renewal18–24 months · 45-hr post-license due

9. Common misconceptions

  • "You must be a U.S. citizen." No.
  • "You must live in Florida." No; nonresidents can be licensed.
  • "Mutual recognition is reciprocity for anyone licensed elsewhere." Only nonresidents licensed in a state with an agreement.
  • "Once licensed you can start working." Not until a broker registers you.

10. Memory sheet

  • 18 · diploma · SSN — no citizenship, no Florida address.
  • 63 hours → pass the exam within 2 years → 75/100 in 3.5 hours.
  • Mutual recognition: nonresident · 40 Q · 30 to pass.
  • Lie on the application = denial/revocation + crime.

lessons.title: FREC and DBPR: structure and powers
lessons.html:
2. Why it matters

Every official action on a Florida license is taken by one of two state bodies. Applications, licenses, records and investigations belong to the DBPR. Rules and discipline belong to the FREC. The exam keeps asking "Which body does X?" and tests the FREC's make-up with exact numbers: 7 members, 4-1-2 seats, 5 and 2 years of experience, one member aged 60 or older, 4-year terms and a quorum of 4.

This is Section III of the official exam outline (License Law and Commission Rules, 2%, about 2 questions). The same "which body" skill comes back in Chapter 6 on complaints and penalties. In practice, it tells you who sent the letter you are holding and what that body can and cannot do.

3. Simple explanation

Two bodies, two kinds of job

  • The DBPR (Department of Business and Professional Regulation) runs the system through its Division of Real Estate. It takes applications, issues licenses, keeps records and investigates complaints. Chapter 455 F.S. is the general law for all the professions the DBPR regulates; Chapter 475 is the real estate license law.
  • The FREC (Florida Real Estate Commission) makes the rules and judges licensees. The DBPR's Division of Real Estate provides its administrative support.

The logic: the people who investigate a case are not the people who decide it, and the profession's rules are written by people who know it, with consumer members at the table.

Who sits on the FREC (s. 475.02, F.S.)

7 members, appointed by the Governor, confirmed by the Senate, for 4-year terms.

Seats Who Requirement
4 Brokers Active license for the 5 years before appointment
1 Broker or sales associate Active license for the 2 years before appointment
2 Consumer members Are not, and have never been, brokers or sales associates
(any seat) At least one of the 7 Aged 60 or older

Quorum and term limits

A quorum is the minimum number of members who must be present before a body can act.

  • Quorum (s. 455.207): 51% or more of the appointed members. For the FREC that is 4. Official action needs a majority of the quorum.
  • Term limit (s. 20.165(5)): no member may serve more than the rest of a predecessor's term plus two consecutive 4-year terms of their own.
  • Terms end on October 31.

Three kinds of power

"Quasi" means "almost": the FREC is not a legislature or a court, but it does work that resembles both.

Power Meaning Who Example
Quasi-legislative Adopting rules with the force of law, within the statute's limits FREC Rule Chapter 61J2 F.A.C.
Quasi-judicial Deciding individual cases and issuing final orders FREC Fining, suspending, revoking
Executive / administrative Running the law day to day DBPR Applications, licenses, records, investigations, support to the FREC

FREC discipline (s. 475.25(1)): denial, reprimand, fine up to $5,000 per count, probation, suspension up to 10 years, revocation.

The complaint path in one line

Complaint → DBPR investigates → FREC probable cause panel decides whether to go forward → FREC final order → review by a District Court of Appeal (notice within 30 days after the order is rendered, s. 120.68). The panel has at least two members, including a current FREC member; a former member may serve; probable cause is decided by majority vote (s. 455.225(4); Rule 61J2-20.009). Chapter 6 covers the details.

What neither body can do

Neither the FREC nor the DBPR can imprison anyone or order a licensee to pay damages to a consumer. Jail (for example, for unlicensed activity, a third-degree felony) comes only from a criminal court. Damages are awarded only by a civil court.

4. Key terms

Term Meaning
FREC Florida Real Estate Commission: 7 appointed members; makes rules, decides discipline
DBPR Department of Business and Professional Regulation: applications, licenses, records, investigations
Division of Real Estate The part of the DBPR that handles real estate and serves the FREC
Consumer member FREC member who is not, and has never been, a broker or sales associate
Quorum Minimum members present for official action; FREC = 4
Quasi-legislative An agency's power to adopt rules
Quasi-judicial An agency's power to decide cases and impose discipline
Probable cause panel FREC panel (at least two members) that decides whether an investigated complaint goes forward
Final order The FREC's written decision in a discipline case

5. Practical example

Part A: two vacancies. The Governor must fill one broker seat and one consumer seat.

Candidate Broker seat? Consumer seat?
Marta, retired teacher in Sarasota, never licensed No Yes
Kevin, a broker first licensed (as a sales associate) 3 years ago and active ever since No: needs 5 years of active licensure No
Paul, a banker who held a sales associate license 20 years ago No No: consumer members must never have been licensed

Kevin could fill the "broker or sales associate" seat (2 years) if it were open.

Part B: a complaint. A buyer says Diego, a sales associate in Orlando, never passed her $8,000 deposit to his broker.

Step Who acts
Complaint filed and investigated DBPR
Probable cause? FREC probable cause panel
$3,000 fine and 6-month suspension FREC final order (within the $5,000-per-count and 10-year limits)
Diego wants the order reviewed District Court of Appeal, notice within 30 days
The buyer wants her $8,000 back Civil court (the FREC cannot award damages)
Diego is charged with a crime Criminal court (only it can impose jail)

Five members attend the FREC meeting that hears the case, so there is a quorum. With only 3, the FREC could not act.

6. Portugal comparison

Familiar principle. In Portugal, one public institute, IMPIC, I.P., both licenses and supervises real estate mediation businesses, and it approves standard mediation contract models.

Florida rule. The work is split three ways: the FREC makes rules and disciplines; the DBPR handles applications, licenses, records and investigations; the courts handle crimes, damages and review of final orders.

Precise difference. Florida separates investigating (DBPR) from deciding (FREC), and the deciding body's seats are fixed by statute (4 brokers, 1 broker or sales associate, 2 consumers). How IMPIC's leadership is appointed and how Portuguese sanctions are decided requires verification.

Exam implication. Never answer "the regulator". Name the body: DBPR investigates, FREC decides, courts jail and award damages.

7. Legal and numerical requirements

Memorize exactly

  • 7 members · Governor appoints · Senate confirms · 4-year terms (s. 475.02).
  • 4 brokers (active 5 years) · 1 broker or sales associate (active 2 years) · 2 consumers never licensed as broker or sales associate · at least one member 60+.
  • Quorum 4 (51% or more of 7, s. 455.207); action needs a majority of the quorum.
  • Term limit: remainder of a predecessor's term + two consecutive 4-year terms (s. 20.165(5)); terms end October 31.
  • Rules → FREC (quasi-legislative). Discipline → FREC (quasi-judicial). Applications, licenses, records, investigations → DBPR.
  • FREC maximums: $5,000 per count, suspension 10 years, revocation (s. 475.25(1)).
  • Probable cause panel: at least two members, including a current FREC member; majority vote (s. 455.225(4)).
  • Review of a final order: District Court of Appeal, 30 days (s. 120.68).

Understand

  • The quorum of 4 and the two-consecutive-term limit are verified (V-13). They come from s. 455.207 and s. 20.165(5), not from s. 475.02 itself.
  • The panel's "at least two members" is verified (V-42), but the current rule's wording on panel size was seen only in fragments.
  • Investigation and decision are kept apart on purpose: the DBPR gathers the facts; the FREC, as judge, decides.

8. Visual explanation

Quorum: a worked calculation

Members present Share of 7 51% or more? Can the FREC act?
3 42.9% No No
4 57.1% Yes Yes: 4 is the quorum

51% of 7 = 3.57. Members are whole people, so "51% or more" means at least 4.

DBPRApplications · licenses · records · investigations
FREC probable cause panelShould the complaint go forward? (at least two members, majority vote)
FREC61J2 rules · final orders: fine, probation, suspension, revocation, reprimand, denial
CourtsJail · damages · review of final orders (30 days)

9. Common misconceptions

  • "Licensees elect the FREC." The Governor appoints and the Senate confirms.
  • "All members are brokers." Only 4 must be; two seats go to consumers who were never licensed.
  • "A former licensee can be a consumer member." No: consumer members must never have been brokers or sales associates.
  • "The FREC investigates complaints." The DBPR investigates; the FREC decides.
  • "Quorum is 3, about half of 7." It is 51% or more, which means 4.
  • "Two terms means 8 years at most." A member may also first serve the rest of a predecessor's term, then two consecutive 4-year terms.
  • "The FREC can award the consumer damages or send a licensee to jail." Only courts can.

10. Memory sheet

  • 7 · Governor + Senate · 4-year terms.
  • 4-1-2: four brokers (5 yrs), one broker or sales associate (2 yrs), two never-licensed consumers. One member 60+.
  • Quorum 4. Term limit: remainder + two consecutive terms (s. 20.165(5)). Terms end Oct 31.
  • Rules = quasi-legislative · discipline = quasi-judicial · both FREC. Paperwork and investigation = DBPR.
  • FREC max: $5,000 per count · 10-year suspension · revocation.
  • DBPR digs, FREC decides, courts jail and award damages. Appeal: 30 days.

lessons.title: License types, registration, group and multiple licenses
lessons.html:
2. Why it matters

You will start as a sales associate, and many violations happen when an associate does what only a broker may do: keep a deposit, take money directly from a customer, or work for a second company on the side. The exam tests look-alike terms (broker associate, group license, multiple licenses) and the exact broker path: 24 months in the preceding 5 years → 72-hour course → broker exam → 60 hours of post-license education. It is also your own route to becoming a broker.

3. Simple explanation

Two levels of license

Chapter 475 issues two license types: sales associate and broker. The difference is independence: a broker works for the public in their own name, while a sales associate works only through an employer.

Sales associate Broker
Works for the public Only under an employing broker (or an owner-developer) In their own name
Opens an office No Yes
Holds escrow deposits No. Deposits go to the broker by the end of the next business day (Rule 61J2-14.009) Yes
Paid directly by the public No. Only a broker may be Yes
Officer or director of a brokerage corporation No Yes

Source note: apart from the deposit deadline (verified, V-36), the rows of this table come from the study manual and are not yet verified.

A broker associate holds a broker license but chooses to work under another broker. It is not a third level of qualification: the person met every broker requirement.

Licensure vs registration

Both must be current before you may work (manual; not yet verified):

  • Licensure is the DBPR's certification that you met the qualifications (course, exam, background).
  • Registration is the DBPR's record of your license: name, address, employer and status.

Licensure is like a diploma; registration records who you work for today.

One employer, and the two "more than one" situations

A sales associate may hold one license and work for one employer at a time.

  • Group license. A sales associate works for several connected entities of one owner-developer (a business that develops and sells its own property). Example: a developer that sells homes through three related companies, one per subdivision.
  • Multiple licenses. A broker holds separate licenses for separate, unconnected brokerages. Only brokers may do this.

The broker path (s. 475.17 and s. 475.181, F.S.)

  1. Experience. During the preceding 5 years, at least 24 months of one of the following:

    • an active sales associate license in the office of one or more brokers licensed in Florida, another US state, territory or jurisdiction, or a foreign national jurisdiction;
    • a current, valid sales associate license while employed by a government agency for a salary, performing licensee duties;
    • a current, valid broker license in another US state, territory or jurisdiction, or a foreign jurisdiction.

    Anyone licensed as a Florida sales associate in the preceding 5 years must also have completed the 45-hour post-license education.

  2. Course. The broker pre-license course (FREC Course II): up to 72 classroom hours of 50 minutes, including the exam (sales associates take 63). If absences exceed 8 classroom hours, no completion notice is issued.

  3. Exam. You must pass the state exam within 2 years after completing the pre-license course, or the course completion becomes invalid. The application also expires 2 years after the DBPR receives it if you have not passed.

  4. Broker post-license. Once licensed, you open your own office or register under another broker as a broker associate. Then, before the first broker renewal, complete 60 hours of Commission-approved broker post-license courses (60 classroom hours of 50 minutes, exam included). DBPR guidance says this may be taken as two 30-hour courses, Broker Investment and Broker Management, in a classroom or by distance learning. The only exemption is a 4-year degree in real estate; attorneys are not exempt.

If the 60 hours are missed, the broker license "shall be considered null and void" (s. 475.17(4)(c)). Flagged: what happens next was not confirmed in the current statute text. Statute and law-book sources say that to be a broker again the person must retake the broker pre-license course and pass the broker exam, and that a way back to a sales associate license exists by completing the 14-hour continuing education course within 6 months after the broker license expired. Treat both as unverified.

4. Key terms

Term Meaning
Sales associate Licensee who performs services only under an employing broker or owner-developer
Broker Licensee who performs services for others in their own name
Broker associate A person with a broker license who works under another broker
Owner-developer A business that develops and sells its own property and may employ sales associates
Licensure The DBPR's certification that a person is qualified
Registration The DBPR record of a license: name, address, employer, status
Group license Lets a sales associate work for connected entities of one owner-developer
Multiple licenses Separate licenses a broker holds for unconnected brokerages

5. Practical example

Beatriz is a sales associate in Tampa. She completed her 45-hour post-license course before her first renewal, worked actively for Bay Shore Realty for 30 months, then went inactive for a year. Now she wants to be a broker. After the first row, each row is a separate "what if".

Situation Rule Result
30 active months, all within the last 5 years 24 months in the preceding 5 years Qualifies
She missed 10 classroom hours of Course II Absences over 8 hours → no completion notice Course not completed
She completes the course but takes 26 months to pass the exam Must pass within 2 years of completion Course completion invalid
She passes in time and rejoins Bay Shore Realty Broker license, working under another broker Broker associate
No 60 hours by her first broker renewal Broker post-license missed Broker license null and void

Three colleagues:

  • Rui was active from 2018 to 2020, then left. Applying in 2027, he has no active months in the 5-year window: not qualified.
  • Lena sells for an owner-developer's three connected companies: group license. She may not also work for an unrelated broker.
  • Carlos is broker of two unconnected brokerages: multiple licenses (brokers only).

6. Portugal comparison

Familiar principle. In Portugal, IMPIC licenses and supervises the mediation business. Consultants inside a licensed agency usually work under the agency's license (requires verification).

Florida rule. Florida licenses each person who performs real estate services. The closest match to the Portuguese licensed agency is the Florida broker, who runs the office, holds escrow and is paid by the public.

Precise difference. Florida has no "working under the agency's license": a sales associate needs a personal license, usable only while registered under one employer.

Your experience and the broker path. The statute counts some foreign experience (an active sales associate license held in the office of a broker licensed in a foreign jurisdiction, or a foreign broker license). Whether a Portuguese career qualifies, when the Portuguese license belongs to the company, requires verification with the DBPR.

Exam implication. Use only the Florida categories (sales associate, broker, broker associate). A Portuguese rule never answers a Florida question.

7. Legal and numerical requirements

Memorize exactly

  • Broker experience: 24 months within the preceding 5 years, in one of the three listed ways; Florida sales associates must also have completed the 45-hour post-license course (s. 475.17(1)).
  • Course II: 72 hours (50-minute hours, exam included). Absences over 8 hours → no completion notice (s. 475.17(2)(a)1.; Rule 61J2-3.008).
  • Pass the exam within 2 years of finishing the course. The application expires 2 years after receipt if the exam is not passed (s. 475.181(2)).
  • Broker post-license: 60 hours before the first broker renewal. Missed → null and void (s. 475.17(4)(c)). Only a 4-year real estate degree exempts; attorneys do not.
  • Sales associate → deposit to broker by the end of the next business day (Rule 61J2-14.009).
  • Two license types; broker associate = broker license under another broker (manual; not yet verified).
  • Only brokers open offices, hold escrow and are paid directly by the public (manual; not yet verified).
  • A sales associate may not be an officer or director of a brokerage corporation; partners and officers who deal with the public must be brokers (manual; not yet verified).
  • Group license = connected entities of one owner-developer; multiple licenses = brokers only (manual; not yet verified).
  • Licensure = DBPR certification of qualification; registration = name, address, employer and status on DBPR records; both must be current to operate (manual; not yet verified).

Understand

  • The 24-month rule is in s. 475.17(1), not s. 475.17(2) as the study manual cites.
  • After a voided broker license, the routes back (retake the broker course and exam; or a sales associate license through 14 hours of CE within 6 months) are unverified.

8. Visual explanation

Experience24 months in the last 5 years (+ 45-hr post-license done)
Course II72 hrs · absences ≤ 8 hrs
Broker examPass within 2 yrs of the course
Broker licenseOwn office, or broker associate
First broker renewal60 hrs post-license, or void
Is the person the broker of the brokerages (not a sales associate or broker associate)?
No → no multiple licenses. A sales associate has one license and one employer (a group license if that employer is one owner-developer's connected entities)
Are the brokerages separate and unconnected?
No → this is not the multiple-license situation
Yes → multiple licenses (brokers only)

9. Common misconceptions

  • "Broker associate is a third license level." It is a broker license used under another broker.
  • "A sales associate can work for two unrelated brokers if both agree." Never: one license, one employer.
  • "Any 24 months of experience counts." It must fall within the preceding 5 years.
  • "I have 2 years to take the broker exam." You must pass it within 2 years.
  • "Missing broker post-license makes the license inactive." It makes it null and void.

10. Memory sheet

  • Sales associate works through an employer. Broker works in their own name. Broker associate = broker license under another broker.
  • Only brokers: office, escrow, paid directly by the public. A sales associate may never be an officer or director of a brokerage corporation.
  • Licensure = qualified. Registration = your employer and address on record.
  • Group = one owner-developer's connected entities. Multiple = brokers only.
  • 24 in 5 → 72 hours (≤ 8 absent) → pass within 2 years → 60 hours before first renewal, or void.
  • Sales 45, broker 60.

lessons.title: Keeping the license: post-license, renewal, CE and license status
lessons.html:
2. Why it matters

A Florida license is not permanent. It must be renewed every 2 years, and the first renewal carries a one-time education deadline that can end the license outright. The exam's most-swapped pair lives here: missed post-license → null and void, but missed CE or renewal → involuntary inactive. Expect questions on the 45, 14 and 28 hours, the 12- and 24-month reactivation bands, and the status words: active, voluntary inactive, involuntary inactive, suspended, revoked, null and void, ineffective.

In practice, the post-license deadline is the one that can end a new career before it starts.

3. Simple explanation

The renewal calendar

Every Florida real estate license expires at midnight Eastern time on March 31 or September 30. A new license is fitted to one of those two dates, so the first renewal period is 18–24 months. Every later period is 24 months.

Stage 1: post-license education (before the first renewal)

  • Sales associates: 45 hours (s. 475.17(3)(a)). The statute caps the requirement at 45 classroom hours (50-minute hours, exam included); it is met with one or more FREC-approved courses totaling at least 45 hours. Courses may be classroom or approved distance learning; a distance course requires passing a timed exam.
  • If absences exceed 10% of classroom hours, no completion notice is issued.
  • Missed? The license "shall be considered null and void." To work again, the person must requalify: complete the 63-hour pre-license course and pass the state exam.
  • Exceptions: the FREC may allow 6 extra months for an individual physical hardship (as defined by rule). Holders of a 4-year or higher degree in real estate are exempt.
  • Attorneys are not exempt from post-license (per DBPR), even though Florida Bar members are exempt from CE.

Why "void" and not "inactive"? Think of post-license as the last piece of qualifying. If qualification is never finished, there is no license left to put on hold.

Stage 2: continuing education (every later renewal)

  • 14 hours (50-minute hours) in each 2-year renewal period, starting after the first renewal (s. 475.182(1); Rule 61J2-3.009).
  • Required split: 3 hours Core Law + 3 hours Ethics and Business Practices + 8 hours specialty. This is mandatory for licenses expiring on or after March 31, 2025, and Core Law must be taken at least once each renewal period.
  • Applies to active and inactive licensees. Approved distance learning is allowed.
  • Florida Bar members in good standing are exempt from CE.
  • Once per renewal cycle, attending one FREC legal agenda session can substitute for 3 hours. This requires 7 days' notice and does not apply if you attend as a party to a disciplinary case.

Missing a renewal: involuntary inactive (s. 475.183; verified, V-11)

If a license is not renewed on time, for example because CE was not finished, it becomes involuntary inactive. The license still exists, but a clock starts:

Time involuntarily inactive To reactivate
12 months or less 14 hours of commission-prescribed CE
More than 12 but less than 24 months 28-hour commission-prescribed reactivation course
More than 24 months License expires (null and void)

The status map

Status How it happens May the person work? What it means
Active Registered with an employing broker (a broker: with an office) Yes Renew every 2 years
Voluntary inactive The licensee chooses it No Renewable indefinitely with 14 hours of CE per cycle
Involuntary inactive Failure to renew No 2-year countdown (table above)
Suspended Discipline: up to 10 years No The license exists but cannot be used
Revoked Discipline No Permanent cancellation (narrow exceptions)
Null and void Post-license missed; involuntary inactive over 24 months No The license no longer exists; requalify
Ineffective License exists but cannot be used, e.g., associate with no employer No Register with an employer (L03-4)

4. Key terms

Term Meaning
Renewal period Time between license expirations: 18–24 months the first time, then 24 months
Post-license education 45 hours (sales associate) due before the first renewal
Continuing education (CE) 14 hours per renewal period after the first: 3 Core Law, 3 Ethics, 8 specialty
Core Law The required 3-hour Core Law part of CE, taken at least once each renewal period
Involuntary inactive Status after failing to renew; void after 24 months
Voluntary inactive Status the licensee chooses while not practicing
Reactivation course 28-hour course for involuntary inactive more than 12 but less than 24 months
Null and void The license has ceased to exist; the person must requalify
Ineffective Exam term for a license that exists but cannot be used

5. Practical example

Sofia and Lucas are licensed as sales associates in Jacksonville in May 2024. Their first expiration is March 31, 2026: the only March 31 or September 30 date that falls 18–24 months later (about 22 months).

Event Rule Result
Sofia finishes her 45 hours in January 2026 and renews Post-license done before the 1st renewal Renewed; next expiration March 31, 2028
Lucas has not finished his 45 hours on March 31, 2026 (no degree, no hardship extension) Post-license missed Null and void: 63-hour course and state exam again
Sofia forgets her CE and does not renew by March 31, 2028 Failure to renew Involuntary inactive
…she reactivates in January 2029 (about 10 months) 12 months or less 14 hours of CE
…or in October 2029 (about 18 months) More than 12 but less than 24 months 28-hour reactivation course
…or does nothing until after March 31, 2030 More than 24 months Null and void

Sofia's 14 hours for 2028 must include 3 Core Law + 3 Ethics and Business Practices + 8 specialty.

6. Portugal comparison

Familiar principle. In Portugal, IMPIC's listed requirements for a mediation license are commercial good standing (idoneidade comercial), civil liability insurance (or an equivalent guarantee) and fees. No state exam or minimum course hours appear.

Florida rule. Florida adds an education pathway with hard deadlines: 63 hours to enter, 45 hours before the first renewal, and 14 hours every 2 years after that.

Precise difference. In Florida, missing an education deadline can void a license. Whether Portugal has any comparable renewal or continuing-education duty requires verification (our comparison data does not cover it).

Exam implication. Never assume a license simply continues. Know 63 / 45 / 14 and which miss voids (post-license) and which inactivates (CE).

7. Legal and numerical requirements

Memorize exactly

  • First renewal: 18–24 months; later periods 24 months; licenses expire March 31 or September 30.
  • Post-license: 45 hours before the first renewal → missed = null and void → 63-hour course + state exam (s. 475.17(3)).
  • Absences over 10% → no post-license completion notice. Individual physical hardship: the FREC may allow 6 extra months. Exempt: 4-year real estate degree. Attorneys not exempt.
  • CE: 14 hours per 2-year period after the first renewal: 3 Core Law + 3 Ethics + 8 specialty (licenses expiring on or after March 31, 2025). Active and inactive licensees. Florida Bar members exempt (s. 475.182; Rule 61J2-3.009).
  • Missed renewal → involuntary inactive. Reactivation: ≤ 12 months → 14 hours; more than 12 but less than 24 months → 28-hour course; more than 24 months → void (s. 475.183; Rule 61J2-3.010).
  • Suspension: up to 10 years (s. 475.25(1)).
  • Voluntary inactive renewable indefinitely (manual; not yet verified). Its CE duty is confirmed by Rule 61J2-3.009.
  • Revocation is permanent with narrow exceptions (manual; not yet verified). "Ineffective" is a course and exam term (manual; not yet verified).

Understand

  • Older materials describe CE only as "14 hours, including core law". The 3 + 3 + 8 split is the current requirement.
  • The study manual mentions only "late CE" for reactivation. The 28-hour course is a verified addition from s. 475.183.
  • The 18–24-month first period comes from an official DBPR sheet (2018). Nothing current contradicts it, but no current-year restatement was found, and the rule citation the manual gives (61J2-1.008 or 61J2-3.020) is unverified.

8. Visual explanation

License issuedUsable once registered with a broker
1st renewal18–24 months · 45-hr post-license or void
Each later renewalEvery 24 months · 14 hrs CE (3 + 3 + 8)
Missed renewalInvoluntary inactive · 24-month clock
First renewal: 45-hour post-license completed (or exempt)?
No → null and void (unless the FREC granted a 6-month hardship extension): 63-hour course + state exam
Later renewal: missed (not renewed on time with 14 hours of CE)?
No → license stays current
Involuntarily inactive more than 12 months?
No (12 months or less) → 14 hours of commission-prescribed CE
More than 24 months?
No (more than 12 but less than 24) → 28-hour reactivation course
Yes → license expired (null and void)

9. Common misconceptions

  • Swapping the two deadlines. Post-license missed → void. CE or renewal missed → involuntary inactive.
  • "Involuntary inactive can be fixed any time." Only for 24 months; after that the license is void.
  • "Attorneys are exempt from post-license, like CE." Florida Bar members are exempt from CE, but not from post-license.
  • "CE is due at the first renewal too." The first renewal requires post-license; CE starts after it.
  • "Voluntary inactive licensees need no CE." They complete 14 hours per cycle.
  • "Any 14 hours will do." It must be 3 Core Law + 3 Ethics + 8 specialty.
  • "A suspended license no longer exists." It exists but cannot be used. Revoked and null-and-void licenses are the ones that are gone.

10. Memory sheet

  • 63 to get in · 45 to stay in · 14 to keep going.
  • POST missed → VOID. CE missed → INACTIVE.
  • First renewal 18–24 months; then every 24. Expiry Mar 31 / Sep 30.
  • CE = 3 Core + 3 Ethics + 8 specialty.
  • Involuntary inactive: ≤ 1 year → 14 · 1–2 years → 28 · past 2 years → dead.
  • Florida Bar members: no CE, but post-license yes. 4-year real estate degree: no post-license.

lessons.title: Licensee duties to the DBPR: address, convictions, changing brokers
lessons.html:
2. Why it matters

The DBPR and the FREC can reach you only through the contact details on record, and they expect you to report some events yourself. This lesson gives you the clocks: 10 days for a change of mailing or e-mail address (and for a change of business address or employing broker), 30 days to report a criminal conviction, finding of guilt or plea, and 60 days when a Florida resident becomes a nonresident.

Exam questions test 10 versus 30, the nolo contendere and "adjudication withheld" traps, and the classic scenario of an associate who keeps showing homes between brokers. In practice, changing brokers is common, and doing it wrong means working without an effective license.

3. Simple explanation

1. Keep your contact details current

  • Under s. 455.275(1), each licensee is solely responsible for notifying the DBPR in writing of their current mailing address, e-mail address and place of practice. Failing to report a change is a violation.
  • Rule 61J2-10.038 sets the deadline: notify the Department in writing of any change to your mailing or e-mail address within 10 days after the change. A first violation gets a citation (a lighter penalty notice instead of a full disciplinary case). Repeat violations lead to disciplinary proceedings.
  • s. 475.23 separately requires notice within 10 days of a change of business address or employing broker, on a Commission form.
  • Moving out of Florida does not end the license (manual; not yet verified). A licensee who changes from Florida resident to nonresident must notify the Commission within 60 days, and the new mailing address is still due within 10 days.

Why so strict? The DBPR can contact you only through the details on record, and the law puts the burden of keeping them current on the licensee alone.

2. Report crimes yourself

  • s. 455.227(1)(t), which covers every DBPR licensee: report in writing to the FREC within 30 days after being convicted or found guilty of, or pleading guilty or nolo contendere to, a crime in any jurisdiction, regardless of adjudication.
  • s. 475.25(1)(p), the real estate law's own version, is narrower: it covers felonies only. Because licensees are bound by both, the rule to learn is the broader one: any crime.
  • Nolo contendere means "no contest". The defendant does not admit guilt but accepts the penalty.
  • Adjudication withheld means the court accepts the plea or finding of guilt but does not formally declare the person convicted. The report is still required.
  • The 30 days run from the plea, finding of guilt or conviction, not from the arrest.

Why? The FREC judges honesty and trustworthiness throughout a career, not only on the application (L02-3).

3. One license, one employer

A sales associate may hold only one license and work for only one broker or owner-employer at a time. A group license lets a sales associate work for several connected entities of one owner-developer; it never allows working for an unrelated broker at the same time (L03-2).

4. Changing brokers

  • When employment ends, the associate's license cannot be used until the new employer's registration is filed. In the gap, it is ineffective.
  • Showing listings, listing or negotiating in the gap is operating without an effective license.
  • The broker must notify the DBPR when an associate leaves.
  • The 10-day notice in s. 475.23 is a reporting deadline, not a 10-day permission to work unregistered.

4. Key terms

Term Meaning
Mailing address The address on DBPR records where official notices are sent
Place of practice Where the licensee practices; it must be on record with the DBPR
Nolo contendere "No contest" plea: no admission of guilt, but the penalty is accepted
Adjudication withheld The court accepts the plea or finding but does not formally declare a conviction
Found guilty A court or jury decides the person committed the crime
Employing broker The broker a sales associate is registered under
Ineffective license A license that exists but cannot be used, e.g., between employers
Citation A lighter penalty notice; used for a first address-rule violation instead of disciplinary proceedings
Nonresident licensee A Florida licensee who does not live in Florida

5. Practical example

Ana, a sales associate from Porto, works for Brickell Bay Realty in Miami.

Date Event Duty Deadline
June 3 Moves apartments and changes her e-mail Written notice to the DBPR of the new mailing and e-mail address June 13 (10 days)
August 1 Pleads nolo contendere to a misdemeanor in Georgia; adjudication withheld Written report to the FREC (any crime, any jurisdiction, regardless of adjudication) August 31 (30 days)
September 15 Leaves Brickell Bay for Coral Gate Realty Change of employing broker on the Commission form September 25 (10 days), but no work until Coral Gate's registration is filed
The next year Moves to Georgia and becomes a nonresident Notify the Commission of nonresidency; update the mailing address 60 days; 10 days

On September 16, before Coral Gate's registration is filed, Ana holds an open house for a former client. Her license still exists, but it is ineffective: she is operating without an effective license. The 10-day notice period does not protect her.

6. Portugal comparison

Familiar principle. In Portugal, IMPIC requires commercial good standing (idoneidade comercial) as a condition of the mediation business's license. Integrity matters in both systems.

Florida rule. Florida makes integrity and contact details a personal, continuing duty of every licensee: crimes reported within 30 days, address and e-mail within 10 days, change of employer on record before working.

Precise difference. Whether Portuguese law requires a consultant or agency to report address changes or criminal matters to IMPIC, and on what deadline, requires verification; our comparison data does not cover it. In Portugal, consultants usually work under the agency's license (requires verification), so moving agencies may feel like a private matter. In Florida, changing brokers is a registration event with the state.

Exam implication. Answer only with the Florida clocks: 10, 30 and 60 days.

7. Legal and numerical requirements

Memorize exactly

  • Mailing or e-mail address change: written notice to the DBPR within 10 days (Rule 61J2-10.038; s. 455.275(1)). First violation → citation; repeat → discipline.
  • Change of business address or employing broker: 10 days, on a Commission form (s. 475.23).
  • Florida resident becomes nonresident: notify the Commission within 60 days (V-34; no statute section given in our sources).
  • Conviction, finding of guilt, or guilty or nolo contendere plea to any crime in any jurisdiction: written report to the FREC within 30 days, regardless of adjudication (s. 455.227(1)(t)). Chapter 475's own rule covers felonies (s. 475.25(1)(p)).
  • One license, one employer at a time for sales associates (manual; not yet verified).
  • No services between brokers until the new employer's registration is filed; the broker notifies the DBPR when an associate leaves (manual; not yet verified). Do not read the 10-day notice period as permission to work in the gap.
  • The license survives a move out of state (manual; not yet verified).

Understand

  • The 10-day address deadline is confirmed in the 2020 rule text. The rule was amended again effective 7/18/2024, and that text was not read directly, so the continuing 10-day period is inferred.
  • According to the DBPR annual report, that 2024 amendment changed the definition of "current mailing address" by removing "residential", so the brokerage office's physical location can serve. The amended text itself was not read. Older materials that require a residential address are likely outdated.
  • "Any crime, regardless of adjudication" comes from s. 455.227(1)(t). Chapter 475 alone would require reporting only felonies, but licensees are bound by both.

8. Visual explanation

Event Deadline Notify Source
Mailing or e-mail address changes 10 days DBPR, in writing Rule 61J2-10.038; s. 455.275(1)
Business address or employing broker changes 10 days Commission form s. 475.23
Florida resident becomes nonresident 60 days Commission V-34 (no section cited in our sources)
Conviction, finding of guilt, guilty or nolo plea (any crime) 30 days FREC, in writing s. 455.227(1)(t)
Has her employment with the old broker ended?
No → she keeps working through her current broker only
Is the new employer's registration still unfiled?
No (it has been filed) → she may work, through the new broker only
Yes → license ineffective: showing, listing or negotiating now is operating without an effective license

9. Common misconceptions

  • "Nolo contendere is not a conviction, so there is nothing to report." It must be reported within 30 days.
  • "Adjudication was withheld, so it doesn't count." The duty applies regardless of adjudication.
  • "Only felonies must be reported." Under s. 455.227(1)(t), any crime must be reported.
  • "A crime in another state doesn't count." Any jurisdiction counts.
  • "The 30 days start at the arrest." They start at the plea, finding of guilt or conviction.
  • "My license is current, so I can keep working between brokers." It is ineffective until the new registration is filed.
  • "The 10-day notice gives me 10 days to work for the new broker unregistered." It is a reporting deadline only.
  • "Only my postal address matters." E-mail address and place of practice must be on record too.

10. Memory sheet

  • Address or e-mail = 10. Employer or business address = 10. Become a nonresident = 60.
  • Crime = 30: conviction, finding of guilt, guilty or nolo plea, any crime, anywhere, adjudication or not, in writing to the FREC.
  • Nolo = report. Withheld = report.
  • No employer = no work. One license, one employer.
  • First address violation = citation; repeat = discipline.

lessons.title: The three brokerage relationships and the transaction-broker presumption
lessons.html:
2. Why it matters

Section 4 of the state exam, "Authorized Relationships, Duties and Disclosure", carries 7% of the score (verified, V-02), which is about 7 of the 100 questions (V-01). Nearly every question in that section depends on one fact: which relationship exists. Once you know that, the duties (L04-2) and the required notices (L04-3) follow.

In practice, Florida's default relationship is not agency. Dealing with both the seller and the buyer in the same sale is common in Portuguese practice (PT-04; requires verification), but in Florida a brokerage that acts as a fiduciary for both sides (dual agency) breaks the law.

3. Simple explanation

First, four words

  • A fiduciary is a person in a relationship of trust who must put another person's interests ahead of their own.
  • A principal is the person a fiduciary agent represents.
  • A customer is a buyer or seller the licensee works with but does not represent as a fiduciary.
  • A presumption is what the law assumes is true unless something else is shown. Here, the "something else" must be in writing.

The three authorized relationships

Florida law (s. 475.278, F.S.) allows exactly three relationships between a licensee and a buyer or seller:

  1. Transaction broker (TB). Limited representation of the buyer, the seller, or both. The licensee helps the deal happen with skill and care, but is not a fiduciary. The parties are customers.
  2. Single agent. Full fiduciary representation of one party only, buyer or seller. That party is the principal.
  3. No brokerage relationship. The licensee deals with the party without representing them at all. A typical case: the brokerage represents the seller as single agent, and an unrepresented buyer comes to see the house.

"Subagent" and "dual agent" are not on the list.

The presumption: transaction broker

Unless a single agent relationship or a no brokerage relationship is established in writing, the licensee is presumed to be a transaction broker.

Why the law works this way. The default is a middle setting. A transaction broker owes enough duties to protect a customer (honesty, skill, limited confidentiality) but no fiduciary loyalty, which is what would make helping both sides impossible. Single agency moves the duties up and no brokerage relationship moves them down. A change like that should be deliberate and visible, so it must be in writing.

The presumption decides the type of relationship. A relationship can begin informally (L04-4). If nobody established a different type in writing, it is transaction broker.

Dual agency is illegal

Dual agency means acting as a single agent (a fiduciary) for both the buyer and the seller in the same transaction. Florida prohibits it. The reason is simple: a fiduciary for the seller must try to get the highest price, and a fiduciary for the buyer must try to get the lowest. No one can owe both kinds of loyalty at once.

The relationship belongs to the brokerage, not only to the individual sales associate. Two associates of the same brokerage therefore cannot each be a single agent for opposite sides of a home sale, because the brokerage would still be acting as a dual agent. There is one narrow exception, designated sales associates, available only in nonresidential deals where the buyer and the seller each have assets of $1 million or more and both sign disclosures requesting it (L04-4). The test is the parties' assets, not the size of the deal.

The lawful way to work both sides is to act as transaction broker for both. If the brokerage started as single agent for one party, that principal must sign a Consent to Transition to Transaction Broker before the change (L04-3).

Industry note (not Florida law)

Since August 2024, NAR (the National Association of REALTORS®) policy requires MLS participants to sign written agreements with buyers before touring homes (course note; not yet verified). This is a practice rule of a private trade association. It does not change Florida's three statutory relationships or the transaction-broker presumption.

4. Key terms

Term Meaning
Brokerage relationship The legal relationship between a brokerage and a buyer or seller; Florida authorizes three
Transaction broker Limited representation of a buyer, a seller or both; not a fiduciary; the presumed relationship
Single agent A fiduciary representing one party only (the principal)
No brokerage relationship The licensee deals with a party without representing them
Fiduciary Someone in a relationship of trust who must put the principal's interests first
Principal The person a single agent represents
Customer A party the licensee works with but does not represent as a fiduciary (TB or no brokerage relationship)
Dual agency Single agent for both buyer and seller in the same transaction; illegal in Florida
Presumption What the law assumes unless shown otherwise; here, transaction broker unless another relationship is established in writing

5. Practical example

Sunshine Realty in Miami has four situations in one week. Associate Paulo handles them.

Situation Written? Relationship Party is a…
Mrs. Alves lists her Coral Gables house and signs a listing agreement establishing single agency Yes Single agent for Mrs. Alves Principal
Mr. Brown, a buyer, calls Paulo, who shows him Brickell condos; nothing about the relationship is signed No Transaction broker (presumed) Customer
Ms. Duarte, a buyer with no agent, wants to see Mrs. Alves's house; Paulo gives her the written No Brokerage Relationship Notice first Yes No brokerage relationship with Ms. Duarte Customer
Mr. Brown now wants to buy Mrs. Alves's house — See below —

The Brown–Alves problem. Sunshine Realty is single agent for the seller. It may not also become Mr. Brown's single agent; that would be dual agency. Colleague Rita offers to "be Brown's single agent while Paulo stays the seller's agent", but this is still dual agency, because both associates belong to the same brokerage and this is a house sale. The lawful route is for Mrs. Alves to sign the Consent to Transition to Transaction Broker before the change. Sunshine Realty then acts as transaction broker for both.

6. Portugal comparison

Familiar principle. In Portuguese practice an agency often deals with both seller and buyer in the same sale, while the mediation contract is signed with one client. This description, and the agency's exact legal duties toward the party who is not its client, require verification (PT-04).

Florida rule. Florida gives each relationship a statutory name and a statutory list of duties. The default is transaction broker unless single agency or no brokerage relationship is established in writing. Fiduciary representation of both sides (dual agency) is prohibited.

The precise difference.

  • In Florida, representing both sides is lawful only as transaction broker for both, or with designated sales associates in nonresidential deals where each party has assets of $1 million or more. (A brokerage may also be single agent for one side and have no brokerage relationship with the other; then it represents only one side.)
  • A Florida relationship with legal duties can exist without any signed contract, because the presumption fills the gap.

Exam implication. Any answer choice containing "dual agent", or "dual agency with written consent", is wrong. Never answer from Portuguese both-sides practice.

7. Legal and numerical requirements

Memorize exactly

  • Three authorized relationships: transaction broker, single agent, no brokerage relationship (manual; not yet verified).
  • Presumption: transaction broker, unless single agent or no brokerage relationship is established in writing (manual; not yet verified).
  • Dual agency is prohibited. Transaction broker for both sides is lawful (manual; not yet verified).
  • Single agent → principal. Transaction broker or no brokerage relationship → customer (manual; not yet verified).
  • A transaction broker is not a fiduciary (manual; not yet verified).
  • Exam weight of Section 4: 7% (verified, V-02).

Understand

  • The default sits in the middle. Writing moves duties up (single agent) or down (no brokerage relationship).
  • The relationship is with the brokerage, so "two associates, one per side" is still dual agency. The only exception is designated sales associates (nonresidential; each party $1 million or more in assets; verified, V-46; L04-4).
  • Moving from single agent to transaction broker requires the principal's prior written consent (verified, V-48; L04-3).

8. Visual explanation

Has a single agent relationship been established in writing?
Yes → Single agent: full fiduciary for ONE party (the principal)
Has a no brokerage relationship been established in writing?
Yes → No brokerage relationship: no representation (the party is a customer)
Neither is in writing?
→ Transaction broker (presumed): limited representation, not a fiduciary
Feature No brokerage relationship Transaction broker Single agent
Represents the party? No Limited Fully
Fiduciary? No No Yes
The party is a Customer Customer Principal
How it arises Established in writing Default (no writing needed) Established in writing
Both buyer and seller in one deal? Not applicable (represents no one) Yes, TB for both No, that would be dual agency
Number of duties (L04-2) 3 7 9

9. Common misconceptions

  • "Dual agency is fine with written consent." Not in Florida. Written consent allows a transition to transaction broker, never dual agency.
  • "Transaction brokers owe loyalty." Only single agents owe loyalty.
  • "No signed agreement means no relationship and no duties." Without writing, the licensee is presumed to be a transaction broker and owes those duties.
  • "Transaction broker means the licensee represents nobody." That describes a no brokerage relationship. A transaction broker gives limited representation.
  • "Two associates in the same brokerage can each be a single agent for one side of a home sale." That is dual agency by the brokerage.
  • "Since NAR requires written buyer agreements, Florida now presumes single agency for buyers." The NAR rule is trade-association practice; the statutory presumption is unchanged.

10. Memory sheet

  • Three relationships: transaction broker (default) · single agent · no brokerage relationship.
  • Nothing in writing = transaction broker.
  • Single agent → principal. TB and no brokerage → customer.
  • Never dual agency. Both sides = TB for both, after the principal's written consent to transition.
  • The relationship belongs to the brokerage.
  • NAR's buyer-agreement rule is industry practice, not Florida law.

lessons.title: The duty lists: 3, 7 and 9
lessons.html:
2. Why it matters

The three duty lists, 3 · 7 · 9, are some of the highest-yield memory material in the course. Exam questions come in three shapes:

  • "How many duties…?"
  • "Which duty is owed by a single agent but NOT by a transaction broker?"
  • A short story followed by "Which duty did the licensee breach?"

In daily practice the lists decide what you may tell the other side in a negotiation, and what you must tell no matter who you represent.

3. Simple explanation

The lists come from s. 475.278 as summarized in the study manual; their exact statutory wording has not yet been checked (manual; not yet verified, V-26).

Build the lists as three floors of one building. Each floor builds on the one below. The top floor upgrades confidentiality from limited to full, adds three new duties, and does not list "additional duties mutually agreed".

Floor 1: the 3 duties every licensee owes (no brokerage relationship)

  1. Deal honestly and fairly.
  2. Disclose all known facts that materially affect the value of residential real property and are not readily observable to the buyer.
  3. Account for all funds entrusted to the licensee.

Why: these protect anyone who deals with a licensee, even a person the licensee does not represent. A fact "materially affects value" if it would change what a reasonable buyer pays or decides. It is "not readily observable" if an ordinary look at the property would not reveal it. L04-4 develops this duty.

Floor 2: the 7 transaction-broker duties

The 3 above, plus:

  1. Use skill, care and diligence.
  2. Present all offers and counteroffers in a timely manner, unless a party has directed otherwise in writing.
  3. Limited confidentiality, unless waived in writing by a party. The licensee may not reveal:
    • that the seller will accept less than the asking price;
    • that the buyer will pay more than the price offered;
    • the motivation of any party for selling or buying;
    • any other information a party asks to be kept confidential.
  4. Any additional duties mutually agreed with a party.

Why "limited": a transaction broker may work for both sides, so the law protects each side's bargaining position without making the licensee take sides.

Floor 3: the 9 single-agent duties

  1. Dealing honestly and fairly
  2. Loyalty: putting the principal's interests first
  3. Confidentiality (full, not limited to four items)
  4. Obedience: following the principal's lawful instructions only
  5. Full disclosure: telling the principal everything the agent knows that could affect the principal's interests or decisions
  6. Accounting for all funds
  7. Skill, care and diligence
  8. Presenting all offers and counteroffers in a timely manner
  9. Disclosing known facts that materially affect the value of residential property and are not readily observable

The four single-agent-only duties are Loyalty, Obedience, full Confidentiality and full disclOsure ("LOCO").

How 7 becomes 9. Start from the transaction broker's 7. Upgrade limited confidentiality to full confidentiality. Drop "additional duties mutually agreed", which is not an item on the single-agent list. Add loyalty, obedience and full disclosure. That gives 5 shared duties + full confidentiality + 3 new = 9.

What no duty can override
