The material-fact disclosure duty is on all three lists. Confidentiality never covers a hidden defect, and obedience never covers an unlawful instruction such as "don't mention the foundation crack".

4. Key terms

Term Meaning
Deal honestly and fairly Baseline duty owed to everyone in every relationship
Accounting Duty to account for all funds entrusted to the licensee
Skill, care and diligence The competence and effort expected of a licensee
Limited confidentiality TB duty not to reveal price flexibility, motivation, or information a party asks to keep confidential; can be waived in writing
Loyalty Single-agent duty to put the principal's interests above everyone else's, including the agent's own
Obedience Single-agent duty to follow the principal's lawful instructions
Full disclosure Single-agent duty to tell the principal all known information that could affect the principal
Readily observable Visible on an ordinary look at the property
Waive To give up a right voluntarily (here, in writing)

5. Practical example

Carla lists her house in Seminole Heights, Tampa, with Gulf Realty. Nothing establishes single agency, so Gulf Realty is a transaction broker. Buyer Mr. Lee also works with Gulf Realty as a transaction-broker customer. Associate Marco handles both.

Event What Marco must do Duty
Carla says, "I'd take $25,000 less; I start a new job in Atlanta in two weeks." Lee asks, "Is she flexible? Why is she selling?" Reveal neither the price flexibility nor the move Limited confidentiality
Lee says, "Offer $450,000, but I'd go to $480,000." Not tell Carla that Lee would pay more Limited confidentiality
Marco knows the attic ductwork leaks into a ceiling cavity, out of sight Disclose it to Lee Material fact, not readily observable
Carla directed in writing: "Don't present offers under $430,000." A $420,000 offer arrives He need not present it; the written direction controls Present offers, unless directed otherwise in writing
Lee hands over a $10,000 deposit check Handle and account for it (deadlines in L05-1) Accounting

What if Carla had signed as Gulf Realty's single-agent principal? Marco would then owe Carla loyalty, obedience, full confidentiality and full disclosure. If Lee had no brokerage relationship with Gulf Realty (he was given the No Brokerage Relationship Notice), Marco would owe Lee only the 3 baseline duties, with no confidentiality. Marco's duty of full disclosure to Carla would then require him to tell her that Lee said he would pay $480,000. The ductwork leak would still have to be disclosed to Lee, because that duty is on every list.

6. Portugal comparison

Familiar principle. In Portuguese practice an agency often deals with both seller and buyer while the mediation contract is signed with one client. That practice, and the agency's exact statutory duties toward the party who is not its client, require verification (PT-04).

Florida rule. The duties are fixed by statute in three numbered lists, and the list depends on the relationship: 3 for no brokerage relationship, 7 for transaction broker, 9 for single agent.

The precise difference. Florida names each relationship and defines its duties by statute (3/7/9). Even the confidentiality a transaction broker owes is a defined list of protected items, and it can be waived only in writing. Fiduciary representation of both sides is unlawful.

Exam implication. Match the duty to the relationship using the Florida lists only. A Portuguese habit or rule never decides a Florida question.

7. Legal and numerical requirements

Memorize exactly

  • No brokerage relationship, 3 duties: honesty and fair dealing; disclosure of known material facts on residential property not readily observable; accounting for all funds (manual; not yet verified).
  • Transaction broker, 7 duties: the 3, plus skill, care and diligence; presenting all offers and counteroffers timely (unless directed otherwise in writing); limited confidentiality (unless waived in writing); any additional duties mutually agreed (manual; not yet verified).
  • Single agent, 9 duties: honesty and fairness; loyalty; confidentiality; obedience; full disclosure; accounting; skill, care and diligence; presenting offers and counteroffers timely; disclosing known material facts (manual; not yet verified).
  • Single agent only: loyalty, obedience, full confidentiality, full disclosure (manual; not yet verified).
  • Limited confidentiality protects: seller will accept less · buyer will pay more · any party's motivation · information a party asks to keep confidential (manual; not yet verified).

Understand

  • Obedience is limited to lawful instructions.
  • Material-fact disclosure is on all three lists. Neither confidentiality nor obedience can override it.
  • A transaction broker is not a fiduciary, which is why it can owe the same limited duties to both sides at once.
  • The lists come from s. 475.278 as summarized in the manual; their exact statutory wording is not yet in the verification log (V-26), hence the flags.

8. Visual explanation

Duty No brokerage (3) Transaction broker (7) Single agent (9)
Deal honestly and fairly ✔ ✔ ✔
Disclose known material facts (residential, not readily observable) ✔ ✔ ✔
Account for all funds ✔ ✔ ✔
Skill, care and diligence — ✔ ✔
Present all offers and counteroffers timely — ✔ ✔
Confidentiality — Limited (waivable in writing) Full
Additional duties mutually agreed — ✔ Not a listed item
Loyalty — — ✔
Obedience (lawful only) — — ✔
Full disclosure — — ✔

Count the entries (ticks and named duties) in each column: 3 · 7 · 9. The bottom three rows, plus "full" confidentiality, are the single agent's LOCO duties.

9. Common misconceptions

  • "A transaction broker owes loyalty (or obedience)." Those belong only to the single agent.
  • "Limited confidentiality lets a licensee hide defects." Material-defect disclosure is owed in every relationship.
  • "Obedience means doing whatever the principal says." Lawful instructions only.
  • "A transaction broker is neutral, so it owes nothing to either side." It owes 7 duties to each customer.
  • "With no brokerage relationship the licensee owes nothing." It owes 3 duties.
  • "Honesty requires a transaction broker to tell the seller the buyer would pay more." No. Limited confidentiality forbids it, and keeping that confidence is not dishonest.
  • "Single agent = the TB's 7 plus loyalty and obedience." Count again: confidentiality becomes full, full disclosure is added, and "additional agreed duties" is not on the 9.

10. Memory sheet

Relationship Count Signature duties
No brokerage 3 Honesty · material facts · accounting
Transaction broker 7 + skill/care · present offers · limited confidentiality · agreed duties
Single agent 9 + Loyalty · Obedience · full Confidentiality · full disclOsure
  • Limited confidentiality: less · more · motive · "keep it secret". Waived only in writing.
  • Offers: present all, timely, unless a party directed otherwise in writing.
  • Defects beat secrets. Obedience stops at the law.

lessons.title: Disclosure notices: timing, transitions, scope and exceptions
lessons.html:
2. Why it matters

Notice questions are timing and scope questions, and the exam builds its wrong answers from near-miss facts:

  • a notice given "at closing" or "within 24 hours";
  • a lease or a 6-unit building offered as a "residential sale";
  • a transaction broker said to need a notice.

The core rules fit in a few lines, but each has a trigger ("whichever occurs first", "before showing", "before the change") that you must read precisely.

In practice, the notice must reach the party before the moment the law names, which for buyers is usually the first showing.

3. Simple explanation

Why notices exist

Transaction broker is the presumed relationship (L04-1). A buyer or seller therefore needs to be told in writing when the licensee offers more than the default (single agent) or less (no brokerage relationship). The law also protects a principal who is about to lose fiduciary loyalty, by requiring written consent before a single agent becomes a transaction broker.

The notices and when each is due

1. Single Agent Notice (s. 475.278(3); verified, V-48)

  • What: a written notice of the single agent relationship and its duties.
  • When: before, or at the time of, entering into a listing agreement or an agreement for representation, or before the showing of property, whichever occurs first.

2. No Brokerage Relationship Notice (s. 475.278(4); verified, V-48)

  • What: a written notice of the duties the licensee owes with no brokerage relationship.
  • When: before the showing of property.

3. Transaction broker: no notice required. It is the default relationship (manual; not yet verified).

4. Consent to Transition to Transaction Broker (s. 475.278(3); verified, V-48)

  • A single agent may become a transaction broker only if the principal gives written consent before the change.
  • Typical use: the brokerage is single agent for a seller, and one of its own buyer customers wants that listing (L04-1).
  • Without the principal's consent, the brokerage may not make the change.

Where the rules apply: "residential sale" (verified, V-20)

The notice requirements apply only to residential sales:

  • improved residential property of 4 units or fewer;
  • unimproved residential property intended for 4 units or fewer;
  • agricultural property of 10 acres or fewer.

Why: these are the transactions where ordinary consumers, who may not understand brokerage relationships, typically buy and sell.

When no notice is required (s. 475.278; verified, V-20)

No notice is required in these situations (several apply even when the property fits the definition):

Situation Condition
The party is already represented The licensee knows the party is represented by a single agent or a transaction broker
Bona fide open house or model-home showing No confidential information, no offer and no representation agreement involved
Unanticipated casual encounter —
General factual questions Responses to general questions about advertised property
General information about the licensee Communications limited to the licensee's qualifications or firm
Auctions —
Appraisals —
Rentals and leases Unless the lease includes an option to purchase property with 4 or fewer residential units
Sale of a business enterprise Except property with 4 or fewer residential units
Nonresidential transactions Anything outside the "residential sale" definition

The study manual's list of exceptions was incomplete. The list above comes from the statute and is a verified addition (V-20). V-20 also mentions a developer's on-site employees selling new units, but that item was not seen in the statute excerpt checked: treat it as unconfirmed (flagged), not as a settled exception.

4. Key terms

Term Meaning
Single Agent Notice Written disclosure of a single agent's duties
No Brokerage Relationship Notice Written disclosure of the duties owed with no brokerage relationship
Consent to Transition to Transaction Broker The principal's prior written consent allowing a single agent to become a transaction broker
Residential sale Sale of ≤4 residential units, unimproved land for ≤4 units, or agricultural property ≤10 acres
Representation agreement A written agreement to represent a buyer or seller (for example, a buyer brokerage agreement)
Bona fide open house A genuine open house or model-home showing with no confidential information, no offer and no representation agreement involved
Option to purchase A right, given in a lease, for the tenant to buy the property later

5. Practical example

Ana is a sales associate at Lakeside Realty in Orlando.

Day Event Notice?
Mon Mr. Reyes lists his 3-bedroom Winter Park house with Lakeside as single agent. The listing is signed before any showing. Single Agent Notice to Mr. Reyes, before or at the signing (the earlier event)
Sat Open house at the Reyes home. Ben asks about square footage and schools; no offer, no confidential or price talk. None (bona fide open house)
Sat A visitor tells Ana she has signed a buyer representation agreement with an agent at another brokerage None (Ana knows the party is already represented)
Next Tue Ben asks Ana to show him a duplex in College Park. Nothing about the relationship is signed. None (Lakeside is a transaction broker by presumption)
Next Wed Ben's sister wants a 12-month apartment lease, with no option to buy None (lease without option)
Next Thu Ben wants to buy the Reyes house Consent to Transition, signed by Mr. Reyes before Lakeside changes to transaction broker for both

Two variations:

  • If Lakeside had chosen to deal with Ben with no brokerage relationship (it represents the seller), Ana would have given Ben the No Brokerage Relationship Notice before his private showing of the Reyes house.
  • The same week a colleague shows a 6-unit apartment building (not a residential sale) and a 9-acre citrus grove (a residential sale: agricultural, ≤10 acres). Only the grove is inside the notice rules.

6. Portugal comparison

Familiar principle. In Portuguese practice the mediation contract is signed with one client, even when the agency deals with both seller and buyer (PT-04; this description requires verification). The comparison base has no entry on Portuguese notice rules.

Florida rule. Florida adds separate statutory notices about the type of relationship and its duties. They are triggered by events such as the first showing, not only by signing a contract, and they apply only to residential sales.

The precise difference. A Florida buyer may be owed a notice before anything is signed, because each notice is due no later than the first showing. Whether Portuguese law requires a written notice of the agent's role to the client or to the non-client party requires verification.

Exam implication. Use only the Florida triggers: whichever comes first for single agent, before showing for no brokerage, before the change for transition.

7. Legal and numerical requirements

Memorize exactly

  • Single Agent Notice: before or at the time of entering into a listing or representation agreement, or before showing property, whichever occurs first (verified, V-48).
  • No Brokerage Relationship Notice: before showing (verified, V-48).
  • Transaction broker: no notice (manual; not yet verified).
  • Consent to Transition: the principal's written consent before the change (verified, V-48).
  • Residential sale: ≤4 units · unimproved land for ≤4 units · agricultural ≤10 acres (verified, V-20).
  • Exceptions: represented party; bona fide open house or model showing; casual encounter; general factual questions; general information about the licensee or firm; auctions; appraisals; leases without an option to buy ≤4 units; business sales (except ≤4 residential units); nonresidential (verified, V-20). A possible exception for a developer's on-site employees is unconfirmed (flagged, V-20).

Understand

  • Each notice is tied to an event, not to a number of days. "At closing" is always too late.
  • Designated sales associates (L04-4) carry the single-agent disclosure requirements even though their deals are nonresidential (verified, V-46).
  • The 24-hour deadline is for delivering a copy of a written listing agreement to the person who signed it (verified, V-49; Chapter 11). It is not a notice deadline.

8. Visual explanation

Is it a residential sale (≤4 units, land for ≤4 units, farm ≤10 acres), or a lease with an option to buy ≤4 units?
No → no brokerage notice required
Does an exception apply (represented party, bona fide open house, casual encounter, general questions, auction, appraisal…)?
Yes → no notice required
Which relationship?
Transaction broker → no notice
No brokerage relationship → No Brokerage Relationship Notice, before showing
Single agent → Single Agent Notice at or before the agreement, or before showing, whichever is first
First contactNo notice yet (TB is presumed)
Agreement or first showingWhichever comes first: Single Agent Notice
Before any showingNo Brokerage Relationship Notice
Before a changePrincipal signs Consent to Transition
ClosingAlways too late for a notice

9. Common misconceptions

  • "Leases always need disclosures." Only a lease with an option to buy property of ≤4 residential units.
  • "A 6-unit building is residential." Not for this rule; the limit is 4 units.
  • "Any farm sale is covered." Only agricultural property of 10 acres or fewer.
  • "Transaction brokers must give a notice." No; it is the default.
  • "The Single Agent Notice can wait until the listing is signed." If a showing happens first, the notice is due before the showing.
  • "The consent to transition can be signed after the change, or at closing." It must come before the change.
  • "Every open house is exempt." Only a bona fide open house with no confidential information, no offer and no representation agreement involved.

10. Memory sheet

  • Residential sale = ≤4 units · land for ≤4 · farm ≤10 acres.
  • Single agent: agreement or showing, whichever first. No brokerage: before showing. TB: no notice.
  • Transition: principal signs before the change.
  • No notice: represented party · bona fide open house · casual encounter · general questions · licensee/firm info · auction · appraisal · lease (unless option ≤4 units) · business sale (unless ≤4 residential units) · nonresidential.

lessons.title: Material facts, designated sales associates, and ending relationships
lessons.manual: M2 §Duties that never go away; §Designated sales associates; §How relationships begin and end
lessons.html:
2. Why it matters

The exam tests three separate topics here:

  1. Must this fact be disclosed? The classic pair: a roof that leaks only in storms (must disclose) and a suicide in the house (need not).
  2. When can one brokerage give single-agent representation to both sides? Only with designated sales associates.
  3. How does a relationship end, and which duties survive?

In practice, you will meet these questions with real sellers who would rather not mention a problem.

3. Simple explanation

A. The duty that never goes away: known material facts

In every relationship, even with no brokerage relationship, the licensee must disclose all facts that meet four conditions (L04-2):

  • known to the licensee;
  • materially affect the value: they would change a reasonable buyer's decision or the price;
  • concern residential real property;
  • not readily observable to the buyer: an ordinary look would not reveal them, as with a latent (hidden) defect.

Examples: hidden roof leaks, flooding, foundation cracks. The study manual traces this rule to the Florida case Johnson v. Davis, under which a seller must disclose known hidden defects that materially affect value (manual; not yet verified).

Consequences:

  • A principal's instruction to stay silent is unlawful. Obedience never covers it.
  • An "AS IS" contract shifts repair obligations. It does not remove the duty to disclose known latent defects.
  • The duty does not depend on the buyer asking.

B. Facts Florida declares NOT material (s. 689.25; verified, V-47)

The following are not material facts that must be disclosed:

  • that an occupant had HIV or AIDS;
  • that a homicide, suicide or death occurred on the property.

Why: these are "stigma" facts. They may disturb a buyer, but they do not change the physical property.

Two cautions:

  • Do not volunteer an occupant's HIV/AIDS status. The study manual says a licensee must not disclose it (manual; not yet verified; V-47 confirms only that it is not material). Disclosing it could also raise fair housing (handicap) issues.
  • The statute removes the duty to disclose, not the duty to deal honestly, which is on every duty list (L04-2). It is no excuse for a false statement.

C. Property tax disclosure (s. 689.261; verified, V-75)

A buyer of residential property must receive a Property Tax Disclosure Summary at or before the contract. It warns the buyer not to rely on the seller's current taxes, because a sale or improvements can raise the assessment (Chapter 11).

D. Designated sales associates (s. 475.2755; verified, V-46)

This is the only way one brokerage can give single-agent representation to both sides of one deal. Three conditions must all be met:

  1. Not a "residential sale" under the L04-3 definition. Examples: an office building, a warehouse, or an apartment building of more than 4 units. Exam questions say "nonresidential" or "commercial".
  2. Buyer and seller each have assets of $1 million or more. The test is the parties' assets, not the price.
  3. The customers request it, and both sign disclosures stating that their assets meet the threshold and asking for this form of representation.

The broker then designates one associate as single agent for the buyer and another as single agent for the seller.

  • Each designated associate owes a single agent's duties (the 9), including the single-agent disclosure requirements.
  • They may not disclose a customer's confidential information except to the broker or persons the broker specifies, or as the law permits or requires.
  • The broker must keep that information confidential and may not use it to the other party's detriment.

E. How relationships begin and end (manual; not yet verified)

Beginning. A relationship is created by agreement:

  • express: a signed listing or buyer agreement; or
  • implied by conduct.

No particular form is needed except where the disclosure rules require writing. Its type defaults to transaction broker (L04-1). A written listing must have a definite expiration date (s. 475.25(1)(r); verified, V-49; Chapter 11).

Ending.

  • performance (closing);
  • expiration;
  • mutual agreement;
  • revocation by the principal or renunciation by the broker (either may end it, but breaching the contract can create liability for damages);
  • death or incapacity of a party;
  • destruction of the property;
  • bankruptcy of the principal.

What survives: confidentiality and accounting for funds.

4. Key terms

Term Meaning
Material fact A fact that would affect a reasonable person's decision or the property's value
Latent defect A hidden defect not discoverable by ordinary inspection
Stigma fact A fact (such as a death on the property or an occupant's HIV/AIDS status) that may affect feelings about a property but not its physical condition
AS IS The buyer takes the property in its current condition; it does not cancel the disclosure duty
Designated sales associate An associate appointed as single agent for one party in a nonresidential deal where each party has $1M+ in assets
Revocation / renunciation The principal ends the relationship / the broker ends it

5. Practical example

Fort Myers: one house, four facts. Mr. Hale sells his house "AS IS" through Palm Realty, a transaction broker. Associate Sofia knows the following:

Fact Disclose? Why
The roof leaks into the attic in heavy rain; the stain is painted over Yes Known, material, not readily observable
A large driveway crack anyone can see Not under this duty, but never misrepresent it Readily observable; honesty still applies
The previous owner died in the house No duty to volunteer s. 689.25
A former tenant had AIDS Do not volunteer s. 689.25; fair housing risk

Mr. Hale says, "Don't mention the roof." Sofia must still disclose it. The buyer also gets the Property Tax Disclosure Summary at or before the contract.

Jacksonville: designated sales associates.

  • A logistics company (assets $20 million) buys a $6 million warehouse from an investor (assets $8 million). Both are customers of the same firm.
  • They ask in writing and both sign the asset disclosures. The broker designates Lucas for the seller and Mia for the buyer, each as a single agent.
  • Later the company's CEO wants to buy a $2.5 million oceanfront house listed by the same firm. No designation is possible, because it is a residential sale. The firm can act as transaction broker for both (if it is the seller's single agent, only after the seller's written consent to transition).

After expiry. A Naples listing expires. Asked for the seller's old bottom line, the former single agent must refuse: confidentiality survives.

6. Portugal comparison

Familiar principle. The comparison base has one Portuguese entry for this chapter (PT-04): in Portuguese practice an agency often deals with both seller and buyer while the mediation contract is signed with one client, and even that description requires verification. Two further Portuguese points also require verification: the agency's and seller's duties to disclose hidden defects or deaths, and whether any structure resembles designated sales associates.

Florida rule. A relationship may begin without any writing (express or implied agreement). Disclosure of known latent defects, the stigma exception and designated sales associates are each fixed by Florida law.

The precise difference. The stigma rule and the both-sides exception are specific Florida statutes. Do not assume a Portuguese practice fills either gap.

Exam implication. Defect = disclose; stigma = not material; designated associates = nonresidential + $1M each.

7. Legal and numerical requirements

Memorize exactly

  • Disclose known facts that materially affect value, are not readily observable, and concern residential property, in every relationship (manual; not yet verified, as part of the duty lists).
  • Johnson v. Davis: the seller must disclose known latent material defects (manual; not yet verified).
  • Not material (s. 689.25; verified, V-47): homicide, suicide or death on the property; an occupant's HIV/AIDS.
  • Property Tax Disclosure Summary: at or before the contract, for residential property (verified, V-75).
  • Designated sales associates (verified, V-46): not a residential sale · buyer and seller each $1 million+ in assets · at the customers' request · both sign disclosures · each associate owes single-agent duties.
  • Ends by: performance, expiration, mutual agreement, revocation or renunciation, death or incapacity, destruction, bankruptcy of the principal. Survive: confidentiality, accounting (manual; not yet verified).

Understand

  • Correction: earlier course notes marked s. 689.25 "per the manual; not independently verified". It is now verified (V-47).
  • The $1 million threshold is the same in every statute edition checked, 2000/2002 through 2026 (V-46).
  • A stigma fact is "not material" only for the disclosure duty. Honesty still forbids a false answer.

8. Visual explanation

Does the licensee KNOW the fact?
No → no disclosure duty (but never misrepresent)
Is it a homicide, suicide or death, or an occupant's HIV/AIDS?
Yes → not material by statute; no duty to disclose (do not volunteer HIV/AIDS)
Does it materially affect the value of residential property?
No → no disclosure duty
Is it readily observable?
Yes → not covered by this duty (honesty still applies)
→ MUST disclose: in every relationship, AS IS or not, whatever the principal says

Designated sales associates need all three: not a residential sale + each party $1M+ in assets + written request and signed disclosures.

9. Common misconceptions

  • "AS IS means no disclosure." Known latent defects must still be disclosed.
  • "If the seller tells me to keep quiet, obedience protects me." Obedience covers lawful instructions only.
  • "A death in the house is a material fact." Florida law says it is not.
  • "The stigma statute lets me deny a death if asked." It removes the duty to disclose, not the duty of honesty.
  • "Designated associates are allowed for any deal over $1 million, or any house sale both parties agree to." The test is each party's assets, and never in a residential sale.
  • "Once the listing expires I can share the seller's bottom line." Confidentiality survives.

10. Memory sheet

  • Defect = disclose. Stigma = not material. Known + material + hidden + residential → disclose, in all relationships.
  • Not material: death / homicide / suicide · HIV/AIDS (s. 689.25). Never lie; never volunteer HIV/AIDS.
  • Tax summary: at or before the contract; don't rely on the seller's taxes.
  • Designated associates: nonresidential + $1M each side + written request and disclosures → two single agents in one firm.
  • Ends: performance · expiration · agreement · revocation or renunciation · death or incapacity · destruction · bankruptcy.
  • Confidentiality and accounting outlive the relationship.

lessons.title: Escrow accounts and the deposit clock
lessons.html:
2. Why it matters

An earnest money check handed to you belongs neither to you nor to your broker. Florida treats it as trust money. It must reach the right place within a fixed number of business days. Apart from a small, capped amount of the broker's own money allowed in the account for bank charges, it must not be mixed with the brokerage's money, and it must never be used as the brokerage's own money. Mixing in more than the allowed amount is a serious violation, and spending escrow money is more serious still.

On the exam, escrow is one of the most predictable topics in Brokerage Activities and Procedures, which carries 12% of the exam (tied for the largest section). Expect a weekday-to-deadline question, and a question on how much of the broker's own money may sit in escrow.

3. Simple explanation

What escrow money is

Escrow (trust) funds are money a broker holds for other people: a buyer's earnest money (binder) deposit, rents collected for a landlord, advance fees. The broker looks after this money but does not own it.

Who holds it, and where

  • A sales associate does not hold escrow. Her job is to pass the deposit to her broker (or employer) quickly.
  • The broker may keep escrow funds in an escrow account at a bank, credit union or savings association doing business in Florida, or place them with a Florida title company or attorney (manual; not yet verified).
  • When a title company or attorney holds the deposit, the contract names it, and the broker still has duties (see below; V-39).
  • A broker is not required to maintain an escrow account at all, but must handle funds properly and keep records either way (manual; not yet verified).
  • An interest-bearing escrow account is allowed only with the written consent of all parties, which also states who receives the interest (manual; not yet verified).

The deposit clock

A business day is any day except Saturday, Sunday and legal holidays. The day the deposit arrives is day 0, and counting starts on the next business day.

Who Deadline Source
Sales associate → broker (or employer) End of the next business day after receipt Rule 61J2-14.009, F.A.C. (verified, V-36)
Broker → escrow account End of the third business day after receipt. FREC rules call this "immediately" Rule 61J2-14.008, F.A.C. (verified, V-37)

Both clocks start on the same day. The course counts the broker's three days from the day the deposit first came into the brokerage, which is the day the associate received it (the manual's worked example). The hand-off to the broker does not restart the clock. If the associate uses her full day, the broker has two business days left.

Why so short? A check in a handbag or a car can be lost or misused, and it is the broker who must account for escrow money. The rules move it quickly to the broker, then into a protected account.

When a title company or attorney holds the deposit

The broker is not the escrow holder, but still has duties under Rule 61J2-14.008(2)(b), F.A.C. (corrected, V-39):

  1. The contract names the holder: its name, address and telephone number.
  2. Within 10 business days after each deposit is due, the broker sends the holder a written request for written verification that the deposit was received. This step is not required if the seller or the seller's agent nominated the title company or attorney in writing.
  3. Within 10 business days of that request, the broker gives the seller's broker (or the seller, if unrepresented) a copy of the verification, or a notice that none was received.

The broker's own money: commingling and conversion

A broker may keep a small amount of personal or brokerage funds in escrow. The manual explains that this covers bank charges. The limits are in Rule 61J2-14.010(2), F.A.C. and s. 475.25(1)(k), F.S. (verified, V-38):

  • up to $1,000 per sales escrow account;
  • up to $5,000 per property management escrow account.

Keeping more than that is commingling: mixing personal money with trust money. Conversion is worse. It means using escrow money for personal or business purposes, even "just until next week".

Records

Whether or not the broker keeps an escrow account, the broker must keep records of the funds handled (manual; not yet verified). Brokerage records are kept for at least 5 years (s. 475.5015, F.S.; V-40; see L06-2).

4. Key terms

Term Meaning
Escrow (trust) funds Money held for others: deposits, rents, advance fees
Earnest money / binder deposit The buyer's good-faith deposit, normally held in escrow
Sales escrow account Escrow account for sale deposits; broker's own funds up to $1,000
Property management escrow account Escrow account for rental money; broker's own funds up to $5,000
Business day Any day except Saturday, Sunday and legal holidays
"Immediately" FREC term: in the escrow account by the end of the 3rd business day after receipt
Commingling Mixing personal or brokerage funds with escrow funds beyond the allowed amount
Conversion Using escrow funds for personal or unauthorized purposes

5. Practical example

Sofia is a sales associate at a Coral Gables brokerage. At a showing on Thursday afternoon, a buyer gives her a $15,000 earnest money check. There are no legal holidays this week.

Step Rule Deadline
Sofia delivers the check to her broker Next business day End of Friday
The broker deposits it in the sales escrow account 3rd business day after receipt: Fri (1), Mon (2), Tue (3) End of Tuesday

Variations:

  • Monday is a legal holiday. Sofia's deadline is still Friday. The broker counts Fri (1), Tue (2), Wed (3), so the deadline is the end of Wednesday.
  • The check is handed over at a Saturday open house. Saturday is day 0 and Sunday does not count. Sofia's deadline is the end of Monday. The broker counts Mon (1), Tue (2), Wed (3), so the deadline is the end of Wednesday.
  • The buyer chose a title company to hold the deposit, due Friday. Within 10 business days after Friday, the broker asks the title company in writing to verify receipt. Within 10 business days of that request, the broker sends the seller's broker the verification, or a notice that none arrived. If the seller had nominated the title company in writing, the request would not be required.
  • Bank fees. The broker keeps $800 of brokerage money in the sales escrow account: allowed. Keeping $1,800 is commingling. Paying the office rent from escrow and "putting it back next week" is conversion.

6. Portugal comparison

Familiar principle. In Portugal, a deposit paid on a contrato-promessa is presumed to be sinal. Under Código Civil art. 442, if the payer defaults, the other party keeps it; if the recipient defaults, the payer can demand double. Who holds the money in practice requires verification.

Florida rule. Earnest money is normally held in escrow by the broker, a title company or an attorney, under strict business-day clocks. Contracts often treat the deposit as liquidated damages if the buyer defaults, and disputes go through the conflicting-demand procedures (L05-2).

The difference. Florida exam content has no automatic "return double" rule. The skills tested are about handling the money: who holds it, how fast it moves, and what must never be mixed with it.

Exam implication. Count business days, and never use the sinal rules to answer a Florida question.

7. Legal and numerical requirements

Memorize exactly

  • Sales associate → broker (or employer): by the end of the next business day after receipt (Rule 61J2-14.009; V-36).
  • Broker → escrow account ("immediately"): by the end of the third business day after receipt (Rule 61J2-14.008; V-37).
  • Saturdays, Sundays and legal holidays are not business days. The day of receipt is not counted.
  • Broker's own funds: up to $1,000 per sales escrow account and up to $5,000 per property management escrow account (Rule 61J2-14.010(2); s. 475.25(1)(k); V-38).
  • Title company or attorney holds the deposit (Rule 61J2-14.008(2)(b); V-39): holder's name, address and phone on the contract; written verification request within 10 business days after each deposit is due (not required if the seller or seller's agent nominated the holder in writing); copy or "none received" notice to the seller's broker (or an unrepresented seller) within 10 business days of the request.
  • Interest-bearing escrow account: written consent of all parties, including who receives the interest (manual; not yet verified).
  • Places to hold escrow: a bank, credit union or savings association doing business in Florida, or a Florida title company or attorney. A broker need not maintain an escrow account (manual; not yet verified).

Understand

  • Corrected manual statement. The manual's single step ("give the holder's statement to the seller within 10 business days") was corrected (V-39). There are two 10-business-day windows, and the copy goes to the seller's broker (see Common misconceptions).
  • One scraped copy of the rule had a general "$5,000 per account" sentence. The account-specific $1,000 sales limit is the rule and matches the statute.
  • The statute gives a broker a reasonable time to correct escrow errors when there is no shortage and no significant threat of economic harm to the public. "Borrowing" escrow money creates a shortage: it is conversion, not an error.
  • The Legislature intends that paying out escrowed funds should not be delayed by a dispute over the broker's own funds in the account.

8. Visual explanation

Thursday · day 0Associate receives the check
Friday · day 1Associate's deadline: check in the broker's hands
Saturday–SundayNot business days: not counted
Monday · day 2Broker may deposit
Tuesday · day 3Broker's deadline: funds in escrow by end of day

The deposit clock for a check received on Thursday, with no legal holidays.

Deposit received Associate → broker by end of Broker deposits by end of
Monday Tuesday Thursday
Tuesday Wednesday Friday
Wednesday Thursday Monday
Thursday Friday Tuesday
Friday Monday Wednesday
Saturday (open house) Monday Wednesday
Thursday, with Monday a legal holiday Friday Wednesday

9. Common misconceptions

  • "Three days includes the weekend." Count business days only, and never the day of receipt.
  • "The broker's three days start when the associate hands over the check." The course counts from the first receipt. The hand-off does not restart the clock.
  • "A short loan from escrow is fine if it is repaid." Using escrow money for any personal or business purpose is conversion, and there is no repayment grace period.
  • "Every escrow account may hold $5,000 of the broker's money." $5,000 is the limit for property management accounts. For sales escrow accounts the limit is $1,000.
  • "None of the broker's own money may ever be in escrow." Up to $1,000 (sales) or $5,000 (property management) is allowed for bank charges. Only more than that is commingling.
  • "The broker may keep the interest." Only if all parties consent in writing, and the consent says who gets it.
  • "If a title company holds the deposit, the broker has nothing to do." The broker must request written verification (unless the seller or seller's agent nominated the holder in writing) and pass it on.
  • "The holder's statement goes to the seller within 10 business days" (the manual's version). There are two windows: the request is due within 10 business days after the deposit is due, and the copy goes to the seller's broker (or an unrepresented seller) within 10 business days of that request.

10. Memory sheet

  • Associate 1, broker 3, in business days. Day of receipt = day 0. Saturdays, Sundays and legal holidays don't count.
  • Both clocks start at the first receipt.
  • Sales 1K, rentals 5K. More = commingling. Spending it = conversion.
  • Interest-bearing account = all parties consent in writing (including who gets the interest).
  • Title company or attorney holds the deposit: holder named on the contract → written request within 10 business days after the deposit is due → copy to the seller's broker within 10 business days of the request.
  • Keep brokerage records at least 5 years.

lessons.title: Conflicting demands and settlement procedures
lessons.html:
2. Why it matters

Deals fail. When the buyer and the seller both claim the deposit, the broker in the middle is holding someone else's money and cannot simply pick a winner. Florida gives the broker a fixed procedure with business-day deadlines. A broker who follows it and then obeys the resulting order is protected from discipline for failure to account. A broker who ignores it can be disciplined.

On the exam this is pure recall: 15 business days to notify, 30 to choose a procedure, the four procedures (M.A.L.E.), when an escrow disbursement order is available, and the two situations in the statute where the broker may simply return the deposit to the buyer.

3. Simple explanation

What starts the procedure

Rule 61J2-10.032, F.A.C. (effective 5/21/2024; verified, V-15) applies when a broker holds the funds in its own escrow account and one of two things happens:

  • Conflicting demands. Two or more parties claim the same deposit. For example, the buyer wants it back and the seller wants to keep it.
  • Good-faith doubt. The broker honestly does not know who is entitled, even if not everyone has made a demand.

The two deadlines

Step Deadline Counted from
Written notice to the FREC 15 business days The last demand (or when the broker came to have good-faith doubt)
Start a settlement procedure 30 business days The last demand

Why the last demand? There is no conflict until the second claim arrives. Suppose the buyer demands the deposit on Monday and the seller counter-demands nine days later. The seller's demand is the last one, so you count from it.

The four procedures: M.A.L.E.

Procedure Who decides How it starts Key point
Mediation The parties themselves, helped by a neutral mediator All parties consent in writing Must be completed within 90 days after the last demand; otherwise the broker promptly uses another procedure. Non-binding (manual; not yet verified)
Arbitration A neutral arbitrator All parties consent Binding (manual; not yet verified)
Litigation (interpleader) A court The broker files it The broker deposits the funds with the court and asks it to decide
Escrow Disbursement Order (EDO) The FREC The broker requests it Available only when the broker holds the funds

Note that the sources state the mediation limit as 90 days, not business days.

After a procedure starts

  • If the matter settles, or goes to court, before an EDO is issued, the broker notifies the FREC within 10 business days.
  • A broker who follows the procedure and the resulting order cannot be disciplined for failure to account.
  • The manual adds that if a broker obeys an EDO and is later sued over the payout, the Recovery Fund may pay the broker's court costs and any judgment (manual; not yet verified).

When the procedure does not apply

  1. Two exceptions in the statute (s. 475.25(1)(d)1, F.S.; corrected, V-16). In these cases the licensee may return the deposit to the buyer without notifying the FREC or starting a procedure:
    • a residential condominium buyer delivers written notice of intent to cancel under s. 718.503. The cancellation periods are taught in L08-5: 15 days for a developer sale, and 7 days for a resale, excluding Saturdays, Sundays and legal holidays, since July 1, 2025 (V-08). Older books say 3 business days for resales, which is outdated.
    • the buyer, in good faith, fails to satisfy the terms of the financing clause. For example, the buyer applied for the loan honestly and was turned down.
  2. A title company or attorney holds the deposit. The broker is not the escrow holder. There is no FREC notice and no EDO. The broker's duty is the written verification procedure from L05-1 (V-39).
  3. "HUD sale." The manual lists this as an exception. It was not found in the statute and is not taught.

4. Key terms

Term Meaning
Conflicting demands Two or more parties claim the same escrowed deposit
Good-faith doubt The broker honestly does not know who is entitled to escrowed funds
Settlement procedure One of the four ways to resolve the dispute (M.A.L.E.)
Mediation A neutral person helps the parties reach their own agreement; requires all parties' written consent
Arbitration A neutral arbitrator decides the dispute; requires all parties' consent
Interpleader A lawsuit in which the broker deposits the disputed funds with the court and asks it to decide
Escrow Disbursement Order (EDO) FREC order deciding who receives disputed funds held by a broker
Financing clause Contract term making the purchase depend on the buyer getting a loan
Failure to account Not accounting for, or not delivering, money held for others; a ground for discipline

5. Practical example

A buyer and seller sign a contract for a house in Orlando. The listing broker holds the buyer's $20,000 deposit in its sales escrow account. The buyer cancels, citing the inspection, and demands the deposit back. The seller says the buyer missed the inspection deadline, and on Wednesday, March 3, 2027 she demands the deposit for herself. Assume no legal holidays fall between March 3 and April 14.

Date Event Broker's duty
Wed, Mar 3, 2027 Seller's demand = last demand (day 0) Start counting
Wed, Mar 24, 2027 15th business day Written notice to the FREC is due
Wed, Apr 14, 2027 30th business day A settlement procedure must have been started
Tue, Jun 1, 2027 90 days after the last demand (calendar days) If mediation was chosen, it must be finished; otherwise the broker promptly uses another procedure

Variations:

  • The broker requests an EDO. Before the FREC issues it, the buyer and seller sign a settlement. The broker notifies the FREC within 10 business days.
  • Financing failure. The buyer applied for the loan in good faith and was denied, and the contract had a financing clause. The broker may return the deposit to the buyer with no FREC notice.
  • Condo resale in Miami. The buyer delivers written notice of cancellation within the s. 718.503 period. The broker may return the deposit with no FREC notice.
  • A title company holds the deposit. The broker is not the escrow holder, so there is no FREC procedure and no EDO.

6. Portugal comparison

Familiar principle. A Portuguese deposit on a contrato-promessa is presumed to be sinal (Código Civil art. 442). If the payer defaults, the other party keeps it. If the recipient defaults, the payer can demand double.

Florida rule. What happens to the deposit depends on the contract. Often the deposit is liquidated damages if the buyer defaults. The broker releases escrowed funds only as the contract provides, on a written agreement of the parties, or through a settlement procedure.

The difference. Florida has no automatic double-return rule, and when demands conflict the broker does not decide who wins: the procedure does.

Exam implication. Suppose a question asks whether the seller receives double the deposit when a buyer defaults. The answer is no. If it asks what the broker does with competing claims, the answer is notice within 15 business days and a procedure within 30.

7. Legal and numerical requirements

Memorize exactly

  • Rule 61J2-10.032 (V-15): written notice to the FREC within 15 business days of the last demand (or of coming to have good-faith doubt); a settlement procedure started within 30 business days after the last demand.
  • M.A.L.E.: mediation (all parties consent in writing; completed within 90 days after the last demand, or the broker promptly uses another procedure), arbitration (all parties consent), litigation (interpleader), escrow disbursement order (only for funds the broker holds).
  • Settled or in court before an EDO is issued: notify the FREC within 10 business days.
  • s. 475.25(1)(d)1 (V-16): return to the buyer with no FREC notice or procedure when a residential condo buyer cancels in writing under s. 718.503, or the buyer fails the financing clause in good faith.
  • Mediation is non-binding; arbitration is binding (manual; not yet verified).

Understand

  • Following the procedure and the resulting order protects the broker from discipline for failure to account.
  • The Recovery Fund paying a broker's costs after the broker obeyed an EDO (manual; not yet verified).
  • The manual's "HUD sale" exception is not in the statute. Do not use it.
  • The manual describes the 10-business-day notice more broadly ("the parties settle before the procedure concludes"). The verified wording ties it to a settlement or lawsuit before an EDO is issued.
  • Condo resale cancellation is now 7 days (since July 1, 2025). Older materials say 3 business days, which is outdated.

8. Visual explanation

Is the deposit in the broker's own escrow account?
No: a title company or attorney holds it → no FREC notice, no EDO; the broker follows the verification steps (L05-1)
Is the case outside both statutory exceptions (a residential condo buyer cancelling under s. 718.503; a buyer failing the financing clause in good faith)?
No, an exception applies → the broker may return the deposit to the buyer; no FREC notice or procedure
Do two or more parties claim the deposit, or does the broker have good-faith doubt?
No → no dispute procedure is needed; handle the funds under the contract
Yes → notify the FREC within 15 business days; start M.A.L.E. within 30 business days
Day 0Last demand
15 business daysWritten notice to the FREC
30 business daysMediation, arbitration, interpleader or EDO started
90 daysMediation must be finished

The two business-day deadlines run from the last demand. The 90-day mediation limit is not stated in business days.

9. Common misconceptions

  • "15 and 30 are calendar days." Both are business days.
  • "The clock starts at the first demand." It starts at the last demand.
  • "The broker can request an EDO when a title company holds the money." An EDO is only for funds the broker holds.
  • "The broker can give the deposit to whoever seems to be right." Once demands conflict, the broker follows the procedure and the resulting order. Only the two exceptions in the statute let the broker return the deposit to the buyer without it.
  • "Any loan denial lets the broker return the deposit." Only if the buyer acted in good faith under the financing clause.
  • "Mediation means someone decides for the parties." Mediation needs everyone's written consent and is non-binding. Arbitration is the binding one (binding/non-binding: manual; not yet verified).
  • "If the seller backs out, the buyer automatically gets double the deposit." That is the Portuguese sinal rule (art. 442), not Florida law. In Florida the contract and, if demands conflict, the settlement procedure decide who gets the deposit.

10. Memory sheet

  • 15 to tell, 30 to choose, both in business days and both from the last demand.
  • M.A.L.E.: Mediation (written consent, 90 days), Arbitration (consent), Litigation (interpleader), EDO (broker-held funds only).
  • Settled or in court before the EDO is issued → tell the FREC within 10 business days.
  • Condo cancellation and good-faith loan denial = return the deposit to the buyer, no notice.
  • Title company or attorney holds it → no FREC procedure, no EDO.
  • No "HUD sale" exception. No sinal.

lessons.title: Advertising rules
lessons.html:
2. Why it matters

As a sales associate you will advertise all the time: yard signs, portal listings, Instagram reels, WhatsApp statuses, flyers. In Florida each of these is a licensee advertisement, and each one must name your brokerage. An ad without the brokerage name is a blind ad, a violation in any medium. The exam tests it often, usually disguised as "it was her personal account" or "the name is in her profile".

3. Simple explanation

The purpose

The idea behind the rules: the public should be able to see which licensed brokerage stands behind an ad. The brokerage is the licensed firm responsible for its associates, so its name is the one element that can never be left out.

The core rules (Rules 61J2-10.025 and 61J2-10.026, F.A.C.; verified, V-44)

  1. The brokerage name goes in every ad. Every real estate advertisement by a licensee must include the licensed (registered) name of the brokerage firm. An ad without it is a blind ad, whatever the medium: yard sign, newspaper, website, Instagram, WhatsApp status.
  2. Your own name. If a licensee's personal name appears, at least the last name must be used as registered (with the DBPR). A registered "Robert Silva" may advertise as "Bob Silva"; "Bob S." does not use the registered last name.
  3. Internet ads. The brokerage name must be placed next to, above or below the contact information in the ad (the phone number, email address and so on). Putting the brokerage name on a profile page one click away does not meet the rule.
  4. Price. The manual adds that an advertised price must be the price agreed with the seller (manual; not yet verified).

Teams and groups

A team is a group of licensees within one brokerage who market together under a team name. The team is not a brokerage, and its advertising must not make it look like one.

Requirement Detail
Allowed words The team name may include "team" or "group"
Banned words "Brokerage", "Realty", "Real Estate", "Properties", "Company" or similar words suggesting a separate brokerage
Size In ads, the team name may not appear larger than the brokerage name
Overall impression Team advertising may not create the impression that the team is an independent brokerage (manual; not yet verified. The verified word and size rules above serve the same purpose)

Who is not covered

An owner who is not a licensee, advertising her own property, is not placing a licensee ad. She has no brokerage to name.

What is not a confirmed rule

The manual says an associate's own name "cannot dominate" over the brokerage identity (manual; not yet verified). The confirmed size limit (V-44) applies to team names: a team name may not appear larger than the brokerage name.

Ads are also covered by rules taught elsewhere: fair housing (L07-1), Do Not Call and CAN-SPAM (L07-2), and credit-advertising trigger terms (L07-3).

4. Key terms

Term Meaning
Advertisement Any marketing message by a licensee about property or real estate services, in any medium
Blind ad A licensee's ad that does not include the licensed brokerage name
Licensed brokerage name The firm's name as registered with the DBPR
Contact information The phone number, email address or other way to reach the brokerage or licensee shown in an ad
Team or group Licensees within one brokerage who market together under a team name

5. Practical example

Joana Ferreira is a sales associate with Atlantic Palm Realty, LLC in Miami, and a member of a team. Does each ad comply?

Ad Complies? Why
Yard sign: "FOR SALE — Call Joana, 305-555-0142" No Blind ad: no brokerage name
Instagram reel with her phone number; the brokerage name is only in her bio No The brokerage name must be next to, above or below the contact details in the ad itself
Website: "Jo Ferreira · Atlantic Palm Realty, LLC · 305-555-0142" Yes Registered last name, and the brokerage name sits beside the contact details
Flyer: "Joana F., your Brickell expert · Atlantic Palm Realty, LLC" No Her registered last name does not appear
Team ad: "THE FERREIRA GROUP" in large letters, brokerage name in small print at the bottom No The team name may not be larger than the brokerage name
The team renames itself "Ferreira Realty Team" No "Realty" suggests a separate brokerage
Her neighbour, not a licensee, posts "House for sale by owner, call 786-555-0199" Not a licensee ad There is no brokerage to name
A price $25,000 below the seller's agreed price, "to get calls" No The price must be the one agreed with the seller (manual; not yet verified)

6. Portugal comparison

Familiar principle. In Portugal, mediation advertising is regulated, and you may be used to seeing an agency's license identification in its ads. Both points, and whether and how Portuguese law requires that identification, require verification.

Florida rule. The required element is the licensed brokerage name. It must appear in every licensee ad, including an associate's personal social media.

The difference. The Florida rule is about the brokerage's name. A license number in an ad does not replace it.

Exam implication. Answer only with the Florida rule. An associate's personal post still needs the brokerage name. An owner advertising her own property needs none.

7. Legal and numerical requirements

Memorize exactly

  • Every real estate ad by a licensee must include the licensed (registered) name of the brokerage firm. Without it, the ad is a blind ad (V-44).
  • Licensee's personal name: at least the last name as registered (V-44).
  • Internet ads: the brokerage name goes next to, above or below the contact information (V-44).
  • Team names (V-44):
    • "team" or "group" allowed;
    • "Brokerage", "Realty", "Real Estate", "Properties", "Company" or similar words banned;
    • team name not larger than the brokerage name.
  • Advertised price = the price agreed with the seller (manual; not yet verified).

Understand

  • The verified rules are in Rules 61J2-10.025 and 61J2-10.026, F.A.C. (V-44).
  • The manual's "an associate's name cannot dominate the brokerage identity" is not yet verified. The size limit for team names is confirmed.
  • The rule is about licensee advertising. An owner who is not a licensee needs no brokerage name.

8. Visual explanation

Is the ad placed by or for a licensee?
No (an owner who is not a licensee selling her own property) → no brokerage name needed
Does the ad include the licensed brokerage name?
No → blind ad
If it is an internet ad, is the brokerage name next to, above or below the contact information?
No → violation
If a licensee's name appears, is at least the registered last name used?
No → violation
If it is a team ad: only "team" or "group", no brokerage-type words, and a team name no larger than the brokerage name?
No → violation
Yes to every check, and the price shown is the one agreed with the seller (manual; not yet verified) → the ad complies

9. Common misconceptions

  • "My personal account is exempt." It is not. A licensee's ad on any account or medium needs the brokerage name.
  • "The brokerage name in my bio or profile is enough." In an internet ad it must sit next to, above or below the contact information.
  • "My license number replaces the brokerage name." The rule requires the brokerage name.
  • "Team names are not allowed." They are allowed. They may use "team" or "group" but not "Realty", "Real Estate", "Properties", "Company" or "Brokerage".
  • "A nickname is illegal." A nickname is allowed if the registered last name appears.
  • "An owner selling by herself must name a brokerage." An owner who is not a licensee has none to name.
  • "An individual licensee's name may never be bigger than the brokerage name." That comes from the manual's "cannot dominate" and is not yet verified. The confirmed size rule applies to team names.

10. Memory sheet

  • No firm name = blind ad, in any medium, including personal social media.
  • Personal name: at least the registered last name.
  • Internet: firm name next to, above or below the contact info.
  • Teams: "team" or "group" only. No Realty, Real Estate, Properties, Company or Brokerage. Never larger than the brokerage name.
  • Owners who are not licensees are not placing licensee ads.

lessons.title: Offices, signs, compensation, kickbacks and rental lists
lessons.html:
2. Why it matters

This lesson covers the office and its sign, and how money moves through a brokerage: who may pay a sales associate, payments to unlicensed people, rebates, kickbacks, commission rates and rental lists. Most violations here start with good intentions, such as a thank-you gift from a seller, a "bonus" for a helpful assistant or a referral fee from a lender. The exam describes exactly these situations and asks whether the payment is lawful.

3. Simple explanation

The office and its entrance sign

An active broker must maintain a registered office, a stationary location where records are kept. Every additional location where the broker does business is a branch office, and each one is registered with a fee (manual; not yet verified).

The entrance sign comes from statute: s. 475.22(1), F.S. (verified, V-45). A sign is required at the entrance of the principal (main) office and of each branch office. It must show:

Element Requirement
Name The broker's name, together with the trade name, if any
A firm (brokerage company) The firm's name plus the name of at least one broker
Words "Licensed Real Estate Broker" or "Lic. Real Estate Broker"

Money flows through the broker

A sales associate may be paid only by her employing broker (or by an owner-developer employer; see L03-2). She is never paid directly by a seller, a buyer, another associate or another brokerage (manual; not yet verified). The path is fixed: customer → brokerage → associate.

  • Pay may be a salary, a commission or both, as agreed with the broker (manual; not yet verified).
  • A pay dispute is a contract matter between the associate and the broker. The associate sues her broker, not the customer. It is not a FREC matter and not a Recovery Fund claim (manual; not yet verified).

Paying unlicensed people

Paying an unlicensed person for real estate services is prohibited (manual; not yet verified). The test is what the payment is for:

  • A salary for clerical work, such as scheduling, filing or answering phones, is fine.
  • A per-closing or per-deal bonus is pay for transactions, and it is unlawful.
  • Paying a past customer a fee for each client referred is unlawful.

The manual treats a small thank-you gift to a past customer for a referral as a gray zone, decided by asking whether the payment was for a real estate service (manual; not yet verified). The statute's exact wording on referral payments to unlicensed persons was not checked in this course (not yet verified).

Lawful payments

  • Rebates. A broker may rebate part of the commission to a party to the transaction (the buyer or seller), with full disclosure to all interested parties (manual; not yet verified).
  • Referrals between licensees. Sharing compensation is lawful broker to broker. An associate may not pay or receive a referral fee directly (manual; not yet verified).

Kickbacks and RESPA

A kickback is a payment for referring business. Under Chapter 475, a kickback from a settlement-service provider (such as an inspector, title company or lender) is allowed only if all parties are fully informed and no other law prohibits it (manual; not yet verified).

Another law usually does prohibit it. RESPA Section 8 (verified, V-53) bans kickbacks and unearned fees for referrals. RESPA covers federally related mortgage loans on 1–4 family residential property, which describes most financed home sales. Because Chapter 475 allows a kickback only when no other law forbids it, full disclosure does not save a payment that RESPA prohibits (see L07-3).

Commission rates are negotiable

There is no "standard", "board-approved" or "customary" rate. Each broker agrees its fee with its own client. Competing brokers who agree on rates are engaged in price fixing, which antitrust law prohibits (manual; not yet verified). The reason: antitrust law protects competition. If competitors agree on a rate, consumers lose the chance to shop around and bargain, so each broker must set its fee independently, client by client.

Rental information lists (s. 475.453, F.S.; verified, V-21)

Some licensees sell lists of available rentals to people looking for a home. A broker or sales associate who sells a rental information list, for a fee paid by the prospective tenant, must give the tenant a contract or receipt. It must provide for:

  • repayment of any amount over 25% of the fee if the tenant does not obtain a rental, so the tenant gets 75% back;
  • repayment of the full fee on demand if the information was not current or accurate in any material respect.

A violation is a first-degree misdemeanor, and the licensee's license is also subject to suspension or revocation. Older editions of the statute (2002/2005) required the tenant to demand the 75% refund within 30 days of the contract. The 2025 excerpts checked did not show that window, so it is not re-confirmed as current. Exam questions written from older materials may still use it.

4. Key terms

Term Meaning
Principal office The broker's registered main office
Branch office Any additional registered location where the broker does business
Trade name A business name the brokerage operates under
Employing broker The broker a sales associate is registered under, and her only source of pay
Rebate Part of the commission returned to the buyer or seller, with full disclosure
Referral fee Payment for sending a client to another licensee; paid broker to broker
Kickback Payment for referring business, especially settlement-service business
Settlement service A service connected with a closing, such as title, lending or inspection
Price fixing Competitors agreeing on commission rates; illegal under antitrust law
Rental information list A list of available rentals sold to prospective tenants for a fee

5. Practical example

Marco is a sales associate at Gulf Harbor Realty, Inc. in Tampa. His broker is Elena Ruiz. Which of these is lawful?

Situation Lawful? Rule
Branch entrance sign: "Gulf Harbor Realty, Inc. · Elena Ruiz · Lic. Real Estate Broker" Yes Firm name, a broker's name and the required words
Sign: "Gulf Harbor Realty · REALTOR®" No No broker's name and no required words. "REALTOR®" does not replace them
A seller hands Marco a $500 gift card at closing "for all your work" No An associate is paid only by the employing broker
The team's unlicensed assistant gets $100 per closed deal for scheduling showings No Per-deal pay to an unlicensed person
The same assistant gets a monthly salary for scheduling Yes Salary for clerical work
Elena rebates $2,000 of the commission to the buyer, disclosed to all parties Yes Rebate to a party, with full disclosure
Marco pays a $1,000 referral fee directly to an agent at another brokerage No Referral fees go broker to broker
A lender offers Elena $250 for each buyer she refers for a federally related home loan, fully disclosed No RESPA Section 8. Disclosure does not cure it
Elena and a rival broker agree neither will take listings below 6% No Price fixing

Rental list calculation. A tenant pays $200 for a list.

Outcome Refund Licensee may keep
Accurate list, no rental obtained 75% × $200 = $150 25% × $200 = $50
Half the listings had already been rented Full fee: $200 $0
Accurate list, tenant rents a unit from it No refund required $200

6. Portugal comparison

Familiar principle. Under Lei 15/2013, art. 19, remuneration is due when the deal the mediation aimed at is concluded and perfected. Under exclusivity it remains due if the deal fails for reasons attributable to the client. Courts require a causal link between the mediator's work and the deal.

Florida rule. Commission terms come from the listing contract. Under an exclusive right of sale the brokerage earns the fee whoever sells; under an open listing only the procuring cause earns it. By law, the money flows customer → brokerage → associate. A sales associate may be paid only by her employing broker.

The difference. In Portugal a statute (art. 19) says when the remuneration is due; in Florida the listing contract sets when the commission is earned. More important for the exam, Florida law fixes who may pay whom: an associate never takes money directly from a customer or another brokerage.

Exam implication. "The associate accepted payment from the seller (or another broker)" → violation. A "standard rate" → price fixing. There is no Portuguese comparison for office signs, rental lists or RESPA in this course (requires verification).

7. Legal and numerical requirements

Memorize exactly

  • Entrance sign (s. 475.22(1); V-45): principal office and each branch; broker's name and any trade name (a firm: its name plus at least one broker); the words "Licensed Real Estate Broker" or "Lic. Real Estate Broker".
  • Rental list (s. 475.453; V-21): contract or receipt; no rental obtained → refund any amount over 25% (75% back); information not current or accurate → full refund on demand; violation = first-degree misdemeanor plus license suspension or revocation.
  • RESPA Section 8 (V-53): no kickbacks or unearned fees for referrals on federally related mortgage loans (1–4 family residential).
  • Associate paid only by the employing broker; no pay to unlicensed persons for real estate services; rebates to parties with full disclosure; Chapter 475 kickbacks only with full disclosure and no other law forbidding them (manual; not yet verified).
  • Registered office; each branch office registered (manual; not yet verified).
  • Rental-list demand window: 30 days of the contract in older editions; not shown in the 2025 excerpts, so not re-confirmed as current.

Understand

  • Commission rates are negotiable; competitors agreeing on rates is price fixing (manual; not yet verified).
  • A Chapter 475 kickback needs full disclosure and no other law against it. On most financed home sales RESPA is that other law.

8. Visual explanation

Is the person receiving the money a licensee?
No → unlawful if it pays for real estate services or referrals. Two lawful cases: a salary for clerical work, and a broker's rebate to the buyer or seller with full disclosure
If the person paid is a sales associate, is the payer her employing broker?
No (gift from a seller, fee from another brokerage) → unlawful
Is the payment free of RESPA problems (not a settlement-service referral payment on a federally related residential loan)?
No → RESPA Section 8 prohibits it, even if disclosed
Lawful: a broker paying its own associates and broker-to-broker referral fees. Any other kickback still needs full disclosure to all parties and no other law forbidding it
CustomerPays the brokerage under the listing or other agreement
Brokerage (broker)Pays its associates, pays other brokers, may rebate to a party with disclosure
Sales associateReceives pay only from the employing broker

Money flows through the broker.

9. Common misconceptions

  • "A gift from a happy seller isn't compensation." Anything of value for the associate's work is compensation. It must come through the broker.
  • "A standard commission rate exists." Rates are negotiated with each client. Competitors agreeing on rates is price fixing.
  • "'REALTOR®' on the main office sign is enough." The sign needs "Licensed Real Estate Broker" or "Lic. Real Estate Broker", and each branch needs one too.
  • "A small per-closing bonus for an unlicensed assistant is fine." Per-deal pay to an unlicensed person is unlawful at any amount. A salary for clerical work is fine.
  • "Disclosure makes any kickback legal." RESPA Section 8 prohibits referral kickbacks on federally related loans even when they are disclosed.
  • "On a rental list, the licensee keeps 75%." It is the reverse: the licensee keeps at most 25%, and the full fee is refunded if the list was inaccurate.
  • "Rental-list violations are second-degree misdemeanors, like most s. 475.42(1) violations." They are first-degree. (Unlicensed practice is a third-degree felony; V-12.)

10. Memory sheet

  • Sign at every office entrance: broker's name + trade name + "Licensed (Lic.) Real Estate Broker". For a firm, at least one broker's name.
  • Money flows through the broker. Associates are paid only by their employing broker.
  • Unlicensed people: salary for clerical work OK, per-deal pay never.
  • Rebate to a party, with full disclosure: OK. Referral fees: broker to broker.
  • RESPA §8: no referral kickbacks on federally related residential loans. Disclosure doesn't cure it.
  • Rates are negotiable. Competitors agreeing on rates = price fixing.
  • Rental lists: keep 25%, return 75%; inaccurate list = 100% back. First-degree misdemeanor plus license discipline. The 30-day demand window is from older text and not re-confirmed.

lessons.title: The complaint process
lessons.html:
2. Why it matters

When someone reports a Florida licensee, the case does not go straight to a penalty. It moves through a fixed sequence of steps, and each step belongs to a different body: the DBPR, a FREC panel, the FREC itself, a judge, and an appeals court. The exam tests the order of the steps, who acts at each step, and the 30-day deadline to appeal.

This lesson, with L06-2 and L06-3, makes up Section 6 of the official exam outline (Violations, Penalties and Procedures, 3%, about 3 of the 100 questions). In practice, if a letter from the DBPR ever arrives, this lesson tells you where you are in the process and which choices are yours.

3. Simple explanation

Why the process has separate steps

A license is a person's livelihood, so the state does not act on an accusation alone. The people who investigate (DBPR) are not the people who decide (FREC); a probable cause panel screens out weak cases before formal charges; the licensee gets a hearing; and an independent court can review the result.

The seven steps

The sequence comes from the study manual and is partially verified: the probable cause panel (V-42) and the appeal (V-43) are confirmed from official sources; the other steps are taught as the manual states them (manual; not yet verified).

  1. Complaint. Filed with the DBPR. It must be legally sufficient: it alleges facts that, if true, would violate a statute or rule. It need not come from someone who was harmed, and an anonymous complaint can be investigated if it is legally sufficient and substantial.
  2. Investigation. The DBPR investigates. The licensee is generally notified and may respond.
  3. Probable cause. A FREC probable cause panel reviews the investigation and decides, by majority vote, whether there is enough evidence to justify formal charges. If not, no formal complaint is filed.
  4. Formal complaint. If probable cause exists, a formal (administrative) complaint is filed against the licensee.
  5. Hearing. The licensee chooses an informal hearing before the FREC when the facts are not disputed, or a formal hearing before an administrative law judge (ALJ) when the facts are disputed. The ALJ writes a recommended order.
  6. Final order. The FREC issues the final order, which sets any penalty (L06-2).
  7. Appeal. A party adversely affected may seek review in a District Court of Appeal. The notice of appeal must be filed within 30 days after rendition (official issuing) of the order (s. 120.68, F.S.).

Withdrawing the complaint does not stop the process. The logic: discipline protects the public, so once the DBPR has a legally sufficient complaint, the case belongs to the state, not to the person who complained.

Who sits on the probable cause panel

Source What it says
s. 455.225(4), F.S.; Rule 61J2-20.009, F.A.C. (verified, V-42) At least two members, including a present FREC member; a former FREC member may serve. Probable cause is decided by majority vote.
Flag The current rule's wording on panel size was seen only in fragments.
Exam answer (manual) Two members, at least one a current FREC member. This fits the verified rule.

The appeal, precisely

  • Deadline: notice of appeal within 30 days after rendition of the final order (s. 120.68; Fla. R. App. P. 9.110(c)).
  • Filing: with the agency clerk; a copy, with the filing fees, goes to the court clerk.
  • Court: the District Court of Appeal for the district where the agency has its headquarters or where a party resides (or as otherwise provided by law).
  • Late notice: an irremediable jurisdictional defect. The court cannot hear the appeal at all.

4. Key terms

Term Meaning
DBPR Department of Business and Professional Regulation: receives complaints and investigates
Legally sufficient Alleges facts that, if true, would violate a statute or rule
Probable cause Enough evidence from the investigation to justify formal charges
Probable cause panel FREC panel (at least two members, at least one current FREC member) that votes on probable cause
Formal (administrative) complaint The formal charges filed after probable cause is found
Informal hearing Hearing before the FREC when the facts are not disputed
Formal hearing Hearing before an administrative law judge when the facts are disputed
Administrative law judge (ALJ) Judge from the Division of Administrative Hearings who conducts formal hearings
Recommended order The ALJ's proposed decision; not the final word
Final order The FREC's decision in the case
Rendition The official issuing of the order; the 30-day appeal clock runs from it
District Court of Appeal The Florida appeals court that reviews the FREC's final order

5. Practical example

Renata, a sales associate in Orlando, sells a townhouse to Mr. Okafor. After closing he learns the community has a mandatory homeowners' association with monthly fees. He says Renata wrote to him that there was none, and he complains to the DBPR.

Step What happens Who acts
1. Complaint Alleges a false statement of a material fact: legally sufficient DBPR
2. Investigation Listing, contract and emails collected; Renata responds DBPR
(meanwhile) Mr. Okafor settles privately and withdraws. The case continues. —
3. Probable cause Two-member panel (one current, one former FREC member) votes yes FREC panel
4. Formal complaint Formal charges filed DBPR
5. Hearing Renata says a later email corrected her mistake. Facts disputed → formal hearing → recommended order ALJ
6. Final order Fine and probation FREC
7. Appeal Notice filed with the agency clerk within 30 days after rendition; copy and fees to the court clerk District Court of Appeal

Variations

  • If Renata agreed with the facts, she could choose an informal hearing before the FREC.
  • A notice filed on day 34 is too late; the court has no power to hear the appeal.
  • Mr. Okafor gets no money from this process. The FREC does not award damages; he would need a civil judgment (and possibly the Recovery Fund, L06-3).

6. Portugal comparison

Familiar principle. You are used to a public regulator supervising real estate intermediaries. In Portugal this is usually associated with IMPIC, I.P., which licenses real estate mediation businesses (requires verification: this course has no checked Portugal comparison for this topic).

Florida rule. A complaint follows a fixed path split across bodies: DBPR investigates, a FREC panel decides probable cause, the FREC issues the final order, and a District Court of Appeal reviews it if a notice is filed within 30 days.

Precise difference. Florida separates investigating, screening, deciding and reviewing, in a fixed order. How a complaint against a Portuguese mediator is investigated, decided and appealed, and with what deadlines, requires verification, so no step-by-step comparison is offered here.
