Exam implication. Answer procedure questions with the Florida sequence and body names only. Never use a Portuguese rule or deadline to answer a Florida question.

7. Legal and numerical requirements

Memorize exactly

  • Complaint → investigation → probable cause → formal complaint → hearing → final order → appeal.
  • The DBPR receives complaints and investigates.
  • Probable cause: majority vote of a panel of at least two members, including at least one current FREC member; a former member may serve (s. 455.225(4); Rule 61J2-20.009; verified, V-42).
  • Informal hearing = facts not disputed, before the FREC. Formal hearing = facts disputed, before an ALJ, who issues a recommended order (manual; not yet verified).
  • The FREC issues the final order and chooses the penalty within s. 475.25(1) (L06-2).
  • Appeal: notice within 30 days after rendition, to a District Court of Appeal; filed with the agency clerk, copy and fees to the court clerk (s. 120.68; Fla. R. App. P. 9.110(c); verified, V-43).

Understand

  • The pipeline as a whole is manual-based and partially verified: the panel (V-42) and the appeal (V-43) are verified; the order of the other steps comes from the manual.
  • Legal sufficiency, complaints from people who were not harmed, anonymous complaints, notice to the licensee, the DBPR filing the formal complaint, the FREC issuing the final order, and "withdrawal does not stop the case" (manual; not yet verified).
  • A missed 30-day notice is an irremediable jurisdictional defect (verified, V-43).
  • Panel size: the verified rule is "at least two members, including a present FREC member" (V-42); the current rule's wording on size was seen only in fragments. The manual's "two members, at least one a current FREC member" fits it and is the exam answer.

8. Visual explanation

1 · ComplaintTo the DBPR · legally sufficient
2 · InvestigationDBPR · licensee may respond
3 · Probable causeFREC panel · majority vote · "no" ends it here
4 · Formal complaintFormal charges filed
5 · HearingInformal (FREC) or formal (ALJ)
6 · Final orderFREC decides the penalty
7 · AppealDistrict Court of Appeal · within 30 days
Informal hearing Formal hearing
When Facts not disputed Facts disputed
Heard by The FREC An administrative law judge
Result FREC final order ALJ recommended order → FREC final order

9. Common misconceptions

  • "Probable cause comes first, then the investigation." The DBPR investigates first; the panel decides probable cause on the results.
  • "The formal complaint starts the case." An ordinary complaint starts it; the formal complaint comes after probable cause.
  • "If the client withdraws the complaint, the case ends." It continues; the case belongs to the state.
  • "Only a harmed client can complain." Anyone may file a legally sufficient complaint; even an anonymous complaint can be investigated if it is legally sufficient and substantial.
  • "The FREC investigates." The DBPR investigates; the FREC decides.
  • "The ALJ decides the penalty." The ALJ recommends; the FREC issues the final order.
  • "Informal hearing means disputed facts." Reversed: disputed facts go to an ALJ.
  • "Appeals go to the Florida Supreme Court or a county court, and a late notice can be excused." A District Court of Appeal, and a late notice is fatal to the appeal.

10. Memory sheet

  • Complaint → Investigation → Probable cause → Formal complaint → Hearing → Final order → Appeal.
  • Traps: I before P (investigation before probable cause); P before F (probable cause before the formal complaint).
  • DBPR digs, panel screens, FREC decides, court reviews.
  • Panel: at least 2 members, at least 1 current FREC member, majority vote.
  • Facts agreed → informal (FREC). Facts disputed → formal (ALJ → recommended order → FREC).
  • Appeal: 30 days after rendition → District Court of Appeal. Late = no appeal.
  • Withdrawn complaint ≠ closed case.

lessons.title: Penalties and the violation vocabulary
lessons.html:
2. Why it matters

When a case reaches the FREC's final order (L06-1), the FREC chooses from a fixed menu of penalties with exact limits. The exam tests those limits ($5,000 per count, 10 years of suspension), the line between administrative penalties (FREC) and crimes (courts), and the labels for misconduct: fraud, misrepresentation, concealment, false promise, culpable negligence, breach of trust.

This is part of Section 6 of the exam outline (3%, shared with L06-1 and L06-3). In practice, one bad habit can become several counts, each with its own fine.

3. Simple explanation

Three separate tracks

Track Who decides Possible result
Administrative (the license) FREC, after the L06-1 process Fine, probation, suspension, revocation and others; fines go to the state
Criminal Criminal court Jail and criminal fines
Civil Civil court Damages paid to the harmed person (and possibly the Recovery Fund, L06-3)

The FREC never imprisons anyone and never awards damages to consumers. The tracks can run together: breaking the rules on selling rental information to prospective tenants is a crime and also exposes the license to discipline (s. 475.453; V-21).

The administrative penalty menu

Under s. 475.25(1), F.S. (verified, V-41) the FREC may deny an application or renewal, issue a reprimand, fine up to $5,000 for each count or separate offense, place a licensee on probation, suspend a license for up to 10 years, or revoke it.

Penalty Meaning Limit or note
Notice of noncompliance Written notice for a first minor violation, letting the licensee correct it Manual; not yet verified
Citation A set fine for a listed minor violation, instead of formal proceedings Manual; not yet verified
Reprimand Formal written disapproval —
Administrative fine A money penalty; the manual says it is paid to the state Up to $5,000 per count
Probation Continued work under FREC conditions —
Required education Courses the FREC orders the licensee to complete Manual; not yet verified
Suspension The license exists but cannot be used Up to 10 years
Revocation The license is cancelled Permanent, with narrow exceptions (manual; not yet verified)
Denial Application or renewal refused —

A count is one separate violation charged. Three counts mean fines of up to 3 × $5,000 = $15,000.

Criminal penalties (courts only)

Conduct Classification Source
Operating as a broker or sales associate without a valid, current, active license Third-degree felony: up to 5 years and $5,000 under the general sentencing statutes s. 475.42(1)(a) (V-12)
Any other violation of s. 475.42(1) Second-degree misdemeanor, unless Chapter 475 sets a different punishment s. 475.42(2) (V-12)
Violating the rules on selling rental information lists to prospective tenants (for example, not making the required refunds) First-degree misdemeanor, plus license discipline s. 475.453 (V-21)

A felony is the more serious class of crime; a misdemeanor the less serious. Note "valid, current, active": the felony is not limited to people who never held a license.

The violation vocabulary

The FREC may discipline a licensee who commits these in any business transaction, not only in real estate (s. 475.25; manual; not yet verified). A licensee who cheats partners in a restaurant venture answers to the FREC too.

Term Meaning Florida example
Fraud Intentional deception Inventing a "second offer" to push a Tampa buyer to pay more
Misrepresentation False statement of a material fact "The roof was replaced last year," when it is 15 years old
Concealment Hiding a material fact A rug placed over a rotten floor section before showings
False promise A promise to induce action that the licensee does not intend to keep or cannot keep "Sign today and the seller will pay all your closing costs," when the seller already refused
False pretenses Pretending a false situation exists to obtain something Charging an owner a "marketing fee" by pretending a buyer is lined up
Dishonest dealing by trick or scheme A planned arrangement to cheat Two contracts for one sale, one with a false price for the lender
Culpable negligence Reckless indifference to others' rights: more than carelessness; no intent to deceive is needed Again and again leaving deposit checks in the car for days because "nothing has gone wrong yet"
Breach of trust Betraying the confidence a principal placed in the licensee Telling a buyer the seller's lowest price while acting as the seller's single agent

Puffing ("the best sunset in Naples") is opinion, not misrepresentation. A one-time careless slip is simple negligence, not culpable negligence.

Other named grounds

  • Commingling (mixing personal or business funds with escrow funds). A broker may lawfully keep up to $1,000 of personal or brokerage funds in a sales escrow account and $5,000 in a property management escrow account (V-38).
  • Conversion (using escrow funds for personal or unauthorized purposes).
  • Failure to account and deliver money or property to the person entitled to it.
  • Operating as a broker while licensed as a sales associate.
  • Conviction of a crime involving moral turpitude (serious dishonesty or immorality).
  • Adjudication of mental incompetence (manual wording: confinement in a mental institution).
  • Records and crime reporting, below.

Records (s. 475.5015; verified, V-40). A broker keeps at least one legible copy of all books, accounts and records for at least 5 years, counted from receipt of entrusted funds or, if none, from the date any party signs the listing, offer, rental management agreement, lease or other agreement engaging the broker. If the records are involved in litigation: at least 2 years after the case and any appeal end, and never less than 5 years in total.

Reporting a crime (s. 455.227(1)(t); verified, V-35). Within 30 days, in writing, to the FREC: any conviction or finding of guilt, or plea of guilty or nolo contendere ("no contest"), to any crime in any jurisdiction, regardless of adjudication (even if the court "withholds adjudication", that is, does not formally enter a conviction). Chapter 475's own rule (s. 475.25(1)(p)) covers only felonies.

4. Key terms

Term Meaning
Count One separate violation charged; fines apply per count
Reprimand Formal written disapproval on the licensee's record
Felony / misdemeanor More serious / less serious class of crime
Material fact A fact that would affect a reasonable party's decision or the property's value
Puffing Exaggerated sales opinion; not a statement of fact
Moral turpitude Serious dishonesty or immorality
Nolo contendere "No contest" plea: no admission of guilt, but the penalty is accepted
Withheld adjudication The court does not formally enter a conviction; the crime must still be reported

5. Practical example

Bruno, a sales associate in Fort Myers, faces a formal complaint with three counts:

  1. On a Friday he received a $10,000 deposit check and kept it in his car until the next Thursday. He had to deliver it to his broker by the end of the next business day: Monday, if not a legal holiday (Rule 61J2-14.009; V-36).
  2. He told the buyer, "The seller replaced the roof last year," knowing it is 15 years old: misrepresentation.
  3. Two months ago he pleaded nolo contendere to a misdemeanor, adjudication withheld, and never told the FREC. Chapter 475's felony-only rule would not reach it; s. 455.227(1)(t) does.
Question Answer
Maximum total fine? 3 counts × $5,000 = $15,000
Other FREC options? Reprimand, probation, suspension up to 10 years, revocation
Can the FREC order him to pay the buyer for the roof? No: the buyer must sue in civil court
Can the FREC jail him? No: only a criminal court

Bruno's unlicensed cousin shows homes for $150 per showing: operating without a license, a third-degree felony for a criminal court.

6. Portugal comparison

Familiar principle. A regulator supervises the sector. In Portugal this role is usually associated with IMPIC, I.P., which licenses real estate mediation businesses (requires verification: this course has no checked Portugal comparison for this topic).

Florida rule. Each licensee holds a personal license, and the FREC disciplines that personal license. Crimes go to the courts; unlicensed practice is a third-degree felony.

Precise difference. Whether the Portuguese license is held by the mediation business rather than by each consultant, how consultants inside an agency operate, and the types, amounts and procedure of Portuguese sanctions all require verification. In Florida the sales associate personally can be fined, and his or her own license suspended or revoked, for conduct in any business transaction.

Exam implication. Use only Florida's limits: $5,000 per count, 10 years, revocation by the FREC; jail only by a court. Never let a Portuguese rule answer a Florida question.

7. Legal and numerical requirements

Memorize exactly

  • FREC (s. 475.25(1); V-41): denial, reprimand, fine up to $5,000 per count or separate offense, probation, suspension up to 10 years, revocation.
  • No valid, current, active license: third-degree felony, up to 5 years and $5,000 (s. 475.42(1)(a); V-12).
  • Other s. 475.42(1) violations: second-degree misdemeanor, unless the chapter sets a different punishment (s. 475.42(2); V-12).
  • Rental information violations: first-degree misdemeanor plus license discipline (s. 475.453; V-21).
  • Records: 5 years; if litigated, 2 years after the case and appeals end, never less than 5 in total (s. 475.5015; V-40).
  • Crimes: written report within 30 days; any crime; guilty or nolo contendere pleas included; regardless of adjudication (s. 455.227(1)(t); V-35).

Understand

  • Outdated figure: the fine cap was $1,000 per count in the 2002 statute; it was $5,000 by 2010 and is $5,000 in the 2024 and 2025 editions. The 2026 edition's penalty text was not retrieved, but the excerpts checked showed no change (V-41).
  • Manual-only (not yet verified): notice of noncompliance and how citations work; ordered education; exceptions to permanent revocation; that fines go to the state; first-degree misdemeanor penalties (up to $1,000 and 1 year); DBPR citations of up to $5,000 and injunctions against unlicensed persons; the violation vocabulary and the "any business transaction" reach; the commingling, conversion, failure to account and deliver, broker-while-associate, moral turpitude and mental incompetence grounds.
  • Rule 61J2-14.012 also requires the broker to keep deposit slips, depository statements and agreements, and to reconcile escrow accounts monthly (V-40).

8. Visual explanation

Which label fits? Work down the questions in order.

Is it only opinion or exaggeration?
Yes → puffing, not misrepresentation
Did the licensee state a false past or present fact, or hide a material fact?
Yes → misrepresentation or concealment (fraud if intentional deception)
Was it an assurance about the future, made to induce action, that the licensee did not intend to keep or could not keep?
Yes → false promise
No intent to deceive, but reckless, repeated disregard of others' rights?
Yes → culpable negligence
One honest slip → simple negligence (other rules may still be broken)

Labels can overlap: a knowingly false assurance about the future is both a misrepresentation and a false promise.

9. Common misconceptions

  • "The FREC can order restitution or jail." Damages need a civil judgment; jail needs a criminal court.
  • "The maximum fine is $5,000 per case." It is $5,000 per count.
  • "The fine cap is $1,000." That was the 2002 cap. ($1,000 is also the personal-funds limit in a sales escrow account, a different rule.)
  • "Suspension and revocation are the same." Suspension is temporary (up to 10 years); revocation cancels the license.
  • "Culpable negligence is any mistake." It is reckless indifference, more than carelessness.
  • "Only real estate deals count." The vocabulary applies in any business transaction.
  • "Only felony convictions must be reported." Any crime, guilty and nolo contendere pleas included, regardless of adjudication.
  • "Records are kept 3 years." At least 5; if litigation is involved, also at least 2 years after it and any appeal end.
  • "Unlicensed practice is a misdemeanor." It is a third-degree felony.

10. Memory sheet

  • Fine 5K per count · suspend 10 · revoke = cancel · records 5 · report crimes in 30.
  • FREC: deny, reprimand, fine, probation, suspend, revoke. Never jail, never damages.
  • No active license = 3rd-degree felony. Other s. 475.42(1) = 2nd-degree misdemeanor. Rental lists = 1st-degree misdemeanor + license action.
  • Fraud = intent · misrepresentation = false fact · concealment = hidden fact · false promise = promise to induce · culpable negligence = reckless · breach of trust = betrayed confidence.
  • Any business transaction. Old $1,000 cap = outdated.

lessons.title: The Real Estate Recovery Fund
lessons.html:
2. Why it matters

The FREC can fine and suspend a licensee, but it cannot give a harmed consumer any money (L06-2). A consumer can win a court judgment against a licensee and still collect nothing if the licensee has no assets or has disappeared. The Real Estate Recovery Fund is the state's last-resort answer to that problem.

The exam asks four things: the two caps ($50,000 and $150,000), what the Fund does not pay, who may not claim, and what happens to the licensee when the Fund pays. It is part of Section 6 of the exam outline (3%, shared with L06-1 and L06-2). In practice, a Fund payment caused by your conduct suspends your license until you pay the money back with interest.

3. Simple explanation

From the foundation up

  1. A licensee harms a consumer in a brokerage transaction (for example, by misrepresentation).
  2. The FREC may discipline the licensee, but it does not award damages.
  3. The consumer sues in civil court and wins a judgment (a court order that the licensee must pay).
  4. The licensee cannot or does not pay: the judgment is unsatisfied.
  5. The consumer applies to the Recovery Fund, which pays within strict limits (s. 475.484, F.S.; verified, V-17).
  6. The licensee's license is automatically suspended until the Fund is repaid in full plus interest (see the note in section 7).

The conditions

The Fund pays a member of the public who:

  • obtained a final civil judgment against a licensee;
  • for a violation arising from a real estate brokerage transaction;
  • and cannot collect it.

What the Fund pays

Rule Detail
Type of loss Actual or compensatory damages only
Not paid Treble damages (triple damages), court costs, attorney's fees, interest
Per claim The lesser of the unsatisfied judgment (actual or compensatory damages) or $50,000
Per transaction $50,000 in total, however many people claim
Per licensee $150,000 in total across all transactions; if claims exceed it, payments are prorated (shared out)

Who may and may not recover

Person May claim?
Buyer, seller or other member of the public harmed by a licensee in a brokerage transaction, with a final judgment they cannot collect Yes
A licensee harmed while acting solely as a buyer or seller (a principal, not an agent) Yes, like any consumer
A licensee who acted as a licensee in the transaction, for example a commission dispute No
A sales associate who sues her broker over an unpaid commission No: she acted as a licensee, and commission disputes are excluded
A licensee's spouse, in certain claims No (manual; details not given)

The logic: the Fund protects the public that deals with licensees. Disputes among licensees about their own pay are business disputes between professionals.

The licensee's consequence

When the Fund pays because of a licensee's conduct, that license is automatically suspended until the licensee repays the Fund in full plus interest. According to the manual, bankruptcy does not restore the license.

A second use: protecting a broker who obeys an EDO

When a broker holding a disputed deposit obtains an Escrow Disbursement Order (EDO) from the FREC, follows it, and is later sued for obeying it, the Fund also pays the broker's defense costs and the judgment (manual; not yet verified).

4. Key terms

Term Meaning
Real Estate Recovery Fund State fund that pays consumers who cannot collect a judgment against a licensee arising from a brokerage transaction
Judgment A court's decision ordering one party to pay another
Unsatisfied judgment A judgment that has not been paid
Actual (compensatory) damages Money that makes up for the real loss suffered
Treble damages Three times the actual damages, awarded under some laws as a penalty
Attorney's fees / court costs The cost of the lawyer and of the lawsuit itself
Aggregate cap A maximum for all claims added together
Prorate Share a limited amount out among several claims
Principal A party to the deal (buyer or seller), as opposed to an agent
Escrow Disbursement Order (EDO) FREC order deciding who receives disputed escrow funds held by a broker

5. Practical example

Lucas, a sales associate in Clearwater, tells Mrs. Duarte that a condo "has never had water damage," knowing the unit flooded twice. She buys it, pays for repairs, and sues him. The court awards her a judgment:

Item Amount
Compensatory damages (repairs and losses) $41,000
Attorney's fees $9,000
Court costs $1,500
Interest $2,000
Total judgment $53,500

Lucas has no assets, so the judgment is unsatisfied. Mrs. Duarte applies to the Fund.

  • Fund pays: the lesser of $41,000 (compensatory damages) or $50,000 = $41,000.
  • Fund does not pay: the $12,500 of fees, costs and interest ($9,000 + $1,500 + $2,000).
  • Lucas: his license is automatically suspended until he repays the Fund $41,000 plus interest.

Two other claims:

  • Ana, a sales associate at Lucas's brokerage, wins a judgment against their broker for unpaid commissions and cannot collect it. She cannot claim: she acted as a licensee, and this is a commission dispute.
  • Paulo, a licensed sales associate, bought a different unit through Lucas for himself, acting only as a buyer, and was misled the same way. After winning his own judgment that Lucas cannot pay, he can claim like any consumer. His claim is a separate transaction, with its own $50,000 cap, and counts toward Lucas's $150,000 total.

6. Portugal comparison

Familiar principle. Both systems want money to be available when a licensed intermediary harms a client. In Portugal, a mediation license is commonly understood to require civil liability insurance (or an equivalent guarantee) (requires verification: this course has no checked Portugal comparison for this topic).

Florida rule. The exam's protection is a state fund. It pays only after a final civil judgment that cannot be collected, only actual or compensatory damages, within $50,000 per transaction and $150,000 per licensee, and the licensee must repay it (automatic suspension until repaid with interest).

Precise difference. The Florida Fund is a last resort that requires a court judgment first, and it is a debt the licensee must repay. Whether and how a Portuguese client claims against a mediator's insurance or guarantee, and any limits on it, requires verification.

Exam implication. For any Florida question about an uncollectable judgment, apply the Recovery Fund rules. Do not answer "the agent's insurance pays", and never let a Portuguese rule answer a Florida question.

7. Legal and numerical requirements

Memorize exactly

  • $50,000 per transaction, all claimants combined (s. 475.484; verified, V-17).
  • $150,000 aggregate per licensee; prorated when exceeded (V-17).
  • Pays the lesser of the unsatisfied judgment for actual or compensatory damages or $50,000 (V-17).
  • Never pays treble damages, court costs, attorney's fees or interest (V-17).
  • Fund payment → license automatically suspended until repaid in full plus interest (V-17: seen in the 2010 statute text, not re-confirmed in the 2026 excerpt; see below).
  • A licensee who acted as a licensee (for example, a commission dispute) cannot recover (manual; not yet verified; the standard exam answer).

Understand

  • The caps and the excluded items are confirmed in s. 475.484 (V-17). The automatic suspension appears in the 2010 statute text; the 2026 excerpt checked did not show that sentence, so its current wording is not re-confirmed. It remains the standard exam answer.
  • The judgment must arise from a violation in a real estate brokerage transaction, and the claimant must be unable to collect it.
  • Who is excluded (licensees acting as licensees, a licensee's spouse in certain claims), the right of a licensee acting solely as a buyer or seller to claim, and the bankruptcy point (manual; not yet verified).
  • The Fund's use for a broker sued after obeying an EDO (manual; not yet verified).
  • The manual says the Fund never pays "punitive damages or interest". The statute's wording, as checked, is actual or compensatory damages only, with treble damages, court costs, attorney's fees and interest excluded (V-17).

8. Visual explanation

Does the claimant have a final civil judgment against a licensee?
No → no Fund claim (sue first; the FREC does not award damages)
Did it arise from a violation in a real estate brokerage transaction?
No → no Fund claim
Is the judgment uncollectable (unsatisfied)?
No → collect from the licensee
Did the claimant act as a licensee in that transaction (for example, a commission claim)?
Yes → excluded
Otherwise → the Fund pays actual or compensatory damages, up to $50,000 per transaction and $150,000 per licensee

Worked calculations

Case Facts Fund pays Why
A Mrs. Duarte: $41,000 compensatory + $12,500 fees, costs and interest $41,000 Below the cap; extras excluded
B One buyer: $68,000 compensatory damages $50,000 Per-transaction cap
C Two buyers in the same transaction: $30,000 + $35,000 = $65,000 $50,000 at most, combined The cap is per transaction, not per claimant
D Four transactions by one licensee, each within its own $50,000 cap: $50,000 + $50,000 + $40,000 + $30,000 = $170,000 $150,000 at most Per-licensee cap; payments are prorated

Check: C exceeds $50,000 by $15,000; D exceeds $150,000 by $20,000.

9. Common misconceptions

  • "Sales associates can claim for unpaid commissions." No. A licensee who acted as a licensee is excluded.
  • "The Fund pays legal fees." No attorney's fees, court costs, interest or treble damages.
  • "Each claimant can get $50,000." $50,000 is the total for the transaction.
  • "$150,000 per transaction." $150,000 is the total per licensee; per transaction it is $50,000.
  • "The FREC orders the Fund to pay after its hearing." The claimant first needs a civil court judgment that cannot be collected.
  • "Once the Fund pays, the licensee is off the hook." The license is automatically suspended until the Fund is repaid in full plus interest.
  • "The Fund payment revokes the license." It suspends it until repayment.
  • "Licensees can never claim." A licensee harmed while acting solely as a buyer or seller may claim.
  • "The cap is $25,000." $25,000 is not a Recovery Fund cap. Use $50,000 per transaction and $150,000 per licensee (V-17).

10. Memory sheet

  • 50 per deal, 150 per licensee. Public only.
  • Judgment first → cannot collect → Fund.
  • Pays actual or compensatory damages only. No treble damages, fees, costs or interest.
  • Licensee acting as licensee (commission dispute) = no claim. Licensee acting solely as buyer or seller = may claim.
  • Payment = automatic suspension until repaid in full plus interest.
  • EDO followed and broker sued → Fund pays defense costs and judgment (manual).

lessons.title: Fair housing
lessons.html:
2. Why it matters

Fair housing law shapes ordinary moments of the job: which homes you show a buyer, how you word an ad, how you answer "what kind of people live here?", and what you do when an owner gives you a discriminatory instruction. Breaking it exposes you and your broker to a HUD complaint or a lawsuit.

On the exam, Section VII (Federal and State Laws Pertaining to Real Estate) is 3%, about 3 questions shared by the four lessons of this chapter. Fair housing questions come in three shapes:

  • vocabulary: steering, blockbusting or redlining?
  • dates: which protected class was added in which year?
  • exemptions: does one apply, and was it lost?

3. Simple explanation

Two federal laws with different reach

  1. Civil Rights Act of 1866. Bans discrimination based on race in the sale or rental of all property, real or personal. It has no exceptions and is enforced by a lawsuit in federal court.
  2. Fair Housing Act of 1968 (Title VIII). Covers housing, protects more classes, and has a few narrow exemptions.

Why this matters: a Fair Housing Act exemption never protects racial discrimination, because the 1866 Act still applies. That is why every exam answer offering a "racial exemption" is wrong.

The protected classes, in order

  • 1968: race, color, religion, national origin.
  • 1974: sex (added by the Housing and Community Development Act).
  • 1988: familial status and handicap (added by the Fair Housing Amendments Act, enacted September 13, 1988). HUD's rules now say disability instead of handicap.

Familial status covers households with children under 18, pregnant women, and people in the process of obtaining custody of a child. Age and marital status are not on the federal fair housing list. They are credit (ECOA) categories, covered in L07-2.

What is prohibited

Because of a protected class, no one may refuse to sell or rent, offer different terms, publish a discriminatory ad, or falsely say a home is unavailable. Three practices have names:

  • Steering: directing buyers or renters toward or away from areas because of a protected class. It targets buyers and renters.
  • Blockbusting (panic peddling): persuading owners to sell by suggesting that a protected class is moving into the neighborhood. It targets sellers.
  • Redlining: a lender refusing loans, or changing loan terms, in certain areas for discriminatory reasons. It targets loans.

Disability: modification vs accommodation

  • Reasonable modification: a physical change to the unit, such as grab bars or a ramp, generally at the tenant's expense.
  • Reasonable accommodation: a change to a rule or policy, such as allowing an assistance animal despite a no-pets rule.

Exemptions, and how they are lost

Exemption Conditions
Private owner of single-family houses Owns no more than 3 such houses at one time. No broker, agent or salesperson is used, and no one "in the business" of selling or renting. No discriminatory advertising. An owner who was not living in the house, or was not its most recent occupant, gets the exemption for only one sale in any 24 months.
"Mrs. Murphy" (owner-occupied) A building with living quarters for no more than 4 families living independently, and the owner lives in one of the units.
Religious organizations May limit noncommercial housing they own or operate to members of the same religion, or give them preference, unless membership is restricted by race, color or national origin.
Private clubs A club not in fact open to the public may limit lodgings it provides as an incidental, noncommercial part of its purpose to its members.
Housing for older persons May exclude children, so the familial status protection does not apply. Two tests: 62+, where all occupants are 62 or older; or 55+, where at least 80% of occupied units have at least one person 55 or older, with published policies and age verification.

A person is "in the business" if, in the preceding 12 months, they acted as principal in 3 or more dwelling transactions, or as agent in 2 or more.

The two exemption killers: using a broker and publishing a discriminatory ad. For the single-family exemption, both are written into the statute. The manual applies the same rule to the other owner and organization exemptions (Mrs. Murphy, religious organizations, private clubs). Housing for older persons is judged differently: by its own tests (62+, or 55+ with 80%, published policies and age verification).

Enforcement

  • A complaint goes to HUD within 1 year after the discriminatory practice occurred or ended.
  • A civil lawsuit must be filed within 2 years. The clock stops while a HUD proceeding on the same practice is pending, and a person may sue without filing with HUD first.
  • Brokerage offices display the equal housing opportunity poster.
  • Florida has its own Fair Housing Act (Chapter 760, F.S.), which mirrors the federal law. Its details were not verified for this course.

4. Key terms

Term Meaning
Protected class A characteristic the law forbids using as a basis for housing decisions
Familial status Household with children under 18, pregnant women, or people obtaining custody
Steering Directing buyers or renters toward or away from areas because of a protected class
Blockbusting (panic peddling) Inducing owners to sell by suggesting that a protected class is moving in
Redlining A lender refusing or changing loans by area for discriminatory reasons
Reasonable modification Physical change to a unit for a person with a disability, generally at the tenant's expense
Reasonable accommodation Change in a rule or policy for a person with a disability
"Mrs. Murphy" exemption Owner-occupied building of no more than 4 units
Housing for older persons 62+ (all occupants) or 55+ (80% of occupied units) housing that may exclude children
HUD U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, which receives fair housing complaints

5. Practical example

Daniela is a sales associate in Tampa. In one week:

Situation Lawful? Why
A couple from Brazil asks for 3-bedroom homes. Without being asked, Daniela shows only homes in "neighborhoods with Brazilian families". No Steering on national origin, even if the buyers seem pleased
An owner of three single-family homes lists one with Daniela and says "no families with kids" No A broker is used, so the exemption is gone. Daniela must refuse the instruction.
An owner lives in one unit of her fourplex and rents another without a broker or ads. She prefers tenants without children. Possibly exempt Mrs. Murphy exemption (familial status). Under the manual's rule, it would end the moment she hired Daniela or ran a discriminatory ad.
The same owner refuses a tenant because of race No 1866 Act: no exemption for race, ever
A tenant with an assistance animal asks to live in a no-pets building Must generally allow Reasonable accommodation (a rule change)
A 55+ community in Sarasota County, where 85% of occupied units have a resident 55 or older and which publishes its policies and verifies ages, turns away a family with a toddler Lawful Housing for older persons (85% is above the 80% minimum). It removes only the familial status protection.
A flyer reads: "A family of [ethnic group] just bought on your street. Sell now!" No Blockbusting

6. Portugal comparison

Familiar principle. Portuguese law forbids discrimination in general, through constitutional equality and specific anti-discrimination legislation. The details require verification.

Florida rule. The exam tests the US federal framework: the 1866 Act (race, no exceptions), the Fair Housing Act's seven classes, three named practices, and narrow exemptions lost when a broker or a discriminatory ad is used.

Precise difference. US law works from a closed list of classes and named practices. General ideas of fairness will not tell you which year sex was added, or whether a fourplex owner is exempt.

Exam implication. No exemption ever applies to race. Answer with the federal list and dates, never by analogy with Portuguese law.

7. Legal and numerical requirements

Memorize exactly

  • 1866: race; all property; no exceptions (manual; not yet verified: V-56 checked only the 1968 Act and its 1974 and 1988 amendments).
  • 1968: race, color, religion, national origin. 1974: sex. 1988: familial status and handicap (disability) (V-56).
  • Single-family owner exemption: no more than 3 houses; no broker (or anyone in the business); no discriminatory ad; a non-occupant owner gets one sale per 24 months (V-54).
  • Mrs. Murphy: no more than 4 units (families living independently), and the owner lives in one (V-54).
  • Older persons: 62+ for all occupants, or 55+ in at least 80% of occupied units, with published policies and age verification (V-55).
  • HUD complaint within 1 year; lawsuit within 2 years (V-57).

Understand

  • Religious organizations lose the exemption if membership is restricted by race, color or national origin. Private clubs: only incidental, noncommercial lodgings.
  • The 80% counts occupied units only; HUD says the other 20% need not be under 55. Older-persons housing is exempt only from the familial status protection.
  • The lawsuit clock pauses while a HUD proceeding is pending; suing does not require a HUD complaint first.
  • "Broker or discriminatory ad ends the exemption" is in the statute for the single-family exemption. The manual extends it to the Mrs. Murphy, religious-organization and private-club exemptions (manual; not yet verified for those). On the exam, a broker or a discriminatory ad means no owner or organization exemption. Housing for older persons is tested on its own conditions.
  • These come from the manual only (manual; not yet verified): the definitions of steering, blockbusting and redlining; the modification/accommodation rules; enforcement of the 1866 Act in federal court; and the poster requirement. The familial status definition (children under 18, pregnant women, people obtaining custody) also comes from the course materials (manual; not yet verified).
  • Florida's Fair Housing Act (Chapter 760, F.S.) has not been verified for this course.

8. Visual explanation

1866Civil Rights Act · race · all property · no exceptions
1968Fair Housing Act · race, color, religion, national origin
1974+ sex
1988+ familial status + handicap (disability)

1978 is the lead-based paint year (L19-2), not a fair housing date.

Is the discrimination based on race?
Yes → never exempt (1866 Act)
Is it 62+ or 55+ housing for older persons that meets its tests, and is the issue only children (familial status)?
Yes → lawful under the older-persons rule
Was a broker or agent used, or a discriminatory ad published?
Yes → no exemption
Does the situation fit an owner or organization exemption (≤3 single-family houses; owner-occupied ≤4 units; religious organization; private club)?
No → the Fair Housing Act applies in full
Yes → exempt from the Fair Housing Act, within that exemption's limits

The broker-or-ad rule belongs to the owner and organization exemptions. Older-persons housing has its own tests (62+, or 55+ with 80%).

Practice Aimed at Typical exam wording
Steering Buyers and renters "showed only homes in areas where…"
Blockbusting Owners (sellers) "sell now, [group] is moving in"
Redlining Loans in an area (by a lender) "the bank will not lend in that ZIP (postal) code"

9. Common misconceptions

  • "Sex and familial status were both added in 1988." Sex was added in 1974. 1988 added familial status and handicap.
  • "1978 is a fair housing date." 1978 is the lead-based paint year (housing built before 1978, L19-2). The fair housing amendments for familial status and handicap came in 1988.
  • "Age and marital status are fair housing classes." Not under the federal Fair Housing Act. They are ECOA (credit) classes.
  • "An owner who qualifies for an exemption can still use a broker." Using a broker ends the exemption.
  • "An exempt owner may refuse a buyer because of race." Never: the 1866 Act has no exceptions.
  • "Showing buyers 'where people like them live' is good service." It is steering, even if the buyer seems pleased.
  • "Blockbusting is done to buyers." It targets owners, pushing them to sell.
  • "The tenant's grab bars are an accommodation." A physical change is a modification. A rule change, like allowing an assistance animal, is an accommodation.
  • "A 55+ community needs a person 55 or older in every unit." It needs one in at least 80% of occupied units. The "everyone" rule belongs to 62+ housing, where all occupants are 62 or older.

10. Memory sheet

  • 1866 race, no exceptions · 1968 race, color, religion, national origin · 1974 sex · 1988 familial status + handicap.
  • Steer buyers · block(bust) sellers · red(line) loans.
  • Modification = physical, tenant usually pays · Accommodation = rules.
  • Exemptions: ≤3 single-family houses (no broker, no ad; one sale per 24 months if not the occupant) · ≤4 units, owner lives in one · religious organizations · private clubs · older persons (62+ all / 55+ 80%).
  • Broker or discriminatory ad = owner/organization exemption lost. Race = never exempt.
  • HUD 1 year · lawsuit 2 years.

lessons.title: ADA, ECOA, HMDA and marketing rules (Do Not Call, CAN-SPAM, fax)
lessons.html:
2. Why it matters

These laws reach three parts of your working day:

  • your office, which must be accessible to the public (ADA);
  • your buyers' loans, which must be granted without discrimination (ECOA) and are reported to regulators (HMDA);
  • your prospecting by phone, email and fax (Do Not Call, CAN-SPAM, junk fax rules).

Prospecting by phone and email is routine in Florida brokerage, so these rules affect most licensees every week.

On the exam (Section VII, 3%, shared with L07-1, L07-3 and L07-4), the questions are of two kinds:

  • matching, such as "a wheelchair ramp at the office: which law?";
  • numbers: 18 months / 3 months for Do Not Call and 10 business days for email opt-outs.

3. Simple explanation

Four laws, four subjects

The exam describes a situation and asks which law governs. Find the subject first.

Subject in the question Law
Housing: selling or renting a dwelling Fair Housing Act (L07-1)
Credit: a loan application ECOA, the Equal Credit Opportunity Act
Public places and businesses: an office, a store ADA, the Americans with Disabilities Act
Lending data: reports on where and to whom lenders lend HMDA, the Home Mortgage Disclosure Act

ADA. Places of public accommodation and commercial facilities, including brokerage offices, must be accessible to people with disabilities. Barriers must be removed where this is readily achievable. The ADA governs business premises, not private homes. Housing is fair housing territory.

ECOA. A creditor (lender) may not discriminate against a credit applicant on any of these bases:

  1. race, color, religion, national origin, sex, marital status, or age (if the applicant is old enough to sign a binding contract);
  2. receipt of public assistance income;
  3. the applicant's good-faith exercise of consumer credit rights.

These bases do not stop a lender from judging whether the applicant can repay. Insufficient income, a poor history of paying debts on time and lack of funds for the down payment are not protected bases, so they can be legitimate reasons to deny a loan.

HMDA. Lenders report data about their mortgage lending. The law is about reporting, not about banning anything. The data reveals patterns such as redlining (L07-1).

CFPB. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau administers the TRID disclosure rules (L07-3).

Marketing rules

Do Not Call. A telemarketing call is a call made to sell something; for you, that means prospecting for listings or buyers. You may not make such a call to a number on the National Do Not Call Registry, or on Florida's list, unless one of two exceptions applies:

  • written permission from the consumer; or
  • an established business relationship (EBR) with your firm.

Two federal rules define the EBR, with almost the same windows:

Rule After a purchase or transaction After an inquiry or application
FCC rule (47 CFR 64.1200) 18 months 3 months
FTC Telemarketing Sales Rule (16 CFR 310.2(q)), since May 16, 2024 540 days 90 days

Under the FCC rule, the relationship must come from a voluntary two-way communication and must not have been ended by either party. A consumer's request to your company not to call ends it for telemarketing, even inside the window.

CAN-SPAM (commercial email):

  • Honor an opt-out (unsubscribe) within 10 business days. Once someone opts out, you also may not sell or transfer their address.
  • The opt-out link or reply address must keep working for at least 30 days after the email is sent.
  • Opting out cannot cost a fee or require more than an email address, a reply email, or a visit to a single web page.
  • Every commercial email must include a valid physical postal address: a current street address, a registered USPS post office box, or a private mailbox registered with a commercial mail receiving agency.
  • Header and subject lines must be truthful, and the email must be identified as an advertisement where required.

Junk Fax Prevention Act. Do not send unsolicited fax advertisements without an established business relationship.

4. Key terms

Term Meaning
ADA Americans with Disabilities Act: accessibility of public accommodations and commercial facilities
Public accommodation A place of business open to the public, such as a brokerage office
Readily achievable The ADA test for when barriers at business premises must be removed
ECOA Equal Credit Opportunity Act: no discrimination in credit
Public assistance income Income from a government assistance program; a protected basis under ECOA
HMDA Home Mortgage Disclosure Act: lenders report lending data
CFPB Consumer Financial Protection Bureau; administers TRID
Telemarketing Calling to sell goods or services, including prospecting calls by licensees
Established business relationship (EBR) A recent transaction or inquiry that allows calls to a registered number for a limited time
CAN-SPAM Federal law on commercial email: opt-outs, postal address, truthful headers
Opt-out A recipient's request to stop receiving commercial email

5. Practical example

Rafael, a sales associate in Miami, plans a morning of calls. Every number below is on the National Do Not Call Registry.

Contact Call? Why
Couple who closed a purchase through Rafael's brokerage 14 months ago Yes Inside 18 months (and inside 540 days)
Woman who emailed about one of his listings 2 months ago Yes Inside 3 months (and inside 90 days)
Man who asked about a rental 5 months ago No The inquiry window has closed
Owner of an expired listing with another brokerage No No relationship with Rafael's firm
Past client from 10 months ago who told the office "please stop calling me" No A company-specific request ends the relationship
FSBO seller who signed Rafael's written permission form at a homeowners' fair Yes Written permission

That afternoon, a newsletter subscriber clicks "unsubscribe". Rafael's brokerage must stop commercial emails to her within 10 business days (business days, not calendar days) and may not sell her address.

His office in Coral Gables needs an accessible entrance: that is the ADA. His buyer's lender may not refuse her because part of her income is public assistance: that is ECOA.

6. Portugal comparison

This course has no verified Portuguese comparison for these laws. Portuguese rules on direct-marketing consent, credit discrimination or office accessibility require verification and must not be used to answer a Florida question. On the exam, apply the US windows (18 months / 3 months; 10 business days) and the US law names exactly.

7. Legal and numerical requirements

Memorize exactly

  • Housing = Fair Housing Act · credit = ECOA · public accommodations = ADA · lending data = HMDA.
  • ECOA bases: race, color, religion, national origin, sex, marital status, age (if able to contract), public assistance income, good-faith exercise of consumer credit rights (V-61).
  • Do Not Call EBR: 18 months after a purchase or transaction; 3 months after an inquiry (FCC rule). The FTC rule since May 16, 2024: 540 days / 90 days (V-58). Exam answer: 18 months / 3 months, unless the question uses days.
  • A company-specific do-not-call request ends the relationship (V-58).
  • CAN-SPAM: opt-out honored within 10 business days; valid physical postal address in every commercial email; opt-out working for at least 30 days after sending (V-59).

Understand

  • Correction: older books give only "18 months / 3 months". That is still literally correct under the FCC rule, but the FTC rule's wording changed in 2024 to 540 days / 90 days. These are close, but not identical, to 18 and 3 months.
  • From the manual only (manual; not yet verified): the ADA rules (public accommodation, readily achievable barrier removal, not private homes); HMDA's description; the CFPB administering TRID; the Florida do-not-call list; the written-permission exception; truthful headers and ad identification under CAN-SPAM; and the junk fax rule.

8. Visual explanation

Law Protects / regulates Key words in the question Example
Fair Housing Act Housing transactions sell, rent, show, advertise a dwelling Refusing to rent to a family with children
ECOA Credit decisions loan, lender, applicant, credit Denying a loan because the applicant is divorced
ADA Public accommodations, commercial facilities office, store, ramp, access No accessible entrance at the brokerage
HMDA Lending data report, data, patterns Data showing few loans in one neighborhood
Has this person asked your company not to call?
Yes → do not call
Is the number on the National (or Florida) Do Not Call list?
No → the registry rules do not block the call
Do you have their written permission?
Yes → you may call
Did they buy, sell or rent through your firm in the last 18 months, or inquire in the last 3 months?
No → do not call
Yes → established business relationship: you may call

9. Common misconceptions

  • "A wheelchair ramp at the office is a fair housing issue." It is an ADA issue. Fair housing covers dwellings.
  • "The ADA requires sellers to make private homes accessible." The ADA governs public accommodations and commercial facilities, not private homes.
  • "Another brokerage's expired listing is fair game." You have no relationship with that owner. Do not call a registered number.
  • "An inquiry gives you 18 months." An inquiry gives 3 months; 18 months follows a transaction.
  • "Past customers on the registry can be called forever." Only within 18 months of the transaction, and never after they ask your company to stop.
  • "540 days is a wrong answer." It is correct under the FTC rule since 2024. Choose by the units the question uses.
  • "ECOA stops a lender from turning down anyone with low income." Insufficient income, poor payment history and lack of down-payment funds are not protected bases. Receiving public assistance income is.
  • "ECOA and the Fair Housing Act protect the same classes." ECOA adds marital status, age, public assistance income and the exercise of credit rights. Familial status and handicap are fair housing classes.
  • "HMDA prohibits redlining." HMDA is a reporting law; its data exposes redlining.
  • "CAN-SPAM gives 30 days to honor an opt-out." 10 business days. Thirty days is how long the opt-out mechanism must keep working.

10. Memory sheet

  • Housing = FHA · Credit = ECOA · Access = ADA · Data = HMDA.
  • ECOA adds: marital status, age, public assistance, exercising credit rights.
  • Do Not Call: 18 after a deal, 3 after a question (FTC: 540 / 90 days). "Stop calling me" ends it. Another firm's expired listing = no call.
  • CAN-SPAM: opt-out in 10 business days · postal address · opt-out works 30 days.
  • Fax ads: only with an established relationship.

lessons.title: RESPA and TILA (TRID)
lessons.html:
2. Why it matters

Most Florida buyers finance, and two federal laws, RESPA and TILA, govern the loan from application to closing. In practice you plan closing dates around the Closing Disclosure wait, you write ads that mention financing, and title companies or lenders may offer you "referral fees".

On the exam (Section VII, 3%, shared with the other lessons of this chapter), expect three themes:

  • the 3 / 3 / 3 business-day rules;
  • trigger terms in advertising;
  • the classic trap: a buyer cannot rescind a purchase mortgage.

3. Simple explanation

Two laws, one set of forms

  • RESPA, the Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act, governs settlement, the American word for the closing. It covers kickbacks and the buyer's free choice of title insurer.
  • TILA, the Truth in Lending Act (Regulation Z), governs the cost of credit: the APR, advertising and the right of rescission.
  • TRID, the TILA-RESPA Integrated Disclosure rule, merged the two laws' forms into two documents: the Loan Estimate and the Closing Disclosure. The CFPB administers it.

RESPA: which loans?

RESPA applies to federally related mortgage loans on residential property of 1 to 4 units (1–4 families). Both parts of that phrase matter:

  • 1–4 residential units. A loan on a single-family home or a duplex can be covered. A loan on a 20-unit apartment building or an office building is outside RESPA.
  • Federally related. This is a defined federal term. Its detailed test is not covered in this course's sources; for the exam, learn the whole phrase "federally related loans on 1–4 unit residential property".

RESPA Section 8: no kickbacks, no unearned fees

  • No one may give or accept a kickback (a fee or anything of value) for referring settlement-service business (title, inspection, lending).
  • No one may accept an unearned fee: a charge, or a share of a charge, for which no service was actually performed.
  • Disclosure does not cure it. A referral kickback is prohibited even if the buyer is told about it in writing.

The idea: the consumer pays for settlement services, so money paid for steering the consumer's business adds cost without adding service.

RESPA Section 9: the buyer chooses the title insurer

A seller may not require the buyer to buy title insurance from a particular title company. A seller who does is liable for 3 times the title insurance charges.

TRID: the two disclosures

Form Deadline "Business day" for this deadline
Loan Estimate Delivered or mailed no later than the 3rd business day after the lender receives the application A day the lender's offices are open for substantially all business
Loan Estimate (second limit) Delivered or mailed no later than the 7th business day before consummation Every day except Sundays and federal public holidays
Closing Disclosure Received at least 3 business days before consummation Every day except Sundays and federal public holidays (Saturdays count)

Consummation is Regulation Z's word for the loan closing.

Further rules on the two disclosures:

  • When the 3-day clock starts. It starts when the lender has all six application items listed in Regulation Z.
  • Denied or withdrawn. If the lender denies the application, or the consumer withdraws it, within the 3-day window, no Loan Estimate is required.
  • Mailed or e-mailed. A disclosure not handed over in person is treated as received 3 business days after it was sent.
  • Waiver. The consumer may waive the Closing Disclosure waiting period only for a bona fide personal financial emergency, and only after receiving the disclosures.
  • Corrected Closing Disclosure. It starts a new 3-business-day wait only if (1) the APR becomes inaccurate, (2) the loan product changes, or (3) a prepayment penalty is added.

TILA: the APR and advertising trigger terms

The APR (annual percentage rate) is the yearly cost of credit, including interest and certain fees. Compare loans by APR, not by the note rate.

There are four trigger terms: the amount or percentage of the down payment; the number of payments or period of repayment; the amount of any payment; the amount of any finance charge. An ad that states any one of them must also state the down payment, the terms of repayment and the APR.

These are not triggers: "no down payment"; "no closing costs"; stating the APR alone; vague phrases like "low monthly payments" or "easy financing".

TILA: the right of rescission

When a loan is secured by the consumer's principal dwelling (main home), such as a home-equity loan or a refinance with a new lender, each owner may cancel the loan:

  • until midnight of the 3rd business day after the latest of three events: consummation, delivery of the rescission notice, or delivery of all material disclosures;
  • business days include Saturdays, but not Sundays or federal public holidays;
  • if the notice or material disclosures are never delivered, the right lasts up to 3 years after consummation (or ends earlier if the property is sold or the consumer's whole interest is transferred).

If the consumer rescinds, the lender's security interest becomes void and no finance charge is owed.

No right of rescission:

  • a residential mortgage transaction, meaning a loan to buy or initially build the principal dwelling;
  • a refinance by the same lender, except for new money above the unpaid balance, earned unpaid finance charges and refinancing costs;
  • investment property, because it is not the borrower's principal dwelling.

The idea: rescission protects owners who pledge a home they already own as security. A loan used to buy or build that home is part of acquiring it, so it is excluded.

4. Key terms

Term Meaning
Settlement / settlement services The closing / services connected with it (title, inspection, lending)
Federally related mortgage loan A loan on 1–4 unit residential property that meets the federal "federally related" test
Kickback Payment or thing of value for referring settlement-service business
Unearned fee A charge, or share of a charge, for which no service was actually performed
TRID TILA-RESPA Integrated Disclosure rule (Loan Estimate and Closing Disclosure)
Loan Estimate Early disclosure of loan terms and costs, due within 3 business days of application
Closing Disclosure Final disclosure, received at least 3 business days before consummation
APR Annual percentage rate: yearly cost of credit including interest and certain fees
Trigger term A specific credit term in an ad that requires full disclosure
Right of rescission Right to cancel certain loans secured by the principal dwelling within 3 business days

5. Practical example

Lucas and Ana buy a single-family home in Orlando, to live in, with a federally related mortgage loan, so RESPA applies. Assume no federal holidays and a lender open Monday to Friday.

Step What happens Rule
Monday The lender receives all six application items The Loan Estimate clock starts
By Thursday Loan Estimate delivered or mailed 3rd business day after application: Tue (1), Wed (2), Thu (3)
Negotiation The seller says: "I'll sign only if you use my cousin's title company" Section 9 violation; the seller would owe 3 times the title charges
Same week A title company offers their sales associate $100 per buyer referred Section 8 kickback, even if disclosed
Closing set for a Thursday Closing Disclosure received by Monday 3 business days before consummation: Wed (1), Tue (2), Mon (3)
If it is e-mailed instead Must be sent by the previous Thursday: received Fri (1), Sat (2), Mon (3) Saturdays count; Sunday does not
Tuesday The lender corrects a fee typo; APR, product and prepayment terms unchanged No new 3-day wait
After closing Ana wants to cancel the purchase loan No rescission right on a purchase loan

Two years later, still living in the home, they take a home-equity loan secured by it from a different lender. They sign on a Friday and receive the notice and all disclosures that day. They may rescind until midnight Tuesday: Saturday (1), Monday (2), Tuesday (3).

Years later, their listing ad for a sale of the home reads "Only $15,000 down". That is a trigger term, so the ad must also state the repayment terms and the APR.

6. Portugal comparison

This course has no verified Portuguese comparison for RESPA, TILA or TRID. Portuguese rules on mortgage-credit disclosures, cooling-off periods or referral fees require verification and must never answer a Florida question. Use the US day counts and business-day definitions above.

7. Legal and numerical requirements

Memorize exactly

  • RESPA: federally related loans on 1–4 unit residential property (V-53).
  • Section 8: no kickbacks or unearned fees for settlement-service referrals (V-53); disclosure does not cure.
  • Section 9: a seller may not require a particular title insurer; liability is 3× the title insurance charges (V-53).
  • Loan Estimate: delivered or mailed within 3 business days after application (and at least 7 business days before consummation) (V-50).
  • Closing Disclosure: received at least 3 business days before consummation. A new wait applies only for an inaccurate APR, a changed loan product, or an added prepayment penalty (V-50).
  • Trigger terms: down payment (amount or %), number of payments / repayment period, payment amount, finance charge. Then disclose the down payment, repayment terms and APR (V-52).
  • Rescission: 3 business days (Saturdays count), principal dwelling, refinance or home equity. Not for loans to buy or build the home, or investment property (V-51).

Understand

  • Different "business day" definitions apply (TRID table in section 3). For the Closing Disclosure and for rescission, Saturdays count; for the 3-day Loan Estimate deadline, only days the lender is open for substantially all its business count.
  • Rescission runs from the latest of consummation, notice and material disclosures (up to 3 years if they are never given). A same-lender refinance can be rescinded only for the new money.
  • No 2025 or 2026 rule changing TRID timing was found. A July 2026 CFPB request for information only asks for comment.
  • From the manual only (manual; not yet verified): "compare loans by APR, not note rate"; the examples of settlement services (title, inspection, lending); and the CFPB administering TRID.

8. Visual explanation

Application6 items received · clock starts
Loan EstimateWithin 3 business days after application
Closing DisclosureReceived ≥ 3 business days before consummation
ConsummationLoan closing
RescissionRefi / home equity only · midnight of 3rd business day

3 after applying · 3 before closing · 3 to rescind a refinance.

Ad wording Trigger?
"Only $15,000 down" · "10% down" Yes: down payment
"Payments of $1,950 a month" Yes: payment amount
"30-year loan" · "360 payments" Yes: repayment period / number of payments
"No down payment" · "Low monthly payments" · "Easy financing" No
"6.5% APR" alone · "No closing costs" No

9. Common misconceptions

  • "A buyer can rescind her purchase mortgage within 3 days." Rescission does not apply to loans to buy or build the home.
  • "Disclosing a referral fee makes it legal under RESPA." RESPA prohibits the kickback outright.
  • "The Loan Estimate comes 3 days before closing." The Loan Estimate comes within 3 business days after application. The Closing Disclosure must be received 3 business days before closing.
  • "Saturdays never count." They count for the Closing Disclosure and for rescission.
  • "Any change to the Closing Disclosure restarts the 3 days." Only an inaccurate APR, a changed loan product or an added prepayment penalty.
  • "'Low monthly payments' is a trigger term." Only specific terms trigger. Stating the APR alone does not.
  • "RESPA covers every real estate loan." Only federally related loans on 1–4 unit residential property.
  • "A seller may insist on her title company if she discloses it." Section 9 forbids it, with 3× liability.
  • "A refinance of a rental property can be rescinded." It is not the principal dwelling.

10. Memory sheet

  • RESPA = closing + no kickbacks (§8) + buyer picks the title insurer (§9, 3×). 1–4 units, federally related.
  • TILA = APR + trigger terms + rescission.
  • 3 after applying (Loan Estimate) · 3 before closing (Closing Disclosure) · 3 to rescind a refinance or home-equity loan.
  • New Closing Disclosure wait only for APR, product, prepayment penalty.
  • Triggers: down, number, payment, finance charge → disclose down payment, repayment terms, APR.
  • Rescind the refi, never the purchase. Saturdays count.

lessons.title: Florida Residential Landlord and Tenant Act
lessons.manual: M5 §Florida Residential Landlord and Tenant Act
lessons.html:
2. Why it matters

Many Florida licensees lease and manage rentals for owners, and almost every sales associate eventually writes a lease. The Florida Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (Chapter 83, F.S.) sets the deadlines a landlord or property manager must meet. Missing one can cost the landlord the right to keep any of the deposit.

On the exam (Section VII, 3%, shared with L07-1 to L07-3), this lesson is mostly day counts: 30 (deposit notice), 15 / 30 / 15 (move-out) and 60 / 30 / 30 / 7 (ending tenancies). Several rules differ from the study manual: the month-to-month notice (15 days in the 2014 statute and in older books, 30 days now), e-mail delivery of deposit notices (since July 1, 2025) and a new flood disclosure for leases (since October 1, 2025).

3. Simple explanation

Holding the tenant's money

A security deposit protects the landlord against damage or unpaid rent. Advance rent is rent paid before the period it covers. In both cases the landlord is holding money that came from the tenant, so the law says how the landlord must hold it and how the tenant must be told.

  • How it is held. The money is kept in a separate Florida bank account, which may or may not pay interest, or the landlord posts a surety bond (a guarantee from a bonding company) instead.
  • Written notice, in the lease or within 30 days of receipt. The notice gives:
    • the name and address of the depository (bank) holding the money, or a statement that a surety bond was posted;
    • whether the tenant is entitled to interest;
    • the disclosure text required by the statute.
  • How the notice is delivered. In person or by mail. Since July 1, 2025 it may also go by e-mail under s. 83.505, but only if both parties signed the statutory e-mail addendum.
  • Changes. If the landlord later changes how or where the money is held, the tenant must be told within 30 days after the change.
  • Exception. This notice rule does not apply to a landlord who rents fewer than five individual dwelling units.
  • Rent is still due. A missing notice is not a defense to paying rent on time.

After the tenancy ends: 15 / 30 / 15

The clock starts when the tenancy ends. V-63 counts from the end of the rental agreement; the study manual says "after the tenant moves out". When the tenant leaves at the end of the lease, these are the same day.

  1. No claim. If the landlord will not claim any of the deposit, it is returned, with interest if required, within 15 days.
  2. Claim. If the landlord intends to keep some or all of it, the landlord sends written notice within 30 days, stating the reason. The notice goes by certified mail (mail with proof of mailing and delivery) to the tenant's last known mailing address. Since July 1, 2025, it may also go by e-mail, if both parties signed the s. 83.505 e-mail addendum and gave e-mail addresses.
  3. Objection. The tenant has 15 days after receiving the notice to object. Without an objection, the landlord deducts the claim and sends the balance within 30 days after the date of the notice.
  4. Missed deadline. A landlord who misses the 30-day notice forfeits the right to claim against the deposit and may not set the damage off against it. The landlord may still sue for damages after returning the deposit.

In a dispute over the deposit, the winning party recovers attorney's fees.

The idea behind the deadlines: the tenant should not wait indefinitely for their own money. A landlord who stays silent past day 30 loses the right to take any of it from the deposit.

Ending a tenancy without a specific term (s. 83.57)

Some tenancies have no end date. They simply renew each week, month, quarter or year. To end one, written notice must be given at least this long before the end of a period:

Tenancy Minimum written notice
Year to year 60 days
Quarter to quarter 30 days
Month to month 30 days
Week to week 7 days

Correction (V-04). The study manual lists 15 days for month to month and 45 days for quarter to quarter. Current law says 30 and 30. Older books show 15 days for month to month because the statute later changed (the 2014 text had 15 days). No version of the statute with 45 days was found. If a practice question uses 15 days for month to month, it reflects the old law: answer with current law (30 days) unless the question says otherwise.

Flood disclosure for leases (s. 83.512, since October 1, 2025)

  • When. Before or at the signing of a residential lease for a term of 1 year or longer. Shorter leases are not covered.
  • Form. A separate document on the statutory form. It covers:
    • flood damage the landlord knows of during the landlord's ownership;
    • flood insurance claims, including claims under the NFIP (National Flood Insurance Program);
    • federal assistance received for flood damage, such as from FEMA (Federal Emergency Management Agency);
    • notices about flood insurance.
  • Remedy. If the landlord does not comply, and the tenant suffers a substantial loss of personal property from flooding, the tenant may end the lease. A substantial loss means repair or replacement costs of 50% or more of the property's market value. The tenant ends the lease by written notice and by giving up possession within 30 days after the damage. The landlord refunds rent paid in advance for the period after termination.
  • Origin. The rule was enacted by CS/CS/SB 948 (ch. 2025-166, Laws of Fla.). A companion House bill, HB 1015, was tabled. Older books will not mention it.

Other lease disclosures (taught elsewhere)

  • Radon: the statutory radon notice appears on at least one document signed at or before a rental agreement for any building (L11-4, L19-2).
  • Lead-based paint, for housing built before 1978: lessors give the disclosure (EPA pamphlet, known lead paint and hazards, available reports), but tenants do not get the buyer's 10-day inspection opportunity (L19-2).

4. Key terms

Term Meaning
Security deposit Money the tenant pays to secure performance of the lease
Advance rent Rent paid before the period it covers
Surety bond A bond posted by the landlord instead of holding the deposit in an account
Depository The bank or institution holding the deposit
Certified mail Mail sent with proof of mailing and delivery
E-mail addendum (s. 83.505) Signed lease addendum allowing notices by e-mail (since July 1, 2025)
Notice of intention to impose a claim The landlord's written notice, within 30 days, stating why part of the deposit will be kept
Forfeit Lose a right by failing to meet a condition or deadline
Tenancy without a specific term A periodic tenancy that renews week to week, month to month, quarter to quarter or year to year

5. Practical example

Carla, a sales associate in Gainesville, manages 8 apartments for one owner. A tenant signs a 12-month lease running July 1 to June 30 and pays a $2,000 deposit.

Moment What Carla must do Rule
At or before signing Give the flood disclosure form Lease of 1 year or longer
In the lease (or within 30 days of receiving the deposit) Give the name and address of the bank holding the deposit (or state that a surety bond was posted) and say whether interest is paid Owner rents 5 or more units
Lease ends June 30, no damage Return the $2,000 by July 15 15 days
Lease ends June 30, broken door ($400) Send notice of the claim by July 30, by certified mail (or e-mail if the addendum was signed) 30 days
Notice sent July 10, received July 13 The tenant may object until July 28 15 days after receipt
No objection Deduct $400 and send $1,600 by August 9 30 days after the date of the notice
Notice sent August 4 instead Too late: no claim against the deposit. Return the full $2,000; the owner may sue for damages separately. Forfeiture

In the same building, a month-to-month tenant's period ends September 30. To end that tenancy, the owner gives written notice at least 30 days before September 30, for example on August 25. A notice sent 15 days ahead follows outdated law.

A snowbird's 6-month seasonal lease does not require the flood disclosure.

6. Portugal comparison

Familiar principle. In Portugal, urban leases are governed by the Civil Code and the NRAU. Their written-form and registration requirements require verification.

Florida rule. A lease of 1 year or less may be oral. A longer lease must be in writing (statute of frauds), but leases no longer need witnesses (s. 689.01, V-05). Florida sets exact day counts: 60 / 30 / 30 / 7 to end tenancies without a specific term, 30 days for the deposit notice, and 15 / 30 / 15 at move-out.

Precise difference. The exam tests these specific Florida day counts. Portuguese notice periods and deposit customs must not be carried over.

Exam implication. A month-to-month tenant in Orlando gets written notice at least 30 days before the end of a monthly period. Use the current s. 83.57 periods.

7. Legal and numerical requirements

Memorize exactly

  • Deposit notice: in the lease or within 30 days of receipt: the depository's name and address (or a surety bond) and whether interest is paid. Not required for landlords who rent fewer than 5 units. A change in how it is held: notice within 30 days (V-62).
  • Move-out: 15 days to return (no claim) · 30 days to send the claim notice (certified mail, or e-mail with a signed s. 83.505 addendum since July 1, 2025) · tenant objects within 15 days of receipt · balance within 30 days of the notice date (V-63).
  • A missed 30-day notice forfeits the claim against the deposit. A separate lawsuit for damages remains possible.
  • Termination notices (s. 83.57): 60 / 30 / 30 / 7 (year / quarter / month / week) (V-04).
  • Flood disclosure (s. 83.512, since October 1, 2025): residential lease of 1 year or longer, at or before signing, separate statutory form (V-07).

Understand

  • Outdated figures:
    • 15 days (month to month) and 45 days (quarter to quarter) are outdated or incorrect.
    • "Certified mail only" is outdated since July 1, 2025 (ch. 2025-16, Laws of Fla.).
    • The old wording, notice of "the manner in which the deposit is held", has been replaced by the current disclosure, but the answer is still 30 days.
  • Flood remedy: a substantial loss (50% or more of market value) lets the tenant terminate within 30 days after the damage, with a refund of prepaid rent.
  • Leases over 1 year must be in writing (statute of frauds), and leases need no witnesses (V-05).
  • From the manual only (manual; not yet verified): the separate Florida account, interest-bearing or not, as a way to hold the deposit; attorney's fees for the prevailing party in a deposit dispute.

8. Visual explanation

Day 0Rental agreement ends
By day 15No claim → deposit returned (with interest if required)
By day 30Claim → written notice by certified mail or e-mail addendum. Missed = claim forfeited
15 days after receiptTenant's deadline to object
30 days after notice dateNo objection → landlord deducts and sends the balance

15 return · 30 claim · 15 object.

Number Means
30 Deposit notice (in the lease or within 30 days) · claim notice · month-to-month and quarter-to-quarter termination · flood-loss termination window
15 Return with no claim · tenant's objection window
60 Year-to-year termination
7 Week-to-week termination
5 Landlords with fewer than 5 units are exempt from the deposit notice
1 year Lease term that triggers the flood disclosure

9. Common misconceptions

  • "Month to month needs 15 days' notice." That is the old law. It is 30 days.
  • "Quarter to quarter needs 45 days." It is 30 days. No version with 45 days was found.
  • "A late claim notice still lets the landlord deduct, because the damage is real." A missed 30-day notice forfeits the claim against the deposit. The landlord must sue separately.
  • "The landlord has 30 days to return the deposit in every case." With no claim, it is 15 days.
  • "The tenant has 15 days from move-out to object." The 15 days run from receiving the notice.
  • "Only certified mail is valid." Since July 1, 2025, e-mail also works if both parties signed the e-mail addendum.
  • "Every landlord must send the deposit notice." Landlords who rent fewer than 5 units are exempt.
  • "No deposit notice means the tenant can stop paying rent." It is not a defense to paying rent.
  • "The flood disclosure applies only in flood zones, or to every lease." It applies to residential leases of 1 year or longer, with no flood-zone condition.

10. Memory sheet

  • Deposit notice: in the lease or 30 days · bank or surety bond · interest yes/no · exempt if <5 units.
  • Move-out: 15 return · 30 claim · 15 object · balance within 30 days of the notice. Late notice = forfeit.
  • Notice delivery: certified mail or e-mail with a signed addendum (since 7/1/2025).
  • End a tenancy: 60 / 30 / 30 / 7 (year / quarter / month / week). 15 and 45 are outdated.
  • Lease of 1 year or more → flood form at or before signing (s. 83.512, since 10/1/2025).

lessons.title: Freehold estates and the bundle of rights
lessons.html:
2. Why it matters

Every listing starts with one question: what exactly does this seller own? In Florida you answer it by reading the deed and the title work, and those documents describe ownership with the vocabulary in this lesson. A seller who holds only a life estate cannot sell the house permanently, and a buyer who receives a fee simple gets something very different from a tenant who signs a lease.

For the exam, this lesson opens Section VIII, Property Rights, which is 8% of the Sales Associate exam (V-02). The questions are short definition tests with a twist. You may be asked to spot the item that is not in the bundle of rights, pick the largest estate, say whether a future interest is a remainder or a reversion, or recognize waste. The same vocabulary returns in Chapter 9 (title and deeds).

3. Simple explanation

Real property is land plus rights

US courses distinguish real estate (land plus permanent improvements) from real property (real estate plus the rights of ownership). Those rights are called the bundle of rights, like a bundle of sticks. There are five:

Right What it lets the owner do Example
Possession Occupy the property Live in the house
Control Decide how the property is used, within the law Repaint, renovate, add a pool
Enjoyment Use it and benefit from it without interference Live there in peace, earn income from it
Exclusion Keep others out Refuse entry to trespassers
Disposition Transfer it Sell it, give it away, leave it by will

The manual's mnemonic is D.E.E.P. C: Disposition, Enjoyment, Exclusion, Possession, Control.

Why call it a "bundle"? Because the sticks can be separated. An owner who leases her condo hands the possession stick to the tenant for a while but keeps disposition, so she can still sell. The bundle is never unlimited: government powers such as taxation, eminent domain and escheat (L09-1) apply to every owner. Escheat is a power of the state, not a right in the bundle.

An estate measures "how much" and "how long"

An estate is an interest in land. It is defined by how much of the bundle it gives and how long it lasts. Estates fall into two families:

  • Freehold estates are ownership for an indefinite time. "Indefinite" does not mean "forever". It means the end date is not fixed in advance. Nobody knows the day a person will die, so an estate that ends at someone's death is still a freehold.
  • Leasehold (nonfreehold) estates are possession without ownership, under a lease (L08-2). An estate for years ends on a date known from the start and gives possession, not ownership, so it is a leasehold however long the term is.
