  • Possession described as open, notorious, hostile, continuous (manual; not yet verified as statutory wording).
  • 20 years = prescriptive easement, case law (V-69), not adverse possession.
  • Testate → devise → devisee. Intestate → descent → heirs. No will and no heirs → escheat (manual; not yet verified).
  • Title passes on delivery and acceptance during the grantor's lifetime, not on signing or recording (manual; not yet verified).
  • A will operates only at death and is revocable until then; homestead devise restrictions (spouse or minor child) override it (manual; not yet verified).

Understand

  • Probate exists so a buyer can trust that an heir or devisee really holds title.
  • Payment in eminent domain does not make it voluntary.
  • Adverse possession is strict because the owner loses land without payment.
  • Source status: the adverse possession rules were checked against ss. 95.16 and 95.18 (V-68), and the 20-year prescriptive easement period is confirmed as Florida case law (V-69). Everything else comes from the study manual (manual; not yet verified; V-26).

8. Visual explanation

The owner has died: where does the real property go?

Did the owner leave a valid will?
Yes → testate: passes by devise to the devisees (probate proves the will; homestead restrictions can override it)
No will. Are there heirs?
Yes → intestate: passes by descent to the heirs under Florida's statute of descent
No will and no heirs → escheat to the state

Source: study manual (manual; not yet verified).

Adverse possession without color of title (s. 95.18, V-68)

Day 0Enters actual possession, claiming the land exclusively; no written instrument
Within 1 yearPays all outstanding taxes and matured installments of special improvement liens
Within 30 days of payingFiles a return with the county property appraiser: DOR form, legal description, notarized attestation
Through year 7Keeps paying all taxes and liens; possession continues without a break
End of year 7Only the land actually possessed (enclosed, cultivated, maintained or improved) is held adversely

With color of title (s. 95.16): a written instrument, decree or judgment (for possession beginning after December 31, 1945, recorded with the clerk of the circuit court in the county), plus 7 years of continued possession (V-68).

9. Common misconceptions

  • "Adverse possession takes 20 years in Florida." It takes 7. Twenty years is the prescriptive easement period, and an easement is only a right to use (V-69).
  • "Seven years of living on the land is enough." Florida also requires color of title (a recorded instrument) or the tax payment, the return and continued payments (V-68).
  • "Paying the taxes on someone's land makes it mine." Taxes are one condition, not a substitute for 7 years of possession; only land actually possessed counts (V-68).
  • "Using the land with the owner's permission still counts." Permission means the possession is not hostile (manual; not yet verified).
  • "Descent means passing property under a will." Descent is the no-will route; a will passes real property by devise (manual; not yet verified).
  • "Bequest and devise mean the same thing." Real property left by will is a devise. "Bequest" usually means a gift of personal property by will (general vocabulary, not in this course's sources; not yet verified).
  • "Escheat and eminent domain are the same." Escheat: owner dies with no will and no heirs. Eminent domain: a taking for public use with just compensation (manual; not yet verified).
  • "Signing a will or recording a deed transfers title." A will operates only at death; a deed transfers title on delivery and acceptance during the grantor's lifetime (manual; not yet verified).

10. Memory sheet

  • Voluntary: deed (sale or gift), will. Involuntary: descent, escheat, eminent domain, foreclosure, adverse possession.
  • 7 years + color of title or taxes (V-68). Color of title = recorded instrument, decree or judgment. No color = taxes within 1 year, return within 30 days, keep paying.
  • Open, notorious, hostile, continuous (exam labels: manual; not yet verified as statutory wording). Only land actually possessed counts (V-68).
  • 20 years = prescriptive easement (V-69), not adverse possession.
  • Devise = will. Descent = no will. Escheat = no will and no heirs → state.
  • Probate proves the will and clears title. Homestead restrictions override the will.
  • Will: effective at death, revocable before. Deed: title passes on delivery and acceptance during life.
  • Items without a V-number: manual; not yet verified.

lessons.title: Deeds: types and requirements
lessons.html:
2. Why it matters

The deed is the document that actually moves ownership at a Florida closing. Two practical questions come up in almost every sale: what kind of deed will the buyer receive, and is the deed valid? The deed type tells your buyer how much the seller promises about the title. A missing witness, or a deed that was never delivered, can stop a closing or leave a buyer without title. Two Florida details deserve special attention because they are easy to get wrong: the grantor signs before two witnesses, and the grantee (the buyer) does not sign the deed at all.

This is a high-priority lesson in Section 9 of the course outline (about 7% of the exam). Expect "Which deed gives the most protection?" (general warranty), "Which deed cures a cloud on title?" (quitclaim) and "How many witnesses?" (two). Expect also the classic trap "Which is essential to a valid deed?", where the grantee's signature, recording and notarization are the wrong answers.

3. Simple explanation

What a deed does

A deed is a written instrument by which the grantor (the person transferring) conveys title to the grantee (the person receiving). Besides transferring title, a deed may contain warranties, also called covenants: promises by the grantor about the quality of the title. The more the grantor promises, and the longer the period the promises cover, the more protection the buyer has. That is the whole logic of the ranking below.

Four deeds, from most to least protection

Rank Deed What the grantor warrants Period covered
1 General warranty Title against defects arising at any time, even before the grantor owned the property. Gives the five covenants below All time
2 Special warranty Only defects arising during the grantor's own ownership The grantor's ownership
3 Bargain and sale Implies that the grantor owns the property, but gives no warranties None
4 Quitclaim Nothing. It conveys whatever interest the grantor has, if any None

(manual; not yet verified)

Why a quitclaim is useful although it promises nothing. A cloud on title is a claim or defect that impairs title, such as an ex-spouse's stray interest or a misspelled heir. The person who might hold that interest signs a quitclaim deed, handing over whatever he or she may have, and the cloud is removed. The other side of the coin: a quitclaim from someone who owns nothing conveys nothing.

The five covenants of a general warranty deed

Covenant Plain meaning
Seisin The grantor owns the property and has the right to convey it
Quiet enjoyment The grantee will not be disturbed by someone with a better claim to the title
Against encumbrances There are no encumbrances (claims such as liens or easements) other than those stated in the deed
Further assurance The grantor will sign or do whatever else is later needed to perfect the grantee's title
Warranty forever The grantor will defend the title against lawful claims, with no time limit

(The list of covenants and the meaning of seisin are from the manual and glossary; the other plain-language meanings are general explanations, not found in this course's sources. Not yet verified.)

What a valid Florida deed requires

Validity answers one question: does this document transfer title from the grantor to the grantee?

# Requirement Why it exists
1 A written instrument Proof of exactly what was transferred
2 A competent grantor: of legal age (18 or older) and mentally competent The grantor is the one giving up rights
3 An identifiable grantee, who may be a minor The grantee only receives, so competence is not required
4 Consideration; a nominal amount (such as ten dollars) is enough Shows that something of value was given; the deed need not show the real price
5 Words of conveyance (the granting clause) Shows the intent to transfer
6 A legal description Identifies the land exactly; a street address is never a legal description
7 The grantor's signature in the presence of two subscribing witnesses (s. 689.01) Florida's statutory formality for conveyances (V-05)
8 Delivery and acceptance during the grantor's lifetime The moment title passes

Rows 1–6 and 8: manual; not yet verified. Row 7: verified (V-05). The legal description systems are covered in a later lesson.

The witnesses, in detail (V-05). A subscribing witness watches the grantor sign and then signs the deed as a witness. Section 689.01 requires two of them for conveyances of freehold estates (ownership estates, L08-1) and of terms over one year. Witnesses may also sign electronically through audio-video technology (s. 117.201). The same section now adds a proviso that no subscribing witnesses are required for a lease of real property, so the general wording about terms over one year no longer makes a lease need witnesses. Older books say a lease over one year needs two witnesses: that rule is outdated (the lease proviso appears in the 2024 text and is absent from the 2010–2019 texts). A lease over one year must still be in writing under the statute of frauds. For the exam, follow V-05: deeds, two witnesses; leases, none.

What is NOT required for validity

  • The grantee's signature. Only the grantor signs.
  • Recording. Recording protects the grantee against the world (L09-3). Delivery makes the deed valid between the parties.
  • A notary's acknowledgment. An acknowledgment is a formal declaration before a notary that the signer signed voluntarily. It is required to record the deed, not to make it valid.

(manual; not yet verified)

Because every buyer wants the deed recorded, a real closing will include the acknowledgment as well. On the exam, keep the two purposes apart: delivery makes it valid; recording warns the world.

4. Key terms

Term Meaning
Deed Written instrument by which a grantor conveys title to a grantee
Grantor / grantee The person conveying / receiving title by deed
Warranty (covenant) A promise by the grantor about the title
General warranty deed Grantor warrants title against defects from any time; five covenants
Special warranty deed Grantor warrants only against defects arising during their ownership
Bargain and sale deed Implies the grantor owns the property, with no warranties
Quitclaim deed Conveys whatever interest the grantor has, with no warranties
Cloud on title A claim or defect that impairs title
Seisin Covenant that the grantor owns the property and has the right to convey it
Encumbrance A claim against or limitation on the property, such as a lien or an easement
Consideration Something of value given for the deed; a nominal amount is enough
Granting clause The words of conveyance that transfer title
Legal description Exact identification of the land; never just a street address
Subscribing witness A person who watches the grantor sign and signs as a witness; Florida deeds need two
Acknowledgment Formal declaration before a notary that the signer signed voluntarily; needed to record
Delivery and acceptance The grantor hands over the deed intending to transfer, and the grantee accepts it; title passes here

5. Practical example

Beatriz, who recently moved from Porto to Orlando, is buying a townhouse in Kissimmee (Osceola County) from Daniel Price, who bought it in 2019. The title work shows that Daniel's ex-wife, Karen, may still hold an interest from their 2021 divorce.

Question Answer Rule applied
Beatriz wants the deed that protects her most. Which one? A general warranty deed: Daniel would warrant against defects from any time, even before 2019 Ranking
The contract allows a special warranty deed instead. What does Daniel promise? Only that no defect arose while he owned it (2019 to the sale). A defect created in 2015 is outside his promise; Beatriz would rely on title insurance (L09-3) Special warranty = grantor's ownership only
How is Karen's possible interest removed? Karen signs a quitclaim deed releasing whatever interest she may have Quitclaim cures a cloud
At closing, the second witness leaves early and Daniel signs before one witness. Is that acceptable? No. The deed must be signed before two subscribing witnesses (s. 689.01, V-05) Witness requirement
Must Beatriz sign the deed? No. The grantee does not sign Grantee's signature not required
The deed says "ten dollars and other consideration", not the real price. Is that a problem? No. Nominal consideration is enough Consideration
When does Beatriz become the owner? When the properly signed deed is delivered to her and she accepts it Delivery and acceptance
The deed is recorded three days later. Did recording make it valid? No. It was already valid. Recording gives constructive notice to the world (L09-3) Recording is not a validity requirement

A different file: the deed in the drawer. In 2022 Ms. Ortiz signed a deed of her Kissimmee condo to her son, but she kept it in her desk. It was found only after her death in 2025. The deed was never delivered during her lifetime, so it did not transfer title. The condo passes under her will or by descent (L09-1), not under the deed.

(All rows except the witness rule: manual; not yet verified.)

6. Portugal comparison

Familiar principle. In Portugal a sale is formalized in a public deed or an authenticated private document, and Portuguese practice does not use graded "warranty deed" types (Portuguese side: requires verification; PT-12).

Florida rule. Florida deeds are ranked by the warranties the grantor gives: general warranty (all time), special warranty (the grantor's ownership period), bargain and sale (implied ownership, no warranties) and quitclaim (no warranties). A valid deed needs the grantor's signature before two witnesses (V-05) and delivery and acceptance.

Precise difference. In Florida, the choice of deed type decides how much the seller promises about the title, and two witnesses are a validity requirement for a deed. Do not assume that a notary's involvement is what makes the transfer valid: in Florida the acknowledgment is needed to record the deed, not for validity (manual; not yet verified). Whether Portuguese formalities give the buyer any comparable promises about title requires verification.

Exam implication. The grantee does not sign; notary acknowledgment is for recording. To clear an ex-spouse's possible interest, the ex-spouse signs a quitclaim deed. Answer every deed question from Florida rules only.

7. Legal and numerical requirements

Memorize exactly

  • Ranking: general warranty > special warranty > bargain and sale > quitclaim (manual; not yet verified).
  • General warranty covenants: seisin, quiet enjoyment, against encumbrances, further assurance, warranty forever (manual; not yet verified).
  • Valid deed: written instrument; competent grantor (18 or older, mentally competent); identifiable grantee (may be a minor); consideration (nominal is enough); words of conveyance; legal description; delivery and acceptance during the grantor's lifetime (manual; not yet verified).
  • Grantor signs before 2 subscribing witnesses (s. 689.01; V-05, corrected). Witnesses may sign electronically through audio-video technology (s. 117.201).
  • Leases: no witnesses required (V-05). "Two witnesses for leases over one year" is outdated. A lease over one year must still be in writing (statute of frauds).
  • Not required for validity: the grantee's signature, recording, acknowledgment. Acknowledgment is required to record (manual; not yet verified).

Understand

  • Validity is about the parties; recording is about the world.
  • A special warranty deed leaves defects from before the grantor's ownership outside the grantor's promise.
  • A quitclaim conveys only what the grantor has, which may be nothing.
  • The grantor must be competent because the grantor gives up rights; the grantee only receives.
  • Source status: everything except the witness rule comes from the study manual (manual; not yet verified; V-26). The witness rule was checked against the 2024–2026 text of s. 689.01 (V-05), which corrected the manual on leases.

8. Visual explanation

General warrantyAll defects, all time, even before the grantor owned it · five covenants · maximum protection
Special warrantyOnly defects arising during the grantor's ownership
Bargain and saleImplies ownership · no warranties
QuitclaimWhatever interest the grantor has, if any · no warranties · cures a cloud on title

From most protection (top) to least (bottom). Source: study manual (manual; not yet verified).

Is it required for a valid Florida deed?

Element Required for validity? Note
Written instrument Yes
Competent grantor Yes 18 or older and mentally competent
Identifiable grantee Yes May be a minor
Consideration Yes Nominal is enough
Words of conveyance Yes The granting clause
Legal description Yes A street address is not enough
Grantor's signature before 2 witnesses Yes s. 689.01 (V-05)
Delivery and acceptance Yes During the grantor's lifetime; title passes here
Grantee's signature No The grantee does not sign
Notary acknowledgment No Required to record
Recording No Gives constructive notice (L09-3)

All rows except the witness row: manual; not yet verified.

9. Common misconceptions

  • "The buyer signs the deed at closing." Only the grantor signs (manual; not yet verified).
  • "A deed is not valid until it is recorded." Delivery and acceptance make it valid; recording protects against the world (manual; not yet verified).
  • "The notary makes the deed valid." The acknowledgment is needed to record, not for validity (manual; not yet verified).
  • "One witness is enough." A Florida deed needs two subscribing witnesses (s. 689.01, V-05).
  • "A lease over one year needs two witnesses." Outdated. Leases need no witnesses now, but a lease over one year must still be in writing (V-05).
  • "A special warranty deed covers every past defect." It covers only defects arising during the grantor's ownership.
  • "A bargain and sale deed gives warranties because it implies ownership." It implies ownership but gives no warranties.
  • "A quitclaim deed proves the grantor owns something." It promises nothing and conveys whatever interest the grantor has, if any.
  • "A signed deed kept in a drawer transfers title." Title passes only on delivery and acceptance during the grantor's lifetime (manual; not yet verified).
  • "A minor cannot receive a deed." The grantee may be a minor; it is the grantor who must be competent (manual; not yet verified).
  • "The deed must state the full price." Nominal consideration is enough (manual; not yet verified).

(Corrections without a V-number: manual; not yet verified.)

10. Memory sheet

  • General > special > bargain & sale > quitclaim.
  • General = all time + 5 covenants (seisin, quiet enjoyment, against encumbrances, further assurance, warranty forever). Special = grantor's ownership only. Bargain and sale = implied ownership, no warranties. Quitclaim = no warranties, cures clouds.
  • Valid deed: writing · competent grantor (minor grantee OK) · consideration (nominal) · granting clause · legal description · 2 witnesses (V-05) · delivery and acceptance.
  • Not required: grantee's signature · recording · acknowledgment (needed to record).
  • Leases: no witnesses (V-05); "2 witnesses for leases over 1 year" is outdated.
  • Delivery makes it valid; recording warns the world.
  • Items without a V-number: manual; not yet verified.

lessons.title: Notice, recording and title evidence
lessons.html:
2. Why it matters

Buyers ask two questions you should be able to answer in plain words: "How do I know the seller really owns this?" and "What protects me if an old problem with the title appears after I buy?" In Florida the answers are the public records and title insurance. Recording also explains why a buyer is bound by an easement recorded decades ago, even if nobody mentioned it during the sale.

For the exam (Section 9 of the course outline, about 7% of the exam), expect questions on constructive versus actual notice, on whether recording is needed for a deed to be valid (it is not), on an abstract with an attorney's opinion versus title insurance, on the owner's versus the lender's policy, and on what title insurance does not cover: problems created after the policy date, and physical damage.

3. Simple explanation

Why recording exists

From L09-2: a properly signed and witnessed deed is valid between grantor and grantee once it is delivered and accepted; recording is not required. But nobody else can see a deed kept in a drawer. Recording places the document in the county public records, where anyone can search it. Recording does not make a deed valid. It warns the world.

Two kinds of notice

  • Constructive notice is notice the law presumes from the public records and from visible possession of the property, whether or not the person actually looked. Once a document is recorded, everyone is treated as knowing it.
  • Actual notice is what a person actually knows, because she was told, read a document or saw something herself.

Why does the law presume knowledge? The records are open to everyone, so a buyer who skips the search cannot rely on her own failure to look. Visible possession works the same way: if someone other than the seller is living on the property, a buyer is expected to find out on what basis, for example a tenant with a lease. (manual; not yet verified)

Who wins when two people claim the same property

Florida's recording system protects a good-faith purchaser who records without notice of prior claims (manual; not yet verified). Follow the logic:

  1. A seller signs and delivers a deed to Buyer A, who does not record it.
  2. The seller dishonestly signs a second deed to Buyer B. B searches the records and finds nothing, has no other knowledge of A's deed, and records.
  3. B is a good-faith purchaser without notice who recorded, so the rule protects B. A's deed was valid between A and the seller, but A carried the risk of not recording.

The protection depends on no notice. If B had actual notice of A's deed, B would not be protected. If A had already moved into the house, A's visible possession would give B constructive notice. The practical lesson: record promptly.

Title evidence: proving marketable title

Marketable title is title a reasonable buyer would accept, free of serious defects and clouds (general definition, not from this course's sources; not yet verified). A Florida buyer evidences it in one of two ways:

Abstract of title + attorney's opinion Title insurance
What it is An abstract is a summary of all recorded documents affecting the title. An attorney examines it and gives an opinion on the title A policy that protects against losses from title defects existing before the policy date
What it rests on What the records show The records, plus the insurer's promise covering defects that existed before the policy date but were undiscovered
Status The traditional method The modern standard

(manual; not yet verified)

An abstract and an opinion can only describe what the records show. Title insurance adds protection against a hidden past defect, such as a forged deed in the property's history.

Owner's policy and lender's policy

Owner's policy Lender's policy
Protects The owner (the buyer) The lender
Amount The purchase price The loan amount
Over time Protects the owner as long as she owns the property Declines as the loan balance is paid down
Transfer Not transferable to the next buyer Follows the loan

(manual; not yet verified)

Title insurance looks backward

Title insurance covers defects existing before the policy date, even undiscovered ones. It never covers defects the owner creates later, such as a lien she allows to attach after closing. It does not cover later events such as a zoning change after closing, and it is not property insurance, so it does not pay for physical damage from a hurricane or flood. Why? The title work examines the property's history up to the policy date. Whatever arises after that date, whether the owner's own debts or outside changes, is outside what the policy insures. (manual; not yet verified)

Related federal rule (V-53, confirmed). Under Section 9 of RESPA (the federal Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act), which applies to federally related mortgage loans on 1–4 family residential property, a seller may not require the buyer to use a particular title insurer. A seller who does is liable for 3 times the title charges. RESPA is covered in a later chapter.

4. Key terms

Term Meaning
Recording Placing a document in the county public records so that the world has notice of it
Constructive notice Notice the law presumes from the public records or visible possession, whether or not the person looked
Actual notice What a person actually knows
Good-faith purchaser A buyer acting honestly and without notice of prior claims
Marketable title Title a reasonable buyer would accept, free of serious defects and clouds
Abstract of title Summary of all recorded documents affecting a property's title
Attorney's opinion An attorney's conclusion on the title after examining the abstract
Title insurance Policy protecting against losses from title defects existing before the policy date
Policy date The dividing line: defects existing before it are covered; problems arising after it are not
Owner's policy Issued for the purchase price; protects the owner while she owns; not transferable
Lender's policy Issued for the loan amount; declines with the balance; follows the loan
Cloud on title A claim or defect that impairs title (L09-2)

5. Practical example

Sofia, a client from Lisbon, buys a house in Fort Myers (Lee County) in November 2026 for $450,000, with a $360,000 mortgage loan.

When Event Result Rule
Before closing The title search shows a utility easement recorded in 1998. Sofia never read it She takes the property subject to the easement Recording = constructive notice
Before closing During a showing, Sofia sees that a man is living in the garage apartment She is treated as knowing whatever rights he has (for example, a lease) and should find out before she buys. If he tells her about his lease, she also has actual notice Visible possession = constructive notice
Closing Two title policies are issued Owner's policy: $450,000 (the price). Lender's policy: $360,000 (the loan) Policy amounts
2028 A man claims that a 2015 deed in the property's history was forged The owner's policy covers the loss Defect existed before the policy date
2029 Sofia does not pay the contractor who built her pool, and a construction (mechanic's) lien attaches to the house Not covered She allowed it to attach after the policy date
2030 A hurricane damages the roof Not a title insurance matter Physical damage is not a title defect
2030 The loan balance is down to $330,000 The lender's coverage has declined with the balance Lender's policy declines
2031 Sofia sells to Marco Her owner's policy does not pass to Marco; his protection must come from a new policy Owner's policy is not transferable

A second file. Sofia's neighbor bought his lot from a seller who, a week earlier, had sold the same lot to someone else by a deed that was never recorded. The neighbor searched the records, knew nothing of the earlier sale, saw nobody occupying the lot, and recorded his deed the same day. As a good-faith purchaser who recorded without notice, he is the one Florida's rule protects.

(All rows: manual; not yet verified.)

6. Portugal comparison

Familiar principle. In Portugal, ownership and charges are recorded in the land registry (registo predial). The degree of protection that registry gives a buyer requires verification (PT-11).

Florida rule. Documents are recorded in county public records, which give constructive notice. Buyers prove marketable title with an abstract plus an attorney's opinion or, usually, title insurance: an owner's policy for the price and a lender's policy for the loan.

Precise difference. Title insurance is a central product in Florida. In Florida, the public records give notice, and protection against a hidden past defect, such as a forged deed, comes from title insurance. The exam tests the owner's versus the lender's policy and what is covered: past defects, not future ones. Example (PT-11): a forged deed from 2015 surfaces after closing, and the owner's title policy covers the loss; a lien the new owner creates in 2027 is not covered. Never use a Portuguese registry rule to answer a Florida question.

Exam implication. Recording protects against third parties; it is not required for a deed to be valid. Memory aid: record to warn the world; insure against the past.

7. Legal and numerical requirements

Memorize exactly

  • Recording = constructive notice to everyone. Visible possession also gives constructive notice. Actual notice = what a person actually knows (manual; not yet verified).
  • Recording is not required for validity between grantor and grantee; delivery and acceptance are (manual; not yet verified).
  • Florida protects a good-faith purchaser who records without notice of prior claims (manual; not yet verified).
  • Title evidence: abstract of title + attorney's opinion, or title insurance (the modern standard) (manual; not yet verified).
  • Owner's policy: purchase price · protects the owner as long as she owns · not transferable (manual; not yet verified).
  • Lender's policy: loan amount · declines with the balance · follows the loan (manual; not yet verified).
  • Title insurance covers defects existing before the policy date, even if undiscovered; never defects the owner creates later (manual; not yet verified).
  • RESPA Section 9: the seller may not require a particular title insurer; liability is 3 times the title charges; applies to federally related mortgage loans on 1–4 family residential property (V-53).

Understand

  • Why the law presumes knowledge: the records are public, so failing to search is no excuse.
  • Notice, actual or constructive, removes the protection the recording system gives a later buyer.
  • An abstract and opinion report what the records show; title insurance also covers hidden defects that existed before the policy date.
  • Title insurance is not property insurance and does not cover later events.
  • Source status: apart from V-53, this lesson rests on the study manual (manual; not yet verified; V-26). This lesson has no deadlines or percentages.

8. Visual explanation

Is the buyer bound by an earlier claim?

Was the earlier claim (a deed, easement or mortgage) recorded in the county public records?
Yes → the buyer is bound: constructive notice, even if she never searched
Not recorded. Did the buyer actually know of it, or would visible possession of the property have revealed it?
Yes → the buyer is bound: actual notice, or constructive notice from possession
No → a good-faith purchaser without notice who records is protected against the unrecorded claim

Source: study manual (manual; not yet verified).

What the owner's policy covers: look at the policy date

2015A forged deed enters the property's history: covered (existed before the policy date, undiscovered)
Nov 2026 · policy dateClosing: owner's policy for the price, lender's policy for the loan
2029A construction lien for pool work the owner did not pay for: not covered (arose after the policy date)
2030Hurricane damage: not covered (physical damage is not a title defect)
2031The owner sells: the owner's policy does not transfer to the new buyer

Title insurance looks backward from the policy date (manual; not yet verified).

9. Common misconceptions

  • "I never saw the recorded easement, so it does not bind me." Recording gives constructive notice to everyone, whether or not they read the records.
  • "Recording makes the deed valid." Delivery and acceptance make it valid; recording warns the world.
  • "If it is not in the records, a buyer can ignore it." Actual knowledge, and visible possession by someone else, also give notice.
  • "Title insurance covers anything that goes wrong with the title." It covers defects existing before the policy date, never defects the owner creates later.
  • "Title insurance pays for hurricane or flood damage." Physical damage is not a title defect.
  • "The owner's policy passes to the next buyer." It is not transferable.
  • "The owner's policy is issued for the loan amount." The owner's policy is for the purchase price; the lender's policy is for the loan amount.
  • "The lender's policy protects the buyer." It protects the lender, declines with the balance and follows the loan.
  • "An abstract of title is the same as title insurance." An abstract summarizes the records and an attorney gives an opinion on them; title insurance is a policy covering losses from pre-policy defects.

(Corrections: manual; not yet verified.)

10. Memory sheet

  • Recording = constructive notice. Visible possession also gives notice. Actual notice = what you know.
  • Delivery makes the deed valid; recording warns the world.
  • Florida protects the good-faith purchaser who records without notice.
  • Evidence of title: abstract + attorney's opinion, or title insurance (modern standard).
  • Owner's: price · while she owns · not transferable. Lender's: loan · declines with the balance · follows the loan.
  • Title insurance looks backward: past defects yes; defects the owner creates later, no; physical damage, no.
  • Seller cannot require a particular title insurer: 3 times the title charges (RESPA Section 9, V-53).
  • Items without a V-number: manual; not yet verified.

lessons.title: Encumbrances: liens, easements, encroachments and restrictions
lessons.html:
2. Why it matters

In practice. Almost every Florida property carries something that limits the owner's title: a mortgage, a strip along the back of the lot for power lines, subdivision rules recorded on the plat, sometimes a neighbour's fence over the line. You will see these in the title evidence and on the survey. You must tell the buyer which ones will be paid off and which ones stay with the land, and spot problems early enough to fix them.

On the exam. This lesson belongs to Section 9, "Title, Deeds and Ownership Restrictions", about 7% of the state exam, roughly 7 of the 100 questions (V-01, V-02). Favourite questions: which lien is paid first from a foreclosure sale, specific versus general liens, what kind of easement a power line is, how long a prescriptive easement takes (20 years, not 7), and what to call a fence over the boundary.

3. Simple explanation

Source status. The prescriptive easement rule is verified (V-69, confirmed), and so are the cross-references to adverse possession (V-68) and homestead (V-66). The other rules in this lesson come from the study manual and are marked (manual; not yet verified).

The foundation: title and encumbrances

Title means ownership. An encumbrance is any claim or limitation on title held by someone else. The owner still owns the property, but subject to that claim. There are two families:

Family What the other person has Examples
Money claims A right to be paid, with the property as security Liens: mortgage, property tax lien, judgment lien
Use and physical limitations A right to use the land, a limit on its use, or an object on it Easements, deed restrictions, encroachments

Liens: money claims against property

A lien is a claim against property as security for a debt. If the property is sold at foreclosure (a forced sale to pay a debt), the lienholders are paid from the sale money in a fixed order called priority.

Specific or general? It depends on how much of the debtor's property the lien reaches (manual; not yet verified):

Specific lien General lien
Attaches to One property All the debtor's property
Examples Property tax lien · special assessment lien · mortgage · vendor's lien · construction (mechanic's) lien Judgment lien · IRS (federal tax) lien · estate lien

A special assessment is a charge on the properties that benefit from a particular local public improvement (a new sidewalk or sewer line). A vendor's lien is the seller's lien for unpaid purchase price. An estate lien is a claim connected with a deceased person's estate. An IRS lien is a lien for unpaid federal taxes (the IRS is the US federal tax agency). A judgment lien comes from a court judgment (for example, a lost lawsuit) and reaches all the debtor's property in the county where the judgment is recorded (course question bank; not yet verified). Florida's homestead protection (V-66) limits what an ordinary judgment creditor can reach: see section 7.

Priority: who is paid first (manual; not yet verified):

  1. Property tax and special assessment liens come first, regardless of date ("superpriority"), even ahead of a first mortgage recorded 20 years earlier.
  2. Every other lien ranks by recording date: first in time, first in right.
  3. Construction liens relate back to the notice of commencement (a public-record document marking the start of a construction project): the lien ranks from the date the notice was recorded, not from the later date the lien claim was recorded.
  4. Subordination: a lienholder can agree to a lower priority, for example so that a new construction loan can take first position.

Why recording order? Recording gives constructive notice to the world: the law treats everyone as knowing what is recorded. A lender who lends after another lien is recorded could have found it, so it accepts the later place. Relation back follows the same logic: once the notice of commencement is recorded, every later lender is warned that construction liens may follow.

Easements: rights to use someone else's land

An easement is a right to use another person's land for a particular purpose (a driveway, utility lines). It is an interest in land. Classify it with two questions.

Who benefits? (manual; not yet verified)

  • Appurtenant: benefits an adjoining parcel. The benefited parcel is the dominant estate; the burdened one is the servient estate. It runs with the land: it transfers automatically when either parcel is sold, because it belongs to the parcel, not to a person.
  • In gross: benefits a person or company, such as a utility. There is no dominant estate.

How did it arise?

  • By necessity: created by law for a landlocked parcel (no access to a road) (manual; not yet verified).
  • By prescription (V-69, confirmed, single-checked): 20 years of actual, continuous and uninterrupted use of a limited, defined area; under a claim of right that conflicts with the owner's use, without the owner's consent (that is what "adverse" means); with the owner's actual knowledge, or use so open, notorious and visible that knowledge is imputed (the law treats the owner as knowing).

The 20 years come from case law, not a statute; s. 95.14, which the manual tentatively cited, is not the source. Florida courts disfavour prescription and resolve doubts in the owner's favour. When Florida cut the adverse possession period to 7 years, the prescriptive period stayed at 20 (V-69).

Adverse possession is different (V-68): 7 years of continuous possession gives title (ownership). With color of title, the possession is under a recorded written instrument; without color of title, the possessor pays the taxes within 1 year of entering, files a return with the property appraiser within 30 days after paying, and keeps paying the taxes. Prescription takes 20 years and gives only a right to use.

License: permission, not an interest in land

A license is revocable personal permission to use land, such as letting a neighbour launch a kayak from your lawn. It is not an interest in land (manual; not yet verified). Since prescription requires use without consent (V-69), use under a license never counts toward the 20 years. False friend: this has nothing to do with your real estate license.

Encroachments and deed restrictions

An encroachment is a physical intrusion: a structure or improvement extending onto another's land (fence, shed, driveway, roof overhang). The public records do not show a physical object, so a survey (a professional measurement of the boundaries and what stands on them) reveals it (manual; not yet verified).

A deed restriction (restrictive covenant) is a private limitation on use, recorded in a deed or on a plat (the recorded subdivision map), that binds future owners (manual; not yet verified). Examples: single-family use only; no boats parked in front yards. It is created by an owner or developer, not by a government.

4. Key terms

Term Meaning
Encumbrance Any claim or limitation on title (lien, easement, restriction, encroachment)
Lien A claim against property as security for a debt
Specific / general lien On one property / on all the debtor's property
Priority The order in which liens are paid from a foreclosure sale
Subordination A lienholder agreeing to a lower priority
Notice of commencement Recorded document marking the start of construction; construction liens relate back to it
Dominant / servient estate The parcel that benefits / the parcel that is burdened
Easement appurtenant Benefits an adjoining parcel; runs with the land
Easement in gross Benefits a person or company (e.g., a utility); no dominant estate
Easement by necessity Created by law for a landlocked parcel
Easement by prescription 20 years of open, continuous, adverse use without consent (case law)
License (land use) Revocable personal permission; not an interest in land
Encroachment Structure or improvement extending onto another's land; found by a survey
Deed restriction Private limitation on use recorded in a deed or plat; binds future owners

5. Practical example

The listing. Marta, a sales associate in Orlando, lists Daniel's lakefront rental house (an investment property, not his homestead) in a platted subdivision in Orange County. The title evidence and a new survey show:

Finding What it is Effect for the buyer
First mortgage, recorded 2016 Specific lien Normally paid from Daniel's proceeds at closing
$40,000 judgment against Daniel, recorded in Orange County, 2021 General lien Reaches Daniel's non-homestead property in the county, including this house; must be dealt with for clear title
Last year's property taxes unpaid Specific lien, top priority Paid first
Strip along the rear line for the electric company Easement in gross Stays on the land
Recorded driveway easement for the rear lot across Daniel's side yard Appurtenant (rear lot dominant, Daniel's lot servient) Runs with the land; binds the buyer
Neighbour's fence 2 feet (about 0.6 m) over the line onto Daniel's lot Encroachment, found by the survey Raise it before closing
Plat rule: no boats in front yards Deed restriction Binds the buyer
Daniel lets a friend launch a kayak from his lawn License Personal permission; no interest in land

What Marta does. She warns Daniel early about the judgment, makes sure the buyer sees the survey and the fence, and hands the buyer the recorded restrictions, because this buyer owns a boat.

If it had gone to foreclosure: (1) the unpaid taxes, (2) the 2016 mortgage, (3) the 2021 judgment. Taxes first, even though the mortgage is older.

6. Portugal comparison

No verified comparison yet. The course's Portugal–Florida comparison file has no entry for encumbrances.

  • Familiar principle (requires verification): from Portuguese practice you will know registered charges such as a mortgage (hipoteca) and rights of way over a neighbour's land (servidões). The general ideas of a money claim on property and a right to use another's land exist in Florida too.
  • Florida rule: tax and special assessment liens first, then recording order; easements appurtenant or in gross, by necessity or by prescription; prescription takes 20 years under case law (V-69).
  • Precise difference: not established. Do not carry over any Portuguese period for acquiring a right by long use, ranking of charges or terminology.
  • Exam implication: answer with the Florida rule only. Easement by prescription (for example, a right of way gained by long use without the owner's consent) = 20 years under Florida case law (V-69).

7. Legal and numerical requirements

Memorize exactly

  • Property tax and special assessment liens first, regardless of date; then recording order ("first in time, first in right") unless a lienholder subordinates (manual; not yet verified).
  • Construction liens relate back to the notice of commencement (manual; not yet verified).
  • Specific: property tax, special assessment, mortgage, vendor's, construction. General: judgment, IRS, estate (manual; not yet verified).
  • Prescriptive easement: 20 years, actual, continuous, uninterrupted use of a limited, defined area; open, adverse, without consent; owner's actual or imputed knowledge. Case law, not statute; not s. 95.14 (V-69).
  • Adverse possession of title: 7 years (V-68). Prescription: 20 years.
  • Appurtenant runs with the land; in gross has no dominant estate; necessity = landlocked; license = revocable, not an interest in land (manual; not yet verified).
  • Encroachment = physical intrusion, found by a survey; deed restriction = private, binds future owners (manual; not yet verified).

Understand

  • Priority follows notice: whoever recorded first was visible to everyone who came later.
  • Prescription is hard to win: courts disfavour it, resolve doubts for the owner, and permission defeats it. The case usually cited is Downing v. Bird, 100 So. 2d 57 (Fla. 1958); its holding was not read directly (V-69). Know the rule, not the case name.
  • Answer choices may mix "who benefits" (appurtenant, in gross) with "how it arose" (necessity, prescription). Pick the one that matches the key clue.
  • Florida's homestead is protected from creditors (V-66) within size limits (inside a municipality, 1/2 acre of contiguous land, residence only; outside a municipality, 160 contiguous acres), so an ordinary judgment creditor generally cannot reach the owner's protected homestead; that is why the examples in this lesson use non-homestead property. The protection does not apply against property taxes and assessments, debts for purchase, improvement or repair, or labour performed on the property: for example the tax lien, a mortgage that financed the purchase, or a construction lien for work on the home.

8. Visual explanation

Worked priority example: a Kissimmee rental house (not a homestead) sold at foreclosure (manual; not yet verified)

1stUnpaid 2025 property taxes and a sidewalk special assessment, whatever their date
2ndFirst mortgage, recorded 2012
3rdJudgment lien against the owner, recorded 2017
4thPool contractor's construction lien: claim recorded July 2023, ranks from the notice of commencement recorded February 2023
5thSecond mortgage recorded April 2023: after the notice of commencement, so behind the construction lien
Clue in the question Answer
Power, phone or water company lines Easement in gross
Shared driveway; "dominant" and "servient" Easement appurtenant
No road access Easement by necessity
20 years of open, continuous use without permission Easement by prescription
Permission that can be withdrawn License
Fence or shed over the line; survey Encroachment
Recorded rule binding all future owners Deed restriction

9. Common misconceptions

  • "The oldest recorded lien is paid first." Property tax and special assessment liens come first regardless of date; recording order governs only the rest.
  • "A first mortgage always stays first." Taxes beat it, its lender can subordinate, and a construction lien ranks ahead of it if the notice of commencement was recorded before the mortgage.
  • "A mortgage is a general lien." No: one property, so specific. A judgment lien is general.
  • "Prescription takes 7 years." No: 7 years is adverse possession of title (V-68); a prescriptive easement takes 20 (V-69), set by case law, not s. 95.14.
  • "A power-line easement is appurtenant." No dominant estate, so it is in gross.
  • "Years of permitted use become an easement." Permission makes it a license; prescription requires use without consent.
  • "An encroachment is a kind of easement." An easement is a right; an encroachment is a physical intrusion found by a survey.
  • "Deed restrictions are government rules." They are private, recorded in a deed or plat.

10. Memory sheet

  • Encumbrance = claim or limit on title: liens (money); easements, restrictions, encroachments (use).
  • Specific = one property (taxes, assessments, mortgage, vendor's, construction). General = everything (judgment, IRS, estate).
  • Taxes and assessments first → recording order → subordination steps a lien down → construction liens date from the notice of commencement.
  • Appurtenant = parcel to parcel, runs with the land. In gross = person or company. Necessity = landlocked.
  • Prescription = 20 years, open, continuous, adverse, no consent; case law (V-69). Adverse possession = 7 (V-68).
  • License = revocable, no interest. Encroachment = over the line, survey. Deed restriction = private, binds future owners.

lessons.title: Fixtures and water rights
lessons.manual: M7 §Wills, water, and what is part of the land
lessons.html:
2. Why it matters

In practice. "Does the chandelier stay?" is a classic fight between buyer and seller. The answer depends on whether the item is a fixture (part of the real property, sold with the house) or personal property (the seller's to take). In commercial leasing you will meet business tenants' equipment bolted to the floor. And Florida has rivers, large lakes and two coastlines, so waterfront buyers ask what they own and what happens when water or a hurricane moves the shoreline.

On the exam. Section 9, "Title, Deeds and Ownership Restrictions", carries about 7% of the exam (V-02). Expect a fact pattern where you apply the fixture tests (intent wins), the trade-fixture trap (equipment bolted down by a business tenant), riparian versus littoral, and accretion versus avulsion after a storm.

3. Simple explanation

Source status. No verification entry covers this lesson. Every rule below comes from the study manual (manual; not yet verified). It is standard exam vocabulary, but it has not been checked against an official Florida source in this course.

The foundation: real property or personal property?

Real property is the land and what is permanently attached to it; personal property is movable. The deed conveys the real property. A fixture is personal property that becomes real property when it is attached: a ceiling fan in a box at the hardware store is personal property; once the owner wires it into the ceiling, it is part of the house. Because a fixture is real property, it goes to the buyer with the land unless the sale contract excludes it (see the chandelier in section 5).

The four fixture tests (intent wins)

When it is unclear whether an item became a fixture, courts apply four tests (manual; not yet verified):

Test Question Points toward a fixture Points away
Intent (dominant) Did the person who attached it mean it to stay permanently? Owner installs a kitchen island to improve the home Seller states in writing that the antique chandelier is excluded
Method of annexation How is it attached? Bolted, wired in, plumbed, cemented Resting on the floor, plugged into a socket
Adaptation to the realty Was it made or fitted for this property? Hurricane shutters custom-made for these windows, on permanent tracks A standard item that fits anywhere
Relationship of the parties Who installed it, in what role? Owner improving their own home Tenant installing equipment for its business

Why intent dominates. The other three tests are really evidence of intent. Bolts, custom fitting and the installer's role are clues; intent is the conclusion. In practice, the clearest evidence of intent is what the parties write: list in the contract what stays and what goes.

Trade fixtures: the business tenant's exception

Trade fixtures are items a business tenant installs for its trade (restaurant ovens, salon chairs, store shelving). They remain the tenant's personal property, even if bolted down, and the tenant must remove them by the end of the lease. If the tenant leaves them behind, they become the landlord's by accession (ownership gained because something was added to, or left on, your property) (manual; not yet verified).

Why? Relationship and intent: a business tenant installs equipment to run its business, not to give it to the landlord. That is why the trade-fixture rule beats the method of attachment.

Emblements: crops as personal property

Emblements are annual crops produced by labour, such as a tenant farmer's tomatoes. They are personal property, and a tenant farmer may harvest crops planted before the tenancy ended (manual; not yet verified).

Water rights: which water, which word

(manual; not yet verified)

Term Type of water Florida example
Riparian rights Rivers and streams A home on the St. Johns River
Littoral rights Oceans, seas and large lakes A condo on the Atlantic; a home on Lake Okeechobee

Memory aid: riparian = river; littoral sounds like "litoral", the coast.

On the coast, the State of Florida owns the land seaward of the mean high-water line (the average high-tide line). The beach seaward of that line is state land, not part of the private lot.

When the water moves the land

Event Speed What happens Boundary
Accretion Gradual Water slowly deposits soil or sand; the owner gains the new land Moves
Erosion Gradual Water slowly washes land away; the owner loses it Moves
Avulsion Sudden A hurricane rips the shoreline or a river suddenly changes channel Does not move

One way to understand it: gradual change cannot be seen from day to day, so the boundary follows the water. A sudden change leaves a clear "before", so the old boundary can still be identified and stays where it was.

4. Key terms

Term Meaning
Real property Land and what is permanently attached to it
Personal property Movable property, not part of the land
Fixture Personal property attached to real property so that it becomes part of it
Method of annexation How an item is attached (bolted, wired, plumbed)
Adaptation to the realty How far an item was made or fitted for this property
Trade fixture Item a business tenant installs for its trade; remains the tenant's personal property
Accession Gaining ownership of what is added to or left on your property
Emblements Annual crops produced by labour; personal property
Riparian rights Rights of owners along rivers and streams
Littoral rights Rights of owners along oceans, seas and large lakes
Mean high-water line Average high-tide line; Florida owns the land seaward of it
Accretion Gradual addition of land by water deposits; owner gains
Erosion Gradual loss of land to water
Avulsion Sudden loss or change; the boundary does not move

5. Practical example

The house. Rui, a sales associate in Jacksonville, lists Linda's home on the St. Johns River. Before writing the listing, he goes through the items with her:

Item Tests Likely result
Ceiling fans wired into the ceilings Method (wired in); owner installed them to improve the home Fixture: stays
Hurricane shutters custom-made for the windows, on permanent tracks Adaptation; method Fixture: stays
Free-standing refrigerator, plugged in Not attached Personal property: goes with Linda unless the contract includes it
Grandmother's chandelier in the dining room Attached, so it looks like a fixture; Linda intends to keep it Make the intent clear: exclude it in writing in the contract, or replace it before showings
TV on a bolted wall bracket Mixed signals Uncertain under the tests: write it into the contract

The shop. Linda also owns a small retail building leased to a hair salon. The salon bolted styling chairs to the floor and plumbed in shampoo sinks. The lease ends next month and Linda is selling the building. These are trade fixtures: they belong to the salon, not to Linda and not to the building buyer. The salon must remove them by the end of the lease; whatever it leaves behind becomes the landlord's by accession.

The river. Over 15 years, sand has slowly built up along Linda's riverbank: accretion, so the new strip is hers. A neighbour's bank has slowly washed away: erosion, so the neighbour lost land. Rui explains that if a hurricane suddenly cut a new channel across a lot, that would be avulsion: the boundary would stay where it was. Linda's rights here are riparian (a river).

The beach. The buyer is also looking at an oceanfront condo at Jacksonville Beach. Those are littoral rights (the Atlantic), and the beach seaward of the mean high-water line belongs to the State of Florida.

6. Portugal comparison

No verified comparison yet. The course's Portugal–Florida comparison file has no entry for fixtures or water rights, so no Portuguese rule is taught here as fact.

  • Familiar principle (requires verification): in Portuguese practice you will have negotiated what "goes with" a property (fitted kitchens, built-in wardrobes, air-conditioning units), and you know that land next to the sea is treated differently from ordinary private land. Portuguese law has its own concepts and terms for both.
  • Florida rule: four tests with intent dominant; trade fixtures stay with the business tenant; riparian (rivers, streams) versus littoral (oceans, seas, large lakes); Florida owns the land seaward of the mean high-water line; gradual change moves the boundary, sudden change does not.
  • Precise difference: not established. Do not assume that a Portuguese classification of an item, or a Portuguese coastal boundary, matches Florida's tests or the mean high-water line.
  • Exam implication: use only the Florida exam vocabulary and tests. A Portuguese rule never answers a Florida question.

7. Legal and numerical requirements

Memorize exactly

There are no numbers in this lesson. All rules below rest on the study manual (manual; not yet verified).

  • Fixture = personal property that becomes real property when attached.
  • Four tests: intent (dominant), method of annexation, adaptation to the realty, relationship of the parties.
  • Trade fixtures: a business tenant's personal property; removed by the end of the lease; left behind → the landlord's by accession.
  • Emblements: annual crops produced by labour = personal property; a tenant farmer may harvest crops planted before the tenancy ended.
  • Riparian = rivers and streams. Littoral = oceans, seas, large lakes.
  • Florida owns the land seaward of the mean high-water line.
  • Accretion (gradual gain) and erosion (gradual loss) move the boundary; avulsion (sudden) does not.

Understand

  • Method, adaptation and relationship are evidence; intent is the conclusion. Bolts alone do not decide.
  • The trade-fixture rule protects the business tenant, but only until the lease ends.
  • In a sale, avoid fixture disputes by listing in the contract what stays and what goes.
  • On the exam keep the textbook distinction: river = riparian, ocean = littoral. Outside the exam you may hear "riparian" used loosely for any waterfront (not verified in this course).
  • When a question asks which water rights a waterfront owner holds, decide by the type of water: river or stream = riparian; ocean, sea or large lake = littoral. Other terms offered as choices are distractors for that question.

8. Visual explanation

Is it a fixture? (manual; not yet verified)

Is it an annual crop produced by labour?
No → go to the next question
Yes → emblements: personal property; a tenant farmer may harvest what was planted before the tenancy ended
Did a business tenant install it for its trade?
No → go to the next question
Yes → trade fixture: the tenant's personal property, even if bolted; remove by the end of the lease or it becomes the landlord's by accession
Weighing method, adaptation and relationship, did the installer intend it to stay permanently?
No → personal property: the seller may take it
Yes → fixture: real property, transfers with the land

Water: which word, and does the boundary move? (manual; not yet verified)

Is the water a river or stream?
No (ocean, sea, large lake) → littoral
Yes → riparian
Did the land change gradually?
No, suddenly → avulsion: the boundary does not move
Yes → accretion (gain) or erosion (loss): the boundary moves

9. Common misconceptions

  • "If it is bolted down, it is a fixture." Not for a business tenant's trade fixtures, and intent, not the method of attachment, is the dominant test.
  • "Trade fixtures pass to the building buyer with the deed." They remain the tenant's personal property.
  • "The tenant can come back for the equipment whenever it likes." It must remove trade fixtures by the end of the lease; what it leaves becomes the landlord's by accession.
  • "Growing crops are always part of the land." Emblements (annual crops produced by labour) are personal property, and a tenant farmer may harvest crops planted before the tenancy ended.
  • "An oceanfront owner has riparian rights." On the exam, ocean, sea or large lake = littoral; river or stream = riparian.
  • "After a hurricane moves the shoreline, the boundary follows the new water line." A sudden change is avulsion: the boundary does not move.
  • "Erosion and avulsion are the same thing." Both lose land, but erosion is gradual (boundary moves) and avulsion is sudden (boundary stays).
  • "A beachfront owner owns down to the water." Florida owns the land seaward of the mean high-water line.

10. Memory sheet

  • Fixture = personal property attached → real property → goes with the land.
  • Tests: intent (wins), method, adaptation, relationship.
  • Trade fixtures stay with the business tenant; remove by lease end or the landlord takes them by accession.
  • Emblements = annual crops = personal property; tenant farmer harvests what was planted before the tenancy ended.
  • Riparian = river. Littoral = ocean, sea, large lake. State owns seaward of the mean high-water line.
  • Gradual (accretion, erosion) moves boundaries; sudden (avulsion) does not.

lessons.title: The three legal description systems
lessons.html:
2. Why it matters

In daily brokerage work you identify a property by its street address. In Florida that is not enough for the documents that move ownership. A valid deed must contain a legal description: words that identify one parcel of land so precisely that it cannot be confused with any other (L09-2; manual; not yet verified). A written listing agreement must also contain a description of the property (s. 475.25(1)(r); V-49, verified). Agents usually take the legal description from the seller's recorded deed or title documents. A wrong lot number or a missing fraction can describe the wrong land, so copy it exactly.

On the exam, Section 10 "Legal Descriptions" carries about 5% of the questions (V-02), which is about five of the 100 questions (V-01). This lesson covers the concepts. The next lesson (L10-2) covers the arithmetic. Typical concept questions:

  • Which system must begin and end at the same point?
  • Which system describes most homes in platted urban subdivisions?
  • Where do Florida's principal meridian and base line intersect?
  • Is a street address a legal description? (Never.)

3. Simple explanation

What a legal description is, and why an address is not one

A legal description identifies a specific parcel so that a surveyor could find its boundaries on the ground. Florida exam materials use three systems: metes and bounds, lot and block, and the government (rectangular) survey (manual; not yet verified).

A street address is never a legal description (manual; not yet verified). The reason: an address tells a mail carrier which door to go to, but it says nothing about where the boundary lines are. Streets can be renamed and numbers can change. One address can cover several parcels, and vacant land often has no address at all.

System 1: Metes and bounds

"Metes" means measurements and "bounds" means boundaries. The description "walks" the boundary of the parcel:

  1. It starts at a point of beginning (POB).
  2. It follows courses (directions, such as "North" or "North 45 degrees East") and distances (in feet) from one corner to the next.
  3. It returns to the POB.

Why must it return to the POB? A boundary line that does not close back on itself does not enclose any land. The return to the POB is what turns a list of lines into a parcel. Metes and bounds is used for irregular parcels, whose shape does not fit a grid or a subdivision map (manual; not yet verified).

System 2: Lot and block

When land is divided into a subdivision, a plat is prepared: a map of the subdivision showing its blocks, lots and streets. The plat is then recorded in the public records. From that moment each lot can be described simply by its lot number, its block number, the subdivision name and a reference to the recorded plat. Lot and block is the usual description in platted urban subdivisions, so a typical subdivision home is described this way (manual; not yet verified).

The condition that matters is a recorded plat. Without a recorded plat, "Lot 14, Block C" points to nothing.

System 3: Government (rectangular) survey

Imagine a giant grid laid over the land, measured from two reference lines:

  • a principal meridian, a reference line running north–south;
  • a base line, a reference line running east–west.

Florida's principal meridian and base line intersect in Tallahassee (N-105; manual; not yet verified, V-26). From these lines the land is divided into townships of 6 × 6 miles, and each township into 36 sections of 1 square mile (640 acres) (N-100, N-101; manual; not yet verified, V-26). A government survey description names a fraction of a section, the section number and its township. L10-2 teaches the numbering and the arithmetic.

Real descriptions also say where the township lies relative to the two lines, for example "Township 12 South, Range 17 East": the township row counted south of the base line and the column (called a range) counted east of the principal meridian. This township-and-range wording is not in the course sources (neither the study manual nor any verification entry): requires verification. None of this course's practice questions use it.

The three systems side by side

Metes and bounds Lot and block Government survey
Starting reference A point of beginning (POB) A recorded plat A principal meridian and base line (Florida: Tallahassee)
How land is described Courses and distances, returning to the POB Lot number in a block on the recorded plat Townships, sections and fractions of sections
Typical use Irregular parcels Platted urban subdivisions Land described by sections (see L10-2)
Clue words in a question "point of beginning", "thence North ... feet" "Lot", "Block", "plat" "Section", "Township", "NW¼"

All rows: manual; not yet verified.

4. Key terms

Term Meaning
Legal description Words that identify one specific parcel precisely enough to locate its boundaries. Required in a deed
Metes and bounds Description using a point of beginning, courses (directions) and distances, returning to the POB
Point of beginning (POB) The starting and ending point of a metes-and-bounds description
Course A direction in a metes-and-bounds description, such as "North 45 degrees East" (face north, then turn 45 degrees toward east). Angles can include minutes: 36°52' means 36 degrees 52 minutes
Distance The length of each boundary line, in feet
Thence Old-fashioned English for "from that point". Metes-and-bounds descriptions use it to introduce the next course, as in "thence North 200 feet"
Lot and block Description by lot and block numbers on a recorded plat
Plat Recorded map of a subdivision showing its blocks, lots and streets
Recorded Entered in the public records, so that anyone can find and rely on it
Government (rectangular) survey System of townships and sections measured from principal meridians and base lines
Principal meridian The north–south reference line of the government survey
Base line The east–west reference line of the government survey
Township A 6 × 6 mile square containing 36 sections
Section 1 square mile, 640 acres

5. Practical example

Luís, a buyer from Porto, asks you to help him buy three Florida properties. You look at the legal description in each seller's recorded deed.

Property Legal description (illustrative) System
A house in an Orlando subdivision, "4127 Heron Pointe Drive" "Lot 14, Block C, HERON POINTE, according to the plat thereof recorded in Plat Book 62, Page 115, of the Public Records of Orange County, Florida" Lot and block
40 acres of pasture in Levy County, no street address "The SW¼ of the NE¼ of Section 22, Township 12 South, Range 17 East" Government survey
An irregular lot on the St. Johns River "Beginning at the point of beginning (POB) on the north line of River Road; thence North 200 feet; thence East 300 feet; thence South 36°52' East 250 feet along the river bank; thence West 450 feet along River Road back to the POB" Metes and bounds

The names, plat book and page numbers, and distances above are invented for illustration.

What you explain to Luís:

  1. The house sits in a platted subdivision, so its description refers to the recorded plat. "4127 Heron Pointe Drive" is the mailing address only. It appears in marketing, but the deed must carry a legal description, and for this platted lot that is the lot-and-block description.
  2. The pasture has no address at all. The government survey locates it within a section of a township measured from Florida's principal meridian and base line, which intersect in Tallahassee (N-105; manual; not yet verified, V-26). In L10-2 you will calculate that "the SW¼ of the NE¼" of a section is 40 acres.
  3. The riverfront lot is irregular, so it is described by metes and bounds. Check that the description ends "back to the POB". If the last course does not return to the starting point, the boundary does not close and the parcel is not properly described. Ask the title company or a surveyor to review it.

6. Portugal comparison

The familiar principle. Any system that transfers land needs a way to identify exactly which land is transferred. How Portuguese documents identify a property is not covered by the course's comparison entries: requires verification. Do not rely on it for any Florida answer.

The Florida rule. The deed carries a legal description in one of three systems: metes and bounds, lot and block (recorded plat) or the government survey (Tallahassee origin). A street address never qualifies (manual; not yet verified).

The precise difference that is verified for this course (PT-17). Units. Portugal uses the metric system (m², hectares; 1 ha = 10,000 m²). Florida descriptions use US customary units: distances in feet, areas in square feet and acres, and miles for townships and sections. For intuition only: 1 acre ≈ 4,047 m² ≈ 0.405 ha, and 1 mile ≈ 1.61 km.

Exam implication. Answer with the three Florida system names and Florida's survey origin (Tallahassee). Read every distance in a metes-and-bounds description in feet. Exam math never uses metric (PT-17).

7. Legal and numerical requirements

Memorize exactly

  • Three systems: metes and bounds, lot and block, government (rectangular) survey (manual; not yet verified).
  • Metes and bounds: POB → courses (directions) and distances → back to the POB. Used for irregular parcels (manual; not yet verified).
  • Lot and block: a lot number in a block on a recorded plat. The usual description in platted urban subdivisions (manual; not yet verified).
  • Government survey: townships and sections measured from a principal meridian and base line. Florida's intersect in Tallahassee (N-105; manual; not yet verified, V-26).
  • A street address is never a legal description (manual; not yet verified).
  • A valid deed requires a legal description (L09-2; manual; not yet verified). A written listing agreement must include a property description (s. 475.25(1)(r); V-49, verified).

Understand

  • Each system answers the same question, "which land, exactly?", from a different starting reference: a point (POB), a map (plat) or a grid (meridian and base line).
  • Metes and bounds must close: without the return to the POB, no area is enclosed.
  • Lot and block depends entirely on the recorded plat. The description is only as good as the map it points to.
  • The government survey is a grid, so its parcels are described by section numbers and fractions. That is why it lends itself to arithmetic (L10-2).
  • Source status: the exam format and weighting (V-01, V-02) and the listing-agreement rule (V-49) are verified; the metric figures are PT-17 arithmetic. Every legal-description rule in this lesson comes from the study manual and is labelled "not yet verified" (the Tallahassee origin and the township and section figures are listed under V-26). The township-and-range wording is outside the course sources (requires verification).

8. Visual explanation

Which system is this description?

1. Does it start at a point of beginning, run by courses (directions) and distances, and return to that point?
No → go to question 2
Yes → metes and bounds
2. Does it name a lot and block on a recorded plat?
No → go to question 3
Yes → lot and block
3. Does it name a section (or a fraction of one) and a township?
No (a street address, a mailbox, "the old Silva grove") → not a legal description
Yes → government (rectangular) survey

Source: study manual (manual; not yet verified).

A metes-and-bounds description "walks" the boundary (the riverfront lot from the practical example in part 5):

StartPoint of beginning (POB)
Course 1North 200 feet
Course 2East 300 feet
Course 3South 36°52' East 250 feet, along the river bank
Course 4West 450 feet, back to the POB: the boundary closes

Distances are invented for illustration. Every metes-and-bounds description ends where it began.

9. Common misconceptions

  • "The street address is enough for the deed." No. A street address is never a legal description.
  • "Metes and bounds just has to list the boundary lines." The lines must start at the POB and return to the POB. That is the classic exam answer to "which description begins and ends at the same point?"
  • "Lot and block works for any parcel." Only for land shown on a recorded plat.
  • "Most subdivision homes are described by metes and bounds." The usual description in platted urban subdivisions is lot and block. Metes and bounds is for irregular parcels.
  • "Florida's survey starts in Miami, Orlando or Jacksonville." Florida's principal meridian and base line intersect in Tallahassee.
  • "I can read the distances in metres, as at home." Florida descriptions use feet and acres (PT-17), and Portuguese practice never answers a Florida question.

10. Memory sheet

  • 3 systems: metes and bounds · lot and block · government (rectangular) survey.
  • Metes and bounds returns to the POB. Courses + distances. Irregular parcels.
  • Lot and block needs a recorded plat. Platted urban subdivisions.
  • Government survey: townships and sections from a principal meridian (N–S) and base line (E–W). Florida's survey origin is Tallahassee.
  • Street address = never a legal description.
  • Documents: a valid deed needs a legal description (manual; not yet verified); a written listing agreement needs a property description (V-49, verified).
  • Source status: every other line is manual; not yet verified (the Tallahassee origin and the township and section figures are listed under V-26).

lessons.title: Townships, sections and land measurement
lessons.html:
2. Why it matters

Rural Florida land is often priced per acre and described by fractions of a section ("the NW¼ of the SE¼ of Section 22"). You must turn that description, or lot dimensions in feet, into acres and then into a price, all in US units, while your Portuguese clients think in hectares.

On the exam, Section 10 "Legal Descriptions" carries about 5% of the questions (V-02), and the study manual treats section-and-township arithmetic as near-certain exam material: "How many acres in ...?", "... AND ...", "What does it cost at $X per acre?", "Where is section 1?"

3. Simple explanation

Step 1: What it represents

The government survey (L10-1) lays a grid over the land (all facts in this step: manual; not yet verified. The township and section figures are N-100 and N-101, listed under V-26):

  • A township is 6 miles × 6 miles = 36 square miles, divided into 36 sections (N-100).
  • A section is 1 mile × 1 mile = 1 square mile = 640 acres (N-101).
  • Sections are numbered in a serpentine pattern (back and forth, like a snake). Section 1 is in the northeast corner. Numbering runs west to section 6, then back east (7–12), west again (13–18), and so on, ending with section 36 in the southeast corner. Section 16 was traditionally reserved for schools.

An aliquot part is a fraction of a section named by direction: halves (N½, S½, E½, W½) and quarters (NE¼, NW¼, SE¼, SW¼). Fractions can be nested: "the NW¼ of the SE¼" is a quarter of a quarter. One section divided into quarter-quarters:

← West East →
NW¼ of NW¼ NE¼ of NW¼ NW¼ of NE¼ NE¼ of NE¼
SW¼ of NW¼ SE¼ of NW¼ SW¼ of NE¼ SE¼ of NE¼
NW¼ of SW¼ NE¼ of SW¼ NW¼ of SE¼ NE¼ of SE¼
SW¼ of SW¼ SE¼ of SW¼ SW¼ of SE¼ SE¼ of SE¼

North is up. Each square is 1,320 ft × 1,320 ft = 40 acres. Each 2 × 2 corner block is a 160-acre quarter section.

To locate a parcel, read the fractions right to left. "The NW¼ of the SE¼": first find the SE¼ of the section (the bottom-right block), then take its NW¼ (the highlighted square).

Step 2: Units

Unit Equals Measures Memory aid
1 mile 5,280 feet Length "Five tomatoes": 5-2-80
1 acre 43,560 square feet Area 43-5-60
1 square yard 9 square feet (3 ft × 3 ft) Area 3 × 3, not 3
1 square mile 640 acres Area 640 in a section
1 section 1 square mile = 640 acres Area
1 township 36 sections = 36 square miles Area 6 × 6

(Manual; not yet verified, V-26. These are standard measurement definitions, but the course has not yet checked them against an official source.)

Feet and miles measure lines. Square feet, square yards, acres and square miles measure areas. An area is length × width, so a square unit is the side length multiplied by itself. Check: 1 square mile = 5,280 ft × 5,280 ft = 27,878,400 sq ft, and 640 acres × 43,560 = 27,878,400 sq ft. The same number, so the constants agree.

Metric intuition (for understanding only): 1 acre ≈ 4,047 m² ≈ 0.405 ha. 640 acres ≈ 259 ha. 1 mile ≈ 1.61 km (PT-17; arithmetic checked with 1 ft = 0.3048 m exactly). Exam math never uses metric.

Step 3: Formula

Task Formula
Acreage of an aliquot part 640 ÷ each denominator (same as 640 ÷ the product of the denominators)
Description joined by AND Compute each parcel separately, then add
Square feet → acres sq ft ÷ 43,560
Acres → square feet acres × 43,560
Feet → miles / miles → feet ÷ 5,280 / × 5,280
Square feet → square yards sq ft ÷ 9
Square miles → acres / acres → square miles × 640 / ÷ 640
Rectangle in feet length × width = sq ft
Price acres × price per acre

The acreage shortcut in action:

  • NW¼ of the SE¼ = 640 ÷ 4 ÷ 4 = 40 acres.
  • S½ of the NE¼ = 640 ÷ 2 ÷ 4 = 80 acres.
