3. Simple explanation

Source status. The assumption, foreclosure and redemption rules come from the study manual (manual; not yet verified). They are also what the course's practice questions test. The closing-statement and tax points in Part 1 are verified (V-18, V-19, V-24, V-25).

Part 1: Taking over an existing loan

A buyer can take over the seller's financing in two ways. The difference between them is personal liability, that is, who can be sued for the debt.

Assumption. The buyer becomes personally liable on the loan. The seller remains secondarily liable: if the buyer fails to pay, the lender can still look to her. This changes only if the lender agrees to a novation, which substitutes the buyer and releases the original borrower.

"Subject to" the mortgage. The buyer takes title and makes the payments but promises nothing, so he has no personal liability. On default the lender forecloses, and only the original borrower faces any deficiency. The buyer keeps paying because otherwise foreclosure takes the property and what he invested in it.

A due-on-sale clause (L12-1) makes the balance due on transfer. If the loan has one, any transfer without the lender's consent lets the lender demand the whole balance.

Assumption Assumption + novation "Subject to"
Buyer personally liable? Yes Yes No
Original borrower still liable? Yes, secondarily No, released Yes: alone faces any deficiency

At the closing table (verified cross-references).

  • An assumed mortgage is a debit to the seller and a credit to the buyer on the closing statement (V-24, which corrected the manual).
  • Note stamps ($0.35 per $100 or portion) are due on new and assumed mortgages (V-18, V-25).
  • The intangible tax (2 mills, i.e. 0.002 × the mortgage amount) applies to new mortgages only. It is not charged again on an assumption when it was paid originally and the debt is unchanged (V-19, V-25).

Part 2: Default and foreclosure in Florida

  1. Default and acceleration. The borrower stops paying, and the acceleration clause makes the entire balance due.
  2. A court case. Florida foreclosure is judicial: a court action that ends in a public sale (the courthouse sale or auction). The lender cannot foreclose without going to court.
  3. Equity of redemption. Until the moment of the sale, the borrower can redeem, that is, stop the foreclosure and keep the property, by paying in full. After acceleration, "in full" means the whole debt, not just the missed payments.
  4. No statutory redemption. Florida gives no right to redeem after the sale. An answer offering "10 days" or "1 year" after the sale is a distractor.

Part 3: After the sale

  • Shortfall. The lender may seek a deficiency judgment (a judgment for the unpaid balance) against the personally liable parties. These are the original borrower (unless a novation released her) and any buyer who assumed the loan. So after an assumption without a novation, the seller is still liable secondarily. A "subject to" buyer is never liable. With an exculpatory clause, the lender's only recourse is the property, so there is no deficiency judgment.
  • Surplus. If the sale brings more than the debt, the surplus goes to the junior lienors first (holders of lower-priority liens, for example a second mortgagee), then to the borrower.

Part 4: Alternatives to foreclosure

  • Short sale. The property is sold, and the lender agrees to accept less than the amount owed.
  • Deed in lieu of foreclosure. The borrower deeds the property to the lender. It is faster, but the lender takes title subject to junior liens, which a foreclosure could have eliminated. So a lender may prefer to foreclose when there is a second mortgage, because otherwise it would own a property still burdened by that lien.

4. Key terms

Term Meaning
Assumption The buyer takes over the loan and becomes personally liable; the seller stays secondarily liable
Novation Substitution of a new party that releases the original borrower
Subject to The buyer takes title and pays the loan without personal liability
Judicial foreclosure Foreclosure through a court action ending in a public sale (Florida)
Equity of redemption The borrower's right to pay off the debt and stop foreclosure, up to the sale
Statutory redemption A right to redeem after the sale. Florida has none
Deficiency judgment Judgment for the unpaid balance after a foreclosure sale
Junior lien A lien with lower priority than the mortgage being foreclosed (e.g., a second mortgage)
Short sale Sale where the lender accepts less than the amount owed
Deed in lieu of foreclosure The borrower deeds the property to the lender to avoid foreclosure; junior liens survive

5. Practical example

Case 1: "subject to" in Tampa. Sofia owes $210,000 on her loan. She sells to Bruno, who takes title subject to her mortgage and makes the payments. Two years later Bruno stops paying, and the foreclosure sale brings $190,000. For simplicity, assume the $210,000 already includes everything the court allows.

  • Shortfall: $210,000 − $190,000 = $20,000.
  • The lender can seek a deficiency judgment against Sofia. Bruno loses the house but is not personally liable.
  • If Bruno had assumed the loan instead, he would be liable and Sofia would remain secondarily liable, unless the lender had granted a novation.

Case 2: an Orlando owner with two mortgages. Lucas owes $280,000 on a first mortgage and $35,000 on a second. The first lender accelerates and files a foreclosure lawsuit.

Option What happens
Redeem Before the sale, he pays the first mortgage in full (for example, by refinancing) and keeps the house
Short sale He finds a buyer at $265,000 and the first lender agrees to accept less than it is owed. The course sources do not say what happens to the second mortgage in a short sale
Deed in lieu The first lender would take title subject to the $35,000 second mortgage, so it may prefer foreclosure, which can eliminate that lien
Sale brings $330,000 Ignoring costs for simplicity, the surplus is $330,000 − $280,000 = $50,000. That pays $35,000 to the second mortgagee, and the remaining $15,000 goes to Lucas

The day after the auction, Lucas's brother offers the full payoff. Too late. In Florida, redemption ends at the sale.

6. Portugal comparison

Familiar principle. The course's Portuguese entry says a lender enforces a hipoteca through court enforcement proceedings (execução). This requires verification (PT-19). If it is accurate, a court-based process will feel familiar.

Florida rule. Foreclosure is judicial. The borrower may redeem by paying in full until the foreclosure sale, and there is no statutory right of redemption after it. Deficiency judgments are possible against personally liable parties (manual; not yet verified).

Precise difference. Portuguese procedure is unverified, so never use it to answer. The exam tests two Florida points: redemption ends at the sale, and junior liens survive a deed in lieu. For example, a full payment offered one day after the courthouse auction is too late in Florida.

Exam implication. There is no post-sale redemption in Florida. "Redeem before the gavel."

7. Legal and numerical requirements

Memorize exactly

  • Assumption: the buyer is personally liable. The seller remains secondarily liable unless a novation releases her (manual; not yet verified).
  • Subject to: the buyer has no personal liability. On default, only the original borrower faces a deficiency (manual; not yet verified).
  • Florida foreclosure is judicial: a court action ending in a public sale. The equity of redemption lasts until the sale, by paying in full. There is no statutory (post-sale) redemption (manual; not yet verified).
  • Deficiency judgment only against personally liable parties. Surplus goes to junior lienors, then to the borrower (manual; not yet verified).
  • Short sale: the lender accepts less than owed. Deed in lieu: faster, but the lender takes title subject to junior liens, which foreclosure could have eliminated (manual; not yet verified).
  • Closing statement: assumed mortgage = debit seller, credit buyer (verified, V-24).
  • Note stamps of $0.35 per $100 or portion on new and assumed mortgages. Intangible tax of 2 mills on new mortgages only, not again on an assumption when it was paid originally and the debt is unchanged (verified, V-18, V-19, V-25).

Understand

  • Liability follows the promise. A "subject to" buyer made none.
  • Because of acceleration, redeeming means paying the whole balance.
  • An exculpatory clause makes the property the lender's only recourse, so there is no deficiency judgment.
  • A deed in lieu is a voluntary transfer, not a foreclosure sale, so junior liens stay.

8. Visual explanation

DefaultThe borrower stops paying
AccelerationThe entire balance is declared due
Court actionJudicial foreclosure: the lender sues in court
Before the saleEquity of redemption: pay in full and keep the property
Public saleRedemption ends here; there is no statutory redemption afterwards
ProceedsShortfall: deficiency judgment vs personally liable parties. Surplus: junior lienors, then the borrower

Redeem before the gavel. After the sale there is nothing left to redeem.

Foreclosure Short sale Deed in lieu
What happens Court action ending in a public sale Property sold; the lender accepts less than owed The borrower deeds the property to the lender
Court process? Yes (judicial in Florida) No court sale; needs the lender's agreement No court order needed
Junior liens Can be eliminated Not covered by the course sources Survive: the lender takes title subject to them
Speed Requires a court case Not covered by the course sources Faster than foreclosure

9. Common misconceptions

  • "After the courthouse sale the borrower has 10 days (or a year) to redeem." False in Florida. Redemption ends at the sale.
  • "A deed in lieu wipes out the second mortgage." False. The lender takes title subject to junior liens. Foreclosure is what can eliminate them.
  • "A 'subject to' buyer owes the deficiency." False. The original borrower does.
  • "An assumption releases the seller." Only a novation does.
  • "A Florida lender can foreclose without court." False. Florida foreclosure is judicial.
  • "Any surplus goes straight to the borrower." Junior lienors are paid first.

10. Memory sheet

  • Assume = liable (the seller stays secondarily liable unless there is a novation). Subject to = not liable.
  • Florida foreclosure = judicial, ending in a public sale.
  • Redeem before the gavel: equity of redemption until the sale; no post-sale redemption.
  • Shortfall: deficiency judgment vs liable parties. Surplus: junior lienors, then the borrower.
  • Short sale = the lender accepts less. Deed in lieu = faster but keeps junior liens.
  • Closing: assumed mortgage = debit seller, credit buyer. Note stamps also on assumptions; intangible tax on new mortgages only.

lessons.title: Qualifying the borrower, usury and predatory lending
lessons.html:
2. Why it matters

Before a buyer falls in love with a house, someone must answer "can they borrow enough?" Lenders answer with two ratios. If you can work them out quickly, you can steer buyers to a realistic price range and understand a lender's "no". Knowing Florida's interest ceiling and the names of the predatory practices also lets you warn homeowners about abusive loan offers.

On the exam, ratio questions are common calculation items (you are given income and payments and asked whether the borrower qualifies), and the usury figures (18%, 25%, $500,000) are exact recall. Residential Mortgages is about 9% of the exam (V-02).

3. Simple explanation

Source status. The qualifying ratios and their benchmarks (28/36 and 31/43) are course conventions from the study manual (manual; not yet verified, V-26). They are teaching benchmarks, not statutes, and real loan-program rules change over time. Florida's usury limits are verified against the statutes (V-72). The names of the predatory practices and the SAFE Act requirement come from the manual (manual; not yet verified).

Step 1: What it represents

A lender asks two questions:

  1. Housing expense ratio: what share of gross monthly income goes to the house payment (PITI)?
  2. Total obligations ratio: what share goes to the house payment plus all other recurring debts?

PITI means Principal + Interest + (property) Taxes + (homeowner's) Insurance. Gross income is income before taxes and deductions, not take-home pay.

Usury is a separate test: is the loan's annual simple interest rate above Florida's legal ceiling?

Step 2: Units

Quantity Unit Conversion
Income US$ per month, gross Annual ÷ 12
Property taxes, insurance $ per month Often quoted yearly, so divide by 12
Principal and interest, recurring debts $ per month Usually given monthly
Ratios Percent Decimal × 100. Round to one decimal place only at the end
Usury Percent per year, simple interest; loan size = principal in $ n/a

Aside: ratios have no units. Just keep every amount monthly and in dollars. There is no metric conversion here.

Step 3: Formula

  • Housing expense ratio = PITI ÷ gross monthly income
  • Total obligations ratio = (PITI + recurring monthly debts) ÷ gross monthly income

For "maximum" questions:

  • From the housing ratio: maximum PITI = income × housing benchmark.
  • From the total ratio: maximum PITI = (income × total benchmark) − recurring debts.
  • The maximum PITI allowed is the lower of the two.

Usury check: annual simple rate = annual interest ÷ principal. Compare it with the ceiling for that loan size.

Step 4: When it applies

Benchmarks (course conventions; manual; not yet verified, V-26)

Loan type Housing expense ratio Total obligations ratio
Conventional 28% 36%
FHA 31% 43%

The borrower must meet both ratios. A ratio exactly at the benchmark passes, because the limit is "should not exceed". The manual's example below qualifies at exactly 36%.

Florida usury (verified, V-72)

  • Loans of $500,000 or less: interest above the equivalent of 18% per year simple interest is usurious and unlawful (ss. 687.02(1), 687.03(1), Fla. Stat.).
  • Loans over $500,000 (a loan, advance, line of credit or forbearance): interest is not usurious unless it exceeds the s. 687.071 rate, which in effect makes the ceiling 25%.
    • A loan counts as over $500,000 if the principal initially exceeds that amount or may reasonably be expected to exceed it during the term (s. 687.03(3)).
  • Criminal usury (s. 687.071), unless otherwise allowed by law. Willfully and knowingly charging:
    • more than 25% but not more than 45% a year is a second-degree misdemeanor;
    • more than 45% is a third-degree felony.
  • Knowingly making an extortionate extension of credit is a second-degree felony.
  • Credit extended in violation of s. 687.071 is not an enforceable debt in Florida.

Predatory lending (manual; not yet verified). The exam names four practices:

  • equity stripping: lending that drains the owner's equity;
  • loan flipping: repeated refinancing to collect fees;
  • packing: hidden add-on products;
  • balloon abuse: misuse of a balloon, which is a lump final payment.

The SAFE Act requires mortgage loan originators to be licensed and registered through NMLS.

Step 5: Worked example

Example A: buyers in Tampa. Their gross income is $102,000 a year. Principal and interest are $1,780 a month, taxes $4,800 a year and insurance $3,240 a year. They pay $520 a month on a car and $90 a month in credit-card minimums.

  1. Gross monthly income: 102,000 ÷ 12 = $8,500
  2. Taxes: 4,800 ÷ 12 = $400. Insurance: 3,240 ÷ 12 = $270
  3. PITI: 1,780 + 400 + 270 = $2,450
  4. Housing ratio: 2,450 ÷ 8,500 = 0.2882 → 28.8%
  5. Total: 2,450 + 520 + 90 = 3,060. Then 3,060 ÷ 8,500 = 0.36 → 36.0%
  6. Conventional: 28.8 > 28 ✗ and 36.0 ≤ 36 ✓, so they do not qualify. FHA: 28.8 ≤ 31 ✓ and 36.0 ≤ 43 ✓, so they qualify.
  7. Maximum conventional PITI: 28% × 8,500 = $2,380. The total ratio would allow 36% × 8,500 − 610 = $2,450. The lower is $2,380, so the PITI must fall by $70.

Example B (study manual). Gross monthly income $7,500; PITI $2,025; car and cards $675.

  • Housing: 2,025 ÷ 7,500 = 27% ✓ (≤ 28).
  • Total: 2,700 ÷ 7,500 = 36% ✓ (≤ 36). The borrower only just qualifies.
  • With $750 of car and card payments instead: 2,775 ÷ 7,500 = 37% ✗.

Step 6: Reasonableness check

  • A result over 100% means you divided upside down. A result of 2% or 3% usually means you used annual income.
  • The total ratio is always at least the housing ratio.
  • Multiply back: 8,500 × 0.288 ≈ 2,448, close to the $2,450 PITI ✓.
  • Boundaries matter. In Example B, $75 more of debt turns a pass into a fail.

Step 7: Common errors

  • Dividing by net or annual income instead of gross monthly income.
  • Leaving taxes and insurance out of PITI, or the recurring debts out of the total ratio.
  • Rounding 36.4% down to "36%" so the borrower appears to qualify.
  • Mixing up the conventional and FHA benchmarks, or checking only one ratio.
  • Applying 18% to a loan over $500,000, or forgetting that a loan expected to exceed $500,000 counts as over.

Step 8: Guided practice

G1. Gross monthly income $6,800; P&I $1,420; taxes $3,720 a year; insurance $1,920 a year. Find the housing ratio. Hint: convert taxes and insurance to monthly first.

Check your answer

Taxes 3,720 ÷ 12 = $310. Insurance 1,920 ÷ 12 = $160. PITI = 1,420 + 310 + 160 = $1,890. Housing ratio: 1,890 ÷ 6,800 = 0.2779 → 27.8%, within the conventional 28%.

G2. The same borrower pays $380 for a car and $120 in credit-card minimums. Find the total ratio. Does the borrower qualify conventionally? Hint: PITI plus every recurring debt.

Check your answer

1,890 + 380 + 120 = $2,390. Then 2,390 ÷ 6,800 = 0.3515 → 35.1%. Both ratios are within 28/36, so yes.

G3. An FHA borrower earns $84,000 a year gross and pays $950 a month on other debts. What is the maximum PITI? Hint: compute both limits and keep the lower one.

Check your answer

Monthly income: 84,000 ÷ 12 = $7,000. Housing limit: 31% × 7,000 = $2,170. Total limit: 43% × 7,000 = $3,010, minus 950 = $2,060. The answer is $2,060; here the total ratio is the binding limit.

Step 9: Independent practice

I1. Gross monthly income $9,200; PITI $2,530; car $610; card minimums $140. Does the borrower qualify conventionally?

Check your answer

Housing: 2,530 ÷ 9,200 = 27.5% ✓. Total: 3,280 ÷ 9,200 = 0.3565 → 35.7% ✓. Qualifies.

I2. Gross income $87,000 a year; P&I $1,690; taxes $3,960 a year; insurance $2,280 a year; other debts $820 a month. Conventional, FHA, both or neither?

Check your answer

Monthly income $7,250. PITI = 1,690 + 330 + 190 = $2,210. Housing: 2,210 ÷ 7,250 = 0.3048 → 30.5%. Total: 3,030 ÷ 7,250 = 0.4179 → 41.8%. Conventional fails both ratios; FHA passes both (≤ 31, ≤ 43). Answer: FHA only.

I3. Gross monthly income $10,000; PITI $2,600. Under the conventional benchmarks, what is the most the borrower may pay on other monthly debts?

Check your answer

Housing: 26% ✓. Total limit: 36% × 10,000 = $3,600, minus 2,600 = $1,000.

I4. A private Florida lender makes a $350,000 loan at 21% per year simple interest, and no other law allows that rate. Is this usury? Is it criminal usury?

Check your answer

The loan is $500,000 or less, so the ceiling is 18%. At 21% it is usurious and unlawful: $73,500 a year of interest (350,000 × 0.21) against a $63,000 maximum (350,000 × 0.18). It is not criminal usury, because the rate is not above 25%.

I5. A line of credit starts at $460,000 but is reasonably expected to reach $540,000 during its term. Its rate is 24% simple. Is it usurious? And at 30%, charged willfully and knowingly?

Check your answer

It counts as over $500,000 (s. 687.03(3)), so the ceiling is effectively 25%, and at 24% it is not usurious. At 30% (more than 25%, not more than 45%) it is criminal usury, a second-degree misdemeanor, unless otherwise allowed by law, and the credit is not an enforceable debt.

Step 10: Exam application

Ratios:

  1. Convert the income to gross monthly.
  2. Build the full PITI.
  3. Compute both ratios.
  4. Compare them with the right set: conventional 28/36 or FHA 31/43. "At or below" qualifies.

For "maximum PITI" questions, keep the lower of the two limits. If a question states different benchmarks, use its numbers.

Usury:

  1. Find the loan size, including any expected growth above $500,000.
  2. Pick the ceiling: 18% or 25%.
  3. If the rate is above 25%, place it in the criminal tiers. They apply only if the rate is charged willfully and knowingly, unless otherwise allowed by law.

4. Key terms

Term Meaning
PITI Principal, interest, taxes, insurance: the monthly housing payment
Gross monthly income Income before taxes and deductions, per month
Housing expense ratio PITI ÷ gross monthly income
Total obligations ratio (PITI + recurring debts) ÷ gross monthly income
Recurring debts Monthly debt payments, e.g. a car loan and credit-card minimums
Usury Charging interest above the legal maximum
Criminal usury Willfully and knowingly charging more than 25% a year, unless otherwise allowed by law (s. 687.071)
Loan flipping / packing Repeated refinancing to collect fees / hidden add-on products
SAFE Act Requires mortgage loan originators to be licensed and registered (NMLS)

5. Practical example

Marta, a nurse in Orlando, earns $90,000 a year gross, and her take-home pay is about $5,700 a month. The home she wants has a PITI of $1,980, and she pays $640 a month on a car and cards.

  • Correct (gross): $90,000 ÷ 12 = $7,500. Housing: 1,980 ÷ 7,500 = 26.4% ✓. Total: 2,620 ÷ 7,500 = 0.3493 → 34.9% ✓. She qualifies under 28/36.
  • Wrong (take-home): 1,980 ÷ 5,700 = 34.7% and 2,620 ÷ 5,700 = 46.0%. These figures would wrongly make her look unqualified, even under FHA.

Her neighbor's phone call. A caller offers her neighbor his third refinance in two years, each with large fees (loan flipping). The fees drain his equity (equity stripping), the paperwork hides an add-on product (packing), and a low monthly payment ends in a huge final payment he could not make (balloon abuse).

The caller also offers a $60,000 second mortgage at 22% simple interest. The loan is $500,000 or less, so the ceiling is 18%. At 22% it is usurious unless otherwise allowed by law: $13,200 a year of interest against a maximum of $10,800. It is not criminal usury, because the rate is not above 25%.

Marta suggests he check the originator in NMLS (SAFE Act) before signing anything.

6. Portugal comparison

Familiar principle. The course's Portuguese entry says Portuguese banks apply a debt-service-to-income limit (taxa de esforço) on net income under Banco de Portugal macroprudential measures. Your own Drive guide says the limit was lowered from 50% to 45% in May 2026. All of this requires verification (PT-18).

Florida rule. The exam convention divides PITI (housing, 28%) and PITI plus recurring debt (total, 36%) by gross monthly income. FHA uses 31/43.

Precise difference. Gross vs net income is the trap, and PITI includes taxes and insurance. For example, take gross income of $8,000 a month, PITI of $2,200 and a $500 car payment. The housing ratio is 2,200 ÷ 8,000 = 27.5% and the total ratio is 2,700 ÷ 8,000 = 33.75%. That borrower qualifies conventionally.

Exam implication. Use gross income, and include taxes and insurance in PITI. Never use a Portuguese percentage or net income in a Florida answer. "Florida divides by GROSS."

7. Legal and numerical requirements

Memorize exactly

  • Housing expense ratio = PITI ÷ gross monthly income. Total obligations ratio = (PITI + recurring debts) ÷ gross monthly income.
  • Conventional 28% / 36% and FHA 31% / 43%: course conventions, not statutes (manual; not yet verified, V-26).
  • PITI = principal, interest, taxes, insurance.
  • Usury: 18% per year simple interest on loans of $500,000 or less. In effect 25% on loans over $500,000, including loans whose principal may reasonably be expected to exceed it during the term (ss. 687.02(1), 687.03(1) and (3); verified, V-72).
  • Criminal usury, unless otherwise allowed by law (s. 687.071(2)-(4); verified, V-72):
    • willfully and knowingly charging more than 25% up to 45% is a second-degree misdemeanor;
    • more than 45% is a third-degree felony;
    • an extortionate extension of credit is a second-degree felony;
    • such credit is not an enforceable debt.
  • Predatory practices: equity stripping, loan flipping, packing, balloon abuse. The SAFE Act requires mortgage loan originators to be licensed and registered (NMLS) (manual; not yet verified).

Understand

  • Pass both ratios. Exactly at the benchmark passes.
  • The maximum PITI is the lower of the two limits.
  • Above 18% on a loan of $500,000 or less is unlawful (civil usury). The criminal tiers begin only above 25%.
  • The benchmarks are teaching conventions. If a question gives other figures, use them.

8. Visual explanation

1. Is the income gross and monthly?
Convert it: use gross, and divide annual figures by 12
Go to 2
2. Does the payment include principal, interest, taxes and insurance?
Add monthly taxes and insurance (annual ÷ 12)
Go to 3
3. Is PITI ÷ income at or below 28% (conventional) or 31% (FHA)?
Does not qualify on the housing ratio
Go to 4
4. Is (PITI + recurring debts) ÷ income at or below 36% (conventional) or 43% (FHA)?
Does not qualify on the total ratio
Qualifies under the course benchmarks

The Florida usury ladder (verified, V-72)

Annual simple rate Loan of $500,000 or less Loan over $500,000 (or expected to exceed it)
Up to 18% Lawful Lawful
Above 18% up to 25% Usurious (unlawful) Lawful
Above 25% up to 45% Usurious; if willful and knowing, 2nd-degree misdemeanor Same
Above 45% Usurious; if willful and knowing, 3rd-degree felony Same

The criminal tiers apply unless otherwise allowed by law. Credit extended in violation of s. 687.071 is not an enforceable debt, and knowingly making an extortionate extension of credit is a 2nd-degree felony.

9. Common misconceptions

  • "Use take-home pay." No. Divide by gross monthly income.
  • "The house payment is P&I." No. PITI adds taxes and insurance.
  • "28/36 is Florida law." No. These are course conventions, not statutes.
  • "FHA uses 28/36 too." No. The FHA benchmarks are 31/43.
  • "18% caps every Florida loan." No. Loans over $500,000, including those expected to exceed it, have an effective ceiling of 25%.
  • "Anything above 18% is a crime." No. The criminal tiers start above 25%.
  • "The Portuguese 45% limit applies here." No. That figure requires verification, uses net income and has no place in a Florida answer.

10. Memory sheet

  • Housing = PITI ÷ gross monthly income. Total = (PITI + recurring debts) ÷ gross.
  • 28/36 conventional · 31/43 FHA: course conventions (manual; not yet verified). Pass both; meeting the benchmark exactly is OK.
  • PITI includes taxes and insurance. Annual figures ÷ 12.
  • Maximum PITI = the lower of (income × housing %) and (income × total % − debts).
  • Usury: 18% simple for loans of $500,000 or less · 25% above (including loans expected to exceed it).
  • Criminal (willful and knowing, unless otherwise allowed by law): above 25% up to 45% = 2nd-degree misdemeanor · above 45% = 3rd-degree felony · extortionate credit = 2nd-degree felony · not enforceable.
  • Predatory: equity stripping, loan flipping, packing, balloon abuse. SAFE Act: originators licensed and registered (NMLS).

lessons.title: FHA, VA and conventional loans
lessons.html:
2. Why it matters

Most of your Florida buyers will bring a pre-approval letter that names a loan program: FHA, VA or conventional. The program tells you a lot before the offer is even written. It tells you how much cash the buyer may need, which insurance or fee the buyer will pay and, for a VA loan, which document sets the property's value (the CRV). If you misunderstand who stands behind the loan, you will also misunderstand the buyer's position. A common example is telling a client that "the government is lending you the money". It is not.

For the exam, Section 13 (Types of Mortgages and Sources of Financing) carries about 4% of the state exam (V-02). That is roughly 4 of the 100 questions (V-01). The favourite traps in this lesson are the verbs (FHA insures, VA guarantees) and the matching of each program to the right charge: MIP, funding fee or PMI.

3. Simple explanation

Source status. All the loan-program content in this lesson comes from the study manual; only the exam-format figures in section 2 are verified (V-01, V-02). The program roles (insure, guarantee, no government backing) and the names of the charges are standard exam vocabulary (manual; not yet verified). The two figures, FHA 3.5% minimum down payment and PMI above 80% LTV, are listed under V-26 as still not independently verified. V-26 also warns that such figures are program rules that change over time. Learn them as the course states them.

Start with the lender's problem

In L12-1 you saw that the mortgage gives the lender a lien on the property. A lien is only as good as the property's value, though. If the borrower stops paying and the home sells for less than the debt, the lender loses money.

The buyer's down payment is the lender's cushion. The down payment is the cash the buyer pays toward the price that is not borrowed. A big cushion means low risk. A small cushion means the lender wants someone else to share the risk of loss. The course teaches three ways to do that:

Who carries the extra risk? Program Exam verb
A federal agency, the FHA FHA loan Insures
A federal agency, the VA VA loan Guarantees
A private insurance company Conventional loan with PMI (private insurance)

In all three cases a private lender supplies the money. That lender may be a bank, a credit union, a savings association or a mortgage banker. The government agencies in this chapter never hand money to buyers.

Measuring the cushion: LTV

LTV (loan-to-value ratio) = loan amount ÷ property value, written as a percentage.

  • A $400,000 home with $40,000 down → loan $360,000 → 360,000 ÷ 400,000 = 90% LTV.
  • When the property's value equals the price and there is only one loan, the down payment percentage and the LTV add up to 100%: 10% down ↔︎ 90% LTV.

FHA: the government insures

  • The FHA (Federal Housing Administration) is part of HUD, the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development.
  • The FHA insures loans made by approved lenders. It never lends.
  • The borrower pays MIP (mortgage insurance premium): an up-front premium and an annual premium.
  • The minimum down payment is 3.5%, with qualifying credit (manual; not yet verified, V-26). Do not drop the qualification: the 3.5% figure is tied to the borrower's credit.
  • Why it works: the insurance protects the lender, so the lender can accept a small cushion.

VA: the government guarantees

  • The VA (Department of Veterans Affairs) guarantees loans to eligible veterans. Private lenders lend. Who counts as eligible is set by VA rules that this course does not cover.
  • The guarantee can take the place of a down payment, so 0 down is possible.
  • The borrower pays a funding fee. This is not MIP and not PMI.
  • The value is set by a Certificate of Reasonable Value (CRV). The VA now calls this document a Notice of Value, but the course and the exam use CRV.

Conventional: no government backing

  • A conventional loan has no government insurance or guarantee.
  • When the LTV is above 80%, the lender requires PMI (private mortgage insurance) (manual; not yet verified, V-26). The borrower pays it.
  • PMI can be cancelled as equity grows, that is, as the borrower's ownership share of the home rises. The course gives no cancellation percentage, so do not invent one.
  • "Above 80%" means more than 80%. A loan at exactly 80% LTV (20% down) does not trigger PMI under the course rule.

Insure vs guarantee: one memory hook

Both protect the lender, not the borrower. The exam uses the verbs as labels, so pair each verb with its charge:

  • Insurance charges a premium: FHA insures → MIP (mortgage insurance premium).
  • A guarantee charges a fee: VA guarantees → funding fee.
  • Private insurance for conventional loans: PMI, only above 80% LTV.

4. Key terms

Term Meaning
FHA Federal Housing Administration, part of HUD. Insures loans made by approved lenders; never lends
HUD U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, the federal department the FHA belongs to
MIP Mortgage insurance premium, paid by the FHA borrower up front and annually
VA Department of Veterans Affairs. Guarantees loans to eligible veterans; never lends
Funding fee The charge a VA borrower pays for the guarantee
CRV Certificate of Reasonable Value: the VA's statement of the property's value. The VA now calls it a Notice of Value; the exam says CRV
Conventional loan A loan with no government insurance or guarantee
Down payment The buyer's own cash toward the price; the part that is not borrowed
LTV (loan-to-value ratio) Loan amount ÷ property value, as a percentage
PMI Private mortgage insurance. Required by the lender on conventional loans above 80% LTV; paid by the borrower; can be cancelled as equity grows
Equity The owner's share of the value: value minus the loan balance
Approved lender A private lender (bank, credit union, mortgage banker) authorized to make FHA-insured loans

5. Practical example

You are showing a $300,000 townhouse in Tampa to three different buyers. Each one has a different pre-approval.

Ana: FHA, first-time buyer with qualifying credit.

  • Minimum down payment: 3.5% × $300,000 = $10,500.
  • Loan: $300,000 − $10,500 = $289,500, so the LTV is 289,500 ÷ 300,000 = 96.5%.
  • The money comes from an FHA-approved bank. The FHA insures the loan, and Ana pays MIP, up front and annually.
  • Ana tells you she was "approved by the FHA". Correct the vocabulary politely: she was approved by an FHA-approved lender, and the FHA insures that lender's loan.

Marcus: VA, eligible veteran.

  • 0 down is possible, so the loan could be the full $300,000. The VA guarantee replaces the down payment.
  • A mortgage banker lends the money and the VA guarantees the loan. Marcus pays a funding fee.
  • The VA's value for the townhouse is set by the CRV. Marcus's lender may call it a "Notice of Value"; it is the same document.

Priya: conventional loan.

  • With 10% down ($30,000), the loan is $270,000, which is 90% LTV. That is above 80%, so the lender requires PMI.
  • With 20% down ($60,000), the loan is $240,000, which is 80% LTV. That is not above 80%, so PMI is not required under the course rule.
  • If Priya does pay PMI, it can be cancelled later as her equity grows.

Your takeaway as the agent. All three buyers borrow from private lenders. The program only decides who shares the lender's risk and what the buyer pays for that protection.

6. Portugal comparison

Familiar principle. You already work with the general lending idea behind this lesson: a larger down payment means less risk for the lender. The course has no Portugal comparison entry for this lesson. How Portuguese banks set down payments, and whether Portugal has a public mortgage-insurance or guarantee program like the FHA or the VA, or private mortgage insurance like PMI, requires verification.

Florida rule. FHA and VA are federal programs, so their roles are the same in Florida as in every other US state. The FHA insures, the VA guarantees, and private lenders lend. A conventional loan above 80% LTV requires PMI.

Precise difference. No verified Portuguese data is available to compare. What is safe to say is that the exam's vocabulary is US-specific: insure/MIP, guarantee/funding fee, PMI above 80% LTV, CRV.

Exam implication. Answer only with these US program terms. Never assume that a Portuguese bank practice answers a Florida question.

7. Legal and numerical requirements

Memorize exactly

  • FHA insures; VA guarantees; neither lends. Private (approved) lenders lend (manual; not yet verified).
  • FHA borrower pays MIP: up-front and annual (manual; not yet verified).
  • FHA minimum down payment: 3.5% with qualifying credit (manual; not yet verified, V-26).
  • VA: eligible veterans; 0 down possible; borrower pays a funding fee; value set by the CRV, which the VA now calls a Notice of Value (the exam answer is CRV) (manual; not yet verified).
  • Conventional: no government backing; PMI required when LTV is above 80% (manual; not yet verified, V-26); PMI can be cancelled as equity grows (manual; not yet verified).
  • Section 13 weight: about 4% of the exam (V-02, verified).

Understand

  • Mortgage insurance and guarantees protect the lender against loss when a borrower defaults. That protection is what allows small or zero down payments.
  • "Above 80%" means more than 80%. Exactly 80% LTV does not trigger PMI under the course rule.
  • V-26 notes that program figures such as FHA's 3.5% and the PMI trigger change over time. The exam tests the course figures, so answer with them.
  • The FHA is part of HUD. Neither the FHA nor HUD makes the loan.

8. Visual explanation

Who does what in each program

FHA VA Conventional
Who lends the money? Approved private lender Private lender Private lender
Government's role Insures Guarantees None
Borrower pays MIP (up-front + annual) Funding fee PMI if LTV above 80%
Down payment (course figures) Minimum 3.5% with qualifying credit (V-26) 0 down possible 20% or more down (one loan, value = price) means LTV at or below 80%, so no PMI (V-26)
Special point Part of HUD Eligible veterans only; value from the CRV (now "Notice of Value") No government backing at all

The money always comes from a private lender. Only the backing and the charge change.

Which charge does the borrower pay?

Is the loan insured by the FHA?
Yes → the borrower pays MIP, up front and annually
Is the loan guaranteed by the VA for an eligible veteran?
Yes → the borrower pays a funding fee; 0 down is possible; the value comes from the CRV
The loan is conventional (no government backing). Is the LTV above 80%?
Yes → the lender requires PMI, which can be cancelled as equity grows
Conventional loan at 80% LTV or less: no PMI under the course rule

PMI trigger and FHA 3.5%: manual; not yet verified (V-26).

9. Common misconceptions

  • "The veteran got his loan from the VA." No. He got it from a private lender, and the VA guaranteed it.
  • "The FHA lends money to first-time buyers." No. The FHA insures loans made by approved lenders.
  • "FHA borrowers pay PMI." No. FHA borrowers pay MIP. PMI belongs to conventional loans.
  • "VA borrowers pay MIP." No. VA borrowers pay a funding fee.
  • "PMI protects the buyer." No. It protects the lender, even though the borrower pays for it.
  • "PMI is required at 80% LTV." No. It is required only above 80%.
  • "PMI lasts for the life of the loan." No. It can be cancelled as equity grows.
  • "A Notice of Value is something different from a CRV." No. It is the VA's current name for the same idea. The exam answer is CRV.
  • "VA loans always mean 0 down." No. 0 down is possible because the guarantee can replace a down payment, but it is not compulsory.

10. Memory sheet

  • FHA (part of HUD) insures → MIP, up-front + annual → minimum 3.5% down with qualifying credit (manual; not yet verified, V-26).
  • VA guarantees → funding fee → 0 down possible → value from the CRV (now "Notice of Value"; answer CRV).
  • Conventional: no government backing → LTV above 80% → PMI (manual; not yet verified, V-26) → cancellable as equity grows.
  • LTV = loan ÷ value. 20% down (one loan, value = price) = 80% LTV = no PMI under the course rule.
  • Insurance → premium (MIP); guarantee → fee.
  • Government agencies never hand money to buyers.

lessons.title: Loan types by repayment and purpose
lessons.html:
2. Why it matters

In Florida practice these loan names come up in real conversations. A seller offers to "carry the paper", that is, to lend the buyer part of the price herself. A developer says each lot will be "released" at closing. A buyer wants one loan for a furnished beach condo and its furniture. A retired client asks about a reverse mortgage. If you can name the loan, you can explain what it does and spot a structure that will not work, such as a wraparound over a loan with a due-on-sale clause.

For the exam, Section 13 carries about 4% of the questions (V-02). Expect vocabulary matching: a described loan to name, or a named loan to explain. The ARM formula (index + margin) is a classic.

3. Simple explanation

Source status. The loan definitions come from the study manual (manual; not yet verified). The reverse-mortgage age of 62 is listed under V-26 as not yet verified. The right of rescission on home equity loans is verified against federal rules (V-51).

Two questions about every loan

Every loan can be described by answering two separate questions:

  1. How is it repaid? This is the loan's shape: amortized, balloon, interest-only or adjustable.
  2. What is it for, and what does it cover? This is the loan's purpose: package, blanket, wraparound, purchase-money, home equity, reverse or construction.

One loan can carry a label from each list. A seller-financed (purchase-money) loan, for example, can also be partially amortized with a balloon.

Repayment shapes

The key fact behind all four shapes is that interest is charged on the unpaid balance. Whatever the payment does to the balance decides the shape.

1. Fully amortized loan. The payments are level (the same every month), and each payment covers that month's interest plus some principal. The last payment brings the balance to zero. Because the balance falls, the interest part falls and the principal part rises, even though the payment stays the same.

Example: a $200,000 loan at 6% for 30 years has a level principal-and-interest payment of $1,199.10.

  • Month 1: interest = $200,000 × 6% ÷ 12 = $1,000.00; principal = $1,199.10 − $1,000.00 = $199.10; new balance $199,800.90.
  • Month 2: interest = $199,800.90 × 6% ÷ 12 = $999.00; principal = $200.10.

2. Partially amortized loan with a balloon. The payments reduce the principal, but not to zero by the end of the term. The remaining balance is due as one large final payment, the balloon payment. This structure keeps the monthly payments lower, but the borrower must then pay off, refinance or sell. Balloon abuse is one of the predatory practices you met in L12-3.

3. Interest-only (term) loan. The payments cover interest only, so the principal never goes down. The whole principal is due at the end of the term.

4. Adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM). The interest rate changes during the loan:

  • Rate = index + margin.
  • The index is an outside market rate. It moves.
  • The margin is the lender's fixed add-on, written in the loan. It does not move.
  • Caps limit the changes. A periodic cap limits how much the rate can change at each adjustment. A lifetime cap limits how much it can change over the whole life of the loan.
  • Some ARMs start with a teaser rate: a low introductory rate that later gives way to index + margin, within the caps.

Example (illustrative contract terms, not legal limits): start rate 6.75% (index 4.25% + margin 2.50%), periodic cap 2%, lifetime cap 5%. At the first adjustment the index rises to 7.00%. Index + margin is now 9.50%, but the periodic cap allows at most 6.75% + 2% = 8.75%. The rate can never exceed 6.75% + 5% = 11.75%.

Purpose types

Loan What it covers or does
Package mortgage Real and personal property in one loan (for example, a furnished condo)
Blanket mortgage Several parcels under one mortgage, with a partial release clause that frees each parcel as it is paid down (a developer's loan)
Wraparound mortgage A new junior loan that includes an existing loan. The buyer pays the wrap lender (often the seller), who keeps paying the old loan. The existing loan must have no due-on-sale clause
Purchase-money mortgage Seller financing: the seller becomes the lender for part of the price
Home equity loan / HELOC Borrowing against equity the owner has already built; a HELOC (home equity line of credit) is drawn as needed
Reverse mortgage For owners 62 or older (manual; not yet verified, V-26). The lender pays the owner; the loan is repaid on sale, move-out or death
Construction loan Money released in stages (draws) as building progresses, then replaced by permanent "take-out" financing

Why does a wraparound need "no due-on-sale clause"? A due-on-sale (alienation) clause lets the lender demand the whole balance when the property is conveyed (L12-1). The wrap only works if the old loan can stay in place after the sale, so a due-on-sale clause would defeat it.

Why does a reverse mortgage balance grow? Money flows to the owner and repayment is not due until sale, move-out or death, so the debt rises over time: the reverse of an amortized loan.

Home equity loans and rescission (verified, V-51). Under the federal Truth in Lending rules, credit secured by the borrower's principal dwelling, such as a home equity loan or a refinance with a new lender, comes with a 3-business-day right of rescission. Saturdays count as business days. The right does not apply to a loan used to buy or build the home.

4. Key terms

Term Meaning
Amortized loan Level payments that cover interest and principal until the loan is fully repaid
Balloon payment The large final payment on a partially amortized loan
Interest-only (term) loan Payments cover interest only; all principal is due at the end
ARM Adjustable-rate mortgage: rate = index + margin, limited by caps
Index The outside market rate that moves an ARM's rate
Margin The lender's fixed add-on to the index
Periodic / lifetime cap Limit on the rate change at each adjustment / over the life of the loan
Junior loan A loan with lower lien priority than an existing loan
Package mortgage Covers real and personal property
Blanket mortgage Covers several parcels; a release clause frees parcels as they are paid
Wraparound mortgage A new junior loan that includes an existing loan
Purchase-money mortgage Seller financing: the seller lends part of the price
HELOC Home equity line of credit
Reverse mortgage The lender pays an owner aged 62+; repaid on sale, move-out or death
Draws / take-out loan Staged payouts of a construction loan / the permanent loan that replaces it

5. Practical example

A developer in Lakeland. Palmetto Ridge LLC finances 20 home sites with one blanket mortgage that has a partial release clause. When a lot sells, part of the proceeds pays down the blanket loan and the lender releases that lot, so the buyer receives it free of the developer's mortgage. Each house is built with a construction loan paid out in draws (foundation, framing, roof, finish); when it is finished, the buyer's permanent loan takes out the construction loan. The furnished model home sells "turnkey", and its buyer finances the house and the furniture with one package mortgage.

A seller in Sarasota. Rosa sells her house for $400,000. She still owes $150,000 on a loan that has no due-on-sale clause. The buyer pays $40,000 down, and Rosa carries a $360,000 wraparound note:

  • $400,000 − $40,000 = $360,000 wrap loan.
  • It includes the $150,000 old loan, so the new credit Rosa herself extends is $360,000 − $150,000 = $210,000. She hands over no cash: this is part of her equity, which she collects over time instead of at closing.
  • The buyer pays Rosa on $360,000. Rosa keeps paying her own lender on the $150,000.

Rosa is the lender, so this is also purchase-money (seller) financing. If her old loan had contained a due-on-sale clause, the sale would let her lender demand the full $150,000, and the wrap would fail.

A retiree in Naples. Mrs. Costa, aged 70, has substantial equity and wants income without moving. A reverse mortgage fits her age (62 or older; manual; not yet verified, V-26): the lender pays her, and the loan is repaid when she sells, moves out or dies.

6. Portugal comparison

Familiar principle. You may have seen variable-rate home loans in Portugal priced as a reference rate plus a bank spread (for example, Euribor plus spread). That description requires verification, because the course has no Portugal comparison entry for this lesson. Whether Portuguese contracts use US-style periodic and lifetime caps, and whether wraparound loans or reverse mortgages are used in Portugal, also requires verification.

Florida rule. An ARM's rate = index + margin, limited by periodic and lifetime caps, sometimes with a teaser rate.

Precise difference. With no verified Portuguese data, the only safe comparison is vocabulary: on this exam the moving part is the index and the fixed part is the margin. Use "margin", not "spread".

Exam implication. Answer in US terms (index, margin, caps). Never let a Portuguese loan practice decide a Florida answer.

7. Legal and numerical requirements

Memorize exactly

All loan definitions in this list: manual; not yet verified. The rescission item is the only verified one (V-51).

  • Amortized: level payments; interest falls, principal rises; fully repaid.
  • Partially amortized → balloon final payment. Interest-only (term) → whole principal due at the end.
  • ARM rate = index (moves) + margin (fixed); periodic and lifetime caps; sometimes a teaser rate.
  • Package = real + personal property. Blanket = several parcels + partial release clauses.
  • Wraparound = new junior loan that includes an existing loan; the existing loan must have no due-on-sale clause.
  • Purchase-money = seller financing. Home equity / HELOC = borrowing against existing equity.
  • Reverse mortgage: owners 62+ (V-26); lender pays the owner; repaid on sale, move-out or death.
  • Construction loan: draws; replaced by permanent take-out financing.
  • Home equity loan or refinance with a new lender on the principal dwelling: 3 business days to rescind, Saturdays count; not for loans to buy or build the home (V-51, verified).

Understand

  • Interest is charged on the unpaid balance. That single fact explains every repayment shape.
  • Caps limit how much the rate can change; they do not freeze it.
  • The purpose label and the shape label are independent: one loan can carry both.
  • A wrap leaves the old loan in place; it does not pay it off.

8. Visual explanation

What happens to the balance?

Shape Monthly payment Balance over time At the end
Fully amortized Level Falls to zero Nothing left
Partially amortized Level Falls, but not to zero Balloon payment
Interest-only (term) Interest only Stays the same All principal due
ARM Can change at each adjustment (index + margin, within caps) Follows the loan's repayment schedule As the loan terms provide
Reverse mortgage The lender pays the owner Rises Repaid on sale, move-out or death

Name that loan

Does one loan cover real property AND personal property (for example, furniture)?
Yes → package mortgage
Does one loan cover several parcels, freeing each as it is paid?
Yes → blanket mortgage with a partial release clause
Is a new junior loan wrapped around an existing loan that stays in place?
Yes → wraparound (the old loan must have no due-on-sale clause)
Is the seller lending part of the price?
Yes → purchase-money mortgage
Does the lender pay an owner aged 62+, with repayment on sale, move-out or death?
Yes → reverse mortgage
Is money paid out in draws while a building goes up?
Yes → construction loan, later replaced by a take-out loan
Is an owner borrowing against equity in a home already owned?
Yes → home equity loan / HELOC
None of these → name the loan by its repayment shape instead (amortized, balloon, interest-only or ARM)

One loan can fit more than one box: Rosa's wraparound is also a purchase-money loan. Definitions from the study manual (not yet verified); age 62 under V-26.

9. Common misconceptions

  • "In an ARM, the margin moves with the market." No. The index moves; the margin is fixed.
  • "The ARM rate is set by the Fed's discount rate." No. The rate is index + margin under the loan contract.
  • "Caps mean the rate cannot rise." No. Caps limit the size of changes, per adjustment and over the life of the loan.
  • "On an amortized loan the payment falls over time." No. The payment is level; only the interest/principal mix changes.
  • "A package mortgage covers several parcels." No, that is a blanket mortgage. A package covers real and personal property.
  • "With a blanket mortgage, nothing can be sold until the whole loan is repaid." No. The release clause frees each parcel as it is paid.
  • "A wraparound pays off the old loan." No. The old loan stays in place inside the wrap, which is why it must have no due-on-sale clause.
  • "In a reverse mortgage the owner makes monthly payments to the lender." No. The lender pays the owner.
  • "The 3-business-day rescission right applies to the loan used to buy the home." No. It applies to credit secured by the principal dwelling, such as a home equity loan, but not to loans to buy or build it (V-51).

10. Memory sheet

  • Interest is charged on the unpaid balance: amortized (to zero) · balloon (lump at the end) · interest-only (all principal at the end).
  • ARM = index (moves) + margin (fixed), within periodic and lifetime caps; teaser = low start rate.
  • Package = real + personal. Blanket = many parcels + release. Wrap = junior loan around an old loan with no due-on-sale clause.
  • Purchase-money = seller lends. HELOC = borrow against existing equity; if secured by the principal dwelling, 3-business-day rescission, Saturdays count (V-51).
  • Reverse = 62+ (manual; not yet verified, V-26); lender pays the owner; repaid on sale, move-out or death.
  • Construction = draws → take-out loan.

lessons.title: Primary and secondary markets, the Fed, and discount points
lessons.html:
2. Why it matters

Mortgage money is not created at the closing table. It flows from savers and investors, through lenders, to your buyer, and the Federal Reserve turns the tap up or down. This affects your daily work in Florida. When credit tightens, rates rise, fewer buyers qualify and listings sit longer. When a buyer's loan is sold after closing, you can explain why a new company may now be collecting the payments. When a loan offer reads "6.50% with 2 points", you can tell the buyer what those points cost in dollars.

For the exam, Section 13 carries about 4% of the questions (V-02). Three question types repeat: sort the entity (primary or secondary market?), name the Fed tool, and compute points (cost in dollars, or how many points a yield change needs).

3. Simple explanation

Source status. The market players, the Fed's tools and the definition of discount points come from the study manual (manual; not yet verified). The two point figures, 1 point = 1% of the loan and about 1/8% of yield per point, are listed under N-125 / V-26 as not yet verified, and the 1/8% figure is a course rule of thumb, not a law.

Why there are two markets

A lender has a limited amount of money. If a bank kept every 30-year loan it made, it would soon have nothing left to lend. The fix is to sell existing loans, get the cash back and lend it again.

  • Primary market: where loans are originated (made) and the borrower deals with the lender.
  • Secondary market: where existing loans are bought and sold, so that primary lenders get fresh money.

Consumers borrow in the primary market only. No buyer ever applies for a mortgage at Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac.

The primary market (lenders the borrower meets)

Player What it does
Commercial banks Lend to borrowers
Credit unions Lend to their members
Savings associations Lend to borrowers
Mortgage bankers Lend their own or borrowed funds and often service loans (collect the payments)
Mortgage brokers Arrange loans between borrower and lender for a fee; lend nothing

The secondary market (buyers of existing loans)

Player What it does
Fannie Mae (Federal National Mortgage Association) Buys loans from lenders (conventional, and also government loans) and issues mortgage-backed securities (MBS)
Freddie Mac (Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corporation) Same role: buys loans and issues MBS
Ginnie Mae (Government National Mortgage Association) Guarantees securities backed by FHA and VA loans

A mortgage-backed security is an investment backed by a pool of mortgage loans. Investors buy it, and their money flows back to the lenders, who lend again.

Intermediation and disintermediation

  • Intermediation: banks and savings institutions pool savers' deposits and lend them out as mortgages.
  • Disintermediation: savers withdraw their deposits to get better returns elsewhere. The lenders lose the money they would have lent, which starves mortgage lending.

The Federal Reserve: three tools

The Federal Reserve (the Fed) is the central bank of the United States. It does not set mortgage rates. It changes how easy or tight credit is, and rates follow.

Tool What it is To tighten credit To loosen credit
Open-market operations Buying and selling government securities. The day-to-day tool The Fed sells securities: buyers pay the Fed, so money leaves the banks The Fed buys securities: money flows into the banks
Discount rate The rate member banks pay to borrow from the Fed Raise it Lower it
Reserve requirements The share of deposits banks must hold instead of lending. The bluntest tool Raise them: banks can lend less Lower them

Tight money → higher rates → real estate slows. Easy money works the other way.

Discount points

Discount points are prepaid interest paid to the lender at closing.

  • 1 point = 1% of the loan amount, never of the price (manual; not yet verified, V-26).
  • Course rule of thumb: each point raises the lender's yield (its effective rate of return) by about 1/8%, which is 0.125% (manual; not yet verified, V-26).

Why do points raise the yield? Suppose a lender charges 2 points on a $315,000 loan. It hands over $315,000 but receives $6,300 back at closing, so it has really advanced only $308,700 while collecting payments on $315,000. Its return is therefore higher than the note rate. Seen from the borrower's side, paying points is how a borrower can get a lower note rate while the lender still earns its target yield.

Three formulas

  1. Cost of points = loan amount × number of points × 1%
  2. Points needed = yield increase wanted ÷ 0.125%
  3. Approximate yield = note rate + (number of points × 0.125%)

Eighths to decimals: 1/8 = 0.125 · 2/8 = 1/4 = 0.25 · 3/8 = 0.375 · 4/8 = 1/2 = 0.50.

Try it

  1. A buyer pays $480,000 for a Fort Lauderdale home with 20% down. The lender charges 1.5 points. What do the points cost?
Check your answer

Loan = $480,000 × 80% = $384,000. Points = $384,000 × 1.5% = $5,760. (Wrong method: $480,000 × 1.5% = $7,200. Points are based on the loan, not the price.)

  1. A loan's note rate is 5.875%. The lender wants an effective yield of about 6.125%. How many points, using the course rule of thumb?
Check your answer

Increase = 6.125% − 5.875% = 0.25%. Points = 0.25% ÷ 0.125% = 2 points.

  1. A lender charges 3 points on a 6% loan. What is its approximate yield?
Check your answer

3 × 0.125% = 0.375%. Yield ≈ 6% + 0.375% = 6.375% (6 3/8%).

4. Key terms

Term Meaning
Originate To make a new loan to a borrower
Primary market Lenders that originate loans: banks, credit unions, savings associations, mortgage bankers (brokers arrange)
Secondary market Buyers of existing loans: Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac buy; Ginnie Mae guarantees MBS backed by FHA/VA loans
Mortgage banker Lends its own or borrowed funds; often services loans
Mortgage broker Arranges loans for a fee; lends nothing
Servicing Collecting the loan payments for the loan's owner
Mortgage-backed security (MBS) An investment backed by a pool of mortgage loans
Intermediation Pooling savers' deposits to make loans
Disintermediation Depositors withdrawing funds for higher yields elsewhere, reducing mortgage money
Federal Reserve (the Fed) The US central bank; steers credit with three tools
Open-market operations The Fed buying or selling government securities; the day-to-day tool
Discount rate The rate member banks pay to borrow from the Fed
Reserve requirements The share of deposits banks must hold; the bluntest tool
Discount points Prepaid interest paid to the lender at closing; 1 point = 1% of the loan
Yield The lender's effective rate of return on the loan

5. Practical example

Daniel is buying a $350,000 condo in Orlando with 10% down ($35,000), so his loan is $315,000.

  1. Who takes his application? Daniel works with a mortgage broker, who shops several lenders but lends nothing. The loan is funded by a mortgage banker, which also services it. Both are primary market. Because the loan is conventional and the LTV is 90%, he will also pay PMI (L13-1; PMI above 80% LTV: manual; not yet verified, V-26).
  2. The rate offer. The lender quotes 6.75% with no points or 6.50% with 2 points. The cost of the points is $315,000 × 2% = $6,300, paid at closing. The offer matches the rule of thumb: 2 points × 0.125% = 0.25%, so 6.50% plus 2 points gives the lender roughly the same yield as 6.75% with no points.
  3. After closing. The mortgage banker sells Daniel's loan to Fannie Mae (secondary market). Fannie Mae pools it with other loans into mortgage-backed securities. The mortgage banker gets its money back and lends it to the next Orlando buyer. The loan's terms were fixed at closing; the sale only moves the loan to a new owner.
  4. Six months later. The Fed sells government securities in the open market. Money leaves the banks, credit tightens and mortgage rates rise. Fewer buyers qualify, and your Orlando listings take longer to sell.

6. Portugal comparison

Familiar principle. From your Portuguese practice you know that banks fund home loans and that interest-rate moves change how many buyers can afford a purchase. The course has no comparison entry for this lesson. The following points all require verification: who sets monetary policy for Portugal (the European Central Bank for the euro area, rather than a national tool kit like the Fed's), whether Portuguese banks sell home loans into a secondary market, and whether up-front bank charges resemble US discount points.

Florida rule. Florida follows the US system: the Fed uses open-market operations, the discount rate and reserve requirements. Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac and Ginnie Mae form the secondary market. 1 point = 1% of the loan.

Precise difference. No verified Portuguese data is available to compare.

Exam implication. Name only the Fed's three tools and the US entities. Never answer with a Portuguese or European institution, and always compute points on the loan.

7. Legal and numerical requirements

Memorize exactly

  • Primary market: commercial banks, credit unions, savings associations, mortgage bankers (lend; often service), mortgage brokers (arrange; lend nothing) (manual; not yet verified).
  • Secondary market: Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac buy loans and issue MBS; Ginnie Mae guarantees securities backed by FHA/VA loans (manual; not yet verified).
  • Consumers borrow in the primary market only (manual; not yet verified).
  • Disintermediation = depositors withdraw for better returns → less mortgage money (manual; not yet verified).
  • Fed tools: open-market operations (day-to-day tool), discount rate, reserve requirements (bluntest). Tight money → higher rates → slower real estate (manual; not yet verified).
  • Discount points: prepaid interest paid to the lender at closing; 1 point = 1% of the loan amount; each point ≈ +1/8% (0.125%) yield, a course rule of thumb (manual; not yet verified, V-26).

Understand

  • The secondary market exists to refill lenders' money so they can lend again.
  • The Fed changes credit conditions; it does not set mortgage rates or make loans.
  • Selling securities, raising the discount rate and raising reserve requirements all tighten credit.
  • Points are based on the loan, so the down payment matters: find the loan first.

8. Visual explanation

How mortgage money flows

Federal ReserveOpen-market operations · discount rate · reserve requirements → credit tight or easy
SaversDeposits pooled by lenders (intermediation); withdrawn for better returns elsewhere (disintermediation)
Primary marketBanks, credit unions, savings associations, mortgage bankers originate; mortgage brokers arrange
BorrowerSigns the note and mortgage at closing; may pay discount points
Secondary marketFannie Mae and Freddie Mac buy loans from primary lenders and issue MBS; Ginnie Mae guarantees MBS backed by FHA/VA loans
InvestorsBuy MBS; their money returns to lenders, who lend again

The borrower deals only with the primary market. The Fed influences the whole chain but lends nothing to home buyers.

Worked calculation: Daniel's points

Step Work Result
1. Find the loan $350,000 − $35,000 down $315,000
2. Convert points to a decimal 2 points = 2% 0.02
3. Cost of points $315,000 × 0.02 $6,300
4. Yield effect (rule of thumb) 2 × 0.125% +0.25%
5. Approximate yield 6.50% + 0.25% ≈ 6.75%
Check $6,300 ÷ $315,000 = 0.02 = 2 points ✓; $6,300 is less than 2% of the $350,000 price ($7,000), as it must be ✓

9. Common misconceptions

  • "A first-time buyer applied for a loan at Freddie Mac." Impossible. Freddie Mac and Fannie Mae are secondary-market buyers of existing loans; consumers borrow in the primary market.
  • "Ginnie Mae buys conventional loans." No. In this course Ginnie Mae guarantees securities backed by FHA/VA loans.
  • "A mortgage broker lends money." No. A broker arranges loans and lends nothing; a mortgage banker lends.
  • "The Fed sets mortgage rates." No. It influences credit through its three tools.
  • "Reserve requirements are the Fed's everyday tool." No. Open-market operations are the day-to-day tool; reserve requirements are the bluntest.
  • "When the Fed sells securities, credit gets easier." No. Selling securities takes money out of the banks and tightens credit.
  • "Disintermediation means more money for mortgages." No. It means depositors pull money out, so there is less.
  • "Points are a percentage of the price." No. 1 point = 1% of the loan.
  • "1 point = 1/8%." Do not mix the two numbers. One point costs 1% of the loan and raises yield by about 1/8%.

10. Memory sheet

  • Primary = loans are made (banks, credit unions, savings associations, mortgage bankers; brokers arrange, lend nothing). Consumers borrow here only.
  • Secondary = loans are bought: Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac buy + issue MBS; Ginnie Mae guarantees FHA/VA-backed MBS.
  • Disintermediation = deposits leave → mortgage money dries up.
  • Fed: open-market operations (everyday) · discount rate · reserve requirements (bluntest). Tight money → higher rates → slower sales.
  • 1 point = 1% of the LOAN ≈ +1/8% (0.125%) yield (course rule of thumb; manual; not yet verified, V-26).
  • Points needed = yield increase ÷ 0.125%.

lessons.title: Math foundations: decimals, fractions, percentages and the percent triangle
lessons.html:
2. Why it matters

In practice. Almost every number you discuss with a Florida client is a percentage of something: the commission on a sale price, a down payment, an offer "5% under list price", or the change in a home's value since it was bought. You already do these calculations in Portugal. Here you must do them quickly, in US number notation, and with the decimal point in the right place.

On the exam. Section 14, "Real Estate Computations and Closing of Transactions", carries 6% of the state exam (V-02). The study manual estimates about ten pure-arithmetic questions across the whole exam, and its twelve math patterns include mortgage, appraisal and tax problems as well as the topics of this chapter (manual; not yet verified). Most of them rest on the one idea in this lesson: the percent triangle. Learn it once and the commission, net-to-seller and profit lessons become variations on it.

3. Simple explanation

Step 1: What it represents

Most exam math is one idea: a part is a rate (a percentage) of a total.

Word Meaning Real estate examples
Total (also called the base or the whole) The amount the percentage is taken of Sale price, purchase cost, original value
Rate The percentage, written as a decimal when you calculate Commission rate, down-payment percentage, profit percentage
Part The piece that results Commission in dollars, down payment in dollars, profit in dollars

Take a 6% commission on a $300,000 sale. The total is $300,000, the rate is 6% (0.06) and the part is the commission: $300,000 × 0.06 = $18,000.

Step 2: Units

Percent means "per hundred": 6% = 6/100 = 0.06. Before you multiply or divide, turn every percent into a decimal.

Conversion How Examples
Percent → decimal Divide by 100: move the decimal point two places left 6% = 0.06 · 0.5% = 0.005 · 125% = 1.25
Decimal → percent Multiply by 100: move the point two places right 0.375 = 37.5% · 0.08 = 8%
Fraction → decimal Divide the top number (numerator) by the bottom number (denominator) 3/8 = 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375 = 37.5%
Decimal → fraction Write it over 10, 100 or 1,000, then simplify 0.25 = 25/100 = 1/4
Percent → fraction Write it over 100, then simplify 12.5% = 12.5/100 = 125/1,000 = 1/8

Equivalents worth knowing by heart: 1/2 = 0.5 = 50% · 1/4 = 0.25 = 25% · 3/4 = 0.75 = 75% · 1/8 = 0.125 = 12.5% · 1/3 = 33⅓% ≈ 0.3333 · 2/3 = 66⅔% ≈ 0.6667.

US notation. The period is the decimal point and commas group the thousands: $1,250.50 is one thousand two hundred fifty dollars and fifty cents.

The part and the total always have the same unit (dollars with dollars). The rate has no unit.

Step 3: Formula

The percent triangle: Part = Total × Rate. Rearranged:

  • Total = Part ÷ Rate
  • Rate = Part ÷ Total

Picture a triangle with Part at the top and Total × Rate at the bottom (Section 8). Cover the number you want. If the two numbers left are side by side, multiply them. If one sits above the other, divide the top one by the bottom one.

Word clues: "of" usually means multiply (6% of the price). "Is" or "was" means equals (the commission was $9,450). "What percent" asks for the rate.

Percentage change is a special case in which the total is the starting value:

Percentage change = (new − old) ÷ old

A positive result is an increase; a negative result is a decrease.

Step 4: When it applies

  1. Identify the total the percentage is taken of. This is the most important decision in all exam math.
  2. If that total is known, multiply to get the part.
  3. If the percentage is applied to the unknown (the total is what you are looking for), divide.
  4. For a change over time, the base is always the original (old) value.
The question says Total (base) Unknown Operation
"a 6% commission on a $300,000 sale" Sale price, known Commission Multiply: $300,000 × 0.06
"the 6% commission was $9,450" Sale price, unknown Sale price Divide: $9,450 ÷ 0.06
"$41,250 down on a $275,000 home" Price, known Rate Divide: $41,250 ÷ $275,000
"value went from $80,000 to $92,000" Old value, $80,000 % change Change ÷ old value

Step 5: Worked example

A. Find the total. A 6% commission was $9,450. What was the sale price?

  1. Part = $9,450. Rate = 0.06. The total is unknown, so Total = Part ÷ Rate.
  2. $9,450 ÷ 0.06 = $157,500.
  3. Check: $157,500 × 0.06 = $9,450 ✓.

B. Find the rate. A buyer in Lakeland pays $41,250 down on a $275,000 home.

  1. Rate = Part ÷ Total = $41,250 ÷ $275,000 = 0.15 = 15%.
  2. Check: $275,000 × 0.15 = $41,250 ✓.

C. Percentage change. A lot bought for $80,000 sells for $92,000.

  1. Change = $92,000 − $80,000 = $12,000.
  2. $12,000 ÷ $80,000 (the old value) = 0.15 = +15%.
  3. Reverse the story: a fall from $92,000 to $80,000 is $12,000 ÷ $92,000 = 0.1304, about −13%.

The dollar change is the same, but the base changes, so the percentages differ.

Step 6: Reasonableness check

  • A commission is a small fraction of the price. If your "price" is smaller than the commission, you multiplied instead of divided. ($9,450 × 0.06 = $567, which cannot be the price of a house.)
  • A rate below 100% always gives a part smaller than the total.
  • Estimate with easy percentages: 10% means moving the point one place left, 1% two places. So 1% of $157,500 is $1,575, and 6% is about 6 × $1,575 = $9,450 ✓.
  • The same dollar change is a bigger percentage of a smaller base.

Step 7: Common errors

Error What it looks like Correction
Decimal placement Using 0.6 for 6% (ten times too big) 6% = 0.06; 0.6 = 60%
Not converting the percent $9,450 ÷ 6 = $1,575 Divide by 0.06, not by 6
Wrong base Measuring the fall from $92,000 against $80,000 Divide the change by the original value
Multiplying when the percent is "of" the unknown $9,450 × 0.06 Divide: $9,450 ÷ 0.06
Rounding too early One-third of $240,000 using 0.33 gives $79,200 instead of $80,000 Keep full decimals (or the fraction); round only the final answer

Step 8: Guided practice

G1. Convert 5/8 to a decimal and to a percent. Hint: divide the top by the bottom, then move the point two places right.

Check your answer

5 ÷ 8 = 0.625 = 62.5%.

G2. Write 0.045 as a percent, and 2.75% as a decimal. Hint: decimal → percent moves the point right; percent → decimal moves it left.

Check your answer

0.045 = 4.5%. 2.75% = 0.0275.

G3. A Clearwater home sold for $318,000 and the total commission was $17,490. What was the commission rate? Hint: Rate = Part ÷ Total.

Check your answer

$17,490 ÷ $318,000 = 0.055 = 5.5%. Check: $318,000 × 0.055 = $17,490 ✓.

Step 9: Independent practice

I1. Express 7/16 as a percent.

Check your answer

7 ÷ 16 = 0.4375 = 43.75%.

I2. A 3.5% commission was $11,725. What was the sale price?

Check your answer

The rate is applied to the unknown price, so divide: $11,725 ÷ 0.035 = $335,000. Check: $335,000 × 0.035 = $11,725 ✓.

I3. A lot bought for $64,000 sells for $72,000. What is the percentage gain?

Check your answer

Change $8,000 ÷ original $64,000 = 0.125 = 12.5%.

I4. A home's value falls from $410,000 to $369,000. What is the percentage decrease?

Check your answer

Change $41,000 ÷ original $410,000 = 0.10 = 10%.

I5. A condo's value rises from $360,000 to $378,000 and later falls back to $360,000. What are the percentage rise and the percentage fall?

Check your answer

Rise: $18,000 ÷ $360,000 = 5%. Fall: $18,000 ÷ $378,000 = 0.0476, about 4.76%. Same dollars, different base.

I6. What is 2.25% of $480,000?

Check your answer

$480,000 × 0.0225 = $10,800.

Step 10: Exam application

  1. Read the last sentence first. Is the question asking for the part, the total or the rate?
  2. Find the total the percentage is "of".
  3. Convert the percent to a decimal.
  4. Choose: multiply if the total is known; divide if the total is unknown or the rate is wanted.
  5. Calculate with full decimals. Round only the final answer, the way the question asks.
  6. Reverse-check by multiplying back.

Wrong answer choices are usually built from the typical mistakes: the multiply-instead-of-divide figure, the wrong-base figure and a misplaced decimal. If your answer matches a choice, still run the reverse check.

One rounding exception you will meet later: documentary stamp tax is charged per $100 "or portion", so you round the amount up to the next $100 before calculating (V-18).

4. Key terms

Term Meaning
Percent (%) "Per hundred": 6% = 6/100 = 0.06
Decimal A number written with a decimal point, such as 0.06
Fraction A top number (numerator) over a bottom number (denominator), such as 3/8
Rate The percentage used in a calculation, written as a decimal
Total (base, whole) The amount the percentage is taken of
Part The result of rate × total
Percent triangle Part on top, Total × Rate below; cover the unknown to see the formula
Percentage change (new − old) ÷ old
Original value The starting amount; the base for any percentage change

5. Practical example

Rita, a sales associate at a Tampa brokerage, meets sellers who bought their St. Petersburg home for $320,000.

  1. "How much has our home gained?" Recent comparable sales suggest about $352,000. Change: $32,000 ÷ $320,000 (what they paid) = +10%.
  2. The offer. They list at $352,000, and a buyer offers 5% below the list price. Discount: $352,000 × 0.05 = $17,600. Offer: $352,000 − $17,600 = $334,400 (or $352,000 × 0.95).
  3. The buyer's down payment. The buyer's lender letter shows $66,880 down. Rate: $66,880 ÷ $334,400 = 0.20 = 20% down.
  4. The commission. If the agreed total commission is 5.5% and the sale closes at $334,400: $334,400 × 0.055 = $18,392.

Each answer used the same triangle. The only real decision each time was: what is the total? The answer was the purchase cost for the gain, the list price for the discount, and the sale price for the down payment and the commission.

6. Portugal comparison

Familiar principle. Percentages, fractions and proportions are the same arithmetic everywhere. The course's Portugal–Florida comparison entries contain nothing that changes this lesson.

Florida rule. Exam numbers are written in US notation: a decimal point and commas between thousands ($1,250.50).

Precise difference. Only the notation. If you usually write a decimal comma (0,06) and a thousands point (1.250), train your eye: on the exam, 0.06 is six hundredths and 1,250 is one thousand two hundred fifty.

Exam implication. No Portuguese rule is involved. Read every number in US format and apply the triangle.

7. Legal and numerical requirements

Memorize exactly

  • Part = Total × Rate · Total = Part ÷ Rate · Rate = Part ÷ Total.
  • Percent → decimal: ÷ 100 (point two places left). Decimal → percent: × 100 (point two places right). Fraction → decimal: top ÷ bottom (3/8 = 0.375 = 37.5%).
  • Percentage change = (new − old) ÷ old.
  • Section 14 (computations and closing) = 6% of the exam (V-02).

Understand

  • No statute governs this lesson: it is arithmetic. The one real skill is choosing the right base.
  • When the percent is taken of the unknown, divide.
  • The base for a change is the original value, so a rise and a fall of the same dollar amount give different percentages.
  • Round only at the end, unless the question or a tax rule says otherwise (documentary stamps: round up to the next $100, V-18).

8. Visual explanation

PARTTop of the triangle: the piece (commission, down payment, profit, change in value)
TOTAL × RATEBottom: the whole the percent is taken of, times the percent as a decimal

Cover the unknown. Part covered → Total × Rate. Total covered → Part ÷ Rate. Rate covered → Part ÷ Total.

Do you already know the amount the percent is taken OF?
No: the percent is applied to the unknown, so DIVIDE (Total = Part ÷ Rate)
Yes: MULTIPLY to get the part (Part = Total × Rate), or divide part by total to get the rate

Same $12,000, two different bases

Movement Change Base (original value) Percentage
$80,000 → $92,000 +$12,000 $80,000 +15%
$92,000 → $80,000 −$12,000 $92,000 about −13%

9. Common misconceptions

  • "6% is 0.6." No. 6% = 0.06; 0.6 is 60%.
  • "A percentage always means multiply." No. When the percentage is taken of the unknown amount, divide.
  • "Percentage change is measured on the new value." No. Always divide by the original value.
  • "A 15% rise is undone by a 15% fall." No. The fall is measured on the larger base: $80,000 → $92,000 is +15%, but $92,000 → $80,000 is only about −13%.
  • "Rounding a rate early (1/3 → 0.33) is fine." No. On $240,000 it gives $79,200 instead of $80,000: early rounding can shift the answer by hundreds of dollars. Round once, at the end.

10. Memory sheet

  • Part = Total × Rate. Cover the unknown: Total = Part ÷ Rate; Rate = Part ÷ Total.
  • Percent ↔︎ decimal: move the point two places. Fraction → decimal: top ÷ bottom (3/8 = 37.5%).
  • Percent of the unknown → divide.
