  5. Multiply, round at the end, and check that the days and shares add up.

A question may ask only for the entry, for example "How do unpaid taxes appear?" The answer is debit seller, credit buyer.

4. Key terms

Term Meaning
Proration Dividing an expense or income between buyer and seller as of closing
In arrears Paid at the end of the period (Florida property taxes, mortgage interest)
In advance Paid at the start of the period (rent, insurance premiums, association dues)
Accrued item An expense that has built up but is not yet paid, such as unpaid taxes
Prepaid item An expense paid ahead for days after closing
Daily rate Annual amount ÷ 365, or monthly amount ÷ days in that month
365-day method Actual days in each month; course convention (V-79)
360-day method Twelve 30-day months; use only when the question says so
Debit An amount a party owes at closing
Credit An amount a party receives at closing
Double entry The same amount debited to one party and credited to the other

5. Practical example

An investor buys a tenant-occupied house in Orlando. Closing is August 12 (non-leap year); the buyer owns the day of closing (course convention, V-79).

Item Facts Work Amount Entry
Property taxes $6,205 for the year, unpaid 6,205 ÷ 365 = $17/day × 223 seller's days (Jan 1 – Aug 11) $3,791 Debit seller, credit buyer
August rent $2,170 collected by the seller on Aug 1 2,170 ÷ 31 = $70/day × 20 buyer's days (Aug 12–31) $1,400 Credit buyer, debit seller
Association dues $2,555 for the year, prepaid by the seller in January 2,555 ÷ 365 = $7/day × 142 buyer's days (Aug 12 – Dec 31) $994 Debit buyer, credit seller

Net effect for the buyer: credits $3,791 + $1,400 = $5,191; debit $994; net $4,197 in the buyer's favor. The seller has the mirror image. Each proration is a double entry, so what one party gains, the other loses.

6. Portugal comparison

Familiar principle: sharing a year's charges fairly between seller and buyer is common sense in any market.

Florida rule: the course convention is 365 days with the buyer owning the closing day (V-79: contract and course practice, not law). Property taxes are paid in arrears, so unpaid taxes are a seller debit and buyer credit.

Difference: this course has no verified comparison entry for how Portuguese practice divides annual property taxes or condominium charges between the parties. Any such Portuguese rule requires verification and is not taught here.

Exam implication: answer only with the Florida method the question gives, or the course convention.

7. Legal and numerical requirements

Memorize exactly

  • 365-day method: actual days in each month; daily rate = annual ÷ 365.
  • The buyer owns the day of closing. Seller's days = Jan 1 through the day before closing.
  • Flag (V-79, unresolved): no statute or rule sets either convention. They come from the contract and the course. Follow the method the question gives; otherwise use the course convention. The FREC syllabus expects both the 360- and 365-day methods. The manual says the FR/BAR contract (a private form) prorates through the day before closing (manual statement; V-79 unresolved).
  • Arrears (property taxes, mortgage interest), unpaid: debit seller, credit buyer for the seller's days.
  • Advance: rent the seller collected → credit buyer, debit seller for the unused days. Prepaid insurance or association dues → debit buyer, credit seller for the days after closing.
  • Property taxes: assessed as of January 1; due November 1 (V-76).

Understand

  • The party who is out of pocket (it paid an expense covering the other's days, or the other collected income belonging to its days) is credited, and the other party is debited by the same amount.
  • No verification entry covers the debit/credit directions. They follow from who has paid, as the manual and the course's practice questions teach.
  • If a question says the seller has already paid the taxes, the direction reverses: debit buyer, credit seller for the buyer's days.

8. Visual explanation

Unpaid taxes, closing August 12 (practical example):

Jan 1Tax year starts; assessment date (V-76)
Jan 1 – Aug 11Seller's days: 223 × $17 = $3,791
Aug 12 · closingBuyer owns this day (course convention, V-79); buyer's days begin
Nov 1Whole year's bill due (V-76); the buyer, now the owner, pays $6,205
Dec 31Tax year ends; buyer's days Aug 12 – Dec 31: 142 × $17 = $2,414

The seller pays the buyer $3,791 at closing (debit seller, credit buyer), and the buyer later pays the full bill: $3,791 + $2,414 = $6,205.

Has the bill for the period been paid?
Not yet (arrears: taxes, interest) → the seller owes for the seller's days: debit seller, credit buyer
Yes, by the seller (prepaid dues, insurance, taxes already paid) → the buyer owes for the buyer's days: debit buyer, credit seller. Rent the seller collected → credit buyer, debit seller

9. Common misconceptions

  • "The seller owns the closing day." Under the course convention, the buyer does, so the seller's days stop the day before closing (V-79).
  • "The 365-day method is Florida law." It is a contract and course convention. Follow the question's method if it gives one.
  • "Unpaid taxes are the buyer's debit because the buyer pays them later." No. Because the buyer will pay the whole bill, the buyer is credited for the seller's share.
  • "Rent collected in advance is a credit to the seller." The seller holds the buyer's money, so the entry is credit buyer, debit seller.
  • "Prorations are single entries." Prorations between buyer and seller are double entries.

10. Memory sheet

  • 365 days · buyer owns closing day (course convention, V-79, not law; follow the question).
  • Seller's days = Jan 1 → day before closing. Buyer's days = closing day → Dec 31.
  • Arrears (taxes, interest) unpaid → debit seller, credit buyer.
  • Advance rent → credit buyer, debit seller.
  • Prepaid dues or insurance → debit buyer, credit seller.
  • Check: days add to 365; shares add to the bill. Round only at the end.

lessons.title: The closing statement: debits and credits
lessons.html:
2. Why it matters

The closing statement is where everything in this chapter comes together: the price, the deposit, the loan, the transfer taxes (L14-6), the prorations (L14-7) and the commission. Buyers want to know the exact cash to close, and sellers want to know their net proceeds. As a sales associate you will review these figures before closing and explain each line.

The exam usually asks for one cell of the statement, for example "How does the binder deposit appear?" or "How is an assumed mortgage entered?" It also asks you to compute the buyer's cash due or the seller's net. Each line follows from simple logic, so learn the logic rather than memorizing a table.

3. Simple explanation

Step 1: What it represents

A closing statement (settlement statement) is the accounting of the sale for each party. Each party has two columns:

  • Debit: an amount the party owes at closing (is charged).
  • Credit: an amount the party receives at closing, or has already paid toward what it owes.

At the bottom, the buyer's debits minus credits is the cash the buyer must bring. The seller's credits minus debits is the cash the seller takes home.

Step 2: Units

  • Money: dollars and cents.
  • Entries: each line goes into one or more cells (buyer debit, buyer credit, seller debit, seller credit).
  • Single entry: the line appears for one party only, because the money moves between that party and an outsider (the lender, the tax collector, the brokerage, the title company).
  • Double entry: the line appears for both parties, as a debit to one and a credit to the other for the same amount, because money or value (such as a debt taken over) moves between buyer and seller.

Step 3: Formula

Result Formula
Cash due from the buyer Total buyer debits − total buyer credits
Cash due to the seller Total seller credits − total seller debits

If the seller's debits are larger than the seller's credits, the result is negative and the seller must bring money to closing.

Step 4: When it applies

Ask for each line: does money or value move between buyer and seller (double entry), or between one party and an outsider (single entry)?

Item Buyer Seller Why
Purchase price Debit Credit Buyer owes it; seller receives it (double)
Binder (earnest money) deposit Credit (single entry) — Already paid into escrow; counts toward the price. The seller is already credited with the full price
New mortgage Credit — Lender's money pays part of the price for the buyer (single)
Assumed mortgage Credit Debit Double entry (V-24, corrected)
Existing mortgage payoff — Debit Seller's own debt paid to the lender from proceeds (single)
Deed doc stamps — Debit Customarily the seller's tax (single)
Note stamps + intangible tax Debit — Customarily the buyer's taxes on financing (single)
Unpaid taxes (proration) Credit Debit Seller owes the buyer for the seller's days (double)
Accrued interest on an assumed loan Credit Debit Paid in arrears; seller owes the buyer (double)
Rent the seller collected in advance Credit Debit Seller holds the buyer's days (double)
Prepaid dues or insurance paid by the seller Debit Credit Buyer owes the seller for days after closing (double)
Commission — Debit (customarily) Seller customarily pays the listing brokerage (single)
Buyer's other closing costs (lender, title) Debit — Paid to outsiders (single)
Seller's other closing costs — Debit Paid to outsiders (single)

Correction (V-24): the study manual's table shows the assumed mortgage as a buyer credit only. That is wrong. An assumed mortgage is a double entry. The buyer is credited because the debt the buyer takes over pays part of the price. The seller is debited because the seller hands over the debt instead of receiving that amount in cash. Compare: a new mortgage is a buyer credit only, and the seller's payoff of an existing loan is a seller debit only.

Step 5: Worked example

An assumption sale (outside Miami-Dade). Price $200,000; deposit $10,000; the buyer assumes the seller's $120,000 loan; unpaid taxes proration $1,500; commission 6% = $12,000; deed stamps 2,000 × $0.70 = $1,400; note stamps on the assumed note (course convention, V-25) 1,200 × $0.35 = $420; intangible tax $0 (not new money).

Line Buyer debit Buyer credit Seller debit Seller credit
Price 200,000 200,000
Deposit 10,000
Assumed mortgage 120,000 120,000
Taxes (proration) 1,500 1,500
Commission 12,000
Deed stamps 1,400
Note stamps 420
Totals 200,420 131,500 134,900 200,000

Buyer brings 200,420 − 131,500 = $68,920. Seller receives 200,000 − 134,900 = $65,100.

Step 6: Reasonableness check

  • Quick estimate for the buyer: start with price − loan − deposit, then add the buyer's other debits and subtract the buyer's other credits. Here 200,000 − 120,000 − 10,000 = 70,000, plus 420 and minus 1,500 = 68,920 ✓.
  • Money in = money out. Cash coming in (buyer's cash + deposit + any new loan) must equal cash going out (seller's net + payoffs + commission + taxes + other costs). Here, in: 68,920 + 10,000 = 78,920. Out: 65,100 + 12,000 + 1,400 + 420 = 78,920 ✓. Double entries between buyer and seller cancel out and never appear in this check.

Step 7: Common errors

Error Correct
Deposit as a seller credit (or a double entry) Buyer credit only. The seller is already credited with the full price
Assumed mortgage as a buyer credit only (the manual's table) Debit seller, credit buyer (V-24)
New mortgage as a seller debit Buyer credit only. The seller's own old loan is the payoff
Unpaid-tax proration as debit buyer Debit seller, credit buyer
Seller's payoff on the buyer's side Seller debit only
Subtracting in the wrong order Buyer: debits − credits. Seller: credits − debits
Forgetting the deposit when computing the buyer's cash The deposit is a credit and reduces the cash due

Step 8: Guided practice

G1. Place each item: (a) buyer's binder deposit; (b) seller's mortgage payoff; (c) unpaid property taxes proration; (d) new first mortgage; (e) intangible tax; (f) mortgage assumed by the buyer. Hint: is money moving between buyer and seller?

Check your answer

(a) Credit buyer (single). (b) Debit seller (single). (c) Debit seller, credit buyer (double). (d) Credit buyer (single). (e) Debit buyer (single). (f) Debit seller, credit buyer (double, V-24).

G2. A home in Lee County. Buyer's side: price $240,000; deposit $12,000; new loan $192,000; note stamps $672; intangible tax $384; other buyer closing costs $3,500; credit for unpaid taxes $1,450. Cash due from the buyer? Hint: list debits and credits separately.

Check your answer

Debits: 240,000 + 672 + 384 + 3,500 = $244,556. Credits: 12,000 + 192,000 + 1,450 = $205,450. Cash due = $39,106.

G3. Seller's side of the same sale: payoff $118,400; commission 5.5%; deed stamps; other seller costs $950; tax proration debit $1,450. Seller's net? Hint: compute the commission and the deed stamps first.

Check your answer

Commission = 240,000 × 0.055 = $13,200. Deed stamps = 2,400 × $0.70 = $1,680. Debits: 118,400 + 13,200 + 1,680 + 950 + 1,450 = $135,680. Net = 240,000 − 135,680 = $104,320.

Step 9: Independent practice

A Sarasota home sells for $260,000. The buyer's deposit is $13,000, and the buyer assumes the seller's loan with a balance of $150,000. Accrued interest owed by the seller on that loan is $375; the unpaid-tax proration is $1,120. The buyer pays note stamps on the assumed note ($525) and other costs of $1,900. The seller pays deed stamps ($1,820), a 6% commission and other costs of $800.

P1. How much cash must the buyer bring?

Check your answer

Debits: 260,000 + 525 + 1,900 = $262,425. Credits: 13,000 + 150,000 + 375 + 1,120 = $164,495. Cash due = $97,930.

P2. How much does the seller receive?

Check your answer

Commission = $15,600. Debits: 150,000 + 375 + 1,120 + 1,820 + 15,600 + 800 = $169,715. Net = 260,000 − 169,715 = $90,285.

P3. If you followed the manual's uncorrected table (assumed mortgage as a buyer credit only), what seller net would you get, and why is it impossible?

Check your answer

$90,285 + $150,000 = $240,285. The seller would be "paid" in cash for a debt the buyer took over. Money in ($97,930 + $13,000 = $110,930) would no longer equal money out. Correct entry: debit seller, credit buyer (V-24).

P4. Which of these is a single entry: the purchase price, the binder deposit, the unpaid-tax proration, the assumed mortgage?

Check your answer

The binder deposit (credit buyer only). The other three are double entries.

Step 10: Exam application

  • One-cell questions: decide whether money or value moves between the parties (double) or to or from an outsider (single), then who owes and who receives.
  • Most-tested cells: deposit = buyer credit only. New loan = buyer credit only. Assumed loan = debit seller + credit buyer. Payoff = seller debit only. Unpaid taxes = debit seller, credit buyer. Commission = seller debit (customarily).
  • Cash questions: write two lists, debits and credits, for the party asked about. Do not mix in the other party's lines.
  • If a practice source shows an assumed mortgage as a buyer credit only, it reflects the manual's error. Answer debit seller, credit buyer. (If a question asks only about the buyer's side, the buyer's entry is a credit.)

4. Key terms

Term Meaning
Closing (settlement) statement The accounting of the sale showing each party's debits and credits
Debit An amount a party owes at closing
Credit An amount a party receives at closing, or has already paid toward the price
Single entry A line that appears for one party only (money to or from an outsider)
Double entry The same amount debited to one party and credited to the other
Binder (earnest money) deposit The buyer's good-faith deposit held in escrow; credited to the buyer at closing
Payoff Paying off the seller's existing loan from the seller's proceeds
Assumed mortgage An existing loan the buyer takes over; debit seller, credit buyer
Cash to close Buyer's debits − buyer's credits
Seller's net proceeds Seller's credits − seller's debits

5. Practical example

A financed sale in Orlando (Orange County). Price $385,000; closing August 12 (non-leap year; the buyer owns the closing day under the course convention, V-79). The buyer's $20,000 deposit is held in escrow by the title company. The buyer has a new $308,000 loan (80% of the price; the appraisal was not lower than the price). The seller's existing loan payoff is $210,000. The listing agreement provides a 5% commission. Annual property taxes of $6,205 are unpaid. The buyer's other closing costs are $4,800, and the seller's are $1,200.

Supporting figures: deed stamps 3,850 × $0.70 = $2,695; note stamps 3,080 × $0.35 = $1,078; intangible tax 308,000 × 0.002 = $616; tax proration $17/day × 223 seller's days = $3,791; commission 385,000 × 0.05 = $19,250.

Line Buyer debit Buyer credit Seller debit Seller credit
Purchase price 385,000 385,000
Deposit 20,000
New mortgage 308,000
Payoff of seller's loan 210,000
Property taxes (proration) 3,791 3,791
Commission 19,250
Deed stamps 2,695
Note stamps 1,078
Intangible tax 616
Other costs 4,800 1,200
Totals 391,494 331,791 236,936 385,000
Balance Buyer brings $59,703 Seller receives $148,064

The associate's check before closing is that money in equals money out (see section 8).

6. Portugal comparison

Familiar principle: in any sale, someone must account for the price, the loans and the taxes so each party knows what it pays and receives.

Florida rule: on the Florida closing statement, deed stamps are customarily a seller debit, and note stamps and intangible tax are buyer debits on financing.

Precise difference (PT-09): in Portugal the buyer pays IMT and Imposto do Selo, so the main transfer taxes sit on the buyer's side. In Florida the main deed tax customarily sits on the seller's side. How a Portuguese sale is documented and settled between the parties is not covered by this course's comparison entries and requires verification.

Exam implication: place deed stamps as a seller debit unless the question says the contract allocates them differently.

7. Legal and numerical requirements

Memorize exactly

  • Debit = what a party owes. Credit = what a party receives.
  • Price: debit buyer, credit seller. Deposit: credit buyer only (single). New mortgage: credit buyer only. Payoff: debit seller only.
  • Assumed mortgage: debit seller AND credit buyer (double entry). This is a correction of the manual's table (V-24).
  • Prorations between the parties: double entries. Unpaid taxes: debit seller, credit buyer.
  • Deed stamps: seller debit. Note stamps + intangible tax: buyer debit. Commission: seller debit. These reflect custom (manual; not yet verified), and contracts can allocate differently.
  • Buyer's cash = buyer debits − buyer credits. Seller's cash = seller credits − seller debits.

Understand

  • V-24 (corrected) verifies the three mortgage lines: assumed = double entry; new = buyer credit only; payoff = seller debit only. The other placements follow the same accounting logic and come from the study manual (manual; not yet verified).
  • A double entry moves value from one party to the other, so it changes both nets but cancels out in the money-in = money-out check.
  • The deposit is a credit to the buyer and not to the seller, because the seller is already credited with the full price, and the deposit is part of that price.

8. Visual explanation

Money in = money out (practical example). Every dollar that arrives at the closing table leaves it again. Double entries between buyer and seller (the price and the proration) cancel and do not appear here.

Money in Amount Money out Amount
Buyer's cash at closing 59,703 Seller's net proceeds 148,064
Deposit held in escrow 20,000 Payoff to the seller's lender 210,000
New loan funds 308,000 Commission 19,250
Deed stamps 2,695
Note stamps + intangible tax 1,694
Buyer's other costs 4,800
Seller's other costs 1,200
Total 387,703 Total 387,703
Does money or value move between buyer and seller?
No (lender, tax, brokerage, title) → single entry: only the party who pays or receives (deposit, new loan, payoff, stamps, commission)
Yes → double entry: debit the party who gives value, credit the party who receives it (price, prorations, assumed mortgage)

9. Common misconceptions

  • "The deposit is credited to the seller." It is a buyer credit only. The seller's credit is the full price.
  • "An assumed mortgage is just a buyer credit, like a new loan." It is a double entry: debit seller, credit buyer (V-24 corrects the manual).
  • "The new loan is debited to the seller." The seller's debit is the payoff of the seller's own old loan, not the buyer's new loan.
  • "Unpaid taxes are a buyer debit." Debit seller, credit buyer: the buyer will pay the whole bill later.
  • "Commission is split between buyer and seller on the statement." It is customarily a seller debit.

10. Memory sheet

  • Debit = owes · credit = receives.
  • Deposit: buyer credit only. New loan: buyer credit only. Payoff: seller debit only.
  • Assumed loan: debit seller + credit buyer (V-24 corrects the manual).
  • Prorations between the parties: double entries (unpaid taxes → debit seller, credit buyer).
  • Deed stamps + commission → seller debits; note stamps + intangible → buyer debits (custom: manual; not yet verified).
  • Buyer brings debits − credits; seller gets credits − debits; money in = money out.

lessons.title: Real estate markets, supply and demand, and pricing tools
lessons.html:
2. Why it matters

In practice. Most client conversations come back to price. A seller asks what her condo is worth. An investor asks whether a neighborhood is heating up or cooling down. A lender with a distressed loan asks you for a value opinion. To answer, you need to read the local market (supply, demand, vacancy), choose the right pricing tool and give it the right name.

On the exam. Section 15 is worth about 1% of the exam (V-02). That is roughly one question out of 100 (V-01). The questions are conceptual: why real estate markets react slowly, what rising vacancy signals, and whether a sales associate may charge for a comparative market analysis. The usual trap is the word "appraisal".

3. Simple explanation

Why real estate is not like the stock market

A market is where buyers and sellers of the same kind of product meet. Every share of a company's stock is identical to every other share, and you can buy one from anywhere in seconds. Real estate is the opposite in almost every way:

Feature What it means What it does to the market
Immobile Land cannot be moved. Markets are local. Empty homes in Pensacola do not fix a shortage of homes in Orlando.
Unique No two parcels are the same (location, lot, view, condition). There is no single quoted price. Every price needs comparison and judgment.
Slow supply New buildings need land, approvals, financing and construction, which often takes years. When demand jumps, prices move first. New supply arrives much later.
Government influence Zoning, interest rates and taxes keep changing. The rules keep shifting while the market adjusts.

Buyers and sellers also rarely have complete information, which slows price adjustment further.

Supply and demand

  • Demand is how much property people want and can pay for, to buy or to rent, at a given price.
  • Supply is how much property is available for sale or rent at a given price.

The basic rule: when demand grows faster than supply, prices and rents rise. When supply grows faster than demand, prices and rents soften (they stop rising or they fall).

Demand drivers Supply drivers
Population (people moving in) Labor (construction workers)
Income Land (available, buildable sites)
Employment (jobs) Materials
Credit availability (how easily buyers get mortgage loans) Construction financing (money lent to builders)

Why the market is slow to adjust. In the short run the number of homes is almost fixed. Suppose a new employer brings thousands of jobs to a county. Demand rises at once, but builders need years to deliver new units, so prices rise in the meantime. Builders react to those higher prices. Because projects take so long, many of them can finish at about the same time, sometimes after demand has cooled. The market then swings the other way, into oversupply.

Vacancy as a signal. The vacancy rate is the share of units that are empty. Rising vacancy means there is more space than users want: oversupply, so prices and rents tend to soften. Falling vacancy means the market is tightening. You will also hear two everyday labels. In a buyer's market, supply exceeds demand and buyers negotiate harder. In a seller's market, demand exceeds supply and sellers have the upper hand.

Three pricing tools, and only one is an appraisal

First, two terms. Comparables ("comps") are similar nearby properties used as evidence of price. A short sale is a sale in which the lender agrees to accept less than the balance owed on the loan.

CMA BPO Appraisal
Full name Comparative market analysis Broker price opinion Appraisal
Prepared by A real estate licensee A real estate licensee A state-licensed or certified appraiser
Usually ordered by / for A seller or buyer deciding on a price (the listing conversation) A lender or investor (short sales, portfolio checks) Whoever needs a formal opinion of value, for example a lender
Standard The licensee's judgment from comparables The licensee's judgment USPAP
May a licensee charge for it? Yes (manual; not yet verified) Yes (manual; not yet verified) Charged by the appraiser
May it be called an "appraisal"? Never Never Yes

What goes into a CMA. A CMA uses three groups of comparables, and each one tells you something different:

  • Recently sold: what buyers actually paid. This is the strongest evidence.
  • Currently listed: the competition that buyers see today.
  • Expired: listings that ended without a sale. They usually show prices the market rejected.

The licensee rule. A licensee may prepare and charge for CMAs and BPOs but must never call them appraisals (manual; not yet verified). The reason is simple. An appraisal is a regulated professional product, prepared by a licensed or certified appraiser under USPAP (the Uniform Standards of Professional Appraisal Practice), and lenders rely on it. If a licensee's price opinion were labeled an "appraisal", the client would think they were getting something they are not.

Federally related transactions. Broadly, a federally related transaction is a real estate financing transaction connected with federally regulated lenders. That is only a rough description: this course's sources do not give the exact federal definition or its exceptions, so the details require verification. Federally related transactions require a state-licensed or certified appraiser following USPAP (manual; not yet verified). What stops a broker is the license class, not the method: a broker does not become eligible by "following USPAP". The manual also says that a licensee who does appraisal work outside federally related transactions must still comply with USPAP (manual; not yet verified).

4. Key terms

Term Meaning
Immobility Land cannot be relocated; the main reason real estate markets are local
Uniqueness No two parcels are identical, so every price needs comparison
Demand The amount of property people want and can pay for at a given price
Supply The amount of property available for sale or rent at a given price
Credit availability How easily buyers can obtain mortgage loans; a demand driver
Vacancy rate The share of units that are empty; rising vacancy signals oversupply
Buyer's / seller's market Supply exceeds demand / demand exceeds supply
Comparables (comps) Similar nearby properties used as price evidence
CMA Comparative market analysis by a licensee to suggest a price range (sold, listed and expired comps)
BPO Broker price opinion, often for lenders or investors; chargeable but not an appraisal
Appraisal A state-licensed or certified appraiser's USPAP-compliant opinion of value
USPAP Uniform Standards of Professional Appraisal Practice, the standards that govern appraisal practice
Short sale A sale in which the lender accepts less than the loan balance

5. Practical example

Sofia is a sales associate in Sarasota. All figures below are hypothetical.

Reading the market. Two years ago condo prices in Sofia's area were climbing, and developers started several new buildings. This year those buildings are finishing at about the same time. Sofia's rental data show the condo vacancy rate rising for three quarters in a row. Her reading: the new supply arrived late, after demand had cooled. That means oversupply, so prices and rents will soften. She tells her sellers to price realistically.

A CMA for Mr. Hughes. Mr. Hughes owns a two-bedroom condo. He wants a written price opinion before deciding whether to list, and Sofia's brokerage charges a fee for written reports.

Comparable group What Sofia found What it tells her
Recently sold 4 units, $312,000 to $328,000 What buyers actually paid
Currently listed 3 units, $329,000 to $345,000 The competition Mr. Hughes would face
Expired 2 units, listed at $355,000 and $360,000 Prices the market rejected

Sofia suggests a range of $315,000 to $325,000. Because vacancy is rising, she recommends the lower half. The cover page says "Comparative Market Analysis". She may charge for it, and she never calls it an appraisal (manual; not yet verified).

Two more requests the same week.

Request Right tool Can Sofia do it?
A lender's asset manager needs a value opinion on a house being sold in a short sale BPO Yes, she may prepare it and charge for it, labeled "Broker Price Opinion" and never "appraisal" (manual; not yet verified)
A buyer's lender says the loan is a federally related transaction and needs an appraisal Appraisal No. She refers the lender to a state-licensed or certified appraiser (manual; not yet verified)

Sofia took an appraisal course and works carefully, but that changes nothing for the federally related loan: her license class does not allow it.

6. Portugal comparison

The familiar principle. Supply and demand, local markets and slow new construction are economics, not law. Your experience reading a local market transfers directly. So does the habit of giving an owner a price opinion before taking a listing.

The Florida rule. A licensee may prepare and charge for a CMA or BPO but must never call it an appraisal. Federally related transactions need a state-licensed or certified appraiser following USPAP (manual; not yet verified).

The precise difference. This course has no verified comparison entry on how Portuguese law regulates property valuations or price opinions from mediadores. Any Portuguese rule on this point requires verification. Do not assume the Portuguese categories line up with Florida's three tools.

Exam implication. Answer only with Florida's three categories. Watch for the word "appraisal": a licensee's CMA or BPO may be charged for, but it is never an appraisal.

7. Legal and numerical requirements

Memorize exactly

  • Real estate markets are local (immobile, unique product) and slow (supply takes years to build). Government (zoning, rates, taxes) keeps changing the field.
  • Demand drivers: population, income, employment, credit availability.
  • Supply drivers: labor, land, materials, construction financing.
  • Rising vacancy → oversupply → softening prices and rents.
  • CMA: a licensee's pricing tool using recently sold, currently listed and expired comparables.
  • BPO: ordered by a lender or investor (short sales, portfolio checks).
  • Appraisal: a state-licensed or certified appraiser's USPAP-compliant opinion of value.
  • A licensee may prepare and charge for CMAs and BPOs and must never call them appraisals (manual; not yet verified).
  • Federally related transactions need a state-licensed or certified appraiser following USPAP (manual; not yet verified).

Understand

  • Prices react first and supply reacts years later. That is why markets overshoot both ways.
  • Expired listings matter because they show the prices buyers refused.
  • The naming rule protects consumers: "appraisal" means a regulated product from an appraiser.
  • For federally related transactions, the obstacle is the license class, not the method used.
  • The manual adds that a licensee doing appraisal work outside federally related transactions must still comply with USPAP (manual; not yet verified).
  • Source status: no verification entry covers this lesson's legal statements, so they are flagged as resting on the study manual. The market concepts are general economics, not law. The Section 15 weight (about 1%) comes from V-02.

8. Visual explanation

Why supply lags demand

StartNew jobs and new residents arrive, and demand rises
Short runSupply is almost fixed, so prices and rents rise and vacancy falls
Builders reactThey buy land, seek approvals and arrange construction financing
Years laterMany projects finish together, and demand may have cooled
ResultVacancy rises, which means oversupply, and prices and rents soften

Illustrative sequence, not a legal rule. Prices adjust first and quantity adjusts later.

Which pricing tool, and what may you call it?

Is the value opinion needed for a federally related transaction?
No: a licensee may prepare a CMA (pricing for a client) or a BPO (for a lender or investor) and may charge for it
Yes: only a state-licensed or certified appraiser following USPAP
Is the licensee about to label a CMA or BPO an "appraisal"?
No: lawful. Call it a CMA or a BPO
Yes: not allowed. A licensee's price opinion is never an appraisal

Both rules: manual; not yet verified.

9. Common misconceptions

  • "Real estate prices adjust quickly, like stocks." No. The product is immobile and unique, and new supply takes years to build.
  • "A housing shortage is fixed as soon as builders start building." No. Construction takes years, and prices rise in the meantime.
  • "Rising vacancy means a hot market." The opposite: it signals oversupply and softening prices and rents.
  • "Only appraisers may charge for a value opinion." No. A licensee, including a sales associate, may prepare and charge for a CMA or BPO (manual; not yet verified).
  • "A CMA is just a cheap appraisal, so the name doesn't matter." It does matter: a licensee must never call a CMA or BPO an appraisal (manual; not yet verified).
  • "An experienced broker who follows USPAP may appraise for a federally related transaction." No. The license class is the barrier, not the standards (manual; not yet verified).
  • "A BPO is ordered by the seller." Usually not. It is ordered by a lender or investor, for example for a short sale or a portfolio check.
  • "Expired listings are useless in a CMA." No. They show the prices the market rejected.

10. Memory sheet

  • Local · immobile · unique · slow supply (years to build) · government shifts the field.
  • Demand: population, income, jobs, credit. Supply: labor, land, materials, construction money.
  • Vacancy rising = oversupply = prices and rents soften.
  • CMA: licensee; sold + listed + expired comps. BPO: lender or investor. Appraisal: appraiser + USPAP.
  • CMA and BPO: yes, may charge. "Appraisal": never (manual; not yet verified).
  • Federally related transaction → licensed or certified appraiser only (manual; not yet verified).

lessons.title: Value: characteristics and principles
lessons.html:
2. Why it matters

In practice. Every pricing conversation with a Florida seller runs on these ideas. An owner says "we spent $85,000 on the pool, so add $85,000", or "the county says it's worth $360,000". You need precise words to explain why neither number is the market value. The same ideas explain why the biggest house on a modest street is hard to sell, and why a developer will pay extra for the lot next door.

On the exam. Appraisal is one of the largest sections of the Florida exam: 8% of the content (V-02, confirmed), so about 8 of the 100 questions (V-01). Questions on principles test vocabulary: you get a one-line scenario and four principle names. This lesson is also the base for L16-2 to L16-4. Substitution sits under all three appraisal approaches, contribution sets the adjustment amounts, and anticipation drives the income approach.

3. Simple explanation

Source status: the definitions and principles in this lesson come from the study manual. No official-source verification entry covers appraisal theory, so they are taught as (manual; not yet verified). The Florida tax facts marked with a V-number are verified.

Value needs four things: DUST

A property has value only when all four elements of value are present at the same time:

Element Meaning If it is missing…
Demand People want it and can pay for it Nobody bids, however nice the property
Utility It can be used; it satisfies a need A parcel with no possible use attracts no buyer
Scarcity Supply is limited Something unlimited (like air) has no market price
Transferability Ownership can legally pass to a buyer If title cannot be conveyed, nobody can buy it

If you remove any one element, value disappears. That is why the exam asks for all four together. Learn the exact words: the S is Scarcity (not "supply") and the T is Transferability (the legal ability to pass ownership to a buyer). Answer options often swap in similar-sounding words.

Value, price and cost are three different numbers

First, one term: an arm's-length sale is a sale between parties who are independent of each other and each act in their own interest (not relatives, not related companies).

  • Market value is the most probable price in an arm's-length sale between informed parties under no unusual pressure. It is an estimate of what should happen in a normal sale.
  • Price is what was actually paid in one particular sale. It is a historical fact. A rushed sale, a sale between relatives or a poorly informed buyer can produce a price far from market value.
  • Cost is what it took to build the property. Building something does not mean anyone will pay that much for it.
  • Assessed value is the value set for property taxes. In Florida, property is assessed as of January 1 (V-76, confirmed). A homestead's assessed value may rise each year by no more than 3% or the CPI change, whichever is lower (Save Our Homes, V-67, confirmed). So a home owned for many years can carry an assessed value far below its market value. (A proposed 2026 amendment, V-23, is pending. It is not law and not exam content.)
  • Insurable value is the value used for insurance coverage. It concerns what can be damaged or destroyed, mainly the building, so it can differ from market value.

The principles of value, and why they work

Substitution is the foundation of appraisal. A buyer will not pay more than the cost of an equally desirable substitute. It works because informed buyers have alternatives. If a similar house two streets away is available for $410,000, few buyers will pay $450,000 for yours. Each approach uses a different substitute: a similar sold property (sales comparison), building a similar property (cost), or buying a similar income stream (income).

Highest and best use (HBU) is the use that is legally permissible, physically possible, financially feasible and maximally productive. Learn the tests in that order. First remove the uses the law does not allow (zoning, for example). Then remove the uses the site cannot physically support, and then the uses that would not pay for themselves. Of the uses left, the one producing the highest value wins. HBU matters because land is valued for the best use the market can make of it, which may not be its current use.

Anticipation says value reflects expected future benefits. Buyers pay today for what they expect to receive later: rent, enjoyment, resale. It is the basis of the income approach (L16-4).

Contribution says a feature is worth what it adds to value, not what it cost. A pool that cost $85,000 but adds $35,000 to market value contributes $35,000.

Increasing and decreasing returns apply contribution to the question "how much should we improve?" At first, improvements may add more value than they cost (increasing returns). Past a certain point, each extra dollar spent adds less than a dollar of value (decreasing returns).

Conformity says value is best protected when a property is reasonably similar to its surroundings in size, style, quality and use. It has two corollaries:

  • Progression: a modest property gains value from better neighbours.
  • Regression: a superior property loses value from lesser neighbours.

Plottage and assemblage. Combining adjacent parcels can create a site worth more than the separate parcels. The act of combining is assemblage. The extra value created is plottage. For example, two lots worth $100,000 each might be worth $260,000 together. The plottage value is then $60,000.

4. Key terms

Term Meaning
DUST Demand, Utility, Scarcity, Transferability: the four elements of value
Arm's-length sale Sale between independent parties, each acting in their own interest
Market value Most probable price in an arm's-length sale between informed parties under no unusual pressure
Price What was actually paid in one sale
Cost What it took to build
Assessed value Value for property taxes (Florida: as of January 1, V-76)
Insurable value Value used for insurance coverage
Substitution A buyer won't pay more than the cost of an equally desirable substitute
Highest and best use Legally permissible, physically possible, financially feasible, maximally productive use
Anticipation Value reflects expected future benefits; basis of the income approach
Contribution A feature is worth what it adds, not what it cost
Increasing / decreasing returns Improvements first add more than they cost, then less
Conformity Value is protected by similarity to surrounding properties
Progression / regression Modest home lifted by better neighbours / superior home dragged down by lesser ones
Plottage / assemblage Value increase from combining parcels / the act of combining them

5. Practical example

Setting. You are a sales associate preparing a CMA for Linda. A CMA is a licensee's pricing tool and is never called an appraisal (manual; not yet verified; see L15-1). Linda owns a 4-bedroom pool home in a Sarasota subdivision of mostly smaller 3-bedroom homes. It has been her homestead since 2012.

What Linda says Value type or principle What you explain
"I paid $280,000 in 2012." Price A historical fact about one sale, not today's market value
"The county's assessed value is $360,000." Assessed value A tax value. As her homestead, its growth has been capped by Save Our Homes (V-67), so it can sit well below market value
"The pool and summer kitchen cost us $85,000." Contribution Recent sales show that similar homes with pools sell for about $35,000 more. The features contribute about $35,000, not $85,000
"Mine is the biggest house on the street." Conformity → regression Smaller neighbours pull a superior house's value down. Her small neighbour benefits (progression)
"Buyers will compare it with the new 4-bedroom homes nearby." Substitution If an equally desirable new home is available at $545,000, informed buyers will not pay much more for hers
"A new interchange is planned near the subdivision." Anticipation Buyers pay today for expected future benefits, such as better access
"A developer bought the two corner lots on the main road to combine them." Assemblage / plottage Assemblage is the act. Any extra value of the combined site is plottage. Whether it can become a shop depends first on what zoning permits (HBU test 1)

Your CMA will show a price range based on comparable sales, not on Linda's purchase price, her costs or the county's figure.

6. Portugal comparison

The familiar principle. In your brokerage work you have probably priced homes by looking at what similar nearby homes sold for, and told owners that a renovation is not worth what it cost them. Those ideas are substitution and contribution. They are market logic, not national law.

The Florida rule. The Florida exam tests these ideas with a fixed US vocabulary: DUST; market value vs price vs cost; assessed and insurable value; the four HBU tests; progression, regression, plottage and assemblage. It expects the exact definitions.

The precise difference. This course has no verified Portugal–Florida comparison entry on valuation. Any statement about how Portuguese law, banks or tax authorities define "value", and any Portuguese tax valuation figure, requires verification. Florida's assessed value is a Florida property-tax concept (January 1 assessment, V-76; Save Our Homes cap, V-67). Do not treat it as equal to any Portuguese figure.

Exam implication. Answer with the exact US term the question is looking for. On this exam "price", "cost" and "market value" are never interchangeable.

7. Legal and numerical requirements

Memorize exactly

Appraisal concepts: manual; not yet verified (no verification entry covers them).

  • DUST: Demand, Utility, Scarcity, Transferability.
  • Market value: most probable price, arm's-length sale, informed parties, no unusual pressure.
  • Price = what was paid. Cost = what it took to build. Assessed value = taxes. Insurable value = insurance.
  • HBU: legally permissible → physically possible → financially feasible → maximally productive.
  • Substitution = the foundation of appraisal. Anticipation = the basis of the income approach.
  • Contribution: worth what it adds, not what it cost.
  • Progression lifts the modest home. Regression drags down the superior one.
  • Plottage = the value gain. Assemblage = the act.

Verified figures:

  • Appraisal = 8% of the exam (V-02).
  • Florida property is assessed as of January 1 (V-76). A homestead's assessed value rises ≤ 3% or the CPI change, whichever is lower (V-67).

Understand

  • Why value needs all four DUST elements at once.
  • Why market value is an estimate while price is a fact.
  • Why over-improving a home rarely pays: contribution, decreasing returns and regression all point the same way.
  • Which principle supports which approach (section 8).

8. Visual explanation

1. Legally permissibleAllowed by zoning and other legal limits? If not, discard it.
2. Physically possibleCan the site's size, shape and soil support it?
3. Financially feasibleWould the use pay for itself?
4. Maximally productiveOf the uses left, which gives the highest value? That use is the HBU.

Highest and best use: four filters, applied in order (manual; not yet verified).

Principle Where you meet it again
Substitution All three approaches: sales comparison (L16-2), cost (L16-3), income (L16-4)
Contribution The size of each adjustment in the sales comparison grid (L16-2)
Anticipation The income approach (L16-4)

9. Common misconceptions

  • "The price paid is the market value." No. Price is one actual sale. Market value is the most probable price in an arm's-length sale between informed parties under no unusual pressure.
  • "It cost $85,000, so it adds $85,000." No. Under contribution, a feature is worth what it adds to value.
  • "Assessed value is market value." No. Assessed value is for taxes and, for a Florida homestead, its growth is capped (V-67).
  • "Progression means prices rising over time." No. It is about neighbours: a modest home lifted by better ones.
  • "Plottage and assemblage mean the same thing." No. Assemblage is the act of combining; plottage is the extra value.
  • "Highest and best use is the most profitable use imaginable." No. It must first be legally permissible, then physically possible, then financially feasible.
  • "Anticipation is about past sales." No. It is about expected future benefits. Past sales are the evidence for substitution.

10. Memory sheet

  • DUST: Demand · Utility · Scarcity · Transferability.
  • Market value (most probable · arm's-length · informed · no pressure) ≠ price (paid) ≠ cost (to build). Also assessed (taxes) and insurable.
  • Substitution underlies everything.
  • HBU: legal → physical → financial → maximally productive.
  • Anticipation = future benefits → income approach.
  • Contribution: worth what it adds, not what it cost.
  • Conformity: progression lifts, regression drags.
  • Plottage = the gain; assemblage = the act.
  • Florida assessed value: January 1 (V-76); homestead cap 3% or CPI, lower (V-67).

lessons.title: Sales comparison approach
lessons.html:
2. Why it matters

In practice. Every time you price a Florida home, you do a rough sales comparison. You look at what similar homes sold for and ask how this one is different. An appraiser does the same work formally, on an adjustment grid: a table that lists each comparable sale and the dollar corrections made to it. When a buyer's lender orders an appraisal, or a seller disputes your CMA (comparative market analysis: a licensee's pricing tool, never called an appraisal; manual; not yet verified), you must be able to read that grid and explain every plus and minus.

On the exam. Appraisal is 8% of the exam (V-02, confirmed), so about 8 of the 100 questions (V-01). Sales comparison questions are short and predictable. They ask which way to adjust, what one comparable's adjusted price is, and which comparable deserves the most weight. The wrong answers are built on two mistakes: adjusting the subject, and adjusting in the wrong direction.

3. Simple explanation

Source status. The appraisal method in this lesson comes from the study manual. No official-source verification entry covers appraisal methods, so the rules are taught as (manual; not yet verified). The arithmetic itself needs no verification.

Step 1: What it represents

The sales comparison approach estimates a property's value from the prices of recent sales of similar properties. It rests on substitution (L16-1): an informed buyer will not pay more than the cost of an equally desirable substitute. So what buyers just paid for similar homes shows what this home is worth.

Term Meaning
Subject (property) The property being valued
Comparable ("comp") A recent sale of a similar property, ideally nearby and an arm's-length sale (independent parties, L16-1)
Adjustment A dollar amount added to or subtracted from a comp's sale price for one difference from the subject
Adjusted sale price The comp's price after all adjustments: what the comp would have sold for if it were just like the subject
Adjustment grid The table showing the comps, their differences and the adjustments

The approach is best for homes and vacant land (manual), because these sell often and buyers really do shop for them by comparison.

Step 2: Units

  • Sale prices and adjustments are in US dollars.
  • A feature adjustment is a lump sum (for example, a pool: $25,000).
  • A size adjustment is dollars per square foot × the difference in square feet. US living area is measured in square feet. Metric aside only: 1 m² ≈ 10.76 sq ft.
  • The amount of each adjustment is the feature's contribution (L16-1): what it adds to market value, not what it cost to build.

Step 3: Formula

Adjusted sale price = comp's sale price − value of what the comp has that the subject lacks + value of what the subject has that the comp lacks

You adjust the comparable, never the subject. The question to ask is: "If this comp were exactly like the subject, what would it have sold for?"

Situation Adjustment to the comp's price Mnemonic
Comp Better (it has a feature the subject lacks, or more of it) Subtract CBS
Comp Inferior (it lacks a feature the subject has, or has less) Add CIA
Both have the same feature No adjustment —

Why subtract when the comp is better? The comp's price already includes the value of its extra feature. The subject does not have that feature, so it would not earn that money. You take it out.

Step 4: When it applies

  • Property types: best for homes and vacant land (manual). Brand-new or special-purpose buildings with few sales point to the cost approach (L16-3); income property points to the income approach (L16-4).
  • Choosing comps: use recent, similar, nearby, arm's-length sales. A licensee's CMA also shows currently listed and expired listings to shape a price range (manual), but only sold properties show what buyers actually paid.
  • Bracketing: the adjusted prices of good comps bracket the subject's value, meaning some fall above it and some below (manual).
  • Weighting: the comp with the fewest and smallest adjustments is the most similar to the subject. It is the most reliable, so it carries the most weight (manual). Judge "smallest" by the size of each adjustment, ignoring the plus or minus sign: +$15,000 and −$15,000 net to zero, but they are still two large adjustments.
  • Final figure: a weighted judgement, never a simple average (reconciliation, L16-4).

Step 5: Worked example

A. The manual's grid example. A comp sold for $410,000. It has a pool worth $25,000 that the subject lacks. The subject has a renovated kitchen worth $15,000 that the comp lacks.

Item Who is better? Amount
Comp's sale price $410,000
Pool (only the comp has it) Comp better → subtract −$25,000
Renovated kitchen (only the subject has it) Comp inferior → add +$15,000
Indicated value from this comp $400,000

B. A three-comp grid in Lakeland. Subject: 1,800 sq ft, 3 bedrooms, 2 baths, 2-car garage, no pool. The appraiser's market data show these contributions: pool $25,000; living area $100 per sq ft; 2-car garage instead of 1-car $8,000.

Comp A Comp B Comp C
Sale price $392,000 $441,000 $388,000
Living area 1,800 (same): 0 1,900, better: −$10,000 1,650, inferior: +$15,000
Garage 1-car, inferior: +$8,000 2-car (same): 0 1-car, inferior: +$8,000
Pool None (same): 0 Pool, better: −$25,000 Pool, better: −$25,000
Adjusted price $400,000 $406,000 $386,000
Number of adjustments 1 2 3
Total size of adjustments $8,000 $35,000 $48,000

Comp A needs the fewest and smallest adjustments, so it carries the most weight, and the indicated value is close to $400,000. The adjusted prices ($386,000 to $406,000) bracket that figure. The simple average of the three ($397,333) is not the method.

Step 6: Reasonableness check

  • Direction test. Comp better → its adjusted price goes down. Comp inferior → it goes up. Ask: "Would the subject sell for more or less than this comp?"
  • Clustering. Adjusted prices should sit closer together than raw prices. In example B the raw prices span $53,000 ($388,000 to $441,000); the adjusted prices span only $20,000.
  • Size. Each adjustment is a market contribution, often much less than what the feature cost.
  • Work backwards. $400,000 − $15,000 + $25,000 = $410,000 ✓.

Step 7: Common errors

Error Correction
Adjusting the subject's value Adjust only the comparables
Adding the value of a feature only the comp has Comp better → subtract (CBS)
Using what the feature cost Use what it adds to market value (contribution)
Adjusting for a feature both properties share No difference, no adjustment
Giving most weight to the highest price or the most recent sale Most weight = fewest and smallest adjustments
Treating a small net adjustment as "few adjustments" Count each adjustment and its size, ignoring signs
Averaging the adjusted prices Weigh them; never a simple average
Using a sale between relatives as a comp Comps should be arm's-length sales (L16-1)

Step 8: Guided practice

G1. A comp sold for $289,000. It has a 2-car garage; the subject has a 1-car garage. The second garage space adds $9,000 of value. What is the comp's adjusted price? Hint: which property is better?

Check your answer

The comp is better → subtract. $289,000 − $9,000 = $280,000.

G2. A Sarasota comp sold for $352,000. The subject has a screened lanai (a covered, screened patio, very common in Florida) worth $7,500 that the comp lacks. The comp has a new roof worth $11,000 that the subject lacks. What is the comp's adjusted price? Hint: one plus, one minus.

Check your answer

Lanai: comp inferior → +$7,500. Roof: comp better → −$11,000. $352,000 + $7,500 − $11,000 = $348,500.

G3. The subject has a pool that adds $28,000; the comp has none. Does the comp's price go up or down, and by how much? Hint: which property is inferior?

Check your answer

The comp is inferior → add. Its price goes up by $28,000. The subject is never adjusted.

Step 9: Independent practice

I1. The subject has 2,100 sq ft of living area. A comp with 1,950 sq ft sold for $415,000. The market pays $95 per sq ft of living area. Find the comp's adjusted price.

Check your answer

Difference: 2,100 − 1,950 = 150 sq ft; the comp is smaller (inferior) → add. 150 × $95 = $14,250. $415,000 + $14,250 = $429,250.

I2. Vacant land in Cape Coral. A comp lot sold for $185,000. It has canal frontage worth $40,000 that the subject lot lacks. The subject lot is 2,000 sq ft larger, and land sells at $6 per sq ft. Find the comp's adjusted price.

Check your answer

Canal: comp better → −$40,000. Size: comp inferior → +(2,000 × $6) = +$12,000. $185,000 − $40,000 + $12,000 = $157,000.

I3. After adjusting: Comp X = $512,000 (4 adjustments, $61,000 in total size); Comp Y = $498,000 (1 adjustment of $4,000); Comp Z = $530,000 (2 adjustments, $27,000 in total size). Which comp carries the most weight? Is the value $513,333?

Check your answer

Comp Y: the fewest and smallest adjustments. $513,333 is the simple average ($1,540,000 ÷ 3); the appraiser weighs the comps instead of averaging, so the final value will lean toward Comp Y's $498,000.

I4. A comp sold for $468,000. It has a pool worth $30,000 that the subject lacks. The subject has a 3-car garage and the comp a 2-car garage (difference: $7,000). The comp has 200 sq ft more living area, worth $110 per sq ft. The subject has a lake view worth $20,000 that the comp lacks. Find the comp's adjusted price.

Check your answer

$468,000 − $30,000 (pool) + $7,000 (garage) − $22,000 (200 × $110) + $20,000 (view) = $443,000.

Step 10: Exam application

If the question says… Answer pattern
"The comparable has a feature the subject lacks" Comp better → subtract from the comparable's price
"The subject has a feature the comparable lacks" Comp inferior → add to the comparable's price
An option that adjusts the subject Trap: never adjust the subject
"Which comparable deserves the most weight?" Fewest and smallest adjustments
"Best approach for a single-family home or a vacant lot?" Sales comparison
A dollar answer Write + or − next to each feature, then total

4. Key terms

Term Meaning
Sales comparison approach Value estimated from recent sales of similar properties; best for homes and vacant land
Subject The property being valued
Comparable (comp) A recent arm's-length sale of a similar property
Adjustment Dollar correction to a comp's price for one difference from the subject
Adjusted sale price The comp's price after all adjustments
Adjustment grid Table of comps, differences and adjustments
CBS / CIA Comp Better → Subtract / Comp Inferior → Add
Bracketing Adjusted comps falling above and below the subject's value
Contribution What a feature adds to value, not what it cost (L16-1)
Most weight The comp with the fewest and smallest adjustments
CMA A licensee's comparative market analysis: a pricing tool, never an "appraisal" (manual; not yet verified)

5. Practical example

Setting. You are preparing a CMA for Mr. and Mrs. Alvarez, who own a 3-bedroom, 2-bath home without a pool in Port St. Lucie. Last year they renovated the kitchen for $55,000. You review possible comps:

Candidate Your decision Rule applied
1. Same subdivision, sold 2 months ago for $398,000, same size, has a pool, older kitchen Use Recent, similar, nearby sale
2. Same model, sold to the seller's daughter at a discount Reject Not an arm's-length sale (L16-1)
3. Same model, but in a different market area across the county Weak; prefer nearby sales Comps should be similar and nearby
4. Active listing at $455,000 Show as competition, not as proof of value A listing is not a sale
5. Expired listing at $470,000 Show: buyers did not pay that price CMAs include expired listings (manual)

Market data show a pool adds about $24,000 and a renovated kitchen about $15,000. For comp 1: comp better (pool) → −$24,000; comp inferior (older kitchen) → +$15,000. $398,000 − $24,000 + $15,000 = $389,000.

Mrs. Alvarez objects: "The kitchen cost us $55,000, so add $55,000." You explain contribution: buyers pay about $15,000 more for a renovated kitchen, so that is the adjustment. Mr. Alvarez asks you to "raise our value because comp 1 has a pool". You explain that the comp is adjusted, never the subject: the pool comes off the comp's price. Finally, you label your work as a CMA. It is not an appraisal, and you may never call it one (manual; not yet verified; see L16-4).

6. Portugal comparison

The familiar principle. You have probably priced homes in Portugal by comparing them with similar nearby sales and adjusting mentally for a terrace, a garage or a renovation. That is the same market logic: substitution and contribution.

The Florida rule. The Florida exam turns that logic into a fixed drill. Adjust the comparables, never the subject; CBS / CIA; the comp with the fewest and smallest adjustments carries the most weight.

The precise difference. This course has no verified Portugal–Florida comparison entry on valuation. Any statement about how Portuguese valuers, banks or tax authorities compare sales, or how sale-price data is obtained in Portugal, requires verification. Sizes also differ: Florida works in square feet, not square metres.

Exam implication. Your experience helps you sense the right size of an adjustment. The exam, however, tests the direction and the vocabulary. Never let a Portuguese practice answer a Florida question.

7. Legal and numerical requirements

Memorize exactly

Appraisal method: manual; not yet verified (no verification entry covers it).

  • Sales comparison approach = best for homes and vacant land.
  • Use recent comparable sales.
  • Adjust the comparables, never the subject.
  • Comp better → subtract (CBS). Comp inferior → add (CIA).
  • The adjusted comps bracket the subject's value.
  • Most weight: the comp with the fewest and smallest adjustments.
  • Manual example: $410,000 − $25,000 (comp's pool) + $15,000 (subject's kitchen) = $400,000.

Verified: Appraisal = 8% of the exam (V-02).

Understand

  • Why a better comp is adjusted downward: its price includes value the subject does not have.
  • Why the adjustment is the feature's contribution, not its cost.
  • Why the most similar comp is the most reliable: fewer estimates, less room for error.
  • Why the final value is weighed, not averaged (L16-4).
  • A CMA is a licensee's pricing tool, not an appraisal (manual; not yet verified).

8. Visual explanation

Do the comparable and the subject differ on this feature?
No → same feature → no adjustment
Is the subject the one that has the feature (or more of it)?
No → the comparable has it → comp better → SUBTRACT its value from the comp's price
Yes → comp inferior → ADD the feature's value to the comp's price. The subject itself is never adjusted.

Adjustment direction drill, applied to one feature at a time (manual; not yet verified).

1. Select compsRecent, similar, nearby, arm's-length sales
2. Adjust each compCBS / CIA, one feature at a time, by contribution
3. Adjusted pricesShould bracket the subject's value
4. WeighMost weight to the fewest and smallest adjustments; never average

The sales comparison approach from start to finish.

9. Common misconceptions

  • "The comp has a pool, so add the pool to the subject." No. The subject is never adjusted. Subtract the pool's value from the comp.
  • "A better comp means a higher value for the subject." No. A better comp is adjusted down to look like the subject.
  • "The adjustment equals what the feature cost." No. It equals what the feature adds to market value.
  • "The highest adjusted price gets the most weight." No. The comp with the fewest and smallest adjustments does.
  • "Average the adjusted prices to get the value." No. Reconciliation weighs; it never simply averages.
  • "Active listings prove value." No. They show competition. Sales show what buyers actually paid.

10. Memory sheet

  • Best for homes and vacant land; based on substitution.
  • Adjust the comp, never the subject.
  • CBS: Comp Better → Subtract. CIA: Comp Inferior → Add.
  • Adjustment = contribution, not cost.
  • Adjusted comps bracket the subject.
  • Most weight = fewest and smallest adjustments.
  • $410,000 − $25,000 + $15,000 = $400,000.
  • Weigh, don't average.

lessons.title: Cost approach and depreciation
lessons.html:
2. Why it matters

In practice. Some Florida properties almost never sell: a church, a school, a fire station. Others are so new that the clearest way to value them is to ask what they would cost to build. The cost approach also gives you the words to explain why a 1970s house in Ocala is worth less than a new house of the same size next door: the old house has suffered depreciation. In appraisal, depreciation means any loss in value, from any cause.

On the exam. Appraisal is 8% of the exam (V-02, confirmed), so about 8 of the 100 questions (V-01). Typical questions are a calculation (land + cost new − depreciation), a classification of depreciation ("an airport is built nearby…") and a definition (reproduction or replacement cost). The traps: depreciating the land, calling external obsolescence curable, and borrowing the tax depreciation periods (V-77) for an appraisal question.

3. Simple explanation

Source status. The cost approach and the three types of depreciation come from the study manual. No verification entry covers appraisal methods, so they are taught as (manual; not yet verified). The tax depreciation facts used for contrast are verified (V-77). The arithmetic itself needs no verification.

Step 1: What it represents

The cost approach asks: what would it cost to create a substitute today? A buyer will not pay more than the cost of buying a similar lot and building an equally useful building (substitution, L16-1). So the value is the land, plus the building as if new, minus the value the existing building has already lost.

Term Meaning
Improvements The buildings and other structures on the land
Land value Estimated separately, by sales comparison of similar lots (L16-2)
Cost new What it would cost today to build the improvements new
Reproduction cost Cost of an exact replica: same design, same materials
Replacement cost Cost of a building with equal utility (usefulness), built with current materials and standards
Accrued depreciation All the value the existing improvements have lost compared with new ones, from any cause
Curable Worth fixing: the cure costs no more than the value it adds
Incurable Not worth fixing (the cure costs more than it adds), or impossible for the owner to fix

The three types of depreciation:

Type Cause Where it comes from Examples Curable?
Physical deterioration Wear and tear The property itself Worn roof, peeling paint, cracked foundation Curable or incurable
Functional obsolescence Outdated design or features The property itself Four bedrooms but one bathroom; no closets Curable or incurable
External (economic) obsolescence Forces outside the property line The neighbourhood or the market A new airport nearby; a weak economy Always incurable

Why is external obsolescence always incurable? Its cause is outside the property. No amount of money spent on the house moves the airport or fixes the local economy.

Land never depreciates (manual). Land does not wear out and cannot go out of style; any change in its value shows up in the separate land estimate. Tax law also never depreciates land (V-77, verified).

Step 2: Units

  • Building size: square feet. Cost new is usually given per square foot: cost new = sq ft × cost per sq ft. Metric aside only: a cost per m² ÷ 10.76 ≈ cost per sq ft.
  • Depreciation: given in dollars, as a percentage of cost new, or through years of economic life (the total number of years the building is expected to add value).
  • Land: dollars, taken from sales of comparable lots.

Step 3: Formula

Value = land value + cost new of the improvements − accrued depreciation

The question gives… Accrued depreciation =
A percentage cost new × the percentage
Separate amounts physical + functional + external
Age and total economic life (cost new ÷ economic life) × age, the same amount each year (straight-line)

Work in this order: cost new → minus depreciation → then add land. The depreciation applies to the improvements only.

Step 4: When it applies

  • Best for: new construction and special-purpose properties such as schools, churches and fire stations (manual). A new building has little depreciation to estimate. A special-purpose building has few comparable sales (so sales comparison is weak) and no rent (so the income approach does not work).
  • Weaker for old buildings: the older the building, the more depreciation must be estimated, and the less reliable the result.
  • Reproduction or replacement? The question says which cost it gives; you must recognise the definition. An exact copy of a historic building's original details is reproduction. A modern building that does the same job is replacement.
  • Not tax depreciation. Appraisal depreciation is a loss of market value. Tax depreciation is an income-tax deduction: residential rental property over 27.5 years, nonresidential over 39 years, straight-line, land never (V-77, confirmed). Do not use these periods in a cost approach question unless the question itself gives them.

Step 5: Worked example

A. Percentage method: a church in Tallahassee. Land: $240,000 (from sales of similar sites). Building: 12,000 sq ft; replacement cost $185 per sq ft. Accrued depreciation: 20%.

  1. Cost new: 12,000 × $185 = $2,220,000.
  2. Depreciation: $2,220,000 × 0.20 = $444,000.
  3. Depreciated building: $2,220,000 − $444,000 = $1,776,000.
  4. Add land: $1,776,000 + $240,000 = $2,016,000.

If you wrongly took 20% off the land as well, you would get $1,968,000: a wrong answer the exam may offer.

B. Straight-line method: a fire station in Polk County. Land: $180,000. Replacement cost new: $1,350,000. The building is 9 years old; its total economic life is 45 years.

  1. Depreciation per year: $1,350,000 ÷ 45 = $30,000.
  2. Accrued depreciation: $30,000 × 9 = $270,000 (9 ÷ 45 = 20%).
  3. Depreciated building: $1,350,000 − $270,000 = $1,080,000.
  4. Add land: $1,080,000 + $180,000 = $1,260,000.

Step 6: Reasonableness check

  • The value is at most land + cost new. It equals that sum only for a building with no depreciation.
  • The land figure passes through unchanged. If your answer changed it, you depreciated land.
  • The depreciation percentage lies between 0 and 100%, and a new building should show little.
  • Shortcut check for A: building value = 80% of cost new: 0.80 × $2,220,000 = $1,776,000 ✓.

Step 7: Common errors

Error Correction
Depreciating the land Depreciate the improvements only; land never depreciates
Forgetting to add the land Value = land + depreciated improvements
Using the original (historical) construction cost Cost new = today's cost
Calling external obsolescence curable It is always incurable
Calling a poor floor plan "external" Inside the property, outdated design → functional
Calling highway noise "functional" Outside the property line → external
Mixing up the two costs Reproduction = replica; replacement = equal utility, current materials
Using 27.5 or 39 years in an appraisal question Those are tax periods (V-77); use the life the question gives

Step 8: Guided practice

G1. Land $75,000. A house of 1,600 sq ft would cost $150 per sq ft to build new. Accrued depreciation: 10%. What is the value by the cost approach? Hint: depreciate the house, not the land.

Check your answer

Cost new: 1,600 × $150 = $240,000. Depreciation: 10% = $24,000. House: $216,000. Plus land: $216,000 + $75,000 = $291,000.

G2. Classify each item: (a) worn carpet and peeling paint; (b) four bedrooms but one bathroom; (c) a landfill opens half a mile away; (d) a cracked foundation that would cost more to repair than the repair would add in value. Hint: inside or outside the property line?

Check your answer

(a) Physical deterioration, curable. (b) Functional obsolescence: curable if adding a bathroom adds at least what it costs, otherwise incurable. (c) External obsolescence, always incurable. (d) Physical deterioration, incurable.

G3. A historic coquina-stone building in St. Augustine would cost $3.2 million to rebuild exactly, with the same stone and hand-carved woodwork. A modern building with the same usefulness would cost $2.1 million. Name each cost. Hint: replica or same utility?

Check your answer

$3.2 million = reproduction cost (exact replica). $2.1 million = replacement cost (equal utility, current materials).

Step 9: Independent practice

I1. Land $110,000. Replacement cost new $420,000. The building is 12 years old, with a total economic life of 60 years (straight-line). Find the value.

Check your answer

$420,000 ÷ 60 = $7,000 per year. × 12 = $84,000 depreciation. Building: $420,000 − $84,000 = $336,000. Value: $336,000 + $110,000 = $446,000.

I2. A house would cost $510,000 new. Accrued depreciation: physical $18,000, functional $22,000, external $35,000. Land: $140,000. Find the value. Which item can the owner never cure?

Check your answer

Depreciation: $18,000 + $22,000 + $35,000 = $75,000. Building: $510,000 − $75,000 = $435,000. Value: $435,000 + $140,000 = $575,000. The external $35,000 is always incurable.

I3. A property's value by the cost approach is $612,000. Land is $150,000 and cost new is $540,000. How much accrued depreciation was taken, and what percentage of cost new is that?

Check your answer

Depreciated building: $612,000 − $150,000 = $462,000. Depreciation: $540,000 − $462,000 = $78,000. $78,000 ÷ $540,000 = 0.1444, about 14.4%.

Step 10: Exam application

If the question mentions… Think Answer
A new building, church, school or fire station: "best approach?" Little depreciation; few sales; no rent Cost approach
An airport, highway, landfill or the economy Outside the property line External obsolescence, always incurable
One bathroom, no closets, outdated layout Design Functional obsolescence
Worn roof, peeling paint Wear Physical deterioration
"Exact replica" Reproduction cost
"Same utility, modern materials" Replacement cost
A dollar answer land + (cost new − depreciation) Never depreciate the land

4. Key terms

Term Meaning
Cost approach Value = land + cost new − accrued depreciation; best for new and special-purpose properties
Improvements Buildings and other structures on the land
Reproduction cost Cost of an exact replica
Replacement cost Cost of a building with equal utility using current materials and standards
Accrued depreciation Total loss in value of the improvements, from any cause
Physical deterioration Wear and tear; curable or incurable
Functional obsolescence Loss from outdated design or features; curable or incurable
External (economic) obsolescence Loss from factors outside the property; always incurable
Curable / incurable Worth fixing / not worth fixing or impossible to fix
Economic life Total years a building is expected to add value

5. Practical example

Setting. Daniel, a buyer you represent in Ocala, compares two homes on the same street:

  • The 1970s home: 1,900 sq ft on a lot worth about $70,000.
  • The new builder home next door: 2,000 sq ft on a lot worth about $72,000.

He asks why the older home is so much cheaper when the sizes are similar. You sketch the cost approach, using a local replacement cost of $165 per sq ft.

1970s home New home
Cost new 1,900 × $165 = $313,500 2,000 × $165 = $330,000
Physical: worn roof (curable: a new roof adds at least what it costs) −$16,000 —
Physical: aged structure (incurable) −$22,000 —
Functional: four bedrooms, one bathroom −$18,000 —
External: four-lane highway built behind the backyard (incurable) −$20,000 —
Depreciated improvements $237,500 $330,000
Land (not depreciated) +$70,000 +$72,000
Cost approach indication $307,500 $402,000

Your explanation to Daniel: the roof is curable, so it can be priced as a repair. A second bathroom might be curable if it adds at least what it costs. The highway is external obsolescence: no owner can cure it, so it will stay in the price when Daniel sells. You add that the cost approach is reliable for the new home, which has almost no depreciation, but weak for a house about 50 years old, so recent comparable sales (L16-2) matter more there. If Daniel's loan is a federally related transaction, the lender's appraisal must come from a state-licensed or certified appraiser, not from you (manual; not yet verified; L16-4).

6. Portugal comparison

The familiar principle. In your own brokerage work you have probably seen buyers discount an old building that needs work, and heard the question "what would it cost to build this today?". That is the logic of cost new minus depreciation: market common sense, not a rule of Portuguese or Florida law.

The Florida rule. The exam uses a fixed formula (land + cost new − accrued depreciation), the reproduction/replacement distinction and three named types of depreciation, with external obsolescence always incurable.

The precise difference. This course has no verified Portugal–Florida comparison entry on the cost approach. Any Portuguese construction-cost reference figure, or Portuguese rule for insurance or tax valuation, requires verification and plays no part on this exam. Units differ as well: Florida costs are quoted per square foot (a cost per m² ÷ 10.76 ≈ cost per sq ft).

Exam implication. Use only the US categories and the formula. Never let a Portuguese rule answer a Florida question.

7. Legal and numerical requirements

Memorize exactly

Appraisal method: manual; not yet verified (no verification entry covers it).

  • Value = land (by sales comparison) + cost new − accrued depreciation.
  • Best for new construction and special-purpose properties (schools, churches, fire stations).
  • Reproduction = exact replica. Replacement = equal utility with current materials and standards.
  • Physical deterioration (wear): curable or incurable.
  • Functional obsolescence (outdated design: one bathroom, no closets): curable or incurable.
  • External (economic) obsolescence (outside the property line: an airport, the economy): always incurable.
  • Land never depreciates.

Verified:

  • Appraisal = 8% of the exam (V-02).
  • Tax depreciation, a different concept: residential rental 27.5 years, nonresidential 39 years, straight-line; land is never depreciated (V-77).

Understand

  • Why external obsolescence cannot be cured by the owner.
  • Why special-purpose buildings point to the cost approach.
  • Curable or incurable is a question of economics: does the cure add at least what it costs?
  • Appraisal depreciation (loss of market value) is not tax depreciation (a deduction).

8. Visual explanation

Is the cause inside the property (the building itself)?
No → outside the property line → external (economic) obsolescence → always incurable
Is the problem an outdated design or feature (layout, one bathroom, no closets)?
No → wear and tear → physical deterioration → curable or incurable
Yes → functional obsolescence → curable or incurable

Classifying depreciation (manual; not yet verified).

Cost new12,000 sq ft × $185 = $2,220,000
− Accrued depreciation20% × $2,220,000 = $444,000
= Depreciated building$1,776,000
+ Land (never depreciated)$240,000
= Value$2,016,000
