Worked example A (the Tallahassee church) as a ladder: depreciate the building, then add the land.

9. Common misconceptions

  • "Apply the depreciation percentage to the whole property." No. Only the improvements depreciate; land never does.
  • "External obsolescence can be cured if the owner spends enough." No. Its cause is outside the property line, so it is always incurable.
  • "Functional obsolescence is always incurable." No. It can be curable or incurable.
  • "Reproduction cost means a modern equivalent." No. That is replacement cost. Reproduction is an exact replica.
  • "Appraisal depreciation uses 27.5 years." No. That is a tax rule (V-77). Use the figures the question gives.
  • "The cost approach is best for an older home." No. It is best for new construction and special-purpose properties.

10. Memory sheet

  • Land + cost new − accrued depreciation. Land by sales comparison; land never depreciates.
  • Best for new and special-purpose (schools, churches, fire stations).
  • Reproduction = replica. Replacement = same utility, current materials.
  • Physical (wear) and functional (design): curable or incurable.
  • External = outside = incurable (airport, economy).
  • Order: cost new → minus depreciation → plus land.
  • Tax depreciation (27.5 / 39 years, V-77) is a different concept.

lessons.title: Income approach, reconciliation and who may appraise
lessons.html:
2. Why it matters

In practice. Investors buying Florida duplexes, small apartment buildings or shops talk in NOI (net operating income) and cap rates, and a seller's flyer often makes both look better than they are. You need to rebuild the numbers yourself. You also need to know where your role ends: you may give a price opinion, but some transactions require an appraisal by an appraiser.

On the exam. Appraisal is 8% of the exam (V-02, confirmed), so about 8 of the 100 questions (V-01). Expect an IRV calculation from raw income and expenses, a GRM question, a reconciliation question and a "who may appraise" question. The manual warns of three planted errors that keep coming back: adjusting the subject (L16-2), treating mortgage payments as operating expenses, and averaging the three approaches.

3. Simple explanation

Source status. The income approach, the multipliers, reconciliation and the "who may appraise" rules come from the study manual. No verification entry covers them, so they are taught as (manual; not yet verified). The tax depreciation facts used for contrast are verified (V-77). The arithmetic itself needs no verification.

Step 1: What it represents

The income capitalization approach values a property by the income it produces. It rests on anticipation (L16-1): an investor pays today for the income expected in the future. It is the approach for income property: rentals and commercial buildings.

Term Meaning
Potential gross income (PGI) All the income the property could earn in a year if fully rented and every tenant paid
Vacancy and collection loss Income lost to empty units and unpaid rent
Effective gross income (EGI) PGI − vacancy and collection loss
Operating expenses Costs of running the property: fixed (property taxes, insurance), variable (utilities, repairs, maintenance, management) and reserves for replacement (money set aside for items such as roofs and appliances)
Net operating income (NOI) EGI − operating expenses
Capitalization (cap) rate NOI ÷ value: the yearly return investors expect from the property's income
Debt service Mortgage payments (principal and interest)
GRM / GIM Gross rent multiplier / gross income multiplier: quick shortcuts from gross income to value

Step 2: Units

  • In the NOI build, every figure is annual dollars. Convert monthly rent: × 12.
  • A vacancy percentage is applied to PGI.
  • The cap rate is a yearly percentage. Turn it into a decimal before dividing: 7.2% = 0.072.
  • GRM uses monthly gross rent. GIM uses annual gross income. Both multipliers are plain numbers, without a dollar sign.

Step 3: Formula

Build NOI: PGI − vacancy and collection loss = EGI; EGI − operating expenses (fixed + variable + reserves) = NOI.

IRV: Income = Rate × Value. Cover the letter you want:

To find Formula
Value NOI ÷ cap rate
Cap rate NOI ÷ value (or sale price)
Income (NOI) value × cap rate

Multipliers: GRM = price ÷ monthly gross rent, so value = monthly rent × GRM. GIM = price ÷ annual gross income, so value = annual gross income × GIM.

Deduct as operating expenses Never deduct
Property taxes and special assessments Debt service (mortgage principal and interest)
Hazard and liability insurance Depreciation
Utilities, repairs, maintenance, management
Reserves for replacement

Why these two are excluded. The building produces the same income whether the buyer pays cash or borrows, so financing (debt service) cannot change the property's value. Depreciation is a tax deduction (residential rental 27.5 years, nonresidential 39 years, V-77), not money spent running the building.

Step 4: When it applies

  • Income approach: income property (manual).
  • GRM: a rougher shortcut for houses and duplexes (manual). GIM: the same idea with annual gross income. Neither looks at expenses or vacancy, which is why they are rough.

Reconciliation. The appraiser's last step is reconciliation: weighing the approaches by their reliability for this property to reach one final value. It is never a simple average. It is also not "always take the highest" or "always use sales comparison". Homes lean on sales comparison (L16-2), new or special-purpose buildings on cost (L16-3), and income property on income.

USPAP. The Uniform Standards of Professional Appraisal Practice govern appraisal practice.

Who may appraise. The manual uses the term federally related transaction without defining it. As a general description only (requires verification), it refers to a real estate financing transaction overseen by federal financial regulators that requires an appraisal, such as a mortgage loan from a federally regulated lender. On the exam, the phrase itself is your cue: a state-licensed or certified appraiser is required.

Work Who may do it May charge? May be called an "appraisal"?
Appraisal for a federally related transaction A state-licensed or certified appraiser, following USPAP Yes Yes
CMA (comparative market analysis): sold, listed and expired comparables shape a price range A real estate licensee Yes Never
BPO (broker price opinion): ordered by a lender or investor, e.g. for a short sale (a sale for less than the loan balance) or a portfolio check A real estate licensee Yes Never

The manual's trap: "an experienced broker may appraise for a federally related transaction if she follows USPAP." No. The licence class is the barrier, not the standards. Per the manual, a licensee who does appraisal work outside federally related transactions must still comply with USPAP (manual; not yet verified).

Step 5: Worked example

A. NOI and IRV: an 8-unit building in Jacksonville. Each unit rents for $1,750 per month.

Line Working Amount
PGI 8 × $1,750 × 12 $168,000
− Vacancy and collection loss 5% × $168,000 −$8,400
= EGI $159,600
− Property taxes (fixed) −$18,500
− Insurance (fixed) −$14,200
− Utilities, common areas (variable) −$6,300
− Repairs and maintenance (variable) −$9,800
− Management (variable) −$9,600
− Reserves for replacement −$4,000
= NOI $159,600 − $62,400 $97,200

The owner's statement also lists mortgage payments of $58,000 and a tax depreciation deduction of $24,000. Ignore both.

Cap rate from a comparable: a similar building sold for $1,250,000 with an NOI of $90,000. R = $90,000 ÷ $1,250,000 = 0.072 = 7.2%.

Value: $97,200 ÷ 0.072 = $1,350,000.

The trap: deducting the mortgage gives an NOI of $39,200 and a "value" of about $544,444, which is badly wrong.

B. GRM: a single-family rental in Orlando. A comparable rental house sold for $297,000 while renting for $2,200 per month: GRM = $297,000 ÷ $2,200 = 135. The subject rents for $2,300 per month: $2,300 × 135 = $310,500.

C. GIM: a small retail building. Annual gross income is $96,000; similar buildings sell at a GIM of 9.5. Value: $96,000 × 9.5 = $912,000.

D. Reconciliation: a Gainesville duplex about 40 years old.

Approach Indication Reliability for this property
Sales comparison $612,000 High: several recent nearby duplex sales
Income $598,000 High: duplex buyers buy rent; good rent and expense data
Cost $655,000 Low: an old building, with much depreciation to estimate

The appraiser gives most weight to sales comparison and income and reconciles to a figure such as $605,000, explaining why. The simple average ($621,667) would be pulled up by the least reliable approach.

Step 6: Reasonableness check

  • PGI ≥ EGI ≥ NOI, always. (EGI equals PGI only when the question gives no vacancy or collection loss.)
  • Work backwards: value × rate = NOI. $1,350,000 × 0.072 = $97,200 ✓.
  • Rate up, value down. The same $97,200 at 8% gives $1,215,000, less than at 7.2%.
  • Size: at 7.2%, the value is about 13.9 times NOI (1 ÷ 0.072). If your value is smaller than the NOI, you multiplied instead of dividing. If it is about 12 times too small, you used monthly income.
  • Multipliers: when rent is the only income, a GRM is 12 times the GIM for the same property.

Step 7: Common errors

Error Correction
Deducting mortgage payments (debt service) Never an operating expense
Deducting depreciation Never an operating expense
Skipping vacancy and collection loss PGI − vacancy = EGI comes first
Using monthly rent in the NOI build Annual figures: × 12
Dividing by 7.2 instead of 0.072 Convert the percentage to a decimal
NOI × rate to find value Value = NOI ÷ rate
Applying a GRM to annual rent GRM = monthly; GIM = annual
Averaging the three approaches Reconcile: weigh by reliability
"A broker following USPAP may appraise for a federally related transaction" Only a state-licensed or certified appraiser

Step 8: Guided practice

G1. PGI $240,000; vacancy and collection loss 4%; operating expenses $78,000; cap rate 8%. Find the value. Hint: EGI first, then NOI, then divide.

Check your answer

Vacancy: 4% × $240,000 = $9,600. EGI: $230,400. NOI: $230,400 − $78,000 = $152,400. Value: $152,400 ÷ 0.08 = $1,905,000.

G2. A house in Tampa rents for $1,950 per month. Similar rentals sell at a GRM of 155. Find the value. Hint: GRM goes with monthly rent.

Check your answer

$1,950 × 155 = $302,250.

G3. A building sold for $2,400,000. Its NOI is $186,000. What cap rate does the sale show? Hint: R = I ÷ V.

Check your answer

$186,000 ÷ $2,400,000 = 0.0775 = 7.75%.

Step 9: Independent practice

I1. Six units at $1,600 per month each. Vacancy and collection loss: 5%. Yearly costs: property taxes $12,400; insurance $9,800; repairs and maintenance $6,900; management $5,500; reserves $2,400; mortgage principal and interest $41,000; owner's tax depreciation $9,000. Cap rate: 8%. Find the value.

Check your answer

PGI: 6 × $1,600 × 12 = $115,200. Vacancy: 5% = $5,760. EGI: $109,440. Operating expenses (taxes, insurance, repairs, management, reserves): $37,000. Mortgage and depreciation are excluded. NOI: $109,440 − $37,000 = $72,440. Value: $72,440 ÷ 0.08 = $905,500.

I2. A small office building sold for $1,140,000 with annual gross income of $120,000. Find its GIM, then value a similar building with annual gross income of $134,000.

Check your answer

GIM: $1,140,000 ÷ $120,000 = 9.5. Value: $134,000 × 9.5 = $1,273,000.

I3. A duplex has two units at $1,400 per month each. Similar duplexes sell at a GRM of 120. Find the value, then the GIM that this value implies.

Check your answer

Monthly rent: 2 × $1,400 = $2,800. Value: $2,800 × 120 = $336,000. Annual rent: $2,800 × 12 = $33,600. GIM: $336,000 ÷ $33,600 = 10 (= 120 ÷ 12).

I4. (a) A lender in a federally related transaction that requires an appraisal asks your broker, who has 20 years of experience and follows USPAP, to appraise the property. Allowed? (b) A lender considering a short sale asks your broker for a BPO and offers a fee. Allowed? What may it never be called?

Check your answer

(a) No. A federally related transaction requires a state-licensed or certified appraiser; experience and USPAP do not change the licence class. (b) Yes. A licensee may prepare a BPO and charge for it, but may never call it an appraisal.

Step 10: Exam application

If the question… Answer pattern
Gives rents, vacancy, expenses and a rate PGI → EGI → NOI → ÷ rate; leave out mortgage payments and depreciation
Gives a rent and a multiplier Monthly rent × GRM, or annual income × GIM
Asks how the final value is reached Reconciliation: weigh by reliability, never average
Asks who appraises for a federally related transaction A state-licensed or certified appraiser (not a broker, however experienced)
Asks about a licensee's CMA or BPO Allowed and chargeable, never called an appraisal

4. Key terms

Term Meaning
Income capitalization approach Value from income; for income property; IRV
PGI Potential gross income: full rent if fully occupied and paid
Vacancy and collection loss Income lost to empty units and unpaid rent
EGI Effective gross income = PGI − vacancy and collection loss
Operating expenses Fixed, variable and reserves; not debt service or depreciation
NOI Net operating income = EGI − operating expenses
Capitalization rate NOI ÷ value
IRV Income = Rate × Value; Value = NOI ÷ rate
GRM / GIM Price ÷ monthly gross rent / price ÷ annual gross income
Reconciliation Weighing the approaches to reach a final value (not averaging)
USPAP Uniform Standards of Professional Appraisal Practice
Federally related transaction Exam cue: the appraisal must be done by a state-licensed or certified appraiser (manual; not yet verified). Broadly, a financing transaction overseen by federal regulators that requires an appraisal (detailed definition requires verification)
CMA / BPO A licensee's pricing analysis / a broker price opinion for a lender or investor: chargeable, never an "appraisal"

5. Practical example

Setting. Sofia, an investor from Porto, asks you about a fourplex in St. Petersburg listed at $860,000. The seller's flyer says: "4 units × $2,100 = $8,400/month. Taxes $15,200, insurance $13,900. NOI $71,700, cap rate 8.3%. Mortgage payments $38,000."

Your rebuild:

Line Amount
PGI: $8,400 × 12 $100,800
− Vacancy and collection loss (5%; the flyer ignored it) −$5,040
= EGI $95,760
− Taxes $15,200, insurance $13,900 −$29,100
− Repairs and maintenance $6,100, management $7,660, reserves $2,400 (all missing from the flyer) −$16,160
= NOI $50,500

The flyer's NOI took only taxes and insurance off the full rent. The mortgage payments are correctly left out of NOI, but they are not the reason for the gap. Recent fourplex sales nearby show a cap rate of 6.25%: $50,500 ÷ 0.0625 = $808,000. As a rougher check, those sales show a GIM of 8.5: $100,800 × 8.5 = $856,800. The GIM ignores expenses, so you rely more on the income figure.

Sofia then asks: "Can you give me an appraisal?" You may prepare a price opinion and charge for it, but never call it an appraisal. If her loan is a federally related transaction, the lender's appraisal must come from a state-licensed or certified appraiser. And her own mortgage payments will never enter the property's NOI.

6. Portugal comparison

The familiar principle. Investors everywhere compare rent with price; you may know this as a "gross yield" (annual rent ÷ price). That is the GIM turned upside down: a GIM of 10 is a 10% gross yield.

The Florida rule. The exam distinguishes a gross measure (GRM on monthly rent, GIM on annual income) from the cap rate, which uses NOI after vacancy and operating expenses but before debt service and depreciation. The appraisal for a federally related transaction requires a state-licensed or certified appraiser.

The precise difference. This course has no verified Portugal–Florida comparison entry on income valuation or on who may value property. Any Portuguese rule on who may value property for banks, courts or tax purposes requires verification.

Exam implication. Do not confuse a gross yield with a cap rate. Answer "who may appraise" questions with the Florida/US rule only; never let a Portuguese rule answer a Florida question.

7. Legal and numerical requirements

Memorize exactly

Appraisal method and appraisal-practice rules: manual; not yet verified (no verification entry covers them).

  • Income capitalization approach = income property. IRV: Value = NOI ÷ cap rate.
  • PGI − vacancy and collection loss = EGI; EGI − operating expenses (fixed, variable, reserves) = NOI.
  • Debt service and depreciation are not operating expenses.
  • GRM = price ÷ monthly gross rent (houses, duplexes). GIM = price ÷ annual gross income.
  • Reconciliation: weigh the approaches by reliability for the property; never a simple average.
  • USPAP governs appraisal practice.
  • Federally related transactions require a state-licensed or certified appraiser.
  • A licensee may prepare CMAs and BPOs and may charge for them, but may never label them appraisals.
  • Per the manual, a licensee doing appraisal work outside federally related transactions must still follow USPAP.

Verified:

  • Appraisal = 8% of the exam (V-02).
  • Tax depreciation periods (27.5 / 39 years, V-77) belong to income tax, not to NOI.

Understand

  • Why financing and depreciation stay out of NOI.
  • Why a higher cap rate means a lower value.
  • Why reconciliation weighs instead of averaging.
  • Why experience and USPAP knowledge do not make a broker an appraiser for a federally related transaction: the licence class is the barrier.
  • Do not confuse "federally related transaction" (the appraisal rule) with RESPA's "federally related mortgage loans" on 1–4 family residential property (V-53). The phrases look alike but belong to different topics: who may appraise here; RESPA's ban on kickbacks and its title-insurer rule there.

8. Visual explanation

PGI $168,0008 units × $1,750 × 12
− Vacancy and collection $8,4005% of PGI
= EGI $159,600What the property really collects
− Operating expenses $62,400Fixed + variable + reserves (no mortgage, no depreciation)
= NOI $97,200The I in IRV
÷ Cap rate 0.072The R in IRV
= Value $1,350,000The V in IRV

Worked example A as a ladder: from potential rent to value.

Is this a federally related transaction that requires an appraisal?
No → a licensee may prepare a CMA or BPO and charge for it, but never call it an appraisal (per the manual, any appraisal work outside federally related transactions must still follow USPAP)
Yes → only a state-licensed or certified appraiser, following USPAP. A broker's experience or USPAP knowledge is not enough.

Who may appraise (manual; not yet verified).

9. Common misconceptions

  • "Mortgage payments are operating expenses." No. Debt service is never deducted to find NOI.
  • "Depreciation is an operating expense." No. It is a tax deduction (V-77), not a cost of running the building.
  • "GRM uses annual rent." No. GRM uses monthly rent; GIM uses annual income.
  • "A higher cap rate means a higher value." No. Value = NOI ÷ rate, so a higher rate gives a lower value.
  • "The final value is the average of the three approaches." No. Reconciliation weighs them by reliability.
  • "An experienced broker who follows USPAP may appraise for a federally related transaction." No. A state-licensed or certified appraiser is required.
  • "A licensee may not charge for a CMA or BPO." No. A licensee may charge, but may never call the work an appraisal.

10. Memory sheet

  • IRV: Value = NOI ÷ rate; Rate = NOI ÷ value; NOI = value × rate.
  • PGI − vacancy/collection = EGI − operating expenses (fixed, variable, reserves) = NOI.
  • NOI excludes debt service and depreciation.
  • GRM monthly (houses, duplexes); GIM annual.
  • Rate up → value down.
  • Reconcile, don't average.
  • USPAP governs appraisal.
  • Federally related transaction → state-licensed or certified appraiser.
  • CMA / BPO: may charge, never "appraisal".

lessons.title: Investment analysis
lessons.html:
2. Why it matters

In practice. Investor clients judge a property by its numbers, not by its kitchen. A retiree buying a duplex in Tampa and a family buying a small retail strip in Ocala will ask the same questions: "What's the cap rate?", "Will it still make money after the mortgage?", "How much should I borrow?" You need to speak this language and know which number goes where.

On the exam. Chapter 17 (investments and business brokerage) is worth about 2% of the exam (V-02), roughly two questions out of 100 (V-01), shared with business opportunity brokerage (L17-2). From this lesson expect a vocabulary question (leverage, liquidity, types of risk) or a short calculation: cash flow = NOI − debt service, or cap rate = NOI ÷ price. This course's practice questions may ask you to type the number, so the arithmetic must be exact.

3. Simple explanation

What an investor actually buys

An investor buys an income stream (rent, year after year) and a future value (the eventual sale price). All figures are in US dollars and per year unless a question says otherwise.

Advantages and disadvantages

Advantages Disadvantages
Income: rent paid by tenants Illiquidity: slow and costly to sell
Appreciation: the value rises over time Management burden: tenants, repairs, vacancies, paperwork
Leverage: borrowed money magnifies the return on the owner's own money Risk: income and value can fall (see the risk table below)
Tax shelter: deductions such as depreciation reduce taxable income

Leverage: borrowed money working for you, or against you

Equity is the owner's own stake: the property's value minus the debt on it. Leverage is using borrowed money to increase the return on that equity.

Here is how it works. Buy a $400,000 property with $100,000 of your own money and a $300,000 loan.

  • If the value rises 10% to $440,000, your equity grows from $100,000 to $140,000. That is +40% on your money.
  • If the value falls 10% to $360,000, your equity shrinks to $60,000. That is −40% on your money.

(Loan repayment and costs are ignored to keep it simple.)

Leverage also works on income. Compare two percentages: what the property earns (NOI ÷ price) and what the loan costs each year (annual debt service ÷ loan amount). If the property's percentage is higher, borrowing raises your return on equity. This is positive leverage. If the loan's percentage is higher, borrowing lowers your return. This is negative leverage. Compare percentages, not dollars: a property can still cover its mortgage payments in dollars and yet earn a lower percentage than the loan costs (see Step 5 of the practical example). Leverage cuts both ways, and more debt also means more financial risk.

Liquidity

Liquidity is how quickly and cheaply an asset can be turned into cash without losing value. Cash is perfectly liquid. Real estate is illiquid: selling takes marketing time, negotiation, inspections, the buyer's financing and a closing, and commissions and closing costs reduce what the seller keeps.

The income ladder: from rent to cash flow

Each line below is defined before it is used, and each one builds on the line above it.

  1. Potential gross income (PGI): all the rent you would collect if every unit were rented all year.
  2. Vacancy and collection loss: rent lost to empty units and to tenants who do not pay.
  3. Effective gross income (EGI) = PGI − vacancy and collection loss.
  4. Operating expenses: the costs of running the property. They include fixed costs (property taxes, insurance), variable costs (repairs, utilities, management) and reserves for replacement (money set aside for items such as roofs and air-conditioning units). Debt service and depreciation are NOT operating expenses (manual; not yet verified).
  5. Net operating income (NOI) = EGI − operating expenses.
  6. Debt service: the total mortgage payments for the year (principal + interest). Monthly payment × 12.
  7. Cash flow (before income taxes) = NOI − debt service.

Cap rate

The capitalization rate (cap rate) = NOI ÷ price (or value), written as a percentage. It is the first-year return the property would give a buyer who paid all cash.

Debt service is left out on purpose. The cap rate measures the property, not the buyer's loan, so two buyers with different mortgages buy the same building at the same cap rate.

The same three numbers can be rearranged. Appraisers call this IRV: Income = Rate × Value.

  • Rate = NOI ÷ Value
  • Value = NOI ÷ Rate
  • NOI = Value × Rate

For the same NOI, a higher cap rate means a lower price, and a lower cap rate means a higher price.

Two more ways an investment grows

  • Equity buildup: each mortgage payment includes some principal, so the loan shrinks and the owner's equity grows.
  • Appreciation: the property's value rises over time, which also increases equity.

Types of risk

Risk What it means Florida-style example
Business risk The property's own operations earn less than expected A major tenant of a strip center closes
Financial risk Risk created by debt: the more you borrow, the larger the fixed payment the income must cover, and the greater the risk of default and foreclosure A highly leveraged duplex loses one tenant and the rent no longer covers the mortgage
Market risk Changes in supply and demand reduce rents or values New apartment buildings open nearby and push rents down
Interest-rate risk Rising rates raise borrowing costs and can push values down An adjustable-rate loan's payment increases
Liquidity risk You cannot sell quickly without cutting the price The owner needs cash fast in a slow market

Tax shelter, in one paragraph

The main tax shelter is depreciation (cost recovery). It is a tax deduction for the building's wear, taken straight-line over 27.5 years for residential rental property or 39 years for nonresidential property. Land is never depreciated (V-77). Depreciation costs no cash in the year it is deducted, so it can shelter part of the cash flow from income tax. It is not an operating expense and does not reduce NOI. Taxation is covered in more detail elsewhere in the course.

4. Key terms

Term Meaning
Equity The owner's stake: value minus debt
Leverage Using borrowed money to increase return on equity; it magnifies gains and losses
Positive / negative leverage The property's percentage return is higher / lower than the loan's percentage cost
Liquidity How quickly and cheaply an asset converts to cash without losing value
Operating expenses Costs of running the property (taxes, insurance, repairs, management, reserves); not debt service, not depreciation
NOI Net operating income = EGI − operating expenses
Debt service Total annual mortgage payments (principal + interest)
Cash flow NOI minus debt service (before income taxes)
Cap rate NOI ÷ price (or value), as a percentage
Equity buildup Growth in equity as the loan principal is repaid
Appreciation Increase in property value over time
Depreciation (cost recovery) Tax deduction for the building over 27.5 or 39 years; never land (V-77)

5. Practical example

Ana is a sales associate in Lakeland. Her investor client, Mr. Duarte, is looking at a fourplex listed at $720,000. All figures are hypothetical and annual.

Step 1: Build the NOI.

Line Amount
Potential gross income: 4 units × $1,850/month × 12 $88,800
− Vacancy and collection loss (5% of $88,800) − $4,440
= Effective gross income $84,360
− Property taxes − $9,600
− Insurance − $8,200
− Repairs and maintenance − $4,800
− Management − $5,060
− Reserves for replacement − $1,500
− Utilities and lawn care − $1,200
= Total operating expenses $30,360
NOI ($84,360 − $30,360) $54,000

The mortgage payment is not on this list, and neither is depreciation.

Step 2: Cap rate at the asking price. $54,000 ÷ $720,000 = 0.075 = 7.5%.

Step 3: Check the price against the market. Ana finds that similar fourplexes in the area sell at about an 8% cap rate. Value = $54,000 ÷ 0.08 = $675,000. The asking price is above what the local cap rate supports, and that gives Mr. Duarte a negotiating point.

Step 4: Add the loan. He would put 25% down ($180,000) and borrow $540,000. The payment is $3,300 a month, so debt service = $3,300 × 12 = $39,600 a year.

  • Cash flow = $54,000 − $39,600 = $14,400.
  • Return on his cash: $14,400 ÷ $180,000 = 8%, compared with 7.5% if he paid all cash. The loan costs $39,600 ÷ $540,000 ≈ 7.33% a year (annual debt service as a percentage of the loan, principal included). That is less than the property earns (7.5%), so this is positive leverage.

Step 5: The bad year. Suppose new apartments open nearby (market risk), vacancy rises, and NOI falls to $42,000. Cash flow = $42,000 − $39,600 = $2,400, about 1.3% on his $180,000. An all-cash buyer would still earn $42,000 ÷ $720,000 ≈ 5.8%. In dollars the NOI still covers the payments, but as a percentage the loan now costs more (≈ 7.33%) than the property earns (≈ 5.8%). That is negative leverage: leverage cuts both ways.

6. Portugal comparison

The familiar principle. Gross rent, vacancy, operating costs, net income, borrowing and the trade-off between return and risk are financial arithmetic. They work the same way in euros as in dollars.

The Florida rule. For the exam: cash flow = NOI − debt service; cap rate = NOI ÷ price; debt service and depreciation are not operating expenses; depreciation runs 27.5 years (residential rental) or 39 years (nonresidential), never on land (V-77).

The precise difference. For the formulas there is no meaningful difference. What differs is the surrounding law. The depreciation periods are US federal tax rules (V-77). How Portugal taxes rental income or allows deductions is not covered by this course's comparison entries and requires verification.

Exam implication. Work in US dollars with annual figures, using the US definitions above. Never use a Portuguese tax rule to answer a Florida question.

7. Legal and numerical requirements

Memorize exactly

  • Advantages: income, appreciation, leverage, tax shelter. Disadvantages: illiquidity, management burden, risk.
  • Cash flow = NOI − debt service.
  • Cap rate = NOI ÷ price. Value = NOI ÷ cap rate.
  • NOI = (PGI − vacancy and collection loss) − operating expenses. Debt service and depreciation are not operating expenses (manual; not yet verified).
  • Other measures: equity buildup and appreciation.
  • Risks: business, financial (debt), market, interest-rate, liquidity.
  • Depreciation: straight-line, 27.5 years residential rental, 39 years nonresidential, land never (V-77).

Understand

  • Leverage helps only when the property's percentage return (NOI ÷ price) is higher than the loan's percentage cost (annual debt service ÷ loan). It magnifies losses as well as gains.
  • The cap rate ignores financing because it measures the property, not the buyer.
  • Annual debt service = monthly payment × 12. Mixing monthly and annual figures is the most common calculation error.
  • For the same NOI, a higher cap rate means a lower value.
  • Source status: the formulas and risk vocabulary are standard course definitions from the study manual, and no verification entry covers them (manual; not yet verified). They are definitions, not statutes. The depreciation periods are verified (V-77), and the chapter weight comes from V-02.

8. Visual explanation

The income ladder, using the Lakeland fourplex

Potential gross income$88,800 (4 × $1,850 × 12)
− Vacancy and collection loss$4,440
= Effective gross income$84,360
− Operating expenses$30,360 (no mortgage, no depreciation)
= NOI$54,000, which divided by the $720,000 price gives a 7.5% cap rate
− Debt service$39,600 ($3,300 × 12)
= Cash flow (before tax)$14,400, which is 8% on $180,000 of equity

The cap rate is measured at NOI, above the loan. Cash flow is measured below the loan.

Leverage cuts both ways (same property, same loan)

Normal year Bad year
NOI $54,000 $42,000
All-cash return (NOI ÷ $720,000) 7.5% ≈ 5.8%
Loan cost ($39,600 ÷ $540,000) ≈ 7.33% ≈ 7.33%
Debt service $39,600 $39,600
Cash flow $14,400 $2,400
Return on $180,000 equity 8% ≈ 1.3%
Leverage Positive (7.5% > 7.33%) Negative (5.8% < 7.33%)

Try it

  1. NOI is $72,400 and annual debt service is $51,900. What is the cash flow?
Check your answer $72,400 − $51,900 = $20,500.
  1. A property sells for $570,000 and its NOI is $45,600. What is the cap rate?
Check your answer $45,600 ÷ $570,000 = 0.08 = 8%. Check: $570,000 × 0.08 = $45,600.
  1. NOI is $38,500 and similar properties sell at a 7% cap rate. What is the indicated value?
Check your answer $38,500 ÷ 0.07 = $550,000. Check: $550,000 × 0.07 = $38,500.
  1. NOI is $36,000 and the mortgage payment is $2,450 a month. What is the cash flow?
Check your answer Debt service = $2,450 × 12 = $29,400. Cash flow = $36,000 − $29,400 = $6,600. (If you subtracted $2,450, you mixed monthly and annual figures.)

9. Common misconceptions

  • "Mortgage payments are an operating expense." No. NOI is calculated before debt service. Subtract debt service only to get cash flow.
  • "Depreciation reduces NOI." No. It is a tax deduction, not an operating expense.
  • "Cap rate = cash flow ÷ price." No. Cap rate uses NOI, before any loan.
  • "A higher cap rate means a more expensive property." The opposite: for the same NOI, a higher cap rate means a lower price.
  • "Leverage always increases returns." Only when the property's percentage return is higher than the loan's percentage cost. Otherwise it lowers returns, and it always magnifies losses.
  • "If NOI covers the mortgage payments, leverage is positive." No. Positive cash flow is not the test. Compare percentages: in the bad year above, NOI covers the payments but the property earns about 5.8% while the loan costs about 7.33%.
  • "Liquidity means profitability." No. Liquidity is how quickly and cheaply an asset converts to cash. A very profitable building can still be illiquid.
  • "The land under a rental building is depreciated too." No. Land is never depreciated (V-77).
  • "Debt service is the monthly payment." For annual analysis it is the monthly payment × 12.

10. Memory sheet

  • Pros: income · appreciation · leverage · tax shelter. Cons: illiquidity · management · risk.
  • PGI − vacancy → EGI · EGI − operating expenses → NOI · NOI − debt service → cash flow.
  • Cap rate = NOI ÷ price · Value = NOI ÷ rate · higher rate = lower value.
  • No mortgage and no depreciation in operating expenses.
  • Leverage cuts both ways: positive only if the property's % return (NOI ÷ price) beats the loan's % cost (debt service ÷ loan).
  • Risks: business · financial (debt) · market · interest-rate · liquidity.
  • Depreciation 27.5 residential / 39 nonresidential, straight-line, never land (V-77).

lessons.title: Business opportunity brokerage
lessons.html:
2. Why it matters

In practice. Florida towns have plenty of small businesses: cafés, salons, dry cleaners, small motels. When the owners sell, they often call the agent who sold their house. Selling a business is not like selling a house. You are selling a working enterprise, and part of the price pays for things nobody can touch. You need to know what is in the package, when a license is needed and which disclosure rules apply.

On the exam. This is a low-priority topic. It shares chapter 17's roughly 2% of the exam (V-02) with investment analysis. Expect probably no more than one question, usually "what is goodwill?" or "does this person need a real estate license?".

3. Simple explanation

What is being sold: a going concern

Business opportunity brokerage means helping someone sell (or buy) a business for compensation. What changes hands is a going concern: a business that is operating today and is expected to keep operating, with customers, staff, suppliers and a name people recognize. The buyer pays for the whole working unit because it already produces income. A café with loyal customers is usually worth more than its tables, machines and coffee beans sold one by one.

The package

Component What kind of property Example: a café How it usually transfers
Real estate (if any) Real property The land and building, if the business owner owns them Deed
Lease of the premises (if the business rents) A leasehold: the business's right, as tenant, to occupy the premises under the lease The café's lease of a shop unit Assignment of the lease, subject to the lease's terms
Goodwill Intangible Reputation, regular customers, the café's name Included in the sale contract
Fixtures Items attached to the premises Walk-in cooler, built-in counters Listed one by one in the contract
Equipment Personal property Espresso machines, ovens, point-of-sale terminals Bill of sale
Inventory Personal property Coffee beans, pastries, packaged goods Bill of sale, usually counted near closing

Fixtures need special care. Whether a counter or cooler goes with the business or stays with the building depends on who owns the building and on what the contract says, so list each item in writing. If the business rents its space, items it installed for its trade (trade fixtures) raise the same question: the lease and the sale contract should say who owns them and whether they pass to the buyer.

Goodwill

Goodwill is the intangible value of a business's reputation and customer base: the reason customers keep coming back. A practical way to picture it is as the part of the price that the identifiable assets do not explain. Goodwill depends on the business continuing to operate, which is why buyers want a going concern and not a closed shop.

Buyers usually pay for the profit a business produces, so the income thinking from investment analysis (L17-1) applies here too: a steady, well-documented income stream supports a higher price.

When a real estate license is needed

Under Chapter 475, brokering business opportunities for compensation requires a real estate license, particularly when real property is included (manual; not yet verified).

Read this carefully. The manual's own sentence says a license is required "when real property is included". That describes the clearest case. It does not say that a business sale without real estate is free of licensing. The course position, and the exam answer, is that a person who sells a business for another person for compensation (such as a commission) needs a real estate license. The exact scope of the statute has not been verified yet.

Brokerage-relationship disclosures

Earlier lessons covered the brokerage-relationship disclosure rules of s. 475.278: for example, the single agent notice, the no brokerage relationship notice, and the principal's written consent before a single agent becomes a transaction broker (V-48). Business sales are outside these disclosure rules, except for property with four or fewer residential units (V-20, verified). So a café in a commercial building is outside them. If the deal also involves property with four or fewer residential units, the business-sale exception does not reach that property, and the rules apply to it.

Practical cautions (good practice, not law)

  • Ask for the financial records (profit and loss statements, tax returns), because the price rests on income.
  • Keep the sale confidential. Staff, suppliers and customers may react badly to rumors.
  • List every component and its price in writing: real estate or lease, goodwill, fixtures, equipment, inventory.

4. Key terms

Term Meaning
Business opportunity brokerage Selling a business for another for compensation (goodwill, inventory, fixtures, possibly real estate)
Going concern A business that is operating and expected to continue, sold as a working whole
Goodwill Intangible value of a business's reputation and customer base
Fixtures Items attached to the premises (counters, coolers); list them in the contract
Trade fixtures Items a business tenant installs for its trade; the lease and the sale contract should say who owns them
Equipment Movable business assets (machines, terminals); personal property
Inventory Goods held for sale or use (stock); personal property
Leasehold A tenant's right to occupy and use property under a lease
Bill of sale The document that transfers personal property
Deed The document that transfers real property

5. Practical example

Rui is a sales associate in Tampa. Helena owns Café Azulejo (a fictional business). It is a busy café in a building she also owns. She asks Rui's brokerage to sell the business for a commission, and Rui handles the listing. All figures are hypothetical.

Component Agreed value
Land and building (commercial) $780,000
Equipment and fixtures (espresso machines, ovens, walk-in cooler, counters) $95,000
Inventory (counted near closing) $25,000
Goodwill (name, reputation, regular customers) $250,000
Total price $1,150,000

Goodwill here is the part of the price that the other assets do not explain: $1,150,000 − $780,000 − $95,000 − $25,000 = $250,000.

Does Rui need a license? Yes. He is brokering a business opportunity for compensation, and real property is included (manual; not yet verified).

Do the brokerage-relationship disclosures apply? This is a business sale and the building is commercial, so it is outside the s. 475.278 disclosure rules (V-20).

Variation 1: the duplex. Suppose Helena's deal also includes a duplex (two residential units) behind the café. That is property with four or fewer residential units, so the business-sale exception does not reach it and Rui follows the disclosure rules for it (V-20).

Variation 2: no building. Suppose instead that Helena rents her shop space, so the deal is the lease, goodwill, equipment and inventory. Rui should not conclude that he can work without a license. For exam purposes, brokering a business opportunity for compensation requires a real estate license. The manual's emphasis on real property is not a safe harbor (manual; not yet verified).

6. Portugal comparison

The familiar principle. In Portugal the sale of an operating shop or café may be familiar to you as a trespasse. That term, the Portuguese legal details, and whether a mediador's license covers this work all require verification: this course has no verified comparison entry on business transfers. The commercial idea is the same in both places: the buyer pays for a working business, including its customers and name.

The Florida rule. Brokering a business opportunity for compensation requires a Florida real estate license, particularly when real property is included (manual; not yet verified). Business sales are outside the brokerage-relationship disclosure rules, except for property with four or fewer residential units (V-20).

The precise difference. It cannot be stated with verified Portuguese facts. Treat any assumption from Portuguese practice as unverified.

Exam implication. A Florida question gets a Florida answer: selling a business for another for compensation means a real estate license is needed. Portuguese practice never decides the answer.

7. Legal and numerical requirements

Memorize exactly

  • Business opportunity brokerage = selling a going concern: real estate (if any) + goodwill + fixtures + equipment + inventory.
  • Goodwill = the intangible value of reputation and customer base.
  • Under Chapter 475, brokering business opportunities for compensation requires a real estate license, particularly when real property is included (manual; not yet verified; the manual's sentence reads "when real property is included").
  • Business sales are outside the s. 475.278 brokerage-relationship disclosure rules, except property with four or fewer residential units (V-20).

Understand

  • A going concern is worth more than its parts because it already produces income. Goodwill measures part of that extra value.
  • Real property moves by deed. Equipment and inventory move by bill of sale. A lease is assigned under its own terms.
  • The manual's "when real property is included" does not mean "only when real property is included". Do not treat a sale with no real estate as license-free.
  • Source status: the licensing statement rests on the study manual and is not yet verified. The disclosure exception is verified (V-20). The chapter weight comes from V-02.

8. Visual explanation

What the buyer of a going concern receives

Real estate (if any)Land and building by deed, or the lease of the premises by assignment
GoodwillReputation, customer base, name: intangible
FixturesAttached items: list each one in the contract
EquipmentPersonal property, by bill of sale
InventoryPersonal property, usually counted near closing

Operating together as one business, these make up the going concern (real estate or a lease only if the deal includes one).

Two quick decisions

Is the person selling (or buying) a business for another, for compensation?
No: this is not business opportunity brokerage as this lesson defines it
Yes: a real estate license is required, particularly when real property is included (manual; not yet verified). The statutory exemptions from licensure (s. 475.011, V-14) are a separate topic.
Does the business sale involve property with four or fewer residential units?
No: outside the s. 475.278 brokerage-relationship disclosure rules (V-20)
Yes: the disclosure rules apply to that property (V-20)

9. Common misconceptions

  • "A business is personal property, so no license is needed." Wrong. Brokering a business opportunity for compensation requires a real estate license, particularly when real property is included (manual; not yet verified).
  • "Only a securities license is needed to sell a business." The course answer is a real estate license.
  • "Only an attorney may sell a business for someone else." No. This is business opportunity brokerage, which is done under a real estate license.
  • "Goodwill is the value of the building." No. Goodwill is intangible: reputation and customer base. The building is real estate.
  • "Goodwill, plottage and equity are the same thing." No. Plottage is the value gain when parcels are combined. Equity is value minus debt. Goodwill is the business's intangible value.
  • "The brokerage-relationship disclosures apply to every sale." Business sales are outside them, except property with four or fewer residential units (V-20).
  • "No building in the deal means no license." Do not assume it. The manual's mention of real property describes the clearest case; it is not an exemption.

10. Memory sheet

  • Business = going concern = goodwill + fixtures + equipment + inventory (+ real estate or lease).
  • Goodwill = reputation + customer base (intangible).
  • Brokering a business for pay → real estate license, particularly with real property (manual; not yet verified).
  • s. 475.278 disclosures: not for business sales, except property with ≤ 4 residential units (V-20).
  • Deed for real property · bill of sale for equipment and inventory · lease assigned under its terms.

lessons.title: Florida property taxation: process and calendar
lessons.html:
2. Why it matters

Every Florida owner pays property tax every year, and buyers will keep asking you, "What will my taxes be?" To answer responsibly you need to know who sets the value, on what date, when the bill arrives, how the early-payment discount works and what happens when the tax is not paid. The calendar also matters in a sale: the January 1 value, the August TRIM notice and the November bill shape what a buyer can expect and what gets prorated at closing.

On the exam, Section 18 (Taxes Affecting Real Estate) carries 3% of the weight (V-02). Expect quick recall questions: the assessment date, the discount for paying in a given month, the delinquency date, what the TRIM notice is, who hears appeals, and the difference between an ad valorem tax and a special assessment.

3. Simple explanation

Labels used here: V-nn = checked against official sources on 2026-10-19/20. "(manual; not yet verified)" = taken only from the study manual.

What is being taxed

Ad valorem means "according to value." A Florida real property tax is an ad valorem tax: the higher the taxable value, the higher the tax. Property taxes fund local government, and Florida has no state property tax (manual; not yet verified).

Three local players share the work:

Who Role
County property appraiser Sets each parcel's just value (Florida's term for market value) as of January 1, certifies the values, mails the TRIM notice
Local taxing authorities (county, city, schools and others) Each sets its own tax rate, called millage
County tax collector Receives the certified tax roll, sends the bills, collects payment

The yearly cycle, step by step

1. January 1: the snapshot. Real property is assessed according to its status and value as of January 1 each year (s. 192.042(1); V-76). Improvements that are not substantially completed on January 1 get no value for that year. Why one fixed date? Every parcel in the county is measured at the same moment, so values are comparable and the roll can be ready for the autumn bills.

2. Summer: certification and the TRIM notice. The appraiser certifies the values (usually July 1). Within 55 days after certification, the appraiser must mail the Notice of Proposed Property Taxes, known as the TRIM (Truth in Millage) notice (s. 200.065(2)(b); V-76). With the usual July 1 certification, the Florida Department of Revenue (DOR) calendar sets the deadline at August 24, which is why the exam says "TRIM in August". A state of emergency allows a 30-day extension. The notice shows the proposed value and the proposed rates. It is information, not a bill. (The timing rule is in s. 200.065(2)(b); s. 200.069 sets what the notice contains. The manual cites s. 200.069 for the timing.)

3. Disagreeing with the value. An owner who believes the value is wrong can first talk informally with the property appraiser and can then petition the county Value Adjustment Board (VAB), the board that hears assessment appeals (manual; not yet verified). This course has no verified VAB filing deadline, so do not guess one on the exam.

4. November 1: the bill and the discounts. Taxes are due and payable November 1, or as soon afterwards as the tax collector receives the certified roll (s. 197.333; V-76). Paying early earns a discount (s. 197.162; V-76):

Paid in Discount
November (or within 30 days after the original tax notice is sent) 4%
December 3%
January 2%
February 1%
March 0% (full amount)

If a discount period ends on a weekend or legal holiday, it extends to the next working day. The discount rewards owners who pay early, so local governments receive the money sooner.

5. April 1: delinquency. Unpaid taxes become delinquent on April 1 of the year after the assessment year, or 60 days after the original tax notice was mailed, whichever is later (s. 197.333; V-76). The 60-day alternative protects owners when bills go out late.

6. After delinquency: tax certificates and tax deeds. Delinquent taxes are enforced through tax certificates and, eventually, a tax deed sale (manual; not yet verified). A tax certificate is a lien sold to an investor to collect the delinquent tax (manual; not yet verified). Its role: the local government collects the money from the investor instead of waiting for the owner, while the unpaid tax stays attached to the property as a lien. If the owner never pays, the process can end with the property itself being sold by tax deed. Homestead status does not stop this: Florida's constitutional homestead protection from creditors gives no protection against property taxes and assessments (V-66).

Ad valorem tax vs special assessment

A special assessment is not an ad valorem tax (manual; not yet verified). It is a charge on the properties specially benefited by a public improvement, such as a new sewer line or street paving, and it is often calculated per front foot (each foot of the lot's frontage along the improvement; a foot is a little under a third of a metre). It is often a one-time charge, and it has lien priority like property taxes (all manual; not yet verified).

Ad valorem property tax Special assessment
Based on Taxable value Benefit from a specific improvement (often front footage)
Who pays Every taxable parcel Only the benefited parcels
How often Every year Often one-time
Status V-76 (calendar) manual; not yet verified

Both are claims that homestead protection does not defeat (V-66: no protection against property taxes and assessments).

Watch item: a ballot measure that is not law (V-23)

A homestead property-tax amendment, CS/HJR 1-F (2026 Special Session F), is on the November 3, 2026 ballot. It needs at least 60% of the vote; if approved, it takes effect January 1, 2027. Until then it is not law and it is not exam content. Exam questions usually lag law changes. (Its Save Our Homes effect is covered in L18-2.)

4. Key terms

Term Meaning
Ad valorem According to value
Just value Florida's term for market value, set by the property appraiser as of January 1
Property appraiser County official who values every parcel and mails the TRIM notice
Millage Tax rate expressed in mills (calculation in L18-2)
Certification of value The appraiser's sign-off on the roll of values, usually July 1; starts the 55-day TRIM clock
TRIM notice Truth in Millage notice: proposed values and rates, mailed within 55 days after certification (usually August)
Value Adjustment Board (VAB) County board that hears assessment appeals
Delinquent Unpaid after the deadline: April 1, or 60 days after mailing if later
Tax certificate Lien sold to an investor to collect delinquent property taxes
Tax deed sale Sale of the property itself when delinquent taxes are never paid
Special assessment Charge on properties specially benefited by a public improvement; not ad valorem
Front foot One foot of lot frontage along the street or improvement

5. Practical example

Carlos's house in Tampa (Hillsborough County), tax year 2026

  • January 1, 2026. Carlos's pool is half built, not substantially completed. The house is valued as it stood that day, and the pool gets no value for 2026. If it is substantially completed by January 1, 2027, it will count in the 2027 value.
  • August 2026. His TRIM notice shows a proposed just value of $455,000. Two similar houses nearby sold for less, so he calls the property appraiser's office. If the informal talk does not resolve it, he can petition the VAB (manual; not yet verified). The TRIM notice is not a bill, so nothing is payable yet.
  • November 2026. The final bill is $6,000. What he pays depends on when he pays:
Pays in Discount Amount
November 2026 4% $6,000 × 0.96 = $5,760
December 2026 3% $6,000 × 0.97 = $5,820
January 2027 2% $6,000 × 0.98 = $5,880
February 2027 1% $6,000 × 0.99 = $5,940
March 2027 0% $6,000
  • April 1, 2027. If he has not paid, the tax is delinquent. (His bill was mailed in November, and 60 days after that falls before April 1, so April 1 controls. If a bill were first mailed on February 15, 2027, delinquency would wait until 60 days after mailing, in mid-April.)
  • Same year, a special assessment. The city extends sewer lines down his street and charges benefited lots $40 per front foot. His lot has 85 feet of frontage: 85 × $40 = $3,400. This charge is based on the benefit and frontage, not on his home's value (manual; not yet verified).
  • 2027, Carlos sells. His buyer must receive the property tax disclosure summary at or before the contract. It warns the buyer not to rely on the seller's current taxes, because a sale or improvements can raise the assessment (s. 689.261; V-75). As the licensee, never quote Carlos's bill as "the buyer's taxes".

6. Portugal comparison

Familiar principle. Portugal also has an annual local tax on property: IMI is an annual municipal tax on the registered taxable value (VPT) (PT-10; the course still marks the Portuguese side of this comparison "requires verification"). IMI rates, exemptions, payment dates and appeal procedures require verification.

Florida rule. Florida's property tax is ad valorem: the county property appraiser sets just value as of January 1 every year, the taxing authorities set millage, the TRIM notice announces proposed figures (usually August), bills go out from November 1 with 4/3/2/1% discounts, and unpaid taxes are delinquent April 1 (or 60 days after mailing, if later).

Precise difference. Florida's base is a just value set as of January 1 each year, and the tax is computed in mills on taxable value after exemptions; school and non-school taxable values can differ (L18-2). Florida's calendar (January 1, TRIM, November discounts, April 1) is set by Florida statutes. Any similarity to IMI's timing requires verification.

Exam implication. Answer every calendar question with the Florida dates above. Do not carry over IMI habits about when or how property tax is paid.

7. Legal and numerical requirements

Memorize exactly

  • Assessment date: January 1 (status and value). Improvements not substantially completed on January 1 get no value that year (s. 192.042(1); V-76).
  • TRIM notice: mailed within 55 days after certification (s. 200.065(2)(b)); usually August (DOR deadline August 24 with July 1 certification); +30 days in a state of emergency. Content: s. 200.069 (V-76).
  • Appeal: informal conference with the appraiser, then petition to the VAB (manual; not yet verified).
  • Due: November 1, or when the tax collector receives the certified roll (s. 197.333; V-76).
  • Discounts: 4% November (or within 30 days after the original notice is sent) · 3% December · 2% January · 1% February · 0% March; a period ending on a weekend or holiday runs to the next working day (s. 197.162; V-76).
  • Delinquent: April 1 of the following year, or 60 days after the original notice was mailed, whichever is later (s. 197.333; V-76).
  • Enforcement: tax certificates, then eventually a tax deed sale (manual; not yet verified). Homestead protection does not cover property taxes and assessments (V-66).
  • Special assessment: not ad valorem; specially benefited properties; often per front foot; lien priority like property taxes (manual; not yet verified).
  • No state property tax; property taxes fund local government (manual; not yet verified).
  • CS/HJR 1-F (November 3, 2026 ballot; 60% needed; would take effect January 1, 2027): not law (V-23).

Understand

  • January 1 fixes both the value and the status of the property for the whole year.
  • The TRIM notice is a warning, not a bill: it is the owner's chance to react before the bills are final.
  • The discount shrinks by one point per month, November to February, and disappears in March.
  • An ad valorem tax follows value; a special assessment follows benefit.
  • Tax certificates let the local government collect now; the lien stays on the property.

8. Visual explanation

January 1Assessment date: status and value fixed (V-76)
Usually July 1Values certified; the 55-day TRIM clock starts
By August 24 (usual)TRIM notice: proposed values and rates, not a bill
After TRIMInformal conference, then VAB petition (manual; not yet verified)
November 1Taxes due · 4% discount in November
December to March3% · 2% · 1% · 0%
April 1, next yearDelinquent (or 60 days after mailing, if later)
AfterwardsTax certificate, eventually tax deed sale (manual; not yet verified)

One Florida property-tax year: the value is fixed on January 1, the bill is paid between November and March, and delinquency starts April 1 of the next year.

9. Common misconceptions

  • "The property is valued on the day the bill is sent." No. It is valued as of January 1.
  • "The TRIM notice is the tax bill." No. It is a notice of proposed taxes, usually in August. Bills come from November 1.
  • "The 4% discount is for paying in October." No. 4% applies in November, or within 30 days after the original notice is sent.
  • "Taxes are delinquent on January 1 (or March 1)." No. They become delinquent on April 1, or 60 days after mailing if that is later.
  • "The TRIM deadline is in s. 200.069." The timing is in s. 200.065(2)(b); s. 200.069 covers the notice's content.
  • "A special assessment is just another ad valorem tax." No. It is based on the benefit from an improvement, often per front foot, not on value.
  • "A homestead cannot be lost for unpaid taxes." Homestead protection gives no protection against property taxes and assessments (V-66).
  • "The November 2026 amendment has already changed the rules." No. CS/HJR 1-F is pending law until approved, and it is not exam content (V-23).

10. Memory sheet

  • Jan 1 assess (status and value) · TRIM within 55 days after certification ≈ August · VAB appeals (manual) · Nov 1 due · 4-3-2-1-0 Nov to Mar · Apr 1 delinquent (or 60 days after mailing, if later).
  • Unfinished on January 1 = no value this year.
  • TRIM = proposed, not a bill.
  • Delinquent → tax certificate → eventually tax deed (manual). Homestead does not protect against taxes or assessments (V-66).
  • Special assessment ≠ ad valorem: benefit-based, often per front foot (manual).
  • No state property tax (manual).
  • CS/HJR 1-F (November 2026 ballot) = not law (V-23).

lessons.title: Exemptions, Save Our Homes and tax computation
lessons.html:
2. Why it matters

In practice. Buyers ask "What will my taxes be?", and in Florida the honest answer is often "more than the seller pays": Save Our Homes may have held a long-time owner's assessed value far below market value. You must explain how a bill is built (value, exemptions, millage), make a rough estimate, and warn buyers not to rely on the seller's current taxes, as the property tax disclosure summary for residential buyers does (V-75).

On the exam. Section 18 is 3% of the exam (V-02), about 3 of 100 questions (V-01). This lesson supplies its math question and its traps: which taxes the second homestead exemption reduces, the current widow/blind/disabled amount, "3% or CPI, whichever is less", and a tax in mills with separate school and non-school values.

3. Simple explanation

Labels: V-nn = checked against official sources on 2026-10-19/20. "(manual; not yet verified)" = from the study manual only. Values, millage rates and CPI changes in the examples are invented for practice.

Step 1: What it represents

A Florida property tax bill is built in layers:

Layer Meaning
Just value Market value, set by the county property appraiser as of January 1 (V-76; L18-1)
Assessed value Where the tax starts. A homestead's can sit below just value, because Save Our Homes limits its growth (V-67)
Exemptions Dollar amounts subtracted from assessed value, for owners who qualify
Taxable value Assessed value − exemptions. A homestead has two: school and non-school
Millage Each taxing authority's rate in mills (school board, county, city and others)

Homestead exemptions (s. 196.031; V-09). The owner must own the property and occupy it as a permanent residence on January 1 (N-140).

  • The first $25,000 of assessed value is exempt from all taxes, school taxes included.
  • An additional exemption of up to $25,000 applies to assessed value above $50,000, for non-school taxes only. Since January 1, 2025 (Amendment 5, approved November 5, 2024) it is indexed to CPI-U (the US Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers, an inflation measure; see Step 2) when the change is positive: $25,722 for 2025 (Florida DOR, 2.9% CPI). Exam math usually uses the round $25,000. Older books say "value between $50,000 and $75,000"; with indexing the top of that band moves ($75,722 for 2025).

Why two taxable values? The additional exemption does not apply to school levies, so school taxes are computed on a base that is normally $25,000 larger.

Other exemptions

  • $5,000 each for a widow or widower, a blind person, or a totally and permanently disabled person who is a Florida resident (s. 196.202; V-10). Raised from $500 by the 2022 Legislature, first for the 2023 tax roll: $500 is outdated, though older printings still show it.
  • Disabled veterans (combat-disabled, or service-connected and totally disabled): larger or total exemptions; details not covered (manual; not yet verified).
  • Green Belt: agricultural land is assessed on use value (its value as farmland), not market value (manual; not yet verified).

Save Our Homes (SOH) (Art. VII, s. 4(d), Fla. Const.; s. 193.155; V-67). After the January 1 reassessment, a homestead's assessed value may rise by no more than 3% of the prior year's assessed value or the percentage change in the CPI for the preceding calendar year, whichever is lower. Why: an owner who stays should not be taxed out of the home by a hot market. Just value − assessed value = the accrued SOH benefit.

  • Reset: on a change of ownership, assessed value resets to just value (N-142).
  • Portability: an owner who sets up a new Florida homestead may transfer the benefit, up to $500,000, if the new homestead is established within 3 years after January 1 of the year the old one was abandoned and the owner had a homestead exemption on January 1 of any of the 3 preceding years; claimed on Form DR-501T with the homestead application (V-67). The 3-year window replaced 2 years from 2021: "2 years" is outdated.
  • Pending, not law (V-23; V-67): CS/HJR 1-F (2026 Special Session F) is on the November 3, 2026 ballot. If at least 60% of voters approve, from January 1, 2027 it would, among other things, let the full accrued benefit transfer for non-school levies (no $500,000 cap for those levies). Until then the 3%/CPI cap and the $500,000 cap remain current. A 2026 House analysis of HB 7031 mentions possible changes to which prior homestead can be ported from; enactment status not verified. Exam questions usually lag law changes.

Step 2: Units

  • Dollars, in US notation: $1,710.50 (comma for thousands, point for decimals).
  • Mill = one-thousandth. 1 mill = $1 of tax per $1,000 of taxable value = 0.001 (manual; not yet verified; N-144). It works like per mille (‰), not like percent.
Millage Tax per $1,000 Decimal Percent
1 mill $1.00 0.001 0.1%
6 mills $6.00 0.006 0.6%
18.4 mills $18.40 0.0184 1.84%
  • Percent for SOH (3% = 0.03). The CPI is the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers, U.S. City Average (V-67).

Step 3: Formula

  1. SOH maximum = last year's assessed value × (1 + the lower of 3% or the CPI change).
  2. Additional exemption = the smaller of $25,000 (or the indexed figure) and (assessed value − $50,000); zero at $50,000 or less.
  3. School taxable value = assessed value − $25,000 (− any other exemption the question applies).
  4. Non-school taxable value = assessed value − $25,000 − additional exemption (− any other exemption the question applies).
  5. Tax = taxable value × mills ÷ 1,000, for each part; then add.

Shortcut: taxable value in thousands × mills = tax (285 × 6 = $1,710). With round figures and an assessed value of $75,000 or more: school taxable = assessed − $25,000; non-school taxable = assessed − $50,000.

Step 4: When it applies

Situation What to do
Homestead Two taxable values, as above
Not a homestead (rental, second home, vacant lot, store) No homestead exemption, no SOH: assessed value × total millage (unless the question gives another exemption)
Widow/widower, blind, totally and permanently disabled Also subtract $5,000. V-10 confirms the amount, not how each levy treats it: apply it as the question states
Last year's assessed value + market and CPI changes given SOH first, then exemptions
Property sold Reset to just value (N-142) at the next January 1 assessment (V-76); the buyer must qualify for homestead on their own (N-140)
Question gives $25,722 Use it; otherwise $25,000

Step 5: Worked example

A. The manual's example. A homestead is assessed at $310,000. School millage 6 mills; county plus city 9 mills.

School Non-school
Assessed value $310,000 $310,000
− first exemption − $25,000 − $25,000
− additional exemption does not apply − $25,000
Taxable value $285,000 $260,000
× mills ÷ 1,000 × 6 × 9
Tax $1,710 $2,340

Total $4,050. Second check with decimals: $285,000 × 0.006 = $1,710; $260,000 × 0.009 = $2,340 ✓.

With the indexed 2025 figure, non-school taxable is $310,000 − $25,000 − $25,722 = $259,278 → $2,333.50; total $4,043.50. Only $6.50 apart, so questions use $25,000 unless they give the indexed figure.

B. The next year, with Save Our Homes. Market value rose 8%; the CPI changed 2.4%. Cap = lower of 3% and 2.4% = 2.4% (ignore the 8%). Maximum assessed value = $310,000 × 1.024 = $317,440 (check: $310,000 × 0.024 = $7,440 ✓). Same millage: school $292,440 × 6 ÷ 1,000 = $1,754.64; non-school $267,440 × 9 ÷ 1,000 = $2,406.96; total $4,161.60.

Step 6: Reasonableness check

  • School taxable ≥ non-school taxable; at assessed values of $75,000 or more the gap is exactly $25,000 (round figures).
  • About $1 per $1,000 per mill: $300,000 at 15 mills ≈ $4,500. Getting $45,000 means you divided by 100.
  • SOH adds at most $3 per $100 of last year's assessed value; more means you used the market rise or the higher rate.
  • An exemption saves exemption × mills ÷ 1,000: $5,000 at 15 mills = $75.

Step 7: Common errors

Error Correction
Taking $50,000 off school taxes School gets only the first $25,000
Full second exemption on a cheap home (assessed $62,000 → $25,000 off) Only value above $50,000 counts: $12,000
Dividing mills by 100 Mills are per 1,000
"Whichever is greater" (CPI 4% → 4%) The lower one: 3%
Applying the cap to market value or to this year's value Apply it to last year's assessed value
Subtracting $500 for a widow $5,000 (V-10)
Estimating the buyer's tax on the seller's capped value Resets to just value after a sale (N-142)

Step 8: Guided practice

G1. A homestead was assessed at $250,000 last year. Market value rose 11%; the CPI changed 1.8%. Maximum assessed value this year? Hint: the lower rate.

Check your answer

1.8% is lower than 3%. $250,000 × 1.018 = $254,500 (check: $250,000 × 0.018 = $4,500 ✓).

G2. An Ocala homestead is assessed at $345,000. School 5.8 mills; non-school 12.4 mills; $25,000 for each exemption. Total tax? Hint: two taxable values, then mills ÷ 1,000.

Check your answer

School taxable $320,000 × 5.8 ÷ 1,000 = $1,856. Non-school taxable $295,000 × 12.4 ÷ 1,000 = $3,658. Total $5,514 (check: 320 × 5.8 + 295 × 12.4 = 1,856 + 3,658 ✓).

Step 9: Independent practice

I1. A rental condo in Fort Lauderdale (nobody's homestead) is assessed at $210,000. Total millage 19.4. Tax?

Check your answer

No homestead exemption: 210 × 19.4 = $4,074 (check: $210,000 × 0.0194 = $4,074 ✓).

I2. Last year's assessed value: $420,000. Market value +6%; CPI +3.7%. Maximum assessed value?

Check your answer

3% is lower than 3.7%. $420,000 × 1.03 = $432,600.

I3. A rural homestead is assessed at $68,000. School 6 mills; non-school 10 mills; round figures. Taxable values and total tax?

Check your answer

Additional exemption = $68,000 − $50,000 = $18,000 (not $25,000). School taxable $43,000 → $258. Non-school taxable $68,000 − $25,000 − $18,000 = $25,000 → $250. Total $508.

I4. A widow's homestead is assessed at $260,000. School 6.5 mills; non-school 9.5 mills; round figures. The question says her $5,000 exemption reduces both taxable values. Total tax? What would the outdated $500 give?

Check your answer

School $230,000 → $1,495. Non-school $205,000 → $1,947.50. Total $3,442.50. With $500: $234,500 → $1,524.25 and $209,500 → $1,990.25, total $3,514.50, a trap answer $72 too high.

I5. Owner A: just value $450,000, assessed value $290,000. Owner B: just value $1,350,000, assessed value $700,000. Each sets up a new Florida homestead in time. How much benefit is portable under current law?

Check your answer

A: $160,000 (all of it). B: $650,000, capped at $500,000 (V-67). CS/HJR 1-F would change B's non-school result only if approved (V-23).

Step 10: Exam application

  1. Homestead or not? SOH involved? Which exemption figures are given?
  2. SOH first: the lower of 3% or CPI, on last year's assessed value.
  3. Exemptions: $25,000 from both values; up to $25,000 more from non-school only; $5,000 if the question includes it.
  4. Each taxable value × its mills ÷ 1,000; add. Round only at the end, to cents.

Wrong choices are built from the Step 7 errors. The annual tax is also what gets prorated at closing (L14-7): use the question's method, otherwise the course convention of a 365-day year with the buyer owning the closing day (V-79: unresolved; a course convention, not law).

4. Key terms

Term Meaning
Just value Florida's term for market value, set as of January 1
Assessed value Value the tax starts from; for a homestead, capped by Save Our Homes
Taxable value Assessed value − exemptions; school and non-school can differ
Homestead exemption $25,000 off all taxes + up to $25,000 (CPI-indexed) off non-school taxes on value above $50,000
Non-school levies County, city and other local taxes (everything except the school board)
Mill / millage 1 mill = $1 per $1,000 = 0.001 / a tax rate in mills
Save Our Homes (SOH) Cap on a homestead's yearly assessed-value increase: 3% or CPI, whichever is less
Accrued SOH benefit Just value − assessed value
Portability Moving up to $500,000 of the benefit to a new Florida homestead (3-year window; Form DR-501T)
Green Belt Agricultural land assessed on use value (manual; not yet verified)

5. Practical example

The Moreira house in Sarasota. Homestead since 2010. On January 1, 2026: just value $540,000, assessed value $275,000. Millage: school 5.9, non-school 9.6. In June 2026 Daniel buys it and moves in. Assume a January 1, 2027 just value of $530,000, unchanged millage, and his own homestead exemption. Use the round $25,000 exemption figures.

Moreira 2026 bill Daniel's 2027 estimate
Assessed value $275,000 $530,000 (reset to just value)
School $250,000 × 5.9 ÷ 1,000 = $1,475.00 $505,000 × 5.9 ÷ 1,000 = $2,979.50
Non-school $225,000 × 9.6 ÷ 1,000 = $2,160.00 $480,000 × 9.6 ÷ 1,000 = $4,608.00
Total $3,635.00 ($3,489.60 if paid in November with the 4% discount) $7,587.50
  • The 2026 bill reflects the Moreiras' January 1, 2026 status and value (V-76) and is prorated at closing (L14-7).
  • From 2027 the assessed value resets (N-142): Daniel's bill could be more than twice theirs even with his own homestead exemption, which is what his property tax disclosure summary warns (V-75). As a rental, with no homestead exemption: 530 × 15.5 = $8,215.
  • The Moreiras move to a smaller home in Venice. Their benefit, $540,000 − $275,000 = $265,000, is under the $500,000 cap. Abandoning the old homestead in 2026, they must establish the new one within 3 years after January 1, 2026 and file Form DR-501T (V-67).

6. Portugal comparison

Familiar principle. Portugal also taxes property every year: IMI is an annual municipal tax on the registered taxable value (VPT) (PT-10; the course still marks the Portuguese side of this comparison "requires verification"). IMI rates and exemptions require verification.

Florida rule. The property appraiser sets just value as of January 1; taxing authorities set millage. Homesteads get the exemptions ($25,000 + up to $25,000 non-school) and the Save Our Homes cap (3% or CPI).

Precise difference. Florida computes the tax in mills on taxable value after exemptions, and school and non-school values can differ: a homestead assessed at $300,000 has school taxable $275,000 and non-school taxable $250,000 (round figures), because the additional exemption applies only to non-school levies (PT-10).

Exam implication. 1 mill = $1 per $1,000; run school and non-school separately when exemptions differ. Never answer a Florida question from IMI habits.

7. Legal and numerical requirements

Memorize exactly

  • Taxable value = assessed − exemptions. Tax = taxable value × mills ÷ 1,000. 1 mill = $1 per $1,000 = 0.001 (manual; not yet verified; N-144).
  • Homestead: $25,000 off all taxes + up to $25,000 off non-school taxes on assessed value above $50,000 (s. 196.031; V-09); CPI-indexed since 2025 ($25,722 for 2025); exam math $25,000. Own and occupy as a permanent residence on January 1 (N-140).
  • $5,000 widow/widower, blind, totally and permanently disabled; Florida resident (s. 196.202; V-10). $500 = outdated (before the 2023 roll).
  • Disabled veterans: larger or total exemptions. Green Belt: use value (manual; not yet verified).
  • SOH: increase ≤ 3% of prior assessed value or the CPI change, whichever is lower (Art. VII, s. 4(d); s. 193.155; V-67). Resets to just value on a change of ownership (N-142).
  • Portability: up to $500,000; within 3 years after January 1 of the year the old homestead was abandoned (2 years = outdated, before 2021); exemption held on January 1 of any of the 3 preceding years; Form DR-501T (V-67).
  • CS/HJR 1-F (November 3, 2026 ballot; 60%; would apply from January 1, 2027): not law (V-23). HB 7031: status not verified.

Understand

  • Exemptions reduce the value, never the tax directly.
  • School taxable value is the larger one: the second exemption skips school levies.
  • SOH caps assessed-value growth, not millage: a higher millage can still raise the bill.
  • SOH protects the owner who stays; a sale resets it; portability lets the owner take part of it along.

8. Visual explanation

Just valueMarket value as of January 1 (V-76)
Assessed valueHomestead: at most last year's × (1 + lower of 3% or CPI) (V-67)
− Exemptions$25,000 all taxes · up to $25,000 non-school above $50,000 · $5,000 widow/blind/disabled
= Taxable valueSchool and non-school, separately
× mills ÷ 1,000Tax for each levy; add them
− Early-payment discount4% Nov · 3% Dec · 2% Jan · 1% Feb (L18-1)

From market value to the amount paid. Save Our Homes works on the second layer; exemptions on the third.

How a homestead's assessed value is sliced (round figures)

Slice of assessed value School taxes Non-school taxes
$0 – $25,000 Exempt Exempt
$25,000 – $50,000 Taxed Taxed
$50,000 – $75,000 Taxed Exempt (top moves with CPI: $75,722 in 2025)
Above $75,000 Taxed Taxed

9. Common misconceptions

  • "Homestead exempts the first $50,000 from all taxes." No. $25,000 from all taxes; the second exemption covers value above $50,000, non-school only. Value from $25,000 to $50,000 gets no homestead exemption.
  • "The widow's exemption is $500." Outdated; it is $5,000 (V-10).
  • "SOH is 3% or CPI, whichever is greater." Whichever is less.
  • "SOH caps the tax bill." It caps assessed-value growth; millage can still rise.
  • "The buyer keeps the seller's low assessed value." It resets to just value (N-142).
  • "Portability has no limit." Up to $500,000, within 3 years. The November 2026 measure would change this for non-school levies only if approved (V-23).
  • "A rental gets Save Our Homes." No. SOH and the homestead exemption are for homesteads.

10. Memory sheet

  • $25k all + up to $25k non-school above $50k (CPI-indexed; $25,722 in 2025). Exam: $25,000. Own and occupy on January 1.
  • $5k widow/widower · blind · totally and permanently disabled (not $500).
  • SOH: 3% or CPI, whichever is less, on last year's assessed value. Sale → reset to just value.
  • Portable: up to $500k, within 3 years (not 2), Form DR-501T. CS/HJR 1-F = not law.
  • Tax = taxable × mills ÷ 1,000. School and non-school separately.
  • Check: school taxable = non-school + $25,000 (assessed $75,000 or more, round figures); about $1 per $1,000 per mill.

lessons.title: Income taxes and real estate
lessons.html:
2. Why it matters

In practice. Income tax drives many sale decisions. An investor wonders whether to sell a fourplex outright or exchange it; a couple asks whether the profit on their home is taxable. You are not a tax adviser, and a client's own figures belong with a CPA or tax attorney, but you must understand the vocabulary well enough to see what is at stake and when to refer.
