On the exam. Section 18 (Taxes Affecting Real Estate) is 3% of the exam (V-02). Questions here are mostly conceptual: 27.5 versus 39 years, land never depreciated, the effect of boot in a 1031 exchange, the $250,000/$500,000 home-sale exclusion with its 2-of-5-years test, and a short adjusted-basis and gain calculation.

3. Simple explanation

Labels: V-nn = checked against official sources on 2026-10-19/20. "(manual; not yet verified)" = from the study manual only. These are US federal income tax rules (Internal Revenue Code, IRS publications), not Florida statutes. Figures in the examples are invented for practice.

Building block 1: basis

Basis is, in general, what the owner paid for the property. Adjusted basis = cost + capital improvements − depreciation taken (manual; not yet verified). Basis is the yardstick the sale is measured against:

  • An improvement (a new roof, an added bedroom) raises basis: the owner has put more money in.
  • Depreciation lowers basis: the owner has already deducted that part of the cost from taxable income.

Building block 2: depreciation (cost recovery)

Buildings wear out, so the tax law lets the owner of a rental or business building deduct the building's cost over a fixed period. This deduction is depreciation, also called cost recovery (26 U.S.C. 168; IRS Pub. 946; V-77):

Property Recovery period Method
Residential rental property (a building where 80% or more of gross rental income comes from dwelling units) 27.5 years Straight-line
Nonresidential real property (offices, stores, warehouses) 39 years Straight-line
Land Never depreciated —

Why never land? Land does not wear out, become obsolete or get used up (V-77). Only the building's cost goes into the depreciable basis, so the purchase price must first be split between land and building.

Straight-line means the same deduction every year: building cost ÷ recovery period. A Kissimmee rental house costs $360,000, of which $85,000 is land: $275,000 ÷ 27.5 = $10,000 a year. An office building's structure costs $780,000: $780,000 ÷ 39 = $20,000 a year.

Finer points (V-77): these are the general-system (GDS, under MACRS) periods; the alternative system (ADS) uses 30 and 40 years. Real tax returns apply the mid-month convention, which adjusts the first and last years; this course's calculations use full years. The 39-year period replaced 31.5 years in 1993, so 31.5 is outdated.

Why investors like it (tax shelter): depreciation costs no cash in the year it is deducted, yet it reduces taxable income, so it shields part of the cash income from tax (manual; not yet verified). The bill comes later, at the sale.

Building block 3: capital gain and recapture

Capital gain = amount realized − adjusted basis (manual; not yet verified). On the exam, the amount realized is the net sale price the question gives.

Because depreciation lowers the basis, it raises the gain. The depreciation taken over the years is recaptured (taxed) at the sale (manual; not yet verified; recapture rates are not covered).

Kissimmee, 6 years later: depreciation taken 6 × $10,000 = $60,000; no improvements. Adjusted basis $360,000 − $60,000 = $300,000. Net sale price $455,000 → gain $155,000. Without the depreciation the gain would be $95,000: the extra $60,000 is the depreciation coming back.

Building block 4: exclude, defer or spread

Tool For what property Effect on the tax
Principal residence exclusion (26 U.S.C. 121; V-78) The seller's main home Gain up to the limit is excluded (not taxed)
1031 like-kind exchange (manual; not yet verified) Investment or business real property Tax deferred (postponed), except on boot
Installment sale (manual; not yet verified) A sale paid over time Tax spread as payments arrive

Principal residence exclusion (V-78). A seller can exclude up to $250,000 of gain, or $500,000 for married filing jointly (a married couple filing one joint federal tax return), if they owned and used the home as their principal residence for at least 2 of the 5 years before the sale: 24 full months or 730 days, and the periods need not be continuous. Qualifications:

  1. Generally not available if the seller excluded gain on another home sold within the 2 years before this sale.
  2. For the $500,000 joint amount, at least one spouse meets the ownership test and both meet the use test and the 2-year look-back rule; otherwise each spouse is tested separately.
  3. A partial exclusion may apply if the tests are failed for qualifying reasons (work, health, unforeseen circumstances).
  4. Gain equal to depreciation claimed or allowable after May 6, 1997 cannot be excluded.
  5. A surviving spouse may use $500,000 if the sale is within 2 years of the spouse's death and other conditions are met.

Source note: confirmed from IRS Publication 523 (2025) and Tax Topic 701; the statute text and any 2026 change were not checked directly (V-78).

1031 like-kind exchange (manual; not yet verified). An owner who exchanges investment or business real property for like-kind property defers the tax on the gain: postponed, not forgiven. A family home is not investment property, so it takes the exclusion, never a 1031. Boot is any value received that is not like-kind: cash, debt relief, personal property. Boot is taxable to the extent of gain (taxed, but never more than the gain), and it does not disqualify the exchange; the like-kind part stays deferred. Other technical requirements of an exchange are beyond this course.

Installment sale (manual; not yet verified). When the seller receives the price over several years (for example, through seller financing), the gain is recognized proportionally as payments are received, so the tax is spread over those years. It is not avoided.

4. Key terms

Term Meaning
Basis In general, the cost of the property
Adjusted basis Cost + improvements − depreciation
Amount realized What the seller receives from the sale (on the exam, the net sale price given)
Capital gain Amount realized − adjusted basis
Depreciation (cost recovery) Yearly deduction of a building's cost: 27.5 years residential rental, 39 years nonresidential, never land
Straight-line The same deduction every year
Recapture Taxing, at the sale, the depreciation taken earlier
1031 exchange Tax-deferred exchange of like-kind investment or business real property
Boot Non-like-kind value received in an exchange (cash, debt relief, personal property); taxable to the extent of gain
Principal residence exclusion Up to $250,000 single / $500,000 married filing jointly of home-sale gain not taxed; 2-of-5-years test
Installment sale Sale paid over time; gain reported as payments are received

5. Practical example

Rita, the investor. Rita bought a fourplex in St. Petersburg for $640,000: $145,000 land and $495,000 building. All of its rent comes from its four dwelling units, so it is residential rental property (80% or more from dwelling units; V-77): $495,000 ÷ 27.5 = $18,000 a year. She later added a new roof for $40,000. Her records show $120,000 of total depreciation taken (building and roof).

Step Calculation Result
Adjusted basis $640,000 + $40,000 − $120,000 $560,000
Amount realized net sale price $860,000
Gain $860,000 − $560,000 $300,000

Her options, in concept:

  • Sell outright. The $300,000 gain is taxable; $120,000 of it comes from the depreciation taken, which is recaptured (manual; not yet verified).
  • 1031 exchange into an apartment building in Tampa (also investment property), receiving $25,000 cash as well. The $25,000 is boot and is taxable, since it is less than her gain; the other $275,000 of gain stays deferred, and the exchange is still valid. (Had her gain been only $15,000, the $25,000 of boot would be taxable only up to $15,000.)
  • Installment sale. She finances the buyer and is paid over several years; the gain is taxed as the payments come in.

She asks which is best. You explain the concepts and refer her to her CPA.

Paulo and Joana, the homeowners. A married couple filing jointly bought their Jacksonville home 3 years ago for $305,000, added a $35,000 pool, and have lived there ever since. No depreciation was taken. They sell for a net $735,000.

  • Adjusted basis $305,000 + $35,000 = $340,000; gain $735,000 − $340,000 = $395,000.
  • Both owned and lived in it at least 2 of the last 5 years, and neither excluded gain on another home sold in the previous 2 years: up to $500,000 can be excluded, so the whole $395,000 is excluded.
  • If Paulo were single, the limit would be $250,000: $395,000 − $250,000 = $145,000 taxable.
  • A 1031 exchange is not available: this is their principal residence, not investment property.

6. Portugal comparison

Familiar principle. Taxing the gain on a property sale is a familiar idea, but this course has no verified Portugal–Florida comparison entry on income taxes, so any Portuguese rule on gains from property sales, rental income, depreciation or reinvesting sale proceeds requires verification.

Florida rule. The rules here are US federal income tax rules: depreciation 27.5/39 years, never land (V-77); the $250,000/$500,000 exclusion with the 2-of-5-years test (V-78); basis, recapture, 1031 exchanges, boot and installment sales (manual; not yet verified).

Precise difference. Not covered by the course's verified sources; any comparison requires verification.

Exam implication. Answer only with the US rules above. A Portuguese rule never answers a Florida exam question, and Portuguese tax treatment is never a guide to a client's US sale.

7. Legal and numerical requirements

Memorize exactly

  • Depreciation: 27.5 years residential rental (80% or more of gross rents from dwelling units); 39 years nonresidential; straight-line; mid-month convention; land never (26 U.S.C. 168; IRS Pub. 946; V-77). ADS: 30/40 years. 31.5 years = outdated (replaced in 1993).
  • Exclusion: $250,000 single / $500,000 married filing jointly; owned and used as the principal residence 2 of the 5 years before the sale (24 months or 730 days; need not be continuous); generally not if used on another home sold within the previous 2 years (26 U.S.C. 121; IRS Pub. 523; V-78).
  • Joint $500,000: one spouse meets ownership; both meet use and look-back. Partial exclusion for work, health or unforeseen circumstances. Depreciation after May 6, 1997 cannot be excluded. Surviving spouse: $500,000 if sold within 2 years of the death and other conditions are met (V-78).
  • Adjusted basis = cost + improvements − depreciation. Gain = amount realized − adjusted basis. Depreciation is recaptured at sale (manual; not yet verified).
  • 1031: investment or business real property, like-kind; tax deferred; boot (cash, debt relief, personal property) taxable to the extent of gain; boot does not disqualify (manual; not yet verified).
  • Installment sale: gain recognized as payments are received (manual; not yet verified).

Understand

  • Depreciation shelters income now but raises the gain later.
  • Exclusion = gain not taxed (up to the limit); 1031 = tax postponed; installment sale = tax spread.
  • The home takes the exclusion; the investment property takes the 1031. Do not cross them.

8. Visual explanation

CostPurchase price, split into land and building
+ ImprovementsRoof, additions, pool: raise the basis
− DepreciationBuilding only: 27.5 or 39 years, straight-line (V-77)
= Adjusted basisThe yardstick for the gain
Amount realized − adjusted basis= Capital gain; depreciation is recaptured

The basis ladder (manual; not yet verified, except the depreciation periods). Each dollar of depreciation lowers the basis and raises the gain by a dollar.

Is the property the seller's principal residence, owned and used 2 of the 5 years before the sale?
No → go to the next question (a partial exclusion may still apply for work, health or unforeseen circumstances).
Yes → exclude up to $250,000 single / $500,000 married filing jointly, generally not available if the exclusion was used on another home sold within the 2 years before this sale (V-78). No 1031 for the home.
Is it investment or business real property exchanged for like-kind property?
No → the gain is taxable at the sale; an installment sale can spread it as payments arrive (manual).
Yes → 1031 exchange: tax deferred; any boot is taxed up to the gain, and the exchange survives (manual).

Which tool fits the sale.

9. Common misconceptions

  • "Land is depreciated with the building." No. Land is never depreciated (V-77).
  • "An apartment building is depreciated over 39 years." No. Residential rental is 27.5 years; 39 is nonresidential.
  • "Nonresidential is 31.5 years." Outdated since 1993: 39 years.
  • "Depreciation lowers the gain at sale." No. It lowers the basis, so the gain is larger.
  • "Receiving cash kills the 1031." No. The cash is boot and is taxed; the exchange survives.
  • "A 1031 makes the gain tax-free." No. It defers the tax.
  • "I can 1031 my family home." No. The home uses the $250,000/$500,000 exclusion.
  • "The 2 years must be the last 2 years in a row." No. 2 of the 5 years before the sale; need not be continuous.
  • "Every married couple gets $500,000." Only married filing jointly, with at least one spouse meeting ownership and both meeting use and the 2-year look-back rule.
  • "An installment sale avoids the tax." No. It spreads it.

10. Memory sheet

  • 27.5 residential rental · 39 nonresidential · straight-line · land never (V-77). 31.5 = outdated.
  • Adjusted basis = cost + improvements − depreciation. Gain = amount realized − adjusted basis. Depreciation recaptured (manual).
  • Home: $250k / $500k, 2 of 5 years, generally not if used on another home sold within the last 2 years (V-78).
  • 1031: investment property, tax deferred; boot taxed, exchange survives (manual).
  • Installment sale = gain taxed as paid (manual).
  • Exclusion excludes · 1031 defers · installment spreads.

lessons.title: Planning, zoning and land-use controls
lessons.html:
2. Why it matters

In practice. Zoning decides what a buyer may do with a property: build an addition near the lot line, run a small daycare from home, keep the shop the seller operates. Permit records and the certificate of occupancy show whether a building, or a later addition, was built legally and may be used. The county or city decides these questions, not you. Your job is to spot them and send the client to the local planning or building department, or to a Florida attorney when rights are at stake.

On the exam. Section 19, "Planning and Zoning", carries 1% of the exam (V-02): about 1 of the 100 questions (V-01), shared with L19-2. Expect a classification: police power or eminent domain? Variance, special exception, nonconforming use or rezoning? Building permit or certificate of occupancy? The study manual calls variance versus special exception "a guaranteed question". With only about one question for the whole section, read that as "the most likely topic", not a promise.

3. Simple explanation

Source status: no verification entry covers the land-use rules in this lesson. Apart from the exam weight (V-01, V-02), everything here comes from the study manual and is labelled (manual; not yet verified). Each Florida county and city adopts its own plan and codes, so local details differ; the exam tests the general concepts.

Foundation: regulating land versus taking it

Owning land never means unlimited freedom. Government can limit how you use land, or it can take the land itself.

Police power Eminent domain
What government does Regulates use for public health, safety and welfare (zoning, building codes, permits) Takes private property for public use
Legal process Ordinances, codes, permits Condemnation
Owner keeps the property? Yes No
Owner paid? No compensation Just compensation (fair payment for what is taken)

(manual; not yet verified)

Why is one paid and the other not? A regulation places similar limits on many owners, and those owners also benefit: your home is safer and more pleasant when the neighbor cannot build a factory. A taking forces one owner to give up property so the public can have a road or a school, so the public pays that owner. "Police power" has nothing to do with the police force; it is the general power to make rules for public health, safety and welfare.

Inverse condemnation. In a normal condemnation the government starts the case. When a regulation goes so far that it destroys all the property's value, the owner may sue, claiming the regulation amounts to a taking that must be paid for. "Inverse" means reversed: the owner starts the case (manual; not yet verified). A mere drop in value is not enough; the course's trigger example is a regulation that destroys all value. This course cites no court decisions on exactly where regulation becomes a taking; know the label and the trigger.

Taxation (Section 18) and escheat (L09-1) are also government powers over property, but not land-use controls.

The comprehensive plan and zoning

  • Comprehensive plan. Every Florida local government (county or city) maintains one: its long-range land-use plan.
  • Zoning implements the plan. A local law (ordinance) divides land into districts: residential, commercial, industrial, agricultural and special districts. Each district lists the uses allowed and dimensional rules such as setback (minimum distance between a building and a lot line or the street) and height.
  • Buffer zones ease the transition between very different districts, for example offices or a park between a shopping center and single-family homes.

(manual; not yet verified)

The plan is the strategy; zoning is the rule book that carries it out, parcel by parcel. Zoning is public law; a deed restriction is a private limit recorded in a deed or plat (L09-4).

When a rule does not fit: four tools

Tool What it is District changes? Why it exists Example
Variance Permission to deviate from a dimensional rule (setback, height) because of a hardship unique to the parcel No; same use Rules written for typical lots can be unfair to an unusually narrow or odd-shaped one Narrow lot: house would sit 3 feet (about 0.9 m) inside the side setback
Special exception (also conditional use) A use the code already permits in the district with case-by-case approval No Some uses serve a neighborhood but fit only on the right site School, church or daycare in a residential district
Nonconforming use A use lawful before the code changed ("grandfathered") No An owner who followed the old rules is not forced out Corner store opened before the street was rezoned residential
Rezoning Changing the district itself Yes The wanted use is not allowed in the district at all Farmland changed to residential for a subdivision

(manual; not yet verified)

Limits of "grandfathered". A nonconforming use may continue, but the code tolerates rather than encourages it: it usually may not expand, and if destroyed or abandoned, it may not resume (manual; not yet verified).

The manual's exam trap: hardship + dimensions → variance; permitted-with-approval use → special exception. Neither is a rezoning (manual; not yet verified).

PUD (planned unit development). A development planned as one unit that mixes uses (homes, shops, offices) and clusters density (buildings grouped closer together) in exchange for open space, such as parks or preserved land (manual; not yet verified).

Construction control

  1. Building permit: needed before construction starts.
  2. Inspections: during the work, against the building codes.
  3. Certificate of occupancy (CO): issued after final inspection; the building may not be used or occupied before it.

Florida contractors are licensed by the CILB (Construction Industry Licensing Board), not by the FREC. (manual; not yet verified)

4. Key terms

Term Meaning
Police power Government power to regulate for health, safety and welfare; no compensation owed
Eminent domain Government power to take private property for public use, with just compensation
Condemnation The legal process for exercising eminent domain
Inverse condemnation Owner's lawsuit claiming a regulation amounts to a taking
Comprehensive plan Local government's long-range land-use plan; zoning implements it
Setback Minimum distance between a building and a lot line or the street
Buffer zone Area easing the transition between very different districts
Variance Permission to deviate from a dimensional rule because of hardship unique to the parcel
Special exception (conditional use) Use allowed in a zone with case-by-case approval
Nonconforming use Lawful use that predates current zoning ("grandfathered")
Rezoning Changing the zoning district itself
PUD Planned unit development mixing uses with clustered density and open space
Certificate of occupancy (CO) Document allowing a building to be occupied after final inspection

5. Practical example

Names, places and distances are invented for practice. Real setbacks and permitted uses come from each local code.

Beatriz, a sales associate in Tampa, helps Mr. and Mrs. Moreira find a home where Mrs. Moreira can run a small daycare. Six land-use questions come up. Each time, Beatriz names the issue, sends the clients to the city or county for the facts, and suggests an attorney where rights are at stake.

Situation Classification What follows
A lot is so narrow that their house plan would sit 3 feet (about 0.9 m) inside the side setback. Variance They may apply; the residential use does not change.
The city code lists daycare as allowed in that residential district with case-by-case approval. Special exception Mrs. Moreira applies for approval; no rezoning needed.
A bakery on the corner opened before the block was rezoned residential; its owner wants to double its size. Nonconforming use It may keep operating but usually may not expand; if it burns down or is abandoned, it may not reopen.
The county takes a 10-foot (about 3 m) strip along the front of another listing to widen the road. Eminent domain The owner receives just compensation.
The city lowers the height limit for every lot on that road; a seller says her lot is now worth less. Police power No compensation for the lower value. If she claims the rule goes so far that it amounts to a taking (the course's example: it destroys all value), her remedy is an inverse condemnation suit; Beatriz refers her to an attorney.
The house they choose has a garage converted into a bedroom. Permit and final inspection Beatriz suggests checking the permit and inspection history with the building department during the inspection period.

(Classifications: manual; not yet verified.)

6. Portugal comparison

Familiar principle. Local control of what may be built where is likely familiar from your work in Portugal. However, this course has no verified Portugal–Florida comparison entry for planning, zoning, expropriation or building control, so any specific Portuguese rule, plan, license or procedure requires verification.

Florida rule. Comprehensive plan → zoning; relief through a variance, special exception, nonconforming-use status or rezoning; regulation unpaid, taking paid; permit → inspections → CO before use (manual; not yet verified).

Precise difference. Not established by the course's verified sources; requires verification.

Exam implication. Answer in US vocabulary only; a Portuguese concept never answers a Florida question. Translate each fact pattern into the Florida tools.

7. Legal and numerical requirements

Memorize exactly

Every item except the last is (manual; not yet verified).

  • Police power = regulate for health, safety and welfare; no compensation.
  • Eminent domain = take for public use through condemnation; just compensation.
  • Inverse condemnation = the owner sues, claiming a regulation is a taking, as when it destroys all value.
  • Every Florida local government has a comprehensive plan; zoning implements it. Districts: residential, commercial, industrial, agricultural, special. Buffer zones ease transitions.
  • Variance = dimensional rule (setback, height) + hardship unique to the parcel.
  • Special exception = conditional use = a use permitted with case-by-case approval (school, church, daycare).
  • Nonconforming use = lawful before the code changed; may continue; usually no expansion; destroyed or abandoned → may not resume.
  • Rezoning = the district itself changes. Variance and special exception are not rezonings.
  • PUD = mixed uses + clustered density traded for open space.
  • Building permit before construction → inspections → CO after final inspection, before use. Contractors: CILB.
  • Section 19 = 1% of the exam (V-02).

Understand

  • Why regulation is unpaid and a taking is paid.
  • The plan comes first; zoning turns it into district rules.
  • Zoning (public) differs from deed restrictions (private, recorded; L09-4).
  • A licensee spots land-use issues and refers clients to the planning or building department or an attorney, rather than guessing what a code allows.

8. Visual explanation

Regulate or take?

Does the government only regulate how the land is used (zoning, height limit, building code), with the owner keeping the property?
No, it takes the property for public use → eminent domain (condemnation): just compensation
Does the regulation destroy all of the property's value?
No → ordinary police power: the owner must comply; no compensation for a loss of value
Yes → the owner may sue for inverse condemnation, claiming the regulation amounts to a taking

Regulation is unpaid; a taking is paid. "Destroys all value" is the course's trigger example for inverse condemnation (manual; not yet verified).

Clue words in exam questions

Clue in the question Answer
Government limits height or use for everyone; owners are not paid Police power
Government acquires land for a road or school and pays the owner Eminent domain
Owner sues, claiming a regulation is really a taking Inverse condemnation
An owner asks to build closer to the line or taller than allowed because of a "hardship" or a "narrow or irregular lot" Variance
"Church, school, daycare", "allowed with approval", "conditional" Special exception
"Existed before the change", "grandfathered" Nonconforming use
"Change the district", "agricultural to residential" Rezoning
"Mixed uses", "clustered", "open space" PUD
"Before construction" Building permit
"Before anyone may move in", "after final inspection" Certificate of occupancy
Comprehensive planLong-range land-use plan
ZoningDistricts, uses, setbacks, heights, buffers
Building permitBefore construction
InspectionsDuring construction
Certificate of occupancyAfter final inspection; then occupancy

From plan to move-in: each step depends on the one before (manual; not yet verified).

9. Common misconceptions

  • "If zoning lowers my property's value, the county must pay me." No. Zoning is police power; a loss of value alone earns no compensation. Inverse condemnation is for a regulation that goes so far it amounts to a taking; the course's trigger example is a regulation that destroys all value.
  • "Eminent domain is voluntary because the owner is paid." No. It is an involuntary transfer; just compensation is not consent (L09-1).
  • "A variance lets me use my lot for a different purpose." No. A variance relaxes a dimensional rule. A different use needs a special exception (if the code lists it) or a rezoning.
  • "Any question that mentions a height limit is about a variance." No. A height limit imposed on everyone is police power; a variance is one owner's request to deviate from it because of a hardship unique to the parcel.
  • "Grandfathered means protected forever." A nonconforming use usually cannot expand and, if destroyed or abandoned, may not resume.
  • "The building permit lets the owner move in." The permit allows construction; occupancy needs the CO after final inspection.
  • "Deed restrictions are part of zoning." Deed restrictions are private and recorded; zoning is police power.

10. Memory sheet

  • Regulate = police power = no pay. Take = eminent domain (condemnation) = just compensation. Regulation destroys all value → owner sues: inverse condemnation.
  • Plan → zoning → permit → inspections → CO. Districts: residential, commercial, industrial, agricultural, special; buffer zones.
  • Hardship + dimensions = variance. Permitted-with-approval use = special exception. Neither is a rezoning.
  • Nonconforming: continues; usually no expansion; destroyed or abandoned → may not resume.
  • Rezoning = new district. PUD = mixed uses, clustered density, open space. CILB = contractors.
  • Section 19 = 1% (V-02). Land-use rules here: manual; not yet verified.

lessons.title: Environmental hazards and regulation
lessons.html:
2. Why it matters

In practice. Selling or renting a home built before 1978 triggers federal lead-based paint paperwork (with some exclusions and exemptions, covered below), and the agents must make sure it is done. Selling or renting any building needs Florida's radon notice. A buyer of an old gas station or factory lot faces a bigger risk: under federal cleanup law, a new owner can pay for contamination someone else caused. You are not an environmental expert, but you must know which forms belong in the file and when to refer a client to an inspector, environmental consultant or attorney.

On the exam. Section 19, "Planning and Zoning", carries 1% of the exam (V-02): about 1 of the 100 questions (V-01), shared with L19-1. Typical questions: the lead-paint year (1978), the buyer's inspection opportunity (10 days, unless waived or changed in writing), whether a new owner can be liable for contamination she did not cause (yes, under CERCLA, unless she has a defense), and intact asbestos (encapsulation).

3. Simple explanation

Source status: lead-based paint (V-60, confirmed; single-checked) and the radon notice (V-73, confirmed) are verified against official sources. Asbestos, CERCLA, brownfields, wetlands, EIS and underground storage tanks come only from the study manual and are labelled (manual; not yet verified).

Foundation: federal rules and Florida rules

Two layers of law apply at once. Federal rules apply in every state; Florida statutes add state rules. Federal agency rules are published in the CFR (Code of Federal Regulations). The EPA is the US Environmental Protection Agency; HUD is the US Department of Housing and Urban Development. Lead paint and CERCLA are federal; the radon notice is Florida law.

Lead-based paint (V-60)

Which housing? Target housing = housing built before 1978 (40 CFR 745.103). The EPA rule is 40 CFR 745 Subpart F; HUD's identical rule is 24 CFR Part 35 Subpart A.

  • Excluded: housing for the elderly or persons with disabilities, and 0-bedroom dwellings (no separate bedroom, such as a studio), unless a child under 6 lives or is expected to live there.
  • Exempt transactions (745.101) include: foreclosure sales; leases of 100 days or less with no renewal; leases of housing certified lead-free; renewals where disclosure was already made.

Duties of the seller or landlord (lessor) (745.107, 745.110, 745.113):

Duty Sale Lease
Give an EPA-approved pamphlet, such as Protect Your Family From Lead in Your Home Yes Yes
Disclose known lead-based paint and lead-based paint hazards Yes Yes
Provide available records and reports Yes Yes
Disclose the same to each agent Yes Yes
Include the Lead Warning Statement and signed acknowledgments in the contract or lease Yes Yes
Allow a 10-day opportunity for a risk assessment or inspection before the buyer is bound Yes No

Timing. If the disclosure comes after an offer, it must be made before the seller or lessor accepts it, so the buyer or tenant has the information while still free to walk away.

The 10-day opportunity. Before the buyer is bound by the contract, the seller must allow 10 days for a lead risk assessment or inspection, unless the parties agree in writing on a different period. The buyer may also waive it in writing. The manual's short version, "may be waived", is correct but incomplete. Tenants get the disclosure but not the 10-day period.

Your duty as a licensee. Licensees share responsibility for compliance: agents must ensure compliance (745.115). Lead paperwork is not only the seller's or landlord's job.

Year trap. 1978 is the lead-paint year. 1988 is when fair housing law added familial status and handicap (V-56). The manual warns that both years may appear among the answer choices.

Radon (V-73)

Radon is a naturally occurring radioactive gas. Florida requires the statutory radon notice on at least one document signed at or before a sale contract or rental agreement, for any building (s. 404.056(5); V-73).

  • Any building: new or old, residential or commercial; sale or rental.
  • The manual says the notice appears "in every sale and lease contract". That points the right way; the verified wording is more precise: at least one document signed at or before the contract or rental agreement.
  • It is a notice. This course's sources describe no testing requirement.

Other Florida disclosures around the contract (flood, property tax summary, energy-efficiency rating information) are in L11-4.

Asbestos (manual; not yet verified)

Asbestos is a fibrous mineral found in older building materials, especially insulation (pre-1980s). It is dangerous when friable: crumbling, so fibers can get into the air and be breathed in. When the material is intact, encapsulation (sealing or covering it so fibers cannot escape) is often safer than removal, because removal disturbs the material and can release fibers.

CERCLA / Superfund (manual; not yet verified)

CERCLA (the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act), known as Superfund, is the federal law on cleaning up contaminated sites.

Feature Meaning Consequence for an owner
Strict liability Liability without fault An owner can be liable without having caused the contamination
Joint and several liability Each liable party can be made to pay the whole cleanup cost, not only its share One owner may face the entire bill

Innocent-landowner defense. A current owner can be liable unless she qualifies for a defense, such as the innocent-landowner defense. It requires due diligence before purchase, such as a Phase I environmental audit (a review of the site and its history before buying). Why so strict? The law gets contaminated land cleaned up and pushes buyers to investigate first; a buyer who skipped the investigation cannot meet the innocent-landowner defense.

Other exam words (manual; not yet verified)

Term Meaning
Brownfield Abandoned or underused contaminated site being redeveloped
Wetlands Land wet or flooded much of the time, such as a marsh or swamp; development there is subject to wetlands permitting
EIS Environmental impact statement: a study of a project's environmental effects, prepared for major federal actions
UST Underground storage tank, for example at a gas station; a leak can contaminate soil and groundwater

4. Key terms

Term Meaning
Target housing Housing built before 1978, covered by the lead-based paint rule (minus the exclusions above)
Lead Warning Statement Required statement, with signed acknowledgments, in the sale contract or lease of target housing
Radon Naturally occurring radioactive gas; Florida requires a notice for the sale or rental of any building
Friable Crumbling; able to release fibers into the air
Encapsulation Sealing or covering asbestos so fibers cannot escape
CERCLA (Superfund) Federal law imposing strict (without fault), joint and several (each party can owe the whole cost) liability for cleaning up contaminated sites
Phase I environmental audit Pre-purchase environmental review; the due diligence the innocent-landowner defense requires
Brownfield Abandoned or underused contaminated site being redeveloped

5. Practical example

Names and properties are invented for practice.

Tiago, a sales associate in Jacksonville, has five files this month.

File Lead-based paint rule? Radon notice? Other points
1. Sale of a 1958 house to a couple with a 2-year-old Yes: pamphlet; known hazards; the seller's old lead inspection report (an available report); Lead Warning Statement and signed acknowledgments; 10-day inspection opportunity Yes The seller completes the disclosure after the offer arrives but before accepting it: on time. The buyers may waive the 10 days in writing, or both sides may agree a different period in writing.
2. 12-month lease of a 1972 condo unit Yes: pamphlet and disclosure, no 10-day period Yes Lease of 1 year or longer: flood disclosure too (V-07)
3. 90-day winter rental of a 1965 beach cottage, no renewal No: lease of 100 days or less, no renewal Yes Radon applies to any rental agreement. Lease shorter than 1 year: no lease flood disclosure (V-07)
4. Sale of a house built in 2023 No: not pre-1978 Yes Radon is not limited to older buildings
5. Investor buying a closed gas station; the back of the lot borders a marsh Not housing Yes (there is a building) Possible USTs; under CERCLA the new owner could be liable for old contamination, so Tiago recommends a Phase I environmental audit before closing. Building in or near the marsh may need wetlands permitting. If this abandoned, contaminated lot is redeveloped, it is the kind of site called a brownfield.

In file 1, the inspector also finds intact, non-crumbling asbestos insulation on old pipes: encapsulation is often safer than removal. Tiago refers the buyers to qualified professionals instead of giving a technical opinion.

Lead, radon and flood points: verified (V-60, V-73, V-07). Asbestos, CERCLA, UST, wetlands and brownfield points: manual; not yet verified.

6. Portugal comparison

Familiar principle. You may have handled technical documents or environmental questions in Portuguese sales. However, this course has no verified Portugal–Florida comparison entry for lead paint, radon, asbestos or contaminated-land liability, so any Portuguese rule on these topics requires verification.

Florida rule. Federal lead rules for pre-1978 housing (V-60); Florida's radon notice for any building (V-73); federal CERCLA liability (manual; not yet verified).

Precise difference. Not established by the course's verified sources; requires verification.

Exam implication. Answer with the US and Florida rules only. A Portuguese rule never answers a Florida question, and Portuguese practice never excuses a missing lead disclosure or radon notice in a Florida deal.

7. Legal and numerical requirements

Memorize exactly

  • Lead (V-60): target housing = built before 1978. Seller or lessor: EPA-approved pamphlet; known lead-based paint and hazards; available records and reports; same disclosure to each agent; Lead Warning Statement and signed acknowledgments. After an offer → disclose before acceptance.
  • Buyer: 10 days for a risk assessment or inspection before being bound; a different period if agreed in writing; may waive in writing. Tenants: disclosure, no 10-day period (V-60).
  • Excluded: housing for the elderly or persons with disabilities and 0-bedroom dwellings, unless a child under 6 lives or is expected to live there. Exempt: foreclosure sales; leases of 100 days or less with no renewal; certified lead-free leases; renewals already disclosed (V-60).
  • Agents must ensure compliance (40 CFR 745.115; V-60).
  • Radon: any building, sale or rental; notice on at least one document signed at or before the contract or rental agreement (s. 404.056(5); V-73).
  • CERCLA: strict, joint and several; an owner can be liable without causing the contamination; innocent-landowner defense requires due diligence before purchase (Phase I environmental audit) (manual; not yet verified).
  • Asbestos: pre-1980s insulation; dangerous when friable; encapsulation often safer than removal (manual; not yet verified).

Understand

  • 1978 (lead) versus 1988 (fair housing: familial status and handicap, V-56).
  • Lead and CERCLA are federal; the radon notice is Florida law.
  • Brownfields, wetlands permitting, EIS for major federal actions, USTs near gas stations (manual; not yet verified).
  • The licensee puts the right forms in the file and refers technical and legal questions to inspectors, environmental consultants or attorneys.

8. Visual explanation

Does the lead-based paint rule apply?

Was the housing built before 1978?
No → no lead disclosure (the radon notice still applies)
Is it target housing? (Excluded: housing for the elderly or persons with disabilities and 0-bedroom dwellings, unless a child under 6 lives or is expected to live there.)
No → excluded
Is the transaction covered? (Exempt: foreclosure sale; lease of 100 days or less with no renewal; lease of housing certified lead-free; renewal where disclosure was already made.)
No → exempt
Is it a sale?
No, a lease → pamphlet, disclosure, available reports, Lead Warning Statement; no 10-day period
Sale → all disclosures + the buyer's 10-day inspection opportunity (different period agreed in writing, or waived in writing)

Lead-based paint, 40 CFR 745 Subpart F (V-60, confirmed). Radon (Florida, V-73) applies to the sale or rental of any building, whatever the answer here.

9. Common misconceptions

  • "The lead-paint year is 1988." No: 1978. 1988 is when fair housing added familial status and handicap (V-56).
  • "Tenants also get 10 days to inspect." No. Tenants get the pamphlet, the disclosure, available reports and the Lead Warning Statement, but no 10-day period (V-60).
  • "The seller can disclose after accepting the offer." No. A disclosure that follows an offer must come before acceptance (V-60).
  • "The radon notice is only for older homes, or only when radon is found, or only for sales." It is for the sale or rental of any building (V-73).
  • "A new owner who did not cause the contamination cannot be liable." Under CERCLA she can be, unless she qualifies for a defense such as innocent landowner (manual; not yet verified).
  • "Asbestos must always be removed at once." Intact, non-friable asbestos is often better encapsulated (manual; not yet verified).

10. Memory sheet

  • 1978 = lead paint (not 1988, fair housing). Sales and leases: pamphlet + known hazards + available reports + Lead Warning Statement. Buyers 10 days (waive or change in writing); tenants: no 10 days. After an offer → before acceptance. Agents ensure compliance (V-60).
  • Lead exempt: foreclosure sale; lease of 100 days or less, no renewal; certified lead-free lease; renewal. Excluded: elderly/disabled housing and 0-bedroom units, unless a child under 6.
  • Radon: any building, every sale and every rental; notice at or before the contract (V-73).
  • CERCLA = owner liable without fault; strict, joint and several; innocent landowner needs a Phase I before buying (manual; not yet verified).
  • Asbestos: friable = danger; encapsulate. Brownfield = contaminated site redeveloped. UST = gas station tanks. EIS = major federal action. Wetlands = permitting (manual; not yet verified).

objectives.text: Explain the difference between federal law, Florida statutes, Florida administrative rules, and court decisions, and give one real estate example of each.
Name Chapter 475 F.S., Chapter 455 F.S., and Rule Chapter 61J2 F.A.C. and say what each governs.
Describe in one sentence each what the FREC, the DBPR and the courts do in real estate regulation.
Identify which source of law answers a given exam question (federal, Florida statute, FREC rule, case law).
List the five categories of real property use (residential, commercial, industrial, agricultural, special-purpose) and classify examples.
Describe the main real estate specializations (brokerage, appraisal, property management, financing, development/construction, counseling).
Explain that REALTOR® is a trademark of NAR membership, not a license, and distinguish it from the state license.
State the three elements that require a license: a real estate service, for another, for compensation.
List the real estate services named in Chapter 475 (A BAR SALE and related acts).
Decide whether a person in a scenario needs a license, paying attention to how they are paid.
List the statutory exemptions in s. 475.011.
Recognize when a change in compensation or role removes an exemption (salary vs per-transaction pay; attorney earning a commission).
State the applicant requirements (age 18, high school diploma or equivalent, SSN) and what is NOT required (citizenship, Florida residency).
State the 63-hour course, its 2-year validity for taking the exam, and the 75/100 passing score.
Explain how criminal history and false applications are treated, and what happens after a denial.
Apply the mutual recognition rules (nonresident at application, 40-question law exam, 30 to pass).
State FREC composition: 7 members, Governor + Senate, 4 brokers (5 yrs), 1 broker or sales associate (2 yrs), 2 consumer members, one member 60+, 4-year terms.
Distinguish quasi-legislative, quasi-judicial and executive/administrative powers, and which body exercises each.
Answer 'which body does X' questions: DBPR investigates; FREC disciplines; courts imprison and award damages.
Distinguish sales associate, broker and broker associate, and what only a broker may do.
Distinguish licensure from registration, and group licenses from multiple licenses.
State the broker path: 24 months active in the preceding 5 years, 72-hour course, broker exam, 60 hours post-license.
State the 45-hour post-license requirement and the consequence of missing it (license null and void).
State the 14-hour CE requirement per 2-year renewal (3 Core Law + 3 Ethics + 8 specialty) and the consequence of missing renewal (involuntary inactive).
State the reactivation rules: ≤12 months 14 hours; 12–24 months 28-hour course; >24 months void.
Distinguish active, voluntary inactive, involuntary inactive, suspended, revoked, null and void, and ineffective.
State the 10-day address-change notice and the 30-day duty to report a conviction or plea (including nolo contendere).
Recognize that a sales associate cannot perform services between brokers until the change is registered.
State that a sales associate may hold only one license and work for one employer at a time.
Name the three authorized relationships and state that transaction broker is presumed unless another is established in writing.
Explain why dual agency is illegal in Florida and the lawful alternative for working both sides.
Distinguish a principal (single agent) from a customer (transaction broker / no relationship).
List the 3 duties owed with no brokerage relationship.
List the 7 transaction-broker duties, including what limited confidentiality protects.
List the 9 single-agent duties and the four that belong only to the single agent (loyalty, obedience, full confidentiality, full disclosure).
Match a described duty to the relationship that owes it.
State when the Single Agent Notice and the No Brokerage Relationship Notice must be given; transaction broker needs no notice.
Explain the Consent to Transition to Transaction Broker and when it is used.
Define 'residential sale' (≤4 units; unimproved for ≤4 units; agricultural ≤10 acres).
Identify situations where disclosure is not required (represented party, open house, casual encounter, general questions, auctions, appraisals, leases without option, business sales).
Decide whether a fact must be disclosed (latent material defect vs stigma such as death or HIV status).
State the designated sales associate conditions: nonresidential, buyer and seller each with assets of $1 million or more, written request/disclosures.
List how brokerage relationships end and which duties survive termination.
State where escrow may be held and the interest-bearing account consent rule.
Compute the sales associate's and broker's deposit deadlines (next business day; end of third business day) from a receipt date.
State the broker's personal-funds limits ($1,000 sales; $5,000 property management) and define commingling and conversion.
State the 15-business-day notice and 30-business-day procedure deadlines, and the 90-day mediation limit.
Name the four settlement procedures and when an EDO is available.
Recognize the statutory exceptions (condo buyer cancellation; good-faith financing failure).
State that every advertisement must include the registered brokerage name; define a blind ad.
Decide whether an ad (sign, social media, website, team ad) complies.
State the office and entrance-sign requirements ('Licensed Real Estate Broker').
Decide whether a payment is lawful (unlicensed assistant, gift from customer, rebate to a party, referral between licensees).
State the rental-list refund rules (75% if no rental, full if inaccurate, demand within 30 days).
Explain why commission rates must be negotiated individually (antitrust/price fixing).
Put the steps in order: complaint → investigation → probable cause → formal complaint → hearing → final order → appeal.
Distinguish informal and formal hearings and who presides.
State the 30-day appeal window to the District Court of Appeal.
State the administrative penalties and limits ($5,000 per violation; suspension up to 10 years; revocation).
State the criminal classifications (unlicensed practice: third-degree felony).
Distinguish fraud, misrepresentation, concealment, false promises, culpable negligence and breach of trust.
State the 5-year record-keeping rule.
State the caps ($50,000 per transaction; $150,000 per licensee) and what is not paid.
Decide who may and may not recover from the Fund.
State the consequence for the licensee (automatic suspension until repaid with interest).
State the protected classes and when each was added (1866 race; 1968; sex 1974; familial status and handicap 1988).
Define blockbusting, steering and redlining and other prohibited practices.
Apply the exemptions and when they are lost (broker used, discriminatory ad; never for race).
Distinguish reasonable modifications from reasonable accommodations.
Match ADA, ECOA, HMDA and fair housing to their subject (public accommodation, credit, lending data, housing).
State the Do Not Call established-business-relationship windows (18 months after a transaction, 3 months after an inquiry; the FTC rule now says 540 / 90 days).
State the CAN-SPAM opt-out rule (honored within 10 business days).
State RESPA's scope (federally related loans, 1–4 residential units) and its kickback prohibition.
State TRID timing: Loan Estimate within 3 business days of application; Closing Disclosure at least 3 business days before closing.
Identify TILA advertising trigger terms and the 3-business-day right of rescission (refinance/home equity on principal residence, not purchase loans).
State how security deposits may be held and the 30-day notice of how they are held.
State the move-out timeline: 15 days to return, 30 days to send a claim by certified mail (or e-mail with a signed addendum), 15 days for the tenant to object.
State the termination notices for tenancies without a specific term: 60 / 30 / 30 / 7 days (current law).
State the landlord's flood disclosure duty for residential leases of 1 year or longer (s. 83.512, since October 2025).
Name the rights in the bundle (possession, control, enjoyment, exclusion, disposition).
Distinguish fee simple absolute, fee simple defeasible and life estates.
Explain the life tenant's rights and duties (waste) and distinguish remainder from reversion.
Distinguish estate for years, periodic tenancy, tenancy at will and tenancy at sufferance.
Distinguish gross, net, percentage, ground, graduated and index leases.
Decide whether a transfer is an assignment or a sublease and who remains liable.
State Florida's defaults: unmarried co-owners with a silent deed = tenancy in common; married couple = tenancy by the entireties.
State the four unities (PITT) and the express survivorship language Florida requires for joint tenancy.
Determine who owns a property after a co-owner dies.
State the size limits (1/2 acre within a municipality; 160 contiguous acres outside).
List the claims that can still reach a homestead (taxes and assessments, purchase or improvement debt, construction liens; federal liens).
Explain the spouse/minor-child protections (spouse joins in deeds and mortgages; devise restrictions).
Distinguish condominium (real property, unit + undivided share) from cooperative (shares + proprietary lease = personal property).
State the cancellation periods: developer condo 15 days; resale condo 7 days excluding weekends and holidays (since July 2025; older texts 3 business days); timeshare 10 days.
State that an HOA disclosure summary must be given before contract, and the buyer's 3-day voiding right if it was not.
Distinguish voluntary transfer (deed, will) from involuntary transfer (descent, escheat, eminent domain, foreclosure, adverse possession).
State Florida adverse possession: 7 years, open, notorious, hostile, continuous, plus color of title or payment of taxes.
Distinguish testate and intestate, devise and descent.
Rank deeds by protection (general warranty, special warranty, bargain and sale, quitclaim) and state what each warrants.
List the requirements of a valid Florida deed, including two witnesses and delivery/acceptance.
Identify what is NOT required for validity (grantee signature, recording, acknowledgment).
Distinguish constructive and actual notice and explain why recording matters.
Compare abstract with attorney's opinion vs title insurance; owner's vs lender's policy.
Distinguish specific and general liens, and state lien priority (taxes and special assessments first, then recording order).
Distinguish easement appurtenant, in gross, by necessity and by prescription (20 years), and a license.
Define encroachment and deed restriction.
Apply the fixture tests (intent, method of annexation, adaptation, relationship) and the trade-fixture rule.
Distinguish riparian and littoral rights, and accretion, erosion and avulsion.
Describe metes and bounds (POB, courses and distances), lot and block (recorded plat) and the government survey.
State that Florida's principal meridian and base line intersect in Tallahassee; a street address is not a legal description.
State township and section facts: 6 × 6 miles, 36 sections, 640 acres per section, section 1 in the northeast corner, serpentine numbering.
Compute the acreage of an aliquot-part description, including 'and' descriptions.
Convert between square feet, acres, square miles, feet and miles (43,560 sq ft; 5,280 ft).
List the essential elements of a valid contract (competent parties, offer and acceptance, legal purpose, consideration).
Distinguish bilateral/unilateral, executory/executed, express/implied; and void/voidable/unenforceable.
State the statute of frauds and the statute of limitations (5 years written, 4 years oral).
Trace whether a contract exists after offers, revocations, counteroffers and rejections.
Explain option contracts (optionor/optionee) and equitable title.
Distinguish the remedies for breach (specific performance, liquidated damages, rescission, compensatory damages).
Distinguish open, exclusive agency, exclusive right of sale and net listings and when commission is earned.
State the Florida written-listing rules: definite expiration date, no automatic renewal, copy to the seller within 24 hours.
State how listings terminate.
Explain the 'AS IS' contract, the effective date and 'time is of the essence'.
List the required disclosures: radon, lead-based paint (pre-1978), property-tax disclosure, energy-efficiency brochure, flood disclosure (s. 689.302), condo/HOA documents.
Apply Johnson v. Davis: known latent defects must be disclosed even in an AS IS sale.
Distinguish the promissory note from the mortgage; mortgagor from mortgagee.
State that Florida is a lien-theory state and the 60-day satisfaction rule.
Define the common clauses (acceleration, due-on-sale, prepayment, defeasance, subordination, release, exculpatory).
Distinguish assumption (with or without novation) from taking 'subject to' a mortgage.
State that Florida foreclosure is judicial, equity of redemption ends at the sale, and there is no statutory redemption.
Compare short sale and deed in lieu of foreclosure (junior liens survive a deed in lieu).
Compute housing-expense and total-obligation ratios using gross monthly income and PITI.
State the usual benchmarks (conventional 28/36; FHA 31/43) as course conventions.
State Florida usury limits (18% simple on loans of $500,000 or less; 25% above) and name predatory practices.
State that FHA insures, VA guarantees, and neither lends; private lenders lend.
State FHA's MIP and 3.5% minimum down payment, VA's funding fee and CRV, and PMI above 80% LTV.
Distinguish amortized, partially amortized (balloon), interest-only and adjustable-rate loans (index + margin, caps).
Distinguish package, blanket, wraparound, purchase-money, home equity, reverse and construction loans.
Sort lenders and agencies into primary vs secondary market (Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, Ginnie Mae).
Name the Fed's tools and their effect on credit.
Compute the cost of points (1 point = 1% of the loan) and the approximate yield effect (1/8% per point, course rule of thumb).
Convert between fractions, decimals and percentages without errors in decimal placement.
Solve Part = Total × Rate for any one unknown.
Compute percentage change using the original value as the base.
Compute area of rectangles, triangles and composite shapes in square feet.
Convert square feet ↔ square yards ↔ acres and feet ↔ yards ↔ miles; compute price per front foot.
Compute total commission and each party's share through a chain of splits.
Compute the sale price needed to net the seller a target amount: Price = Net ÷ (1 − rate).
Compute profit or loss percentage on cost.
Recover the original cost from a sale price and a profit or loss percentage (divide, do not multiply).
Compute simple interest (I = P × R × T) and the interest/principal split of a monthly payment.
Compute LTV using the lesser of price or appraised value, and the down payment.
Compute the cost of discount points.
Compute deed stamps ($0.70 per $100 or portion, on the full price; Miami-Dade single-family $0.60).
Compute note stamps ($0.35 per $100 or portion) on new and assumed mortgages (course convention).
Compute intangible tax (0.002 × new mortgage only).
State who customarily pays each tax.
Prorate an annual expense with the 365-day method, the buyer owning the day of closing.
Decide which party is debited and credited for items paid in arrears vs in advance.
Prorate rent and mortgage interest.
Place each closing item as debit/credit for buyer and/or seller (single vs double entry).
Compute the cash due from the buyer and to the seller.
Explain why real estate markets are local and slow to adjust; name the supply and demand factors.
Distinguish a CMA, a BPO and an appraisal, and what a licensee may charge for.
State the four elements of value (DUST) and distinguish market value, price, cost, assessed and insurable value.
Explain substitution, highest and best use, anticipation, contribution, conformity, progression/regression and plottage/assemblage.
Adjust comparables (never the subject): comparable better → subtract; inferior → add.
Explain which comparable deserves the most weight.
Compute value = land + cost new − accrued depreciation.
Distinguish reproduction from replacement cost and the three types of depreciation (external obsolescence always incurable).
Build NOI (PGI − vacancy & collection loss − operating expenses) and apply IRV.
Apply GRM (monthly) and GIM (annual).
Explain reconciliation and the federally related transaction rule (licensed/certified appraiser).
Explain leverage, liquidity and the types of risk.
Compute cash flow (NOI − debt service) and cap rate.
Explain what a business brokerage transaction includes (going concern, goodwill, fixtures, inventory) and when a real estate license is needed.
State the January 1 assessment date, TRIM notice in August, VAB appeals, November bills with 4%→1% discounts, April 1 delinquency.
Explain ad valorem taxes vs special assessments and the role of tax certificates.
State the homestead exemptions ($25,000 all taxes + up to $25,000 CPI-indexed non-school above $50,000) and the $5,000 widow/blind/disabled exemption.
State the Save Our Homes cap (3% or CPI, whichever is less; portable).
Compute a tax bill with separate school and non-school taxable values (1 mill = $1 per $1,000).
State depreciation periods (27.5 residential rental; 39 nonresidential; land never).
Distinguish a 1031 exchange (investment property, boot taxable) from the principal-residence exclusion ($250,000/$500,000; 2 of 5 years).
Explain basis, adjusted basis, capital gain and installment sales.
Distinguish police power from eminent domain (just compensation; inverse condemnation).
Distinguish variance, special exception, nonconforming use and rezoning; describe a PUD.
Explain comprehensive plans, building permits and certificates of occupancy.
State the lead-based paint rules (pre-1978, pamphlet, 10-day inspection right) and the Florida radon disclosure.
Explain CERCLA liability, asbestos, brownfields, wetlands and underground storage tanks.

questions.q: Which source contains Florida's real estate license law?
questions.ex: Chapter 475 F.S. is the real estate license law passed by the Legislature. Chapter 455 covers all DBPR professions generally; 61J2 contains FREC's rules made under Chapter 475.

1: Chapter 455 is the general law for all DBPR-regulated professions, not the real estate license law.
2: 61J2 is FREC's administrative rule chapter, adopted under the authority of Chapter 475.
3: The Fair Housing Act is federal anti-discrimination law.

questions.q: The rule that a broker must deposit escrow funds by the end of the third business day is found in a rule adopted by the FREC. What kind of law is this?
questions.ex: Rules adopted by an agency (here the FREC, in Chapter 61J2 F.A.C.) are administrative rules. They carry the force of law but must stay within the statute that authorizes them.

0: Escrow deadlines for Florida brokers are state rules, not federal statutes.
2: Court decisions interpret law; they do not set escrow deadlines.
3: The Florida Constitution does not contain escrow rules.

questions.q: A licensee is accused of stealing escrow money. Which of the following can impose a prison sentence?
questions.ex: Only a court can impose criminal penalties such as imprisonment. The FREC imposes administrative discipline (fines, suspension, revocation); the DBPR investigates.

0: The FREC disciplines the license but cannot imprison anyone.
1: The DBPR investigates and administers; it cannot imprison.
3: The probable cause panel only decides whether to file a formal complaint.

questions.q: In Florida, a seller who knows of a hidden defect that materially affects the value of a home must disclose it to the buyer. The original source of this duty is:
c: Rule Chapter 61J2 of the Florida Administrative Code
A Florida Supreme Court decision, Johnson v. Davis
The federal Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act
The Florida Realtors/Florida Bar contract form
questions.ex: Johnson v. Davis (Fla. 1985) created the seller's duty to disclose known latent defects materially affecting value. It is case law. The contract forms reflect it but did not create it.

0: 61J2 regulates licensees' conduct; the seller's disclosure duty comes from case law.
2: RESPA governs settlement procedures and kickbacks for federally related loans.
3: Contract forms reflect the duty; a disclosure duty exists even without a form.

questions.q: Which statement about the term REALTOR® is correct?
c: It is the official title on a Florida sales associate license
It identifies a member of the National Association of REALTORS®
Every Florida broker must use it
It is issued by the FREC after the broker exam
questions.ex: REALTOR® is a trademark identifying NAR members who subscribe to its Code of Ethics. Florida licenses are 'sales associate' and 'broker'.

0: The license title is 'sales associate'; REALTOR® is a trade-association membership mark.
3: The FREC issues nothing related to the trademark.

questions.q: A church, a school and a hospital are best classified as which category of property?
questions.ex: Properties with a unique, limited use such as churches, schools and hospitals are special-purpose properties.

3: Mixed-use combines residential and commercial uses.

questions.q: A licensee who leases units, collects rents and arranges maintenance for an owner is working in which specialty?
questions.ex: Property management covers leasing, rent collection and maintenance on behalf of owners.

3: Counseling is giving real estate advice for a fee.

questions.q: A Florida real estate license is required when a person performs a real estate service:
c: for compensation, even on their own property
for another, even without any compensation
only if the person advertises to the public
questions.ex: All three elements are needed: a real estate service, for another, for compensation (paid, promised or expected). Remove any one and no license is needed.

0: Owners dealing with their own property are exempt.
2: Without compensation (or the expectation of it) no license is required.
3: Advertising is one service, but the test is service + for another + compensation.

questions.q: Marco, unlicensed, finds a buyer for his neighbour's house. The neighbour promises Marco a used car 'if the deal closes'. The deal closes and Marco receives the car. Which is correct?
c: No license was needed, because compensation means a payment of money
No license was needed, because a single favour for a neighbour is exempt
Marco violated the law by performing a real estate service for compensation
Only the neighbour violated the law, by paying an unlicensed person
questions.ex: Compensation means anything of value, including a car. Marco found a buyer (a real estate service) for another for compensation. One-time activity is not an exemption.

0: Compensation includes anything of value, not just money.
1: There is no 'one-time favour' exemption when compensation is paid.
3: Marco is the one who performed services without a license.

questions.q: Which activity is a real estate service under Chapter 475?
c: Painting a house before it is listed
Leasing a property for another for a fee
Inspecting a roof for a buyer
Lending money secured by a mortgage
questions.ex: Leasing for another for compensation is a listed service (A BAR SALE: Advertise, Buy, Appraise, Rent, Sell, Auction, Lease, Exchange).

0: Painting is construction work, not a brokerage service.
2: Home inspection is a separate licensed profession.

questions.q: A builder pays Sofia a fixed salary to sell homes in its subdivision. The builder then changes her pay to $1,000 for each home that closes. What is the effect?
c: She remains exempt because she works for the owner
She now needs a real estate license
She needs a license only if she sells more than 10 homes a year
She may continue if the builder holds a broker license
questions.ex: Salaried employees of an owner can be exempt, but commissions or per-transaction pay remove the exemption. Paid per closing, she is performing services for compensation tied to transactions and needs a license.

0: The owner's-employee exemption depends on salary, not commission.
3: Even working for a broker, she would need her own license.

questions.q: Which person is exempt from real estate licensure under s. 475.011?
c: A property manager paid 8% of collected rents to manage homes for several different owners
A salaried employee of the owner who leases units from the apartment community's onsite office
An unlicensed assistant whom the broker pays $200 for each showing she conducts for buyers
A friend of the broker who receives a referral fee each time she sends a buyer to the brokerage
questions.ex: s. 475.011 exempts salaried employees of an owner (or of a broker for an owner) of an apartment community working in an onsite rental office in a leasing capacity.

0: Managing property for several owners for a percentage of rents requires a license.
2: Per-showing pay for real estate services requires a license.
3: Paying an unlicensed person for referrals of real estate business is not allowed.

questions.q: An attorney at law handles a client's closing and also negotiates the sale of the client's property, charging a 3% commission on the price. Which is correct?
c: Exempt, because attorneys at law are always exempt from Chapter 475
Exempt, because the commission was earned while handling the closing
Not exempt: earning a brokerage commission requires a real estate license
Exempt, as long as the attorney is a member in good standing of The Florida Bar
questions.ex: Attorneys are exempt when acting within their legal duties. Charging a commission for brokerage services takes the attorney outside that exemption.

0: The exemption covers legal services, not brokerage for a commission.
1: Handling the closing does not cover earning a sales commission.
3: Bar membership is what makes them a lawyer; it does not authorize brokerage commissions.

questions.q: Under s. 475.011, an attorney in fact (holding a power of attorney) is exempt when:
c: acting only to execute contracts or conveyances for the owner
selling the owner's properties in exchange for a commission
advertising and negotiating the sale of the owner's property for a fee
managing the owner's rentals for a percentage of the rents collected
questions.ex: The statute exempts attorneys in fact acting to execute contracts or conveyances only. Brokerage activity for compensation is not covered.

1: Earning commissions is brokerage, not signing on the owner's behalf.
2: Advertising for several owners for pay is a real estate service.
3: Property management for a percentage requires a license.

questions.q: Which is NOT a requirement to apply for a Florida sales associate license?
c: A high school diploma or its equivalent
questions.ex: Florida residency and U.S. citizenship are not required. Applicants must be 18+, have a high school diploma or equivalent, and a Social Security number.

1: A diploma or equivalent is required.
2: A Social Security number is required.

questions.q: A student completed the 63-hour pre-license course 26 months ago and has not taken the state exam. What is the status of the course for exam purposes?
c: Still valid — course completion never expires for exam purposes
Expired — it is valid for 2 years for purposes of the state exam
Still valid — course completion is valid for 3 years for the exam
Still valid — it remains valid until the student takes the exam
questions.ex: s. 475.181(2): the course completion becomes invalid if the state exam is not passed within 2 years after completing the course. At 26 months without a pass it has expired.

0: Course completion is valid for 2 years.
3: It expires after 2 years unless the exam has been passed; taking it is not enough.

questions.q: An applicant with a 7-year-old misdemeanor conviction answers 'No' to the criminal-history question. Which is the most accurate consequence?
c: No consequence, because misdemeanors older than five years need not be disclosed
The false answer is itself grounds for denial or revocation and may be a crime
No consequence, because the FREC cannot consider any record older than 5 years
No consequence, because only felony convictions must be disclosed on applications
questions.ex: Criminal history must be disclosed. An old record does not automatically disqualify, but a false answer on the application is grounds for denial or revocation and is itself a crime.

0: Criminal history, including misdemeanors, must be disclosed.
2: There is no 5-year rule; the FREC weighs the record and the applicant's honesty.
3: Misdemeanors can also be considered; honesty is the issue.

questions.q: Lucas holds an active license in a state with a Florida mutual recognition agreement. He moved to Orlando last year and now wants a Florida license through mutual recognition. Which is correct?
c: He may use mutual recognition and must pass a 40-question law exam
He cannot use mutual recognition because he is a Florida resident when applying
He must take only the 63-hour course
He may practice in Florida immediately under his home-state license
questions.ex: Mutual recognition is only for applicants who are NOT Florida residents at the time of application. As a resident, Lucas must follow the normal path (63-hour course and state exam).

0: The 40-question exam path is only for nonresidents.
2: Residents must complete the course AND pass the state exam.
3: No out-of-state license authorizes practice in Florida.

questions.q: A nonresident licensee applying under mutual recognition must pass a Florida law exam of:
questions.ex: The mutual recognition exam is 40 questions on Florida law; 30 correct (75%) passes.

0: 100/75 is the full sales associate exam.
2: It is 40 questions with 30 to pass.

questions.q: How many members of the FREC must be licensed brokers who have held active licenses for the preceding 5 years?
questions.ex: Four members must be brokers active for the 5 preceding years; one is a broker or sales associate active for 2 years; two are consumer members who have never been licensed.

0: 2 is the number of consumer members.
3: 5 is the years of experience, not the number of members.

questions.q: Which statement about FREC membership is correct?
c: Members are elected by Florida licensees at the annual meeting, for 2-year terms
Members are appointed by the Governor, confirmed by the Senate, for 4-year terms
Members are appointed by the DBPR Secretary and serve until they choose to resign
Members are appointed by the Governor, and all seven must be licensed brokers
questions.ex: The Governor appoints FREC members, subject to Senate confirmation, for 4-year terms. Two members are consumers who have never held a license.

0: Members are appointed, not elected, and terms are 4 years.
2: The Governor appoints; terms are 4 years.
3: Two members must never have been licensed.

questions.q: When the FREC adopts a rule setting advertising requirements, it is exercising which power?
questions.ex: Rule-making is quasi-legislative. Deciding discipline cases is quasi-judicial.

0: Quasi-judicial is deciding cases and imposing discipline.
2: Executive/administrative functions (licensing, records) are mostly DBPR's.
3: Prosecution is done by DBPR attorneys (discipline) or state attorneys (crimes); adopting rules is not prosecution.

questions.q: A buyer files a complaint against a sales associate. Which body investigates it?
questions.ex: The DBPR receives and investigates complaints. The FREC (through a probable cause panel and final orders) decides discipline.

0: The FREC decides discipline; it does not investigate.

questions.q: A person holds a broker license but works under another broker's supervision. This person is a:
questions.ex: A broker associate holds a broker license but operates as an associate under another broker.

0: A sales associate holds a sales associate license.
2: Transaction broker is a brokerage relationship, not a license type.
3: Designated sales associate is a role in certain nonresidential deals.

questions.q: To qualify for a broker license, a sales associate must have held an active license for at least:
questions.ex: 24 months of active sales associate licensure during the preceding 5 years, then the 72-hour broker course and broker exam.

questions.q: Which person may hold multiple licenses?
c: A sales associate working for two unrelated brokers
A broker who is a broker for two unconnected brokerages
A broker associate working for two brokers
A sales associate under a group license
questions.ex: Only a broker may hold multiple licenses (for separate, unconnected brokerages). A sales associate can work for one employer at a time; a group license covers connected entities of one owner-developer.

0: A sales associate may work for only one employer at a time.
2: An associate works under one employer.
3: A group license is one license covering connected entities.

questions.q: A sales associate fails to complete post-license education before the first renewal. The license:
questions.ex: Missing the 45-hour post-license requirement makes the license null and void. Missing CE at a later renewal makes it involuntarily inactive.

0: Involuntary inactive is the result of missing a later renewal/CE.
3: The license does not remain active.

questions.q: After the first renewal, a sales associate must complete how many hours of continuing education each renewal period?
questions.ex: 14 hours of CE every 2-year renewal period after the first: 3 hours Core Law, 3 hours Ethics and Business Practices, 8 hours specialty.

1: 28 hours is the reactivation course after more than 12 months of involuntary inactivity.

questions.q: Rita's license has been involuntarily inactive for 18 months. What must she do to reactivate it?
c: Nothing yet; she may simply pay the renewal fee within 2 years
Complete the regular 14 hours of commission-prescribed CE
Retake the 63-hour pre-license course and pass the state exam
questions.ex: More than 12 but fewer than 24 months involuntarily inactive: 28-hour reactivation course. 12 months or less: 14 hours. More than 24 months: the license expires.

0: She must complete education to reactivate.
1: 14 hours applies only if inactive 12 months or less.
3: Requalifying is required only after the license expires (more than 2 years).

questions.q: Which license status can be renewed indefinitely without the holder working for a broker?
questions.ex: A licensee may choose voluntary inactive status and keep renewing it (with CE) indefinitely. Involuntary inactive expires after 2 years.

2: Suspension is discipline for a set time.
3: A void license no longer exists.

questions.q: A sales associate let her license lapse (involuntary inactive) 26 months ago. What is her status?
c: Null and void; she must requalify
Active once she pays the fee
questions.ex: Involuntary inactive status lasts at most 2 years. After 26 months the license has expired (null and void).

0: The 28-hour course applies only between 12 and 24 months.
1: She did not choose voluntary status.
3: Paying a fee cannot revive an expired license.

questions.q: A licensee changes her mailing address. Within how many days must she notify the DBPR?
questions.ex: Address changes must be reported within 10 days. Convictions and pleas must be reported within 30 days.

3: 30 days is the deadline for reporting a conviction or plea.

questions.q: A sales associate pleads nolo contendere to a misdemeanor and adjudication is withheld. What must she do?
c: Nothing, because she was not convicted
Report it at her next renewal
questions.ex: Licensees must report a conviction, a guilty plea, or a plea of nolo contendere within 30 days, whether or not adjudication is withheld.

0: A nolo plea must be reported even without a conviction.

questions.q: Tom's employing broker closes the office. While looking for a new broker, Tom keeps showing his clients' listings. Which is correct?
c: Lawful, because his license remains current and active until it expires
Lawful for up to 30 days while he registers with a new employing broker
Unlawful: his license is ineffective until registered with a new employer
Lawful, as long as each client consents in writing to his continued help
questions.ex: A sales associate may act only under a registered employer. When employment ends, the license cannot be used until the new employer's registration is filed.

0: A current license is not enough; it must be registered with an employer.
3: Client consent cannot authorize unlicensed activity.
