verification.citation: 12 CFR 1026.24(d)(1)-(2), Regulation Z (eCFR current text, 2026), and Supplement I comment 24(d)(1)
verification.teach: Triggers: down payment amount or percentage, number of payments or repayment period, payment amount, finance charge amount. Using one requires the down payment, repayment terms and APR. The APR alone, 'no down payment' and 'no closing costs' are not triggers.

verification.manual: RESPA applies to federally related mortgage loans on 1-4 family residential property; Section 8 prohibits kickbacks and unearned fees; Section 9 bars sellers from requiring a particular title insurer [12 USC 2602, 2607, 2608; 12 CFR 1024]
verification.finding: Scope: under 12 USC 2602(1), a 'federally related mortgage loan' is a loan, other than temporary financing such as a construction loan, that is secured by a first or subordinate lien on residential real property designed principally for one to four families, including condominium and cooperative units. The loan must also have a federal connection, for example a federally insured or regulated lender, a federally related program, or intended sale to Fannie Mae, Ginnie Mae or Freddie Mac. Regulation X (12 CFR 1024.2) adds that a loan secured by property outside a State is not covered. Section 8, 12 USC 2607: (a) no person may give or accept any fee, kickback or thing of value under an agreement to refer settlement-service business; (b) no person may give or accept any portion, split or percentage of a settlement-service charge other than for services actually performed. Under 12 CFR 1024.14, a charge for no or nominal services, or a duplicative fee, is an unearned fee. Freeman v. Quicken Loans (2012) limits 2607(b) to fees split between two or more persons. Section 9, 12 USC 2608(a): a seller of property bought with a federally related mortgage loan may not require, directly or indirectly as a condition of sale, that the buyer purchase title insurance from a particular title company. Under 2608(b), a violating seller owes the buyer 3 times all title insurance charges. 12 CFR 1024.16 restates this rule.
verification.citation: 12 USC 2602(1), 2607(a)-(b), 2608(a)-(b) (U.S. Code, 2023 edition, govinfo); 12 CFR 1024.2, 1024.14, 1024.16 (Regulation X, current)
verification.teach: Federally related mortgage loans on 1–4 family residential property. Section 8: no kickbacks or unearned fees for referrals. Section 9: a seller may not require the buyer to use a particular title insurer (liable for 3 times the title charges).

verification.manual: Fair Housing Act exemptions: owner of no more than 3 single-family houses selling/renting without a broker and without discriminatory ads (one sale per 24 months if not the occupant); owner-occupied dwellings of no more than 4 units; religious organizations; private clubs [42 USC 3603(b), 3607]
verification.finding: 3603(b)(1): section 3604 does not apply to a single-family house sold or rented by a private owner, but only if four conditions are met. (1) The owner does not own more than three such houses at one time, and does not own an interest in or receive proceeds from more than three at once. (2) An owner who was not living in the house, or was not its most recent occupant, gets the exemption for only one such sale in any 24-month period. (3) No broker, agent or salesperson, and no person in the business of selling or renting dwellings, is used. (4) No advertising that violates 3604(c) is published. Under 3603(c), a person is 'in the business' if, in the preceding 12 months, they acted as principal in 3 or more dwelling transactions or as agent in 2 or more. 3603(b)(2): rooms or units in a dwelling with living quarters for no more than four families living independently are exempt if the owner actually lives in one of them. 3607(a): a religious organization, or a nonprofit it operates, supervises or controls, may limit sale, rental or occupancy of dwellings it owns or operates for a noncommercial purpose to members of the same religion, or give them preference, unless membership in the religion is restricted by race, color or national origin. A private club not in fact open to the public may limit lodgings it provides as an incidental, noncommercial part of its purpose to its members, or give them preference. 24 CFR Part 100 repeats both exemptions.
verification.citation: 42 USC 3603(b)-(c) and 3607(a) (U.S. Code, 2023/2024 editions, govinfo)
verification.teach: Private owner of no more than 3 single-family homes, no broker, no discriminatory ads (one sale per 24 months if not the occupant); owner-occupied building with no more than 4 units; religious organizations; private clubs (members, non-commercial lodging).

verification.manual: Housing for older persons: 55+ with at least 80% of occupied units having at least one person 55+; or 62+ for all occupants [42 USC 3607(b); 24 CFR 100.304-305]
verification.finding: The familial status protections do not apply to 'housing for older persons'. 42 USC 3607(b)(2) defines that housing three ways: (A) housing provided under a qualifying state or federal elderly program; (B) housing intended for, and solely occupied by, persons 62 or older; (C) housing intended and operated for persons 55 or older. Under (C), at least 80% of occupied units must have at least one person 55 or older, and the facility must publish and follow policies showing that intent and comply with HUD's age-verification rules. The Housing for Older Persons Act of 1995 (Pub. L. 104-76) added the 80% test, which replaced the old 'one person 55+ per unit' wording. HUD rules are as follows. 24 CFR 100.303: 62+ housing must be solely occupied by persons 62 or older; exceptions cover residents who were under 62 on Sept. 13, 1988 (if all new occupants are 62+) and vacant units reserved for persons 62+. 24 CFR 100.304-305: the 80% is measured on occupied units only; a temporarily vacant unit counts as occupied if the primary occupant lived there in the past year and intends to return; fractions round up; new construction need not comply until 25% of units are occupied; HUD says the other 20% need not be occupied by people under 55. 24 CFR 100.306-307 require published policies and verification by reliable surveys and affidavits.
verification.citation: 42 USC 3607(b)(1)-(2) (U.S. Code, 2023 edition); 24 CFR 100.303-100.307 (CFR 2025 edition / eCFR current)
verification.teach: 62+: all occupants 62 or older. 55+: at least 80% of occupied units have at least one person 55 or older, with published policies and age verification.

verification.topic: Fair housing protected classes by year (42 USC 3604)
verification.manual: Sex added to the Fair Housing Act in 1974; familial status and handicap added in 1988 [HUD / 42 USC 3604 history]
verification.finding: The U.S. Code amendment notes to 42 USC 3604 say Pub. L. 93-383, the Housing and Community Development Act of 1974 (section 808), inserted ', sex' after 'religion' throughout 3604(a)-(e). The Fair Housing Amendments Act of 1988 (Pub. L. 100-430, enacted Sept. 13, 1988, effective 180 days later) did three things. It added 'familial status' to 3604(a)-(b). It added 'handicap, familial status' to 3604(c)-(e). It added 3604(f), which bars discrimination because of handicap. The 1968 Act originally covered race, color, religion and national origin. Current protected classes: race, color, religion, sex, familial status, national origin and handicap (HUD rules now say 'disability').
verification.citation: 42 USC 3604, Amendments notes (U.S. Code 2023 edition, govinfo); Pub. L. 93-383 sec. 808 (1974); Pub. L. 100-430, 102 Stat. 1619 (1988)
verification.teach: 1968: race, color, religion, national origin. 1974: sex. 1988: familial status and handicap (disability).

verification.manual: Fair housing complaint to HUD within 1 year of the discriminatory act; civil action within 2 years [42 USC 3610(a), 3613(a)]
verification.finding: 42 USC 3610(a)(1)(A)(i): an aggrieved person may file a complaint with the HUD Secretary no later than one year after an alleged discriminatory housing practice occurred or terminated. 42 USC 3613(a)(1)(A): a civil action in federal or state court must be filed no later than 2 years after the practice occurred or terminated, or after breach of a conciliation agreement, whichever is later. Under 3613(a)(1)(B), the 2-year period does not run while a HUD administrative proceeding on the same practice is pending; this tolling does not apply to suits for breach of a conciliation agreement. Under 3613(a)(2), a person may sue whether or not a HUD complaint was filed. For comparison, Attorney General suits on referred matters under 3614(b)(1)(B) have an 18-month limit.
verification.citation: 42 USC 3610(a)(1)(A)(i) and 3613(a)(1)(A)-(B) (U.S. Code, 2020/2021 editions, govinfo)
verification.teach: HUD complaint within 1 year; civil lawsuit within 2 years (the clock stops while a HUD proceeding is pending).

verification.topic: Do Not Call: established business relationship (16 CFR 310.2; 47 CFR 64.1200)
verification.manual: Do Not Call established business relationship: up to 18 months after the consumer's last purchase/transaction and up to 3 months after an inquiry [16 CFR 310.2; 47 CFR 64.1200]
verification.finding: The FTC rule's wording has changed, while the FCC rule's wording has not. FTC Telemarketing Sales Rule, 16 CFR 310.2(q), as amended by the final rule published April 16, 2024 (89 FR, doc. 2024-07180) and effective May 16, 2024, defines an established business relationship as either (1) a purchase, rental, lease or financial transaction with the seller within the 540 days before the telemarketing call, or (2) an inquiry or application about the seller's goods or services within the 90 days before the call. The 2024 rule replaced '18 months' with 540 days and 'three months' with 90 days. Sellers relying on the inquiry prong must keep records under 310.5. The FCC rule, 47 CFR 64.1200(f)(5) (current eCFR), still uses 18 months after a purchase or transaction and 3 months after an inquiry or application. Under the FCC rule, the relationship must come from a voluntary two-way communication and must not have been ended by either party; a company-specific do-not-call request ends it for telemarketing purposes. Exam answer: '18 months / 3 months' is still literally correct under the FCC rule. The TSR now says 540 days / 90 days, which is roughly but not exactly the same.
verification.citation: 16 CFR 310.2(q) (as amended eff. May 16, 2024; eCFR current 2026); 47 CFR 64.1200(f)(5) (eCFR current)
verification.teach: FCC rule: 18 months after a purchase or transaction, 3 months after an inquiry. FTC rule since May 16, 2024: 540 days and 90 days. Exam answer: 18 months / 3 months, unless the question uses days.

verification.manual: CAN-SPAM opt-out requests must be honored within 10 business days; email must include a valid physical postal address [15 USC 7704; 16 CFR 316]
verification.finding: 15 USC 7704(a)(4)(A): once a recipient opts out, the sender, and anyone acting on its behalf, may not send that recipient commercial email more than 10 business days after receiving the request. The sender also may not sell or transfer the address. The FTC's 2008 rulemaking considered cutting this to 3 days and kept 10 business days; its 2019 review kept the Rule without changes. Under 7704(a)(3), the opt-out mechanism must keep working for at least 30 days after the message is sent. Under 16 CFR 316.5, the sender may not charge a fee or require more than an email address, a reply email, or a visit to a single web page to opt out. 15 USC 7704(a)(5)(A)(iii): every commercial email must include the sender's valid physical postal address. 16 CFR 316.2 defines this as a current street address, a registered USPS Post Office box, or a private mailbox registered with a commercial mail receiving agency.
verification.citation: 15 USC 7704(a)(3)-(5) (U.S. Code 2020 edition, govinfo); 16 CFR 316.2, 316.5 (CAN-SPAM Rule, current)
verification.teach: Honor opt-outs within 10 business days; include a valid physical postal address; the opt-out must keep working for at least 30 days after sending.

verification.topic: Lead-based paint disclosure (40 CFR 745 Subpart F)
verification.manual: Housing built before 1978: disclose known lead-based paint hazards, provide the EPA pamphlet, give buyers a 10-day opportunity to inspect (may be waived); applies to sales and leases [40 CFR 745 Subpart F; 24 CFR 35]
verification.finding: The rule covers target housing, defined in 40 CFR 745.103 as housing built before 1978. Excluded are housing for the elderly or persons with disabilities and 0-bedroom dwellings, unless a child under 6 lives or is expected to live there. Sellers and lessors must, under 745.107: give an EPA-approved pamphlet such as 'Protect Your Family From Lead in Your Home'; disclose known lead-based paint and hazards; provide available records and reports; and disclose the same to each agent. If disclosure comes after an offer, it must be made before the seller or lessor accepts it. Under 745.113, contracts and leases must include the Lead Warning Statement and signed acknowledgments. 10-day rule (745.110): before a purchaser is bound by the contract, the seller must allow 10 days for a risk assessment or inspection, unless the parties agree in writing on a different period. The purchaser may waive the opportunity in writing. The 10-day opportunity applies to sales only; EPA says lessees get disclosure but not this period. Exemptions in 745.101 include foreclosure sales, leases of 100 days or less with no renewal, leases of housing certified lead-free, and renewals where disclosure was already made. HUD's identical rule is 24 CFR Part 35, Subpart A. Agents must ensure compliance under 745.115.
verification.citation: 40 CFR 745.101, 745.103, 745.107, 745.110, 745.113 (Subpart F; CFR 2025 edition / eCFR current); 24 CFR Part 35 Subpart A
verification.teach: Housing built before 1978: EPA pamphlet, disclosure of known lead paint and hazards and of available reports, Lead Warning Statement. Buyers get a 10-day inspection opportunity (may be waived or changed in writing). Tenants get the disclosure but not the 10-day period.

verification.manual: ECOA prohibits credit discrimination based on race, color, religion, national origin, sex, marital status, age (if able to contract), or receipt of public assistance income [15 USC 1691]
verification.finding: 15 USC 1691(a) makes it unlawful for a creditor to discriminate against any applicant in any aspect of a credit transaction on three grounds: (1) race, color, religion, national origin, sex, marital status, or age, provided the applicant can contract; (2) because all or part of the applicant's income comes from a public assistance program; (3) because the applicant has in good faith exercised a right under the Consumer Credit Protection Act. The manual's list leaves out ground (3). Under 1691(b), creditors may ask about age or public assistance income to judge the amount and likely continuance of income, among other permitted uses. Regulation B (12 CFR 1002.2(z)) defines 'prohibited basis' the same way. A CFPB final rule published April 22, 2026 and effective July 21, 2026 removed the disparate-impact 'effects test' from 1002.6(a) and narrowed discouragement under 1002.4(b) to statements of intent to discriminate. It did not change the protected bases.
verification.citation: 15 USC 1691(a)-(b) (U.S. Code, 2020 edition, govinfo); 12 CFR 1002.2(z), Regulation B (as amended eff. July 21, 2026)
verification.teach: Race, color, religion, national origin, sex, marital status, age (if able to contract), receipt of public assistance income, and good-faith exercise of consumer credit rights.

verification.topic: Security deposit: disclosure of how it is held (s. 83.49(2))
verification.manual: Landlord must give the tenant written notice of how the security deposit is held within 30 days of receipt [s. 83.49(2), F.S.]
verification.finding: Confirmed, with qualifications. The landlord must give the tenant written notice disclosing the advance rent or security deposit either IN THE LEASE AGREEMENT or within 30 days after receiving it. The notice must: (a) be given in person or by mail, or by e-mail under s. 83.505 (e-mail added effective 7/1/2025, ch. 2025-16, and only allowed if both parties signed an e-mail addendum); (b) give the name and address of the depository holding the funds, or state that a surety bond was posted; (c) say whether the tenant is entitled to interest; and (d) contain the statutory disclosure. If the landlord later changes how or where the deposit is held, the tenant must be told within 30 days after the change. EXCEPTION: this subsection does not apply to a landlord who rents fewer than five individual dwelling units. Failure to give this notice is not a defense to paying rent when due. The older wording 'manner in which the landlord is holding' (2011 text) was replaced by the 'in the lease or within 30 days' disclosure.
verification.citation: s. 83.49(2), Fla. Stat. (2025; same structure in 2026 edition); s. 83.505, Fla. Stat. (2025), created by ch. 2025-16, Laws of Fla. (CS/CS/CS/HB 615)
verification.teach: In the lease or within 30 days of receipt: where the deposit is held (or that a surety bond was posted) and whether interest is paid. Not required for landlords who rent fewer than 5 units.

verification.topic: Security deposit after the tenancy ends (s. 83.49(3))
verification.manual: After move-out: return deposit within 15 days if no claim; otherwise certified-mail notice of intent to impose a claim within 30 days; tenant has 15 days to object; failing the 30-day notice forfeits the claim [s. 83.49(3), F.S.]
verification.finding: The deadlines are unchanged, but the notice method has been widened. (a) If the landlord does not intend to claim against the deposit, it must be returned, with interest if required, within 15 days after the rental agreement ends. (b) If the landlord intends to impose a claim, written notice must be given within 30 days after the agreement ends, stating the reason. It goes by certified mail to the tenant's last known mailing address OR, since 7/1/2025, by e-mail under s. 83.505 (only if both parties signed the statutory e-mail addendum and gave e-mail addresses). (c) Unless the tenant objects within 15 days after receiving the notice, the landlord may deduct the claim and must send the balance within 30 days after the date of the notice. (d) If the landlord misses the 30-day notice, the landlord forfeits the right to claim against the deposit and may not seek a setoff against it, but may sue for damages after returning the deposit. What changed: HB 615 (ch. 2025-16, effective 7/1/2025) added the e-mail option. Certified mail is no longer the only valid method.
verification.teach: 15 days to return it if there is no claim; 30 days to send notice of a claim by certified mail, or by e-mail if both parties signed the e-mail addendum (s. 83.505, since July 1, 2025); the tenant has 15 days to object; missing the 30-day notice forfeits the claim.

verification.manual: Timeshare purchaser may cancel within 10 days; the right cannot be waived [s. 721.10, F.S.]
verification.finding: The purchaser may cancel the contract until midnight of the 10th CALENDAR day after the later of (a) the date the contract is signed or (b) the date the purchaser receives the last of the documents the developer must provide. No purchaser, and no one acting for the purchaser, may waive this right. Trying to obtain a waiver, or holding a closing before the cancellation period ends, is unlawful, and such a closing is voidable at the purchaser's option. The excerpts disagree on how long it stays voidable (1 year versus 5 years); this does not affect the 10-day rule.
verification.teach: Until midnight of the 10th calendar day after the later of signing the contract or receiving the last required document. Cannot be waived.

verification.manual: HOA disclosure summary must be provided before contract execution; if not, the buyer may void the contract within 3 days after receipt or before closing [s. 720.401, F.S.]
verification.finding: Confirmed, with an added qualifier. A prospective buyer of a parcel in a community subject to a mandatory homeowners' association must receive the disclosure summary before signing the contract. If it was not provided first, the buyer may void the contract by written notice to the seller or the seller's agent within 3 days after receiving the disclosure summary or before closing, WHICHEVER OCCURS FIRST. The buyer may not waive this right, but it ends at closing. Each covered sale contract must contain a conspicuous clause describing this right. The section does not apply to associations regulated under chapters 718, 719, 721 or 723.
verification.teach: Given before the contract is signed. If not, the buyer may void the contract within 3 days after receiving it or before closing, whichever occurs first. Not waivable; ends at closing.

verification.topic: Homestead protection from creditors (Art. X, s. 4, Fla. Const.)
verification.manual: Homestead creditor protection: 1/2 acre contiguous within a municipality, 160 contiguous acres outside; exceptions for taxes and assessments, obligations for purchase, improvement or repair, and labor on the realty [Art. X, s. 4, Fla. Const.]
verification.finding: Homestead owned by a natural person is exempt from forced sale under court process, and no judgment, decree or execution is a lien on it. The limits: outside a municipality, up to 160 acres of contiguous land plus improvements, which cannot be reduced without the owner's consent if the land is later brought into a municipality; inside a municipality, up to one-half acre of contiguous land, with the exemption limited to the residence of the owner or the owner's family. Exceptions: taxes and assessments on the property; obligations contracted for its purchase, improvement or repair; and obligations for house, field or other labor performed on the realty. Section 222.01(5), F.S. restates the same exceptions, citing Art. X, s. 4. The section also exempts $1,000 of personal property, and the exemptions pass to the surviving spouse or heirs (s. 4(b)).
verification.citation: Art. X, s. 4(a)-(b), Fla. Const. (current, as published by the Florida Senate); s. 222.01(5), Fla. Stat. (2025)
verification.teach: Inside a municipality: 1/2 acre of contiguous land (residence only). Outside: 160 contiguous acres. No protection against property taxes and assessments, debts for purchase, improvement or repair, or labor performed on the property.

verification.topic: Save Our Homes cap and portability (Art. VII, s. 4(d); s. 193.155)
verification.manual: Save Our Homes: homestead assessment increases capped at the lesser of 3% or CPI change; benefit portable to a new Florida homestead (limits, e.g. up to $500,000, within a set number of years) [Art. VII, s. 4, Fla. Const.; s. 193.155, F.S.]
verification.finding: Current law as of 2026-10-20. After the January 1 reassessment, the annual change in a homestead's assessed value may not exceed the lower of 3% of the prior year's assessed value or the percentage change in the CPI for All Urban Consumers (U.S. City Average) for the preceding calendar year. Portability: an owner who sets up a new Florida homestead may transfer the accrued SOH benefit (just value minus assessed value), up to $500,000. The new homestead must be established within 3 years after January 1 of the year the prior homestead was abandoned, and the owner must have had a homestead exemption as of January 1 of any of the 3 preceding years. The 3-year window replaced 2 years from 2021. The transfer is claimed on Form DR-501T with the homestead application. PENDING CHANGE: CS/HJR 1-F (2026 Special Session F) is on the November 3, 2026 ballot. If at least 60% of voters approve, it takes effect January 1, 2027 and would, among other things, let the full accrued SOH benefit transfer for non-school levies (no $500,000 cap for those levies). Until then, the $500,000 cap and the 3%/CPI cap remain current. A 2026 House analysis of HB 7031 also mentions possible changes to which prior homestead can be ported from; its enactment status was not verified.
verification.citation: Art. VII, s. 4(d), Fla. Const.; s. 193.155(1) and (8), Fla. Stat. (2026); Fla. Dept. of Revenue brochure PT-112; CS/HJR 1-F (2026F) staff analysis
verification.teach: Homestead assessed value rises no more than 3% or the CPI change, whichever is lower. Portability: up to $500,000 of the benefit moves to a new Florida homestead established within 3 years after January 1 of the year the old one was abandoned. A November 2026 ballot measure (V-23) could change this from 2027.

verification.manual: Adverse possession in Florida: 7 years of continuous possession under color of title, or without color of title with payment of taxes and a return filed with the property appraiser [ss. 95.16, 95.18, F.S.]
verification.finding: WITH COLOR OF TITLE (s. 95.16): the possessor entered under a claim of title founded on a written instrument (a conveyance), decree or judgment, and has been in continued possession for 7 years of the property included in it. For possession beginning after December 31, 1945, the instrument must be recorded with the clerk of the circuit court in the county where the land lies. Land counts as possessed if it is usually cultivated or improved, or protected by a substantial enclosure. WITHOUT COLOR OF TITLE (s. 95.18): 7 years of actual continued possession under a claim of title exclusive of any other right, not founded on a written instrument. The possessor must: (a) pay all outstanding taxes and matured installments of special improvement liens within 1 year after entering possession; (b) file a return with the county property appraiser within 30 days after making that payment, on the DOR form with a legal description and a notarized attestation; and (c) keep paying all taxes and liens for the rest of the 7-year period. Only the land actually possessed (enclosed, cultivated, maintained or improved) is held adversely.
verification.citation: ss. 95.16 and 95.18, Fla. Stat. (2025; 95.18 also shown in 2026 edition)
verification.teach: 7 years of continuous possession. With color of title: under a recorded written instrument. Without color of title: pay the taxes within 1 year of entering, file a return with the property appraiser within 30 days after paying, and keep paying the taxes.

verification.manual: A prescriptive easement in Florida requires 20 years of continuous, open, adverse use [Florida case law / s. 95.14?]
verification.finding: Confirmed as case law; no statute sets this period, and s. 95.14 is not the source. Official Florida legislative staff analyses state that a prescriptive easement requires: actual, continuous and uninterrupted use of a limited and defined area of land for 20 years; use under a claim of right that conflicts with the owner's use, without the owner's consent; and the owner's actual knowledge, or use so open, notorious and visible that knowledge is imputed. A 2013 House analysis notes that when the adverse possession period was cut to 7 years, the prescriptive easement period stayed at 20 years. Florida courts disfavor acquiring rights by prescription and resolve doubts in the owner's favor. The leading case usually cited is Downing v. Bird, 100 So. 2d 57 (Fla. 1958), but its holding was not read directly.
verification.citation: Florida common law, as summarized in the Fla. House staff analysis of HB 799 (2024); Fla. Senate analysis of SB 1142 (2011); House final analysis of HB 903 (2013)
verification.teach: 20 years of continuous, open, adverse use without the owner's consent. This comes from case law, not a statute.

verification.manual: Statute of limitations: action on a written contract 5 years; oral contract 4 years [s. 95.11(2)(b), (3), F.S.]
verification.finding: WITHIN 5 YEARS (s. 95.11(2)(b)): a legal or equitable action on a contract, obligation or liability founded on a written instrument. Exceptions: claims on payment bonds follow their own provisions, and deficiency judgments are governed by a separate paragraph. WITHIN 4 YEARS (s. 95.11(3)): a legal or equitable action on a contract, obligation or liability NOT founded on a written instrument, including actions for the sale and delivery of goods, wares and merchandise, and on store accounts. This is paragraph (3)(j) in the 2025 compilation according to the search excerpt; the lettering changed after 2023 amendments, so cite only subsection (3) unless verified.
verification.teach: Written contract: 5 years. Oral contract: 4 years.

verification.manual: Mortgagee must record a satisfaction within 60 days after full payment [s. 701.04, F.S.]
verification.finding: Within 60 days after receiving full payment of the mortgage (current text also covers payment of the payoff amount in an estoppel letter), the mortgagee, holder or servicer must: sign a written satisfaction or release; have it acknowledged; record it in the county official records; and send the recorded satisfaction to the mortgagor or record owner. The prevailing party in a suit to enforce this recovers attorney fees and costs. Subsection (3) sets a parallel 60-day duty to record satisfactions of liens and judgments after full payment.
verification.teach: The lender records the satisfaction within 60 days after full payment and sends it to the borrower.

verification.manual: Usury: 18% per annum simple interest on loans of $500,000 or less; 25% on larger loans; criminal usury above 25% (45% felony) [ss. 687.02, 687.03, 687.071, F.S.]
verification.finding: Interest above the equivalent of 18% per annum simple interest is usurious and unlawful (ss. 687.02(1), 687.03(1)). For a loan, advance, line of credit or forbearance over $500,000, interest is not usurious unless it exceeds the rate in s. 687.071, which in effect makes the ceiling 25%. A loan counts as over $500,000 if the principal initially exceeds that amount or may reasonably be expected to exceed it during the term (s. 687.03(3)). CRIMINAL USURY (s. 687.071), unless otherwise allowed by law: willfully and knowingly charging more than 25% but not more than 45% per annum is a second-degree misdemeanor (subs. (2)); more than 45% per annum is a third-degree felony (subs. (3)); knowingly making an extortionate extension of credit is a second-degree felony (subs. (4)). Credit extended in violation of s. 687.071 is not an enforceable debt in Florida. The 2026 edition shows the same subsection (2) wording.
verification.teach: 18% simple interest for loans of $500,000 or less; 25% for larger loans. Criminal usury: more than 25% up to 45% = misdemeanor; more than 45% = felony.

verification.manual: Radon gas notification must be provided at or before contract for sale or rental of any building [s. 404.056(5), F.S.]
verification.finding: Under the heading 'Notification on real estate documents,' the notice must appear on at least one document, form, or application signed at or before the contract for sale and purchase of any building, or at or before signing a rental agreement for any building. The statute sets the exact notice wording: radon is a naturally occurring radioactive gas that can present health risks when it builds up in a building in sufficient quantities over time; radon levels above federal and state guidelines have been found in Florida buildings; more information on radon and radon testing is available from the county health department. Use the statutory text word for word, not a paraphrase. The leg.state.fl.us page labeled 2026 carries this subsection (5) text. The 2025 flsenate.gov excerpt was cut off before subsection (5), but the 2010, 2014, and 2026 texts are the same.
verification.citation: s. 404.056(5), Florida Statutes (2026 edition on Online Sunshine; 2025 edition on flsenate.gov)
verification.teach: The statutory radon notice appears on at least one document signed at or before a sale contract or rental agreement for any building.

verification.manual: Prospective purchaser of real property with a building for occupancy must receive the energy-efficiency rating information brochure at or before contract [s. 553.996, F.S.]
verification.finding: The current s. 553.996 is titled 'Energy-efficiency information provided by building energy-efficiency rating systems providers.' It requires that a prospective purchaser of real property with a building for occupancy on it be given energy-efficiency information at or before signing the contract for sale and purchase. The information tells the buyer of the option to have the building's energy-efficiency rated. Its content covers how to analyze the rating, comparisons to statewide averages for new and existing construction of that class, and ways to improve the rating. For residential buyers it adds a notice that a rating may qualify them for an energy-efficient mortgage from lending institutions. Qualification on wording: the timing rule ('at or before' the contract) and the trigger are the same as before. The current statute says 'information' prepared and distributed by building energy-efficiency rating system providers, not a free 'information brochure' prepared by the department as in older editions (e.g., 2012). The 2021 and 2025 texts already use the provider wording. Calling it a 'brochure' is outdated terminology, but the operative rule is unchanged.
verification.citation: s. 553.996, Florida Statutes (2025; also 2021 edition)
verification.teach: The buyer of a building receives information on the option of an energy-efficiency rating at or before signing the contract. Older books call it a 'brochure'.

verification.manual: Property tax disclosure summary required in residential sale contracts: buyer should not rely on seller's current taxes [s. 689.261, F.S.]
verification.finding: s. 689.261(1): a prospective purchaser of residential property must be given a disclosure summary at or before signing the contract for sale. The summary may be separate or included in the contract, and either way must be substantially similar to the statutory 'PROPERTY TAX DISCLOSURE SUMMARY.' That form warns the buyer not to rely on the seller's current property taxes as the amount the buyer will owe in the year after purchase, and states that a change of ownership or property improvements triggers reassessments that could result in higher property taxes. Unless the summary is included in the contract, the seller must provide it. If it is not in the contract, the contract must refer to it and incorporate it by reference, and must say in prominent language that the buyer should not sign the contract until reading the summary. 2026 update (does not change this rule): the 2026 Florida Statutes text of s. 689.261, from 2026 CS/SB 856, adds listing-platform rules. Beginning February 1, 2027, any residential property shown on an online listing platform must include estimated ad valorem taxes, calculated by DOR formula or the countywide average millage rate, with a disclaimer. Such platforms may not show the current owner's taxes unless they use a qualifying estimator, and must link to the property appraiser's estimator. The current owner's taxes may not appear in printed listing materials.
verification.citation: s. 689.261, Florida Statutes (2025; 2026 edition adds new listing-platform subsection effective Feb. 1, 2027)
verification.teach: Buyer of residential property receives the summary at or before contract: do not rely on the seller's current taxes; a sale or improvements can raise the assessment.

verification.manual: Assessment date January 1; TRIM notice in August; tax bills from November 1 with 4/3/2/1% discounts Nov-Feb; delinquent April 1 [ss. 192.042, 200.069, 197.162, 197.333, F.S.]
verification.finding: Assessment: real property is assessed as of January 1 each year. Improvements not substantially completed on January 1 get no value (s. 192.042(1), 2025; same in the 2026 text). TRIM: the property appraiser must mail the Notice of Proposed Property Taxes (TRIM notice, form under s. 200.069) within 55 days after certification of value (s. 200.065(2)(b)). With the usual July 1 certification, DOR's calendars set the deadline at August 24. A state of emergency allows a 30-day extension. Note that the timing rule is in s. 200.065(2)(b); s. 200.069 sets the notice's content. Due date: taxes are due and payable November 1, or as soon after as the tax collector receives the certified roll (s. 197.333). Discounts (s. 197.162): 4% in November or within 30 days after the original tax notice is sent; 3% in December; 2% in January; 1% in February; 0% in March. A period ending on a weekend or holiday extends to the next working day. Delinquency: taxes become delinquent April 1 of the year after assessment, or 60 days after the original tax notice was mailed, whichever is later (s. 197.333).
verification.citation: ss. 192.042(1), 200.065(2)(b), 200.069, 197.162(1), 197.333, Florida Statutes (2025; 2026 text same for 192.042, 197.162 and 197.333); Fla. DOR Property Appraiser and TRIM calendars
verification.teach: Assessed as of January 1; TRIM notice mailed within 55 days after certification (usually August); due November 1; discounts 4% / 3% / 2% / 1% in November–February; delinquent April 1 (or 60 days after the bill was mailed, if later).

verification.manual: Straight-line recovery periods: residential rental property 27.5 years, nonresidential real property 39 years; land not depreciable [IRS Publication 946; 26 USC 168]
verification.finding: Under GDS (MACRS), the recovery period is 27.5 years for residential rental property and 39 years for nonresidential real property. Both use the straight-line method and the mid-month convention (26 U.S.C. 168(b)(3), (c), (d)(2); IRS Pub. 946 (2025)). Residential rental property means a building where 80% or more of gross rental income comes from dwelling units. Nonresidential real property is section 1250 property that is neither residential rental property nor property with a class life under 27.5 years. The 39-year period replaced 31.5 years in 1993 (Pub. L. 103-66). Under ADS the periods are 30 years (residential rental) and 40 years (nonresidential). Pub. 946 says land is not depreciable because it does not wear out, become obsolete, or get used up, so only the building's cost goes into the depreciable basis.
verification.citation: 26 U.S.C. 168(c) (U.S. Code 2024 ed., govinfo); IRS Publication 946 (2025), How To Depreciate Property; Instructions for Form 4562 (2025)
verification.teach: Residential rental: 27.5 years. Nonresidential: 39 years. Straight-line. Land is never depreciated.

verification.topic: Home sale gain exclusion (26 USC 121; IRS Pub. 523)
verification.manual: Exclusion of gain on sale of principal residence: $250,000 single, $500,000 married filing jointly, if owned and used as main home 2 of the last 5 years [IRS Publication 523; 26 USC 121]
verification.finding: IRS Pub. 523 (2025) and Topic No. 701: a seller can exclude up to $250,000 of gain, or up to $500,000 for married filing jointly, if they owned and used the home as their principal residence for at least 2 of the 5 years before the sale (24 full months or 730 days; the periods need not be continuous). Qualifications: (1) the exclusion is generally not available if the seller excluded gain on another home sold within the 2 years before this sale; (2) for the $500,000 joint amount, at least one spouse must meet the ownership test and both must meet the use test and the look-back rule; otherwise each spouse is tested separately; (3) a partial exclusion may apply if the tests are failed for qualifying reasons (work, health, unforeseen circumstances); (4) gain equal to depreciation claimed or allowable after May 6, 1997 cannot be excluded; (5) a surviving spouse may use $500,000 if the sale is within 2 years of the spouse's death and other conditions are met. The search budget ran out before I could pull the 26 U.S.C. 121 statutory text directly. This confirmation rests on the official IRS publication excerpts, and I could not check for any 2026 statutory change.
verification.citation: IRS Publication 523 (2025), Selling Your Home; IRS Tax Topic No. 701; 26 U.S.C. 121(a)-(b)
verification.teach: $250,000 single, $500,000 married filing jointly; owned and used as the main home 2 of the 5 years before the sale; generally not if used on another home within the last 2 years.

verification.topic: Proration conventions (365-day year; who owns the closing day)
verification.manual: Florida prelicense convention: 365-day year and buyer responsible for the day of closing (the FR/BAR contract prorates through the day prior to closing) [FR/BAR contract; not a statute (report as unresolved if no official source)]
verification.finding: No official government source was found or checked. This is a private-contract and course convention: the Florida Realtors/Florida Bar (FR/BAR) contract is a privately published form, not a statute or FAC rule, so no official domain would state it as law. The 365-day-year method and buyer-owns-closing-day convention can only be verified against the current FR/BAR contract text, which is not on an allowed official domain. The shared web-search budget also ran out before any search for this item could run. Keep it labeled as a course and contract convention, not a legal rule.
verification.citation: None (FR/BAR 'AS IS' Residential Contract for Sale and Purchase is a private form; no Florida Statute or FAC rule identified)
verification.teach: No statute or rule sets these; they come from the contract and the course. Follow the method the question gives; otherwise use the course convention (365-day year, buyer owns the day of closing). The FREC syllabus expects both the 360- and 365-day methods.

verification.topic: Exam retakes, reviews and pilot questions
verification.manual: Retake and scheduling rules for the sales associate exam (waiting period, fees), and whether the exam includes unscored pretest items
verification.finding: PARTLY CONFIRMED. (1) Pretest items: the January 2025 Sales Associate booklet says pilot (experimental) questions may be included. If they are, they are NOT counted toward the score, and candidates get extra time to answer them. They are used to build the question bank for future exams. (2) Passing: graded on 100 points; 75 or higher passes. (3) Scheduling: to cancel, candidates must contact Pearson VUE at least 2 days before the appointment. Cancelling later or not showing up can forfeit exam fees. (4) Review: a failed candidate may review the questions they missed at a Pearson VUE center, usually with half the exam time. The request must come within 21 days of the grade release, and only the most recent failed exam qualifies. A candidate who files a challenge must wait until the challenge results are official before taking another exam. (5) Time limits: the s. 475.175, F.S. excerpts seen (2024 and 2026 compilations; 2025 wording not retrieved separately) say the application expires 2 years after receipt if the applicant has not passed the exam. They also say the course completion becomes invalid for licensure if the exam is not passed within 2 years of completing the course. UNRESOLVED: (a) Waiting period: no official source states a mandatory waiting period between state-exam attempts or a cap on attempts. The only 30-day wait found applies to the prelicense end-of-course exam (Rule 61J2-3.008, from 2017 FREC meeting material), not the state exam. (b) Fees: the 2016 DBPR CBT fee table lists Real Estate Sales Associate at 3.5 hours, with a $36.75 Pearson VUE administration fee and a $35.00 review fee. The booklet says CBT exam fees went up effective January 3, 2023, and links to an updated fee table that could not be retrieved, so the current retake fee is unverified. The statute caps the initial application-plus-exam fee at $100 (s. 475.125). No Pearson VUE page was checked because pearsonvue.com is not on the allowed official-domain list.
verification.citation: Florida DBPR, Candidate Information Booklet: Real Estate Sales Associate Examination (eff. Jan 2025); DBPR CBT Examination Administration and Review Fees (2016); s. 475.175, Fla. Stat. (2024/2026 compilations); DBPR Examination Reviews and Hearings page
verification.teach: Pilot questions may appear; they are not scored and come with extra time. Cancel at least 2 days before the appointment. Review of a failed exam: request within 21 days. No official waiting period or attempt limit was found; the current retake fee was not verified.
